en: The Five Lamps Adorning the Lineage, Volume One:

The Seven Buddhas and Ancient Buddhas appeared in the world throughout an infinite succession of time; it is impossible to know them all or enumerate them exhaustively. Therefore, we shall now discuss those who appeared more recently.
In the Bhadrakalpa, there are one thousand Tathāgatas; yet from [the beginning] up to Śākyamuni, only seven Buddhas are recorded. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it says:
"By the power of the diligence of the seven Buddhas, they emit light that extinguishes the darkness. Each sat beneath a tree and therein attained perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī is the primordial teacher of the seven Buddhas.

When the Great Being Suṇhīta of the Golden Flower ascended the summit of Mount Song to practice the Way, he was moved by a vision of the seven Buddhas leading before him and Vimalakīrti following behind. Thus, the present compilation begins with the seven Buddhas.
Vipaśyin Buddha (the 998th of the Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) spoke in verse: "The body arises from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is fundamentally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, having no place of abiding."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, of the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was Bandhumat and his mother was Bandhumatī; he resided in the city of Bandhumatī.

Seated beneath a Pāpala tree, he preached the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering three hundred and forty-eight thousand people. He possessed two disciples of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the first of whom was named Khaṇḍa.
Tea. His second name was Tiṣya. His attendant was Aśoka. His successor was Fangying.

Śikhin Buddha (the nine hundred and ninety-ninth honored one of the *Zhuāngyán* Kalpa) spoke in verse: "All wholesome dharmas that arise are fundamentally illusory; The various evil karmas one creates are likewise illusory.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind. Illusorily produced, they have no root and no real nature. —From the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Kautilya (or Kauṇḍinya).

His father was Mingxiang (Vimalaprabha), and his mother was Guangyao (Prabhāvatī). He resided in the city of Guangxiang (Prabhāsa). He sat beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree and preached the Dharma in three assemblies.
He delivered two hundred and fifty thousand people. He had two disciples with supernormal powers: the first was named Abhibhū and the second was named Vāsavu.
His attendant was Kṣāntivādin, and his son was Ananta.
The Buddha Viśvabhū (the first of the thousand Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) spoke in verse: "The body is provisionally formed by borrowing from the four great elements;

the mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects. If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist; sin and merit are like illusions, arising and then ceasing.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that this Buddha appeared in the world when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste and belonged to the Kauṛilya clan.

His father was named Good Lamp; his mother was named Renowned Virtue. He resided in the city of Anupama and sat beneath a *bimba* tree to preach the Dharma in two assemblies, delivering one hundred and thirty thousand people.
His two disciples with supernormal powers were Upavaṃśa and Uttara. His attendant was Śānti, and his son was Sujñāta.
K Krakucchanda Buddha (the first honored one of the present Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body;
To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. When one realizes that the nature of both body and mind is empty, How can such a person differ from the Buddha?
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Brahmin caste and the clan Kāśyapa.
His father was named Datta; his mother, Subhaddā. He resided in the city of Anurādhapura and sat beneath a Sāl tree to preach the Dharma.

In a single assembly, he delivered the teaching and saved forty thousand people. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Sāṇa and Vīra. His attendant was Sumana, and his chief disciple was Uttara.
The Buddha Kanakamuni (the second honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha;

If there were truly a knowing subject, there would be no Buddha apart from it. The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; They remain composed and unafraid of birth and death. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the caste of Brahmins, and his clan name was Kāśyapa.
His surname was Śāla; his father was Mahāpuṇya and his mother was Sujayā.

He resided in the city of Viśuddha and sat beneath an Udumbara tree as a brahmin to preach the Dharma in a single assembly, delivering thirty thousand people across. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Śūrpaka and Uttara.
His attendant was Saumya, and his son was Vināyaka.
Kāśyapa Buddha (the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Brahmin caste, with the clan name Kāśyapa; his father was Brahmā.

The Buddha was named Śrīdatta. His maternal uncle, the householder Dhanapati, resided in the city of Vārāṇasī. While seated beneath a nyagrodha tree, he delivered a single discourse on the Dharma, through which twenty thousand people attained liberation.
He possessed two disciples with supernormal powers: first Tiṣya and second Bharadvāja. His attendant was Subhūti, and his son was Saṃjaya.
Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was Śuddhodana; his mother was Mahāmāyā.
Having attained the rank of a Bodhisattva in his final birth, he was born in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was named Sudānta-devaputra, also known as the Great Being Vajrapāṇi.

He delivered the various hosts of devas and expounded the practices of a Bodhisattva in his final birth. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he manifested his body and preached the Dharma, universally illuminating all.
The Sūtra says: When the Buddha was first born into the family of a Kṣatriya king, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Golden lotuses sprang up from the earth, spontaneously supporting his two feet. He walked seven paces each toward the east and west, as well as the north and south.
Pointing his fingers at heaven and earth, he let out a lion’s roar: "In the zenith and nadir, and in the four intermediate directions, there is none who can surpass me. Thus it is said.

In the forty-second year of King Zhao of Zhou, the year of Jiayin (the twenty-fourth year of his reign), on the eighth day of the fourth month, at the age of nineteen, he desired to leave the household life. He thought to himself, "What further encounter shall I have?
Thereupon, he went out to observe the sights at the four gates and beheld the four signs; his heart was moved by both sorrow and joy, and he reflected: "This is old age and sickness..."

Death is ultimately something to be weary of and renounced. Then, at the hour of midnight, a celestial being named Śuddhāvāsa appeared within the window, joined his palms, and said, "The time for your renunciation has arrived;
you may depart. Upon hearing this, the Prince felt joy in his heart and immediately leaped over the city wall and left.
He went to Mount Daṇḍaka to practice the Way, beginning his training under Ārāḍa Kālāma.
For three years he studied under Ārāḍa Kālāma, but when he realized that the state of meditative concentration was not the ultimate, he abandoned it.
He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra and for three years studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; realizing this too was not the way, he likewise abandoned it.

He then went to Mount Elephant Head, where he joined the various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), subsisting on only sesame and wheat for six years. Thus the Sūtra says: "Without mind or intention, and without the activity of sensation, he completely subdued them all."
The various non-Buddhists first underwent trials of heterodox methods, were shown various skillful means, and had their diverse views aroused, so that they might reach Bodhi.

Thus, the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states: "On the eighth day of the second month, at the time when the morning star appeared, the Bodhisattva attained enlightenment and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
he was then thirty years of age. This was the year *Guiwei*, the third year of King Mu’s reign. Subsequently, at the Deer Park...
In a wild garden, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five disciples, including Kauṇḍinya, whereby they realized the fruits of the Path.
He remained in the world preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years. Later, he addressed his disciple Mahākāśyapa:
"I entrust to you my pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, and the subtle, sublime True Dharma of the signless reality-essence. You must protect it."

"Maintain it, and command Ānanda to act as your deputy in transmitting the transformation [of the Dharma], so that it shall not be severed. Then he spoke this verse: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-dharma;
No-dharma is also dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting no-dharma, How has dharma ever been dharma?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further addressed Kāśyapa: "I shall take my golden-threaded saṃghāṭī robe and transmit it to you..."
“You must transmit this to the one who succeeds you, until the appearance of the Buddha Maitreya, so that it does not fall into decay.

When Kāśyapa heard these verses, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and said, “Excellent, excellent! I shall follow your instructions out of reverence for the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One—
Arriving at the city of Kuśinagara, he addressed the great assembly: "I now suffer from back pain and wish to enter parinirvāṇa.

He then proceeded to the banks of the Hiranyavatī River, beneath a pair of *śāla* trees, where he lay on his right side with his feet叠疊 (one upon the other), entering a state of profound stillness and tranquility. Subsequently, he rose once more from his coffin.
He preached the Dharma for his mother, specifically manifesting his two feet to convert Bāhika, and spoke the verse on impermanence:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.

At that time, the disciples vied with one another to cremate him with fragrant wood. After the embers were spent, the golden coffin remained as it was. Then the great assembly, before the Buddha, [offered...]

The verse of praise says: "How could the fierce and blazing fires of ordinary mortals be able to incinerate [this body]? We pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi shall cremate this golden-hued body.
At that time, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees and moved back and forth through the air.
Through the *Agninirmāṇa-samādhi*, ashes were produced in an instant, and eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra* were obtained.

This was on the fifteenth day of the second month in the *wenshen* year, the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign. It was one thousand and seventeen years after the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One.
The teaching reached the Central Lands (China) in the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han, the *wuchen* year. Just as the World-Honored One...
Upon being born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, walked seven steps, and looked in the four directions, saying:

"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the most honored. One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the great assembly had gathered, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:
"Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. The World-Honored One.
One day, he ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, "In this assembly, there are two bhikṣus who have violated the disciplinary rules; for this reason, I do not preach the Dharma.
Using his power of reading others' minds, Ānanda observed these bhikṣus and then had them expelled. The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again: "Just now..."
"Two bhikṣus have come who have violated the Vinaya; these two bhikṣus have already been expelled. Why does the World-Honored One not preach the Dharma?
The World-Honored One said, "I vow never to preach the Dharma for those of the Two Vehicles or for śrāvakas.

He then descended from his seat. One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the great assembly gathered in silence. Kāśyapa struck the gavel and announced, "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma. Thereupon, the World-Honored One...
The assembly descended from their seats. For ninety days, the World-Honored One had remained in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother.

As he was about to depart from the celestial realm and descend, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings all went to the sky to welcome him. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā thought to herself: "I am a nun;
I will certainly be behind the great monks when seeing the Buddha. It would be better to use my supernormal powers to transform myself [into a male form]."
The Wheel-Turning Sage King, surrounded by a thousand sons, was the first to behold the Buddha, and thus his vow was fulfilled.
As soon as the World-Honored One saw him, he rebuked him, saying: "Lotus-Color Bhikṣuṇī, how is it that you have bypassed the great monks to see me?
Though you see my physical body (rūpakāya), you do not yet see my Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Subhūti, sitting in meditative seclusion within the mountain cave, has instead seen my Dharma."
[Śāriputra] said: "World-Honored One, in the past, when Mañjuśrī arrived at the place where the Buddhas had gathered, he encountered the various Buddhas each returning to their own abodes.
There was only one woman who sat near that Buddha, having entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Why is it that this person is permitted to sit near the Buddha, while I am not? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: 'You need only awaken this woman and cause her to arise.'"
He arose from samādhi. "Ask her yourself," [the Buddha said]. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once;

he then supported her up to the Brahma Heaven, yet despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not bring her out. The World-Honored One said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs..."
Nor can anyone else deliver this woman from her samādhi. Forty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of worlds below, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalanetra, who is able to deliver this woman from her samādhi.
In an instant, the Mahāsattva Vimalanetra surged forth from the earth.
He prostrated before the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One commanded Wangming to come forward. Wangming went back to the woman and snapped his fingers once;

thereupon, the woman emerged from her meditative concentration. Because of this, King Prasenajit asked the World-Honored One: "Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), is there conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
If one says there is not, then wisdom should not be dual. If one says there is, then wisdom should not be singular."

Regarding the meaning of "one" and "two," what is their significance? The Buddha said, "Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Dragon Light (Nāgaprabha), you once asked about this meaning.
Now I have nothing to say, and you have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and hearing is called the 'meaning of one' and the 'meaning of two.
One day, the World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī standing outside the gate and said, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī..."
“Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter through the gate? Mañjuśrī replied, “I do not see a single dharma outside the gate; how can you instruct me to enter?
One day, while the World-Honored One was sitting, he saw two men carrying a pig past him.
He asked, “What is this? They replied, “The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom; yet you do not even recognize a piglet. The World-Honored One said, “You ought to have questioned me on this.”
The World-Honored One was asked by a certain heterodox teacher, "Are all phenomena eternal? The World-Honored One did not answer.
He was asked again, "Are all phenomena impermanent? He likewise did not answer. The heterodox teacher said, "The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom; why do you not answer me?"

The World-Honored One said, "All that you have asked is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One day, the World-Honored One showed a mani-jewel that reflected the colors of its surroundings and asked the celestial kings of the five directions, "This jewel is unique;
what color is it? At that time, the celestial kings of the five directions each described it as a different color.
The World-Honored One then hid the jewel in his sleeve, raised his hand, and asked, "What color is this jewel? The celestial kings replied: [it is the color of our hands].
There were no pearls in the Buddha’s hand; where, then, could there be color? The World-Honored One sighed and said, "How can you be so utterly deluded?
I shall show you the worldly pearl," and they each insistently claimed it was blue, yellow, red, or white. When I showed them the true pearl, they knew nothing at all.
At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all attained enlightenment. It was because of a gandharva that the World-Honored One [acted thus].
The king presented music. At that time, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all became the sound of the lute.
Kāśyapa rose and danced. The king asked Kāśyapa, "Are you not an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted? Why do you still have residual habits?
The Buddha said, "In truth, there are no residual habits; do not slander the Dharma. The king again played the lute three times, and Kāśyapa likewise danced three times.
The King said, "When Kāśyapa performed a dance, was that not so? The Buddha said, "In truth, he never performed a dance.

The King said, "World-Honored One, how could you speak falsely? The Buddha said, "It is no falsehood. When you plucked the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all wood and stone became the sound of the lute;
was that not so? The King said, "It was. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa was just like this. Therefore, it is truly not..."
[The Buddha] once performed a dance, and the king then believed and accepted it. Later, when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "What Dharma did you teach yesterday?
he replied, "I taught the Dharma of certainty. The non-Buddhist asked, "What Dharma do you teach today? He replied, "The Dharma of uncertainty.

The non-Buddhist said, "Yesterday you taught the Dharma of certainty; why do you teach the Dharma of uncertainty today? The World-Honored One said, "Yesterday was certain; today is uncertain. Thus it was.

The World-Honored One was questioned by a seer possessing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā). "The World-Honored One possesses six supernormal powers; I possess five. What is this one supernormal power?
The Buddha summoned the seer with the five supernormal powers, who responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Ask me about that one supernormal power."
The World-Honored One, because the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) desired to see Samantabhadra but could not find him—
even after entering meditative concentration three times and searching throughout the trichiliocosm— was unable to perceive Samantabhadra, and thus came to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If you simply give rise to a single thought within the samādhi of stillness, you will immediately see Samantabhadra.
Thereupon, as soon as Puyan gave rise to a single thought, he saw Samantabhadra riding upon a six-tusked white elephant in mid-air.

Furthermore, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreats in three different places; when Kāśyapa was about to strike the gavel to expel him, just as he raised the gavel, he beheld [him].
There were hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs; although Kāśyapa exhausted his supernatural powers, he could not lift the mallet.
The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa was speechless. This was because of the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha.

He proposed to debate the meaning of the doctrine and made a formal agreement, saying: "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head. The World-Honored One asked: "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? He replied:
"My tenet is that I do not accept anything at all. The World-Honored One asked: "Do you accept this view [that you do not accept anything]?"

Zhi brushed his sleeves and departed. When he reached the middle of the road, he realized his error and said to his disciples, "I must go back and cut off my own head to apologize to the World-Honored One.
His disciples said, "Since you were victorious before the assembly of devas and humans, why would you cut off your head?"
The Master said: "I would rather have my head cut off before a person of wisdom than achieve victory before one who lacks wisdom.
He then sighed and said: "In both cases, my doctrine falls into defeat. If this view is accepted, the door of defeat is gross; if this view is not accepted, [the same fault remains]."
The point where he was defeated was subtle; all humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles did not know where his own doctrine fell into error.
Only the World-Honored One and the great bodhisattvas knew where his doctrine fell. Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "My doctrine has fallen into defeat at two points;
therefore, I shall cut off my head to apologize. The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing as this. You should turn back."

Their minds turned toward the Path. Thereupon, together with their five hundred followers, they simultaneously threw themselves at the Buddha’s feet to leave the household life and attained the state of Arhat.

Formerly, when the World-Honored One intended to lead the assembly of noble ones to the Sixth Heaven to preach the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, he commanded all the fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands, this land, the human realm, and the heavens to assemble entirely, receive the Buddha’s entrustment, and provide protection.
To protect the True Dharma, should there be any who do not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings shall fly hot iron wheels to pursue them and compel their assembly.
Once assembled, there shall be none who do not comply with the Buddha’s command; each shall make a great vow to uphold the True Dharma.
There was, however, only one Māra King who said to the World-Honored One: "Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have become Buddhas. The assembly...
The realm of sentient beings is empty; there is no such thing as the name "sentient being. It was for this reason that I resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
Once, while the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, they came upon an ancient stūpa of a Buddha. The World-Honored One paid his respects to it. Ānanda asked, "Whose stūpa is this?
The World-Honored One replied, "This is the stūpa of the Buddhas of the past. Ānanda said, "The Buddhas of the past were..."
"Whose disciple am I? The World-Honored One said, "You are my disciple. Ānanda said, "It should be so.

At that time, a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One a question, yet he did not ask whether there was something to be said or nothing to be said. The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while.

The non-Buddhist praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; you have cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way]. He then prostrated himself in worship.
[The monk] departed. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what principle did the outsider praise [you] and then depart?

The World-Honored One said, "It is like a fine horse of the world that gallops upon seeing the shadow of the whip. One day, the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda, "The time for the meal is approaching;
you should enter the city with your almsbowl. Ānanda replied, "As you command. The World-Honored One said, "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the example of the past."
Regarding the ritual of the Seven Buddhas: Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven past Buddhas?
The World-Honored One called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded. The World-Honored One said, "Take the bowl and go. Because of this, a bhikṣu asked the World-Honored One:
"Within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, I see that there is a place of 'abiding,' yet the place of 'realization' is not yet present. What should the World-Honored One point out to me?"
The Venerable One said: "Bhikṣu so-and-so, what should be shown to you regarding this question of yours?
After the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment, he was sitting cross-legged beneath a tree in the Jeta Grove. At that time, there were two merchants with five hundred wagons."
As they passed by the edge of the forest, two ox-carts refused to move forward. The merchants, seeing this, were surprised.

A mountain deity informed them, "Within this forest there is a sage who has attained the Way. Forty-nine days have passed since he began his practice, yet he has not eaten; you should provide him with offerings.
The merchants entered the forest and indeed saw a man sitting upright and motionless. They then asked him, "Are you Brahmā?"
“Is it a demon? Is it Śakra? Is it a mountain deity? Is it a river deity? The World-Honored One smiled and held up the corner of his *kāṣāya* robe to show them.
The merchants prostrated themselves and subsequently presented offerings. Because Jīvaka was skilled at distinguishing sounds, the World-Honored One went to a cemetery and saw five skulls.
He struck one skull and asked Jīvaka, “Where was this person born after death? Jīvaka replied, “This person was born...”
"Human realm. The World-Honored One struck again once and asked, "Where was this life born? [Jīva] replied, "This life was born in the heavenly realm.
The World-Honored One struck another time and asked, "Where was this life born? Jīva was ignorant of where he had been born.
Thereupon, the Brahmin Kāla, employing his supernormal powers, took two *saṃpuṣpita* *aśvattha* trees in his left and right hands and came to make an offering to the Buddha.
The Buddha summoned the rishi. The brahmin assented. The Buddha said, "Let go. The brahmin then let go of one flower from his left hand.
The Buddha again summoned the rishi, saying, "Let go. The brahmin then let go of one flower from his right hand.
The Buddha again summoned the rishi, saying, "Let go. The brahmin said, "World-Honored One, both my hands are now empty."
"What else do you have to put down? The Buddha said, "I am not instructing you to cast away those flowers;

rather, you should cast away the six external objects, the six internal sense organs, and the six consciousnesses in between. Abandon them all at once. When there is nothing left to abandon, that is the place where you escape birth and death.
At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This occurred during the assembly on Vulture Peak.
There were five hundred bhikṣus who had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernormal powers, yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

By means of their supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), each of them saw for themselves how they had committed patricide, matricide, and other grave offenses in the past.
Within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to penetrate or realize the profound Dharma. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, proceeded...
Holding a sharp sword in his hand, he pressed it against the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One then said to Mañjuśrī, "Stop, stop!
You should not commit an act of parricide. Do not seek to harm me. If I am to be harmed, let it be for the sake of goodness that I am harmed.
Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning, there has been no self or person; it is only because of the internal mind that you perceive a self or person. When the internal mind arises, my mind..."
"Suffering" is precisely what is called "harm. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized for themselves that their original mind is like a dream and like an illusion;
within this dream-illusion, there is no self, no person, nor even parents who give birth or are born from. Then the five hundred bhikṣus praised him in unison, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source of the Dharma. With his own hand he grasps the sharp [sword]..."
A sword—holding it to threaten the body of the Tathāgata—the sword and the Buddha are likewise identical. They are of one mark and not two; they are markless and unarisen.
Within this, how could there be killing? When the World-Honored One was on the path of practice, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara.
Seeing the place where the hair was spread, Dīpaṃkara then signaled for the assembly to withdraw and pointed to the ground, saying: "In this single plot of land, one [Buddha] should be established."

At the site of the Brahma-shrine (*brahmavihāra*), there was at that time an elder among the assembly named Xianzhu (Wise-Elder). Holding a marker, he inserted it into the ground where his finger had pointed and declared, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is complete.
Then the various devas scattered flowers and praised him, saying, "This son of a concubine possesses great wisdom!

Subsequently, when the World-Honored One was wandering through the Śītavana cemetery with the Seven Virtuous Maidens, one of the maidens pointed to a corpse and said: "The corpse is right here; where has the person gone? One [of the others] said: [The person has gone to the realm of the dead.]
The woman said, "What? What? Sisters, observe closely! Each of them attained realization.
Moved by this, Śakra devānām indra scattered flowers and said, "I pray that you, Holy Sister, tell me what it is you require; I shall provide for you for the rest of my life.
The woman said, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided. I require only three things: first, a single rootless tree; second..."
"I require a place where there is no distinction between yin and yang; I require a mountain valley so deep that a shout does not echo.
Śakra said, "I possess everything you might need, yet as for these three things, I truly have none.
The woman said, "If you lack these, how can you hope to save others? Śakra was at a loss. He then went with her to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Kauśika, I..."
The various disciples and great arhats did not understand this meaning; only the great bodhisattvas understood it.
Because Devadatta slandered the Buddha, he entered hell in his physical body. Consequently, the World-Honored One had Ānanda ask him: "Are you at peace within hell? He replied:
"Although I am in hell, it is like the bliss of the third dhyāna heaven. The Buddha then further instructed him to ask:
“Will you still seek to leave? He replied, “I shall leave as soon as the World-Honored One arrives. Ānanda said, “The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms;
how could he have any portion [of karma] that leads him into hell? He replied, “Since the Buddha has no portion that leads him into hell, how could I have any portion that leads me out of hell?
Because Mañjuśrī suddenly gave rise to the view of a Buddha and the view of dharmas, he was restrained by the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One.
Facing the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), there was an old woman to the east of the city who had been born at the same time as the Buddha, yet she did not wish to see him.
Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately avoid him; nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha.
He then covered his face with his hand; within the palms of his ten fingers, they were all entirely Buddhas.
When Aṅgulimāla arrived at the gate of a certain elder’s house carrying his alms bowl, the woman of the household was in the midst of a difficult labor, and mother and child had not yet separated.
The elder said, "Disciple of Gautama, you are a most holy one. What dharma do you possess that can alleviate this difficulty of childbirth? Aṅgulimāla spoke.
The elder said, "I have only recently entered the Path and do not yet know this Dharma. Wait until I return to ask the World-Honored One, and then I shall come back to inform you.
Upon his return, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla, "Go quickly and tell her:
'Since I first came to the noble and holy Dharma, I have never killed a living being. Aṅgulimāla obeyed the Buddha’s words and went swiftly to inform her; when his wife heard this, she was moved.
At that time, [the matter] was resolved. Once, while the World-Honored One was sitting beneath a Nyagrodha tree, two merchants asked him, "Did you see any carriages pass by?
He replied, "I did not see them. The merchants asked, "Did you hear them? He replied, "I did not hear them. The merchants asked, "Were you in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?
He replied, "I was not in meditative concentration. They asked, "Were you asleep? He replied, "I was not asleep. The merchants...
The person sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent! The World-Honored One has awakened yet remains unseen. He then offered two pieces of white woolen cloth.

When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude. At that time, the entire assembly remained silent; only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, which is truly..."
The Dharma-gate of form and formlessness is subtle and wondrous; it does not rely on words and letters, but is a separate transmission outside the teachings, entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
When the World-Honored One went before the Many-Sons Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit with him, then wrapped him in his *saṃghāṭī* robe and said:
"I now secretly entrust to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. You must protect and uphold it."
To be transmitted to future generations: When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, the Great Being Mañjuśrī requested that the Buddha turn the wheel of the Dharma once more.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying, "Mañjuśrī, during the forty-nine years I have dwelt in this world, I have never spoken a single word.
You ask me to turn the wheel of the Dharma again; have I ever turned the wheel of the Dharma before? At the assembly for his nirvana, the World-Honored One...
He rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the assembly, saying: "You should all carefully observe my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold.

Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied; do not let yourselves have cause for regret later. If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciples. If you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa,"
"Nor are they my disciples. At that time, an assembly of one hundred million beings all attained realization.
The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. His clan name was Brahmin; his father was named Yin... [text fragment ends].
Zé’s mother, Xiāngzhì, was formerly a goldsmith who was highly skilled in understanding the nature of gold and how to temper it until it became pliant and malleable.
The *Fǎfǔchuán* (Biographies of the Transmission of the Dharma) states that once, in the distant past, after the Parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the fourfold assembly erected a stūpa.
Within the stūpa, the face of a golden image had become damaged and discolored. At that time, there was a poor woman who took a gold bead to the goldsmith’s workshop and requested [his assistance].
They adorned the Buddha’s face. Thereupon, they made a vow together: "May we two become husband and wife without marriage.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas their bodies were all golden in color; subsequently, they were born in the Brahma Heaven.

When their celestial lifespan ended, they were born in a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Madhyadeśa in Magadha, named Kāśyapa—translated as "Drinking Light" (Drinking Radiance) or "Victorious Honored One. This was because...
He was named after his golden complexion. Consequently, he resolved to seek renunciation, hoping to cross over the various realms of existence (*bhava*). The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
and his hair and beard fell away naturally, while the *kāṣāya* robe clothed his body. He was constantly praised as the foremost among the assembly. Furthermore, [the Buddha] said:
"I entrust this to you with my pure Dharma-eye; you must propagate it so that it does not perish. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Kāśyapa was not present among the assembly. The Buddha addressed the great disciples:
'When Kāśyapa arrives, you should have him proclaim the Treasury of the True Dharma-eye. At that time, Kāśyapa was at the Śīrṣa..."
At the Piṇḍola Cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he beheld a sublime radiance and immediately entered into samādhi.

With his purified divine eye, he saw that the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River. He then addressed his disciples, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa;
how swift was it! He then went to the space between the twin śāla trees and wailed in grief and longing. The Buddha emerged from the golden coffin.
He displayed his two feet. At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus: "The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; the adamantine *śarīra* relics are not our concern.
We ought to convene a council of the Dharma-eye so that it may not be severed. He then spoke this verse: "Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter nirvāṇa.
Those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) should attend the council. Thereupon, those who had attained supernatural powers...
They all assembled at the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. At that time, Ānanda was unable to enter the assembly because his outflows were not yet exhausted;
later, having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he was thereby able to enter. Kāśyapa then addressed the assembly, saying:
"This bhikṣu Ānanda is of great learning and possesses dhāraṇī; he has great wisdom and constantly follows the Tathāgata.

His pure conduct is immaculate, and whatever Dharma he hears from the Buddha is retained without omission, like water being passed from one vessel to another. He is praised by the Buddha as foremost among those who are quick-witted and intelligent.
It would be appropriate to request him to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka. The great assembly remained silent. Kāśyapa then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now proclaim the Eye of the Dharma. Hearing these words, Ānanda accepted them with faith. Observing the minds of the assembly, he spoke in verse:
"O monks and all your followers, Without the Buddha you lack adornment, Just as in the midst of the sky, The multitude of stars is without the moon."
Having spoken these verses, he prostrated at the feet of the assembly of monks, ascended the Dharma seat, and proclaimed these words: "Thus have I heard.

At one time the Buddha was dwelling in such-and-such a place, preaching such-and-such a sutra and teaching, until [the mention of] humans, devas, and others, who paid homage and practiced accordingly.
Then Kāśyapa asked the bhikṣus, "Is what Ānanda has said free from error? They all replied, "It is no different from that which the World-Honored One [taught]."
Having spoken thus, Kāśyapa addressed Ānanda, saying: "The time for my life is not long; I now entrust the True Dharma to you.
Guard it well. Listen to my verse: 'All dharmas are originally dharmas; there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.'"
"How can there be both the Dharma and non-Dharma within a single dharma? Having spoken this verse, he took up his saṃghāṭī robe and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya;
this was the year Bingshen, the fifth year of King Zhou Xiao.
When a non-Buddhist asked the Venerable One, "What is my self?", he replied, "The one who seeks the self is your self. The non-Buddhist said:
"This is my self," [the Master] said. "Where is your self, Teacher? He replied, "You seek me by asking about me.
One day, while the Venerable was treading mud, a novice saw him and asked, "Venerable Sir, why do you do this yourself? The Venerable said, "If I do not do it myself, who will do it for me?"
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Kṣatriya; his father was King Droṇodana, who was indeed the younger brother of the Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Ānandita, which here means "Joyous" or "Rejoicing.

He was born on the night the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, and thus he was given this name. He was widely learned and profoundly erudite, possessing unimpeded wisdom. The World-Honored One regarded him as...

He was foremost in dhāraṇī and had always been praised for it. Furthermore, due to his great merit from past lives, he had received and upheld the Dharma-treasury like water being passed from one vessel to another.
The Buddha then appointed him as his attendant. One day, the Venerable addressed the Buddha, saying, "Today, upon entering the city, I witnessed a most extraordinary thing.
The Buddha asked, "What extraordinary thing did you see? He replied, "As I entered the city, I saw a..."
A troupe of musicians was performing a dance. Upon leaving the city, [the Buddha] saw that they had all met with impermanence.
The Buddha said, "Yesterday, when I entered the city, I also witnessed a remarkable event. [The interlocutor] asked, "I do not know what remarkable event you witnessed.
The Buddha said, "When I entered the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; when I left the city, I also saw musicians performing a dance. One day, he questioned Kāśyapa.
He asked: "Elder brother, apart from the transmission of the golden-brocade *kāṣāya* robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. Later, King Ajātaśatru addressed him, saying:
"Virtuous one, both the Tathāgata and the venerable and supreme teacher Kāśyapa have already entered *nirvāṇa*, yet I am burdened by many affairs."

None were able to see him. When the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he wished to take his leave. The Venerable One granted this. Later, he thought to himself: "My body is fragile and brittle, like a mass of foam;
how much more so now that I am aged and infirm—how could it endure for long? King Ajātaśatru has made an appointment with me;
I shall go to the royal palace to bid him farewell. He then went to the palace and said to him: "I wish to enter parinirvāṇa; I have come to say my farewells."
The gatekeeper said, "The King is asleep; it would not be proper to inform him. The man said, "Wait until the King awakens, and I shall speak for you.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw in a dream a precious parasol adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions.
He circumambulated it in veneration. Suddenly, a violent wind and rain arrived, blowing the handle off and causing the precious jewels and necklaces to fall entirely to the ground.

His heart was filled with great wonder and alarm. Upon waking, the gatekeeper reported these events in detail. When the King heard this, he cried out in lamentation, his grief moving both heaven and earth.
He immediately went to the city of Vaiśālī and saw the Venerable One sitting cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River.
He sat down. The king then paid homage and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms, who has left me and come here.
For the sake of your compassionate vow, please do not enter parinirvāṇa for a while. At that time, King Vaiśālī was also by the riverbank. He spoke this verse:
"How can you, O Venerable One, return so swiftly to the field of quiescent extinction? I pray that you remain for a brief moment and accept our offerings."
The Venerable One, seeing that the two kings had both come to entreat him, spoke this verse: "O Two Kings, dwell well-composed; do not give way to sorrowful longing.
Nirvāṇa is my purity, for it is free from all states of existence. The Venerable One further reflected:
"If I were to favor one kingdom over the other, the various nations would fall into strife; such a thing must not be. I should deliver all beings through impartiality."
He then proceeded to enter parinirvāṇa in the middle of the Ganges River. At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.
Five hundred sages from the Snowy Mountains, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air to arrive; they prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One.
Kneeling on his right knee, he addressed him, saying, "I shall testify to the Buddha-dharma for you, Elder. I pray that you will grant us great compassion and deliver us.

The Venerable One accepted the request in silence and immediately transformed the Ganges River so that it became entirely golden ground. For the sake of that assembly of sages, he preached the various Great Dharmas.
The Venerable One then thought, "The disciples I have previously delivered should now gather here. In a brief moment, five...
One hundred arhats descended from the sky and conferred the full precepts upon the renunciants among the sages. Within that assembly of sages were two arhats:
one named Śāṇakavāsin and the other named Madhyāntika. Knowing them to be vessels for the Dharma, the Venerable One said to them:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Great Eye of the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; Kāśyapa has now entered meditative concentration."
I have entrusted this to you. Now that I am about to pass away, I transmit it to you. Receive my teaching and listen to these verses:
"The Dharma originally entrusted exists; Once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken for themselves; Upon awakening, there is neither existence nor non-existence."

When the Venerable One had finished transmitting the Treasury of the Dharma-Eye, he leaped into the void and manifested eighteen transformations. He entered the Samādhi of the Swift Play of Wind and divided his body into four parts:
one part he offered to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; one part he offered to the Palace of the Sāgara Dragon King;
one part he offered to King Viśākhā; and one part he offered to King Ajātaśatru. Each of them constructed a precious stūpa to make offerings to it.
This was the year of Guisi (癸巳), the twelfth year of King Li’s reign.
The third patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā; he was also named Śāṇavāsa.
His clan name was Viśvāmitra; his father was Vanavāsī and his mother was Kauśeya. He was born after being in the womb for six years.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Śaṇakha; this translates as "Naturally-Grown Garment," which is the name of a nine-branch exquisite grass from the Western Regions.
Whenever a sage descends to be born, this grass grows in pure and clean places. When Andhaka-Vṛṣṇi was born, this auspicious grass appeared in response. Formerly, like...
He came to travel and convert others, arriving at the kingdom of Mathurā. Seeing a grove of blue trees with lush branches and leaves, he said to Ānanda:
"This forest is named Uruvilvā. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma here.
Later, in the hundredth year, Śāṇakavāsin was indeed born; he left the household life, realized the Way, and received great celebration.
The Venerable Dhammasena delighted in the Dharma-eye and transformed sentient beings. While residing in this forest, he subdued two fire-dragons who submitted to the Buddha’s teaching.

The dragons subsequently offered him their land, upon which he established a Brahma-palace. As the Venerable One’s period of transformative activity drew to a close, he reflected upon the entrustment of the True Dharma.
He then sought out Upagupta in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā and took him as his attendant.
He asked Upagupta, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old. The master said, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or is your nature seventeen?
He replied, "My teacher’s hair has turned white; is it the hair that is white, or is the mind white? The master said, "It is only my hair that is white, not my mind."
Pāṇḍaraka said, "My body is seventeen [years old], but my nature is not seventeen.

The Venerable One, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, ordained him by shaving his hair and bestowing the full precepts three years later, and then told him: "In the past, the Tathāgata, with the unsurpassed eye of Dharma..."
I have entrusted this to Kāśyapa, who passed it down through successive generations until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; do not let it be severed.
Receive my teaching and listen to these verses of mine: "It is neither dharma nor mind; there is neither mind nor dharma.
When speaking of this mind-dharma, this dharma is not a mind-dharma. Having spoken these verses, he immediately vanished at the White Elephant [Cave] south of Kaśmīra.
Later, while in the mountains and within samādhi, he saw his disciple Guptaka with five hundred followers who were frequently indolent and arrogant.
The Venerable One then went to them and manifested the Dragon’s Agility Samādhi (*nāgavikrīḍita-samādhi*) to subdue them, and spoke this verse:
"Penetrating realization is neither this nor that; in the Ultimate Sage there is no long or short. Cast away your thoughts of contempt, and you shall swiftly attain Arhatship.
Upon hearing these verses, the five hundred bhikṣus followed the teaching and practiced accordingly, all of whom attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

The Venerable One then manifested the eighteen transformations and entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi) to cremate his own body. Kujūta collected the relics and enshrined them at Vaṅkāla.
At the mountain, five hundred bhikṣus each held a banner to escort [the relics] there, where they erected a stūpa and made offerings;
this was in the twenty-third year of King Xuanshi, the year of Yiwu (515 CE).
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. He was also named Upagupta and alternatively called Upagupta.
His clan name was Śūdra; his father’s name was Kalyāṇabhadra. He left home at the age of seventeen and realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty.

Traveling to convert beings according to their circumstances, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, where those who attained deliverance were exceedingly numerous. Consequently, the palace of Māra shook and trembled.
Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear; he then exhausted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma. The Venerable One immediately entered *samādhi* to observe its origins.
Pāpīyān again sought an opportunity and secretly took a necklace, placing it around [the Venerable’s] neck. When the Venerable emerged from *samādhi*, [he saw it].
He then took the three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands. He spoke with words of consolation to Pāpīyas, saying:
"The necklaces you gave me were truly exquisite; I have these flower garlands to offer in exchange. Pāpīyas was greatly delighted and stretched out his neck to receive them.
Immediately, they transformed into three kinds of putrid corpses, infested with maggots and rotting away. Pāpīyas felt loathing and great revulsion arose within him.
Distressed and troubled, he exerted all his supernatural powers but was unable to move it. He then ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and informed the various lords of those heavens;

he further went to the Brahmā King to seek deliverance. They each replied, "The miraculous transformations performed by a disciple of the One of Ten Powers—how could we, who are common and lowly, be able to remove them?
Pāpīyān asked, "If that is so, then what should be done? The Brahmā King said, "You should return [to the Buddha]."
The Venerable One was able to sever it immediately. He then spoke a verse to cause him to redirect his merit, saying:
"If one falls upon the ground, one must rise from the ground; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible.

Having received these instructions, Pāpīyas descended from the celestial palace, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One, and offered a piteous confession. The Venerable One told him: "From this day forward, regarding the Tathāgata..."
"Will you no longer cause harm to the True Dharma? Pāpīyān replied, "I vow to turn toward the Buddha-way and forever sever all unwholesome deeds.
The Venerable One said, "If that is so, you may yourself proclaim with your own mouth your refuge in the Triple Gem.
The Māra joined his palms and recited it three times; his flower garlands were completely removed. Thereupon, he leaped for joy and, prostrating before the Venerable One, spoke this verse:
I prostrate to the Honored One of Samādhi, the noble disciple endowed with the ten powers. I now dedicate my merit, praying that no one shall fall into weakness.

While the World-Honored One was in the world, he transformed and guided beings so that the number who realized the fruits of the path was greatest; for every person he delivered, he placed a tally-stick within a stone chamber.
That chamber was eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width, until it was filled to capacity. At the very end, there remained one long [tally].

"O son, one named Gandharvasena has come to pay homage to the Venerable One, seeking to leave the household life. The Venerable One asked: 'Do you leave the household life with your body, or do you leave it with your mind?

He replied: 'I have come to leave the household life, not for the sake of body or mind. The Venerable One said: 'If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that leaves the household life?
He replied: 'As for leaving the household life, it is because there is no self and no "mine. Because there is no self and no "mine," [one leaves the household life].'"
"The mind itself is neither born nor extinguished. That the mind is neither born nor extinguished is the eternal Way.

All Buddhas are likewise eternal; the mind has no form or appearance, and its essence is the same. The Venerable One said, "You shall attain great awakening and the mind will naturally reach full penetration.

You should rely upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to perpetuate the noble lineage. He then performed his tonsure, conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*), and further told him: "Your father once..."
"You were born on a day when gold appeared in a dream; you may be named Tiṭṭhaka.
He further said to him, "The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse:

'The mind is itself the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma. If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; if there is no mind, there is no original dharma. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, [he passed away]."
He then leaped into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations; returning to his original seat, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
Kātyāyanīputra used the tally-sticks from within the room to cremate the Master’s body. He collected the relics and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
This was the year Gengzi, the thirty-first year of King Ping’s reign.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhika, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. In the Sanskrit language he is called Diṭṭhika; in this [Chinese] language it means "Measure of Penetrating Reality.
At the time of his birth, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth.

Before him stood a great mountain, adorned with various jewels; from the summit of the mountain, a spring gushed forth, flowing in torrents in the four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Gupta.
To explain this: "The mountain of jewels" is my own body; "the gushing spring" is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma.
"The sun rising from the house" is the sign that you have now entered the Path. "Illuminating heaven and earth" is the transcendence of your wisdom.
Having heard the teacher’s explanation, the Venerable One was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, singing this verse: "Majestic is the mountain of the seven treasures."
"Constantly issuing from the spring of wisdom, it is transformed into the flavor of the True Dharma; it is able to deliver all those with whom there is a karmic connection.
The Venerable Gupta also spoke a verse, saying: "I transmit my Dharma to you; you shall manifest great wisdom. Like the golden sun rising from the house, it shall illuminate heaven and earth.
Hearing his teacher’s sublime verse, Tiṭṭibha prostrated and received it into his keeping. Later, he traveled to Central India. There...
In the kingdom there were eight thousand great sages, with Mīḍhika at their head. Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage.
They said to the Venerable One, "In the past, we were born together in the Brahma Heaven. I encountered the sage Asita, who transmitted the methods of the sages to me."
The Master encountered a disciple of the Ten Powers (Daśabala) who was practicing dhyāna. From that point on, their karmic destinies diverged, and six kalpas have already passed.
The other said, "Separated by many kalpas—truly not in vain! Now you may abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox to enter the Buddha-vehicle."
Mecaka said, "In the past, the seer Asita gave me this prophecy: 'Six kalpas hence, you shall meet a fellow student and attain the fruit of the outflows-free state.
That we have now met—is this not due to our past affinity? I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me liberation.
Thereupon, [the Buddha] ordained him as a renunciant and commanded the noble ones to bestow the precepts upon him. The remaining assembly of seers had only just begun to give birth to me.
Māna. The Venerable One displayed great supernatural powers (*mahā-ṛddhi*). Thereupon, they both gave rise to the bodhicitta and simultaneously left the household life.
[The Venerable One] then addressed Mucilinda, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-eye (*mahādharmanetra-kośa*) to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and cherish it. He then spoke this verse: "Thoroughly penetrating the fundamental..."
The Dharma-mind: there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and likewise no dharma.
Having spoken this verse, he leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations. Entering the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), he spontaneously incinerated his own body.
Miśraka, together with eight thousand bhikṣus, collected the relics and erected a stūpa for veneration on Mount Paṇḍava. This was during the reign of King Zhuang.
It was the year Jichou (609 CE), the seventh year [of the reign].

The Venerable Ṣaḍdarśanācārya (Six-View Master) Mīzhējiā (Mihirakula) was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled for the sake of conversion until he reached the kingdom of Northern India.
Seeing auspicious golden clouds above the city walls, he sighed and said, "This is the breath of a person of the Way."
"There must be a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city. In the midst of the marketplace, there was a man holding a vessel of wine.
Approaching him, he asked, "From where have you come, Master? Where do you intend to go? The Patriarch said, "I have come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere.
The man asked, "Do you recognize this object in my hand? The Patriarch said, "This is a vessel for contact that carries purity."
He asked, "Does my teacher recognize me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, it would not be me.
He further said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your original cause. He answered with a verse:
"From immeasurable kalpas past, until my birth in this land, My original surname was Bharadvāja, and my name was Vāsukīta. The Patriarch said, "My teacher..."
Tidūka said: "In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through Northern India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'Three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa in this country, there will be a holy man of the Bharadvāja clan named Vasumitra. He shall become the seventh patriarch in the lineage of dhyāna.
The World-Honored One predicted this of you; you ought to leave the household life. Thereupon, [Vasumitra] set down his bowl and prostrated before the Master. To the side...
Standing, he said: "I recall a past kalpa when I served as a donor (*dānapati*) and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata.

That Buddha prophesied to me, saying: 'In the Śākya Dharma of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall propagate the ultimate teaching. This now accords with the Master’s words; I pray that you grant me liberation.
The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He then told him: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye..."
"I now entrust this to you; do not let it be severed. He then spoke a verse, saying: "No mind can be grasped; What is spoken cannot be called a dharma.

If one realizes that mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas. Having spoken the verse, the Patriarch entered the Lion’s Boundless Vigor Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).
He leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, then returned to his original seat and transformed himself into fire to cremate his own body.
Vasumitra collected the sacred relics and enshrined them within a casket of the seven precious gems; he then erected a stupa and placed them upon its upper level.
This was the year Jia-shen, the seventeenth year of King Xiang’s reign.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India. His family name was Bharadvāja.
He constantly wore pure garments and carried vessels for wine as he wandered through the streets and neighborhoods, sometimes chanting and sometimes whistling; people regarded him as mad.

Upon meeting the Venerable Mithyaka, who proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past prophecies, he reflected upon his own prior karmic conditions. He cast aside his vessels, left the household life to receive the Dharma, and traveled to propagate the teachings.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kāmarūpa, he extensively promoted Buddhist activities. Before the Dharma seat, there suddenly appeared a man of wisdom who declared, "My name is Buddhānandi;
I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "O worthy one, where there is debate, there is no true meaning; where there is true meaning, there is no debate.
If you intend to debate the meaning, it will ultimately not be a discourse on the meaning. Knowing that the Master’s principle was superior, Buddhānandi submitted with deep reverence.
He said, "I wish to seek the Way and be moistened by the flavor of the nectar of immortality. The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and conferred the full precepts upon him.
He further told him, "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it. Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
With a mind equal to the realm of empty space, you manifest dharmas identical to empty space; when you realize the time of empty space, there is neither "is" nor "non-is.
You then enter the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind. At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together to pay homage and spoke these verses:
"O Ancestor of the Sages of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position. Venerable One, have compassion for us; we pray that you [will act as our leader]."
He proclaimed the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). The Venerable One arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma I have attained is not existent;
if one recognizes the Buddha-ground, it is because it is free from existence and non-existence. Having spoken, he re-entered samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa.
At that very seat, Nandi immediately erected a stūpa of the seven treasures to enshrine his entire body. This was the year of Xīnwèi, the nineteenth year of the Reign of Stability (*Dìngwáng*).
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmala. His surname was Gautama.
He possessed a fleshly protuberance upon his crown and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Initially, he met Vasumitra, from whom he left the household life and received instruction.

Subsequently, leading his disciples on a tour of propagation, he arrived at the house of Viśāla in the kingdom of Tiṅga. Observing a white light ascending from the roof of the house, he said to his disciples:
He said, "In this family there is a sage who speaks no words; he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He does not walk upon the four crossroads, for he knows that contact is defiling.
Having finished speaking, the elder came forth to pay his respects and asked, "What do you require?

The Patriarch said, "I seek an attendant. The elder replied, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra; he is already fifty years old, yet he has never spoken with his mouth, nor has he ever walked with his feet."

[The Master] had never stepped on it before. The Patriarch said, "According to what you have said, you are truly my disciple. When Vuddha heard this, he immediately rose and prostrated himself, reciting a verse:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my path; [I am now my own kin, and the Way is my own path].
"Who is the one who has attained the supreme Way? The Patriarch answered with a verse: "What you say is intimate with the mind;
even your parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Way; the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like what you have."
"I wish to recognize your original mind; it is neither joined nor separated. Having heard this verse, Votada immediately took seven steps.

The Patriarch said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past, and his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to part with, he remained silent and did not walk.
Let the elder now release him so that he may leave the household life. The Patriarch then conferred full ordination upon him and further told him:
"I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s treasury of the eye of the true Dharma; do not let it be severed. He then spoke a verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one thoroughly understands space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Bodhidharma, receiving this entrustment, praised him with a verse: "Among the patriarchs of Chan, I shall become the first."
8. He transformed immeasurable multitudes through the Dharma, and they all attained arhatship.

At that time, Buddhadatta manifested supernatural transformations and then returned to his original seat, remaining solemnly in nirvana. The assembly erected a jeweled stupa and interred his entire body;
this was the year of Bingyin, the twelfth year of Emperor Jing’s reign.
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Tika. His secular surname was Viśrāva.

Having received the entrustment of the Eighth Patriarch, he later traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma. At that time, there was an elder named Gandhacchattra who brought his son to pay homage to the Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years; therefore, he shall be named Duṣprasaha (Difficult to Be Born). He once met with a rishi.
"This child is no ordinary person; he shall become a vessel for the Dharma. Now that he has met the Venerable One, he may be ordained.
The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred the precepts. At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty-seven *śarīra* relics appeared before them.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all weariness. Subsequently, the Patriarch said to him: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata..."
"I now entrust this to you; you must protect and keep it in mind. He then spoke a verse, saying: "The True Principle is originally nameless; It is through names that the True Principle is revealed.
Having received the Dharma of reality, It is neither true nor false. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he immediately entered the samādhi of cessation and passed into parinirvāṇa.
The assembly used fragrant oils and sandalwood to cremate him, collected the relics, and erected a stupa.
Regarding Nālandā Monastery: it was in the thirty-fifth year of King Śrīharṣa, the year of Jia-yin (654 CE).
The tenth patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of Central India. His original name was Durlabha.

When he was first about to be born, his father dreamed that a white elephant with a jeweled throne upon its back entered through the gate; atop the throne sat a brilliant pearl, its light illuminating the four quarters.
When the assembly awoke, he was born. Later, he encountered the Ninth Patriarch and attended upon him at his side, never once sleeping;

it was said that his ribs did not even touch his mat, and thus he was titled the Venerable Kāśyapa. When he first arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand, telling the assembly:
"When this ground turns golden in color, a sage shall enter this assembly. Having finished speaking, he immediately—
He transformed into the color of gold. At that time, there was a son of a householder named Pūrṇayaśas, who stood before him with palms joined.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Where do you dwell?

He replied, "My mind does not abide anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Are you not settled? He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise. The Patriarch said, "Are you not a Buddha? He replied, "All [Buddhas are likewise]."
The Buddha was not [the one]. The Patriarch then spoke a verse, saying: "This ground turns to the color of gold; it is known in advance that a Sage has arrived.

He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and having perfected himself through the flowers of awakening—" Yaśas then spoke another verse, saying: "The Master sits upon the golden ground, constantly preaching the meaning of ultimate reality.
May he turn his light back to illuminate me, causing me to enter samādhi. The Patriarch understood his intent and immediately ordained him.
He left the household life and further perfected the categories of the precepts. Then he addressed him, saying: "The Great Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you;
you must protect and keep it in mind. He then spoke a verse, saying: "The true essence is naturally true;

Because of this truth, there is the principle of teaching. Having realized the dharma of true truth, There is neither practice nor cessation. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested spiritual transformations and entered nirvāṇa. Thus was he transformed.
The fire consumed itself. The fourfold assembly each took the relics in their robes and, at various locations, erected stupas to make offerings to them.
This was the year of Jihai, the twenty-second year of King Jeong.
The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Punyayasas, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. His clan name was Gautama; his father was named Ratnagātra.
Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Pārśva, he soon traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa came forward to pay his respects and asked:
"I wish to recognize the Buddha; which one is he? The Patriarch replied: "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, do not..."

[Asanga] said, "This is consciousness. Vasubandhu replied, "Since the Buddha did not recognize it, how can you know that this is it? Vasubandhu said, "Since he did not recognize the Buddha, how can you know that this is not it?

[Asanga] said, "This is the meaning of the saw. Vasubandhu said, "That is the meaning of the wood. Vasubandhu asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? [Asanga] replied, "It is leveled together with the Master.
Vasubandhu then asked, "What is the meaning of the wood? Vasubandhu said, "You have been cut by me," and thus Asanga was defeated.
He was suddenly awakened to understanding and, prostrating himself, took refuge [in the Triple Gem]. He then requested ordination.
The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly the King of Viśālā. In that kingdom, there was a class of people who were like naked horses.

The King exercised his supernatural power and divided his body into silkworms, so that they might obtain clothing. Later, the King was reborn in Central India; the 'horse-people' remained filled with longing for him."
He cried out in lamentation, and for this reason he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry). The Tathāgata had prophesied, saying:

"Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a worthy one named Aśvaghoṣa in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. He shall subdue the heterodox paths and deliver immeasurable people, continuing my transmission of the Dharma.
Now is precisely that time. He then addressed him, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you. Thus it was said.

He spoke in verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are never separate. Now I entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation; it is neither one nor two.
Having thus entrusted the Dharma, the Venerable One manifested supernatural transformations and entered profound, perfect nirvana. The assembly then erected a precious stupa.
His entire body was enshrined in a sealed stupa; this was the year Wuxu, the fourteenth year of King An.
As for the twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, he was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

He was also named Kātyāyanīputra (Gongsheng), a name derived from the fact that his various merits—both conditioned and unconditioned—were most preeminent. Having received the Dharma from the venerable Saṃgharakṣita...
Later, while he was turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, a certain old man suddenly prostrated himself on the ground before him.
The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person; there shall surely be a sign of distinction. Having spoken, the man vanished.
A moment later, a golden figure emerged from the earth, which then transformed into a woman. She pointed her right hand toward the Patriarch and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Elder."
"Venerable One, you shall receive the Tathāgata’s prediction. Now, upon this ground, I have proclaimed and disseminated the ultimate truth.
Having spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished. The Patriarch said, "A demon is about to come to compete with me in strength. After a short while, a violent wind and rain arrived.
Heaven and earth grew dark and murky. The Patriarch said, "The arrival of Māra is indeed certain; I shall eliminate him.

He then pointed toward the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic power and shaking the mountains and peaks. The Patriarch remained seated with solemn dignity, and the demonic disturbances were instantly extinguished.
After seven days, a small insect as large as a mayfly appeared, hiding beneath his seat. The Patriarch took it up with his hand.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation of Māra, who has come to eavesdrop upon my Dharma. He then released him to depart, but the Māra was unable to move.
The Patriarch said to him, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers.
Thereupon, he returned to his original form, prostrated himself, and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name? How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is..."
Kapimala had three thousand followers. The Patriarch asked, "Exert all your supernatural powers;
what kind of transformations can you perform? He replied, "I could transform the vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat. The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the Ocean of Nature (xinghai)?

He asked, "What is meant by the 'Ocean of Nature'? I have never known such a thing. The Patriarch then explained the Ocean of Nature for him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it."
The samādhis and the six supernormal powers manifested from this. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra gave rise to faith and, together with three thousand followers, requested ordination.
The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts upon him. He further addressed him, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now to be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the very source.'"
The Dharma: light and darkness are fundamentally non-dual. Now, having entrusted this Dharma of realization, it is neither to be grasped nor abandoned.
