Having finished the entrustment, he immediately entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi (*nāga-vikrīḍita-samādhi*). Standing upright in mid-air like the orb of the sun, he then manifested his passing into extinction.
The fourfold assembly enshrined his true body in a dragon-shaped grotto; this was the year of the Jia-wu cycle, the thirty-seventh year of King [Jing]’s reign.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.

Initially, he was a follower of non-Buddhist paths, possessing three thousand disciples and being well-versed in various heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his followers to Western India.
He had a crown prince named Meghasvāmin, who, hearing the Venerable One’s name, invited him to the palace to provide offerings.
The Elder said, “The Tathāgata has taught that śramaṇas must not draw near to kings, ministers, or families of power.
The Prince said, “To the north of our city there is a great mountain. On that mountain is a stone cave where you may practice meditative seclusion.”

"Is this so? The Patriarch replied, "Yes. He then entered that mountain and traveled several *li* when he encountered a large python. The Patriarch walked straight ahead without looking back; the serpent coiled itself around his body. The Patriarch then conferred the Three Refuges upon it, and having heard them, the serpent departed. As the Patriarch was about to reach a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain white robes came forth, joined his palms in greeting, and asked, "What is your purpose here? The Patriarch said, "I am seeking the Dharma. The old man said, "The Dharma is not to be found here; you should go to the place where the Fifth Patriarch resides. The Patriarch asked, "Where is that? The old man replied, "It is thirty *li* to the east of here. The Patriarch thanked him and proceeded. Upon reaching the mountain, he saw a monk sitting facing a wall. He called out, "Venerable One, please attend to me! The monk turned his head slightly and said, "Who are you? The Patriarch replied, "I am a seeker of the Way. The monk said, "If you seek the Way, you must first wash your feet. The Patriarch washed his feet and then went forward. The monk said, "Who are you? The Patriarch replied, "I am a seeker of the Way. The monk said, "If you seek the Way, you must first wash your face. The Patriarch washed his face and went forward again. The monk said, "Who are you? The Patriarch replied, "I am a seeker of the Way. The monk said, "If you seek the Way, you must first wash your heart. The Patriarch said, "My heart has long been pure; what more could it need washing? The monk said, "If you have already washed your heart, you may enter. The Patriarch entered and bowed to the ground. The monk said, "Arise! Why do you bow? The Patriarch replied, "Because I am a seeker of the Way. The monk said, "If you seek the Way, you must first understand the Way. What is the Way? The Patriarch replied, "The Way is simply the absence of obstruction. The monk said, "Since there is no obstruction, why do you bow? The Patriarch remained silent. The monk said, "You have come from afar; you should rest for a while. The Patriarch stayed for three days. On the third day, the monk said, "You have come from afar seeking the Way. The Way is not something that can be transmitted. However, I possess the robe and bowl of the Sixth Patriarch, which serve as proof of succession. You may take them and go to the East to transmit the Dharma. The Patriarch took the robe and bowl and departed. When he reached the river, he thought, "How shall I cross? At that moment, a young woman carrying a pitcher of water came by. Seeing the Patriarch, she set down her pitcher, bowed, and said, "Venerable One, please cross over. The Patriarch crossed the river and proceeded toward the East. After traveling some distance, he arrived at the monastery of the Fifth Patriarch. He presented the robe and bowl to the Patriarch and said, "The Master has commanded me to transmit these to you. The Fifth Patriarch wept and said, "I am an old man of declining years; how could I possibly be worthy of such a great Dharma? You must not speak thus. The Patriarch replied, "The Master has commanded me to transmit the robe and bowl to you; how could I dare disobey? The Fifth Patriarch then accepted the robe and bowl and hid them in a storeroom. He then summoned the assembly and said, "I am now old and infirm. I wish to retire and pass away. I have entrusted the robe and bowl to the Great Master Hongren. You should all pay homage to him and receive the Dharma from him. Having spoken, he passed away. The Patriarch then ascended the high seat and preached the Dharma for the assembly. After seven days, he descended from the seat and retired to his quarters. He then sent a messenger to invite the former master, who had been the attendant to the Fifth Patriarch, to come and oversee the funeral arrangements. The messenger returned and reported this to the Patriarch. The Patriarch said, "He is a man of the Way; I should go to see him. He went to the room of the former master and bowed to the ground. The former master said, "Why do you bow? The Patriarch replied, "Because I am a seeker of the Way. The former master said, "If you seek the Way, you must first understand the Way. What is the Way? The Patriarch replied, "The Way is simply the absence of obstruction. The former master said, "Since there is no obstruction, why do you bow? The Patriarch remained silent. Zhi replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in stillness.

A novice bhikṣu came frequently to request instruction, but I grew weary of responding to him and conceived thoughts of resentment. When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have dwelt in this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts, I have come to express my gratitude. The Patriarch asked:
He asked, "Who else dwells upon this mountain? He replied, "Ten li to the north, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas.
This king of trees is named Nāgavṛkṣa (Dragon Tree), and he constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas; I too have listened to and received it."
The Patriarch then proceeded with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is desolate and solitary, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.
Great Virtue, Most Honored One, why do you deign to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am not a most honored one; I have come to visit a worthy man.
Nāgārjuna reflected silently, "Has this master attained the nature of certainty and clarified the eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?"
The Patriarch said, "Although you spoke with your mind, I have already known it with my mind. Simply prepare for your renunciation; why worry that I am not a sage?
Having heard this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately ordained him, and together with five hundred dragon followers, he conferred the full precepts upon them.
He spoke to him again, saying: "I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury. Listen attentively to these verses:
'The dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest—this is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). To awaken to this dharma of hiding and manifesting is neither ignorance nor wisdom.'"
Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and used fire to cremate his body. Nāgārjuna collected the five-colored śarīra relics and erected a stūpa there;
this was the year of Renchen (the 41st year of Emperor Nǎn).
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was a native of Western India. He was also named Nāgasena.
Having first received the Dharma from Venerable Māra, he later traveled to Southern India. The people of that country were largely devoted to meritorious deeds;

when the Patriarch preached the Dharma for them, they said to one another, "If a person possesses meritorious deeds, they are foremost in the world. To speak in vain of Buddha-nature—who can [realize it]?"
He beheld him. The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride. The man asked, "How large or small is the Buddha-nature?
The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small; it is neither broad nor narrow. It has no merit and no retribution; it neither dies nor is born.
Upon hearing these principles, which were superior, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then manifested a sovereign body from his seat, appearing like the orb of the full moon.
The entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and did not behold the physical form of the Patriarch.

Among the assembly was the son of an elder named Kāṇadeva, who said to the assembly, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "We have never seen it with our eyes; how could we possibly identify it?"
Deva said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to show us. How do we know this?
It is because through the signless samādhi, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.
Having finished speaking, the wheel-mark vanished, and he returned to his original seat, whereupon he spoke a verse: "The body manifests the form of the full moon, To symbolize all..."
The essence of the Buddha is formless when preaching the Dharma; its function is discernment beyond sound and color.

When the assembly heard these verses, they suddenly realized non-arising (*anutpāda*) and all vowed to leave the household life in their quest for liberation. The Patriarch then shaved their heads and commanded the holy ones to confer the full precepts upon them.
Previously, there had been more than five thousand followers of external paths in that country who practiced great illusory arts and were venerated by the masses; the Patriarch transformed them all.
He caused them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. He further composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, which he bequeathed to the world.
Later, he addressed his chief disciple, Kāṇadeva, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to my verse:
'To clarify the principles of concealment and manifestation, one must first explain the logic of liberation; regarding the Dharma, the mind does not [cling]...'"
He realized the state where there is neither anger nor joy. Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi and extensively manifested miraculous transformations.
He then returned to his original seat and remained in profound meditative stillness. Kanadeva, together with the fourfold assembly, constructed a precious stupa to enshrine him.
This was the year Jichou (493 CE), the thirty-fifth year of the reign of the First Emperor of Qin.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds while also delighting in philosophical debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he was about to reach the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent his attendant to place a bowl filled with water before the seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [took it].
He cast a single needle into it and it advanced; they joyfully reached a profound accord. Nāgārjuna immediately preached the Dharma for him.

Without rising from his seat, he manifested the form of a lunar disc; they heard only his voice but did not see his physical form. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This auspicious omen of today..."
The Master manifested the Buddha-nature, signifying that the preaching of the Dharma transcends sound and form. Having received the Dharma, the Patriarch later traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There was an elder there named Brahmā Śuddhadeva. One day, mushrooms grew from the trees in his garden; they were exceedingly delicious.
Only the elder and his second son, Rāhulabhadra, took them and ate them; once taken, they grew back immediately.
When they had perished, they were reborn; none of their other relatives could see them. The Patriarch, knowing the cause from their past lives, went to their home.
The elder then asked for the reason, and the Patriarch said: "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu. However, this bhikṣu’s vision of the Way was not yet clear;
because he had received the faithful offerings in vain, his retribution was to become wooden mushrooms. Only you and your son [may see them]."
Only those who offer with sincerity and devotion may partake of it; others cannot. He then asked the elder how old he was, and the elder replied, "I am seventy-nine.
Zuzo then spoke this verse: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, they shall return in person to repay the offerings of the faithful."
"You are eighty-one years old; this tree will not grow. Having heard this verse, the elder was even more deeply moved by his admiration and submission.
He said, "I am an old man and cannot serve you as a disciple. I wish to give up my second son so that he may follow you and leave the household life.
The Patriarch said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. That we have met now is surely..."

Fu, following his past karmic affinity, immediately shaved his head and attended upon him. Upon reaching the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.
After deliberating for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered among their assembly. They asked the Patriarch, "Why do you not go forward?
The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not stay behind? They said, "You seem like a lowly person. The Patriarch replied, "You seem like those of noble status."

The man asked, "What Dharma do you understand? The Patriarch said, "You do not understand anything at all. The man said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. The Patriarch said, "I have certainly attained Buddhahood.
The man said, "It is not fitting for you to attain it. The Patriarch said, "Originally I say that I have attained it; you truly have not attained it.
The man said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? The Patriarch said, "Because you harbor a sense of self, therefore..."
"It cannot be obtained; since I am without a self, I shall obtain it by myself. When his arguments were thus exhausted, he asked the Patriarch, "What is your name?
The Patriarch replied, "My name is Kanadeva. Having previously heard of the Patriarch's reputation, he repented his errors and offered his thanks.
At that time, those in the assembly still raised various challenges and difficulties, but the Patriarch refuted them with unimpeded eloquence, whereupon they all submitted and took refuge in him.
He then addressed his senior disciple, Rāhulabhadra, and transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "I have explained the principle of liberation To one who is a successor of the Dharma;
In truth, there is no realization of the Dharma, Neither end nor beginning. Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch entered the Samādhi of Vigorous Prowess.
His body emitted eight rays of light as he returned to nirvāṇa. The assembly of disciples erected a stūpa to make offerings to him. This is the preceding account.
The nineteenth year of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty was the *gengchen* year.
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, was a native of Kapilavastu. While traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
There was a river there called Suvarṇodaka (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine; in its midstream, the reflections of five Buddhas appeared. The Patriarch—
He addressed the assembly, saying, "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away; there dwells the holy one Saṃghanandin.
The Buddha prophesied that after one thousand years, he shall succeed to the position of the Holy One. Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples upstream.
Upon reaching that place, they saw Saṃghanandin sitting peacefully in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him for three [days].

After seven days, he finally arose from his concentration. The Patriarch asked him, "Was it your body that was concentrated, or was it your mind? Daiten replied, "Both body and mind were concentrated.

The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind were concentrated, how could there be entering and exiting [the state]? Daiten replied, "Though there is entering and exiting, the characteristic of concentration is not lost;
it is like gold in a well—the essence of the gold remains eternally still. The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or whether the gold has been taken out of the well,"
"Gold has neither motion nor stillness; what is it that enters and exits? Daitetsu said, "If you say gold has motion and stillness, what is it that enters and exits?

If you say gold enters and exits, then gold itself is neither motion nor stillness. The Patriarch said, "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold has come out of the well..."
"What is it that remains? Daiten said, "If the gold has come out of the well, what remains is not the gold; if the gold is still in the well, what has come out is not the object.
The Patriarch said, "This interpretation is not correct. Daiten said, "That interpretation is not attached [to the truth]. The Patriarch said, "This interpretation shall fall [into error]."
Tianqi said, "Your thesis is not established. The Patriarch said, "Your thesis is not established; my thesis is established.
Tianqi said, "Although my thesis is established, the Dharma is not me. The Patriarch said, "My thesis is already established, for I am without a self (*anātman*).
Tianqi said, "If you are without a self, what thesis is thereby established? The Patriarch said, "Because I am without a self, your thesis is established. Tianqi said, "Virtuous One..."
"Who is your teacher? Who has attained this non-self? The Patriarch replied, "My teacher is Kanadeva;
he has realized this non-self. Nandī praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Deva, from whom you have emerged, O Benevolent One.
Because you, Benevolent One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch answered with a verse: "Since I am already without self, you must see my 'self. You..."
"If you take me as your teacher, you shall know that 'I' and 'non-I' are both 'I'. At these words, Nandi’s mind was suddenly enlightened;
he immediately sought liberation. The Patriarch said, "Your mind is sovereign; it is not bound by me.

Having spoken, he took his right hand, lifted the golden bowl up to the Brahma Heaven, and took fragrant food from there to serve the great assembly. However, the assembly suddenly felt a sense of revulsion. The Patriarch—
He said, "This is not my fault; it is the result of your own karma. He then commanded Nandi to share his seat and eat together with him.

The assembly again marveled at this, and the Patriarch said, "That you were unable to eat was entirely due to this reason. You should know that he who shared his seat with me is the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he has manifested his traces here, and you all likewise belong to the Bhadrakalpa."
They had attained the third fruit [of the path] but had not yet realized the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. The assembly said, "The supernatural power of our teacher is indeed trustworthy.
However, they harbored secret doubts regarding what he called the "Buddhas of the past. Knowing that sentient beings were conceited, Nandika said:
"When the World-Honored One was alive, the world was level and even; there were no hills, rivers, ditches, or moats. All water was sweet, and the grasses and trees..."

The land flourished and was abundant. For over eight hundred years since he manifested his parinirvāṇa between the twin trees, people have practiced the ten wholesome deeds while free from the eight sufferings;

yet now the world has become desolate and the trees withered. People lack profound faith, their right mindfulness is feeble, and they do not believe in *tathatā* (suchness), loving only supernatural powers.
Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the *vajra-maṇḍala*, and took—
The Amṛta-water was carried in a lapis lazuli vessel to the assembly hall. When the great multitude saw it, they immediately felt deep admiration; repenting their errors, they prostrated themselves.
Thereupon, the Patriarch charged Saṃghanandi with the transmission of the Dharma-eye, speaking this verse:

"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has neither the mark of existence nor non-existence; How could it arise from within or without? The Patriarch then transmitted the Dharma.

Having finished [his teaching], he sat peacefully and returned to stillness. The fourfold assembly erected a stupa for him; this was in the twenty-eighth year of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, the Wuchen year (428 CE).
The seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents in verse, saying:
"I prostrate to my father of great compassion; I pay homage to my mother of flesh and bone. I now wish to leave the household life; I pray you will have pity on me.

His parents tried to dissuade him, but he subsequently refused to eat for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the household life while remaining at home, and he was given the name Seng.
Ganḍi then appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He often thought to himself, "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light shone down from above, and he saw a path that was level and smooth.
Without realizing it, he walked slowly along it for about ten *li* until he reached a great cliff where there was a stone cave.
He then entered into silent meditation within. When the father lost his son, he immediately banished Śrīlāta from the country and went abroad in search of him, but did not know where he was.
After ten years had passed, the Patriarch had attained the Dharma and received his prediction;

while traveling to the country of Mathurā to propagate the teachings, a cool breeze suddenly swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of joy and comfort to both body and mind. Not knowing its cause, the Patriarch said: "This is the Way..."
"This is the wind of virtue. Surely a sage shall appear in this world to continue the ancestral lamp.
Having spoken thus, he employed his supernatural powers to lead the great assembly through the mountains and valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak.
He said to the assembly, "Upon the summit of this peak there is purple cloud like a canopy; a sage dwells here. He then wandered with the assembly for a long while until they beheld the mountain.
He left. A young boy holding a round mirror went straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? He replied, "One hundred years.
The Patriarch said, "You are still a child; why do you say you are one hundred years old? The boy said, "I do not understand principle; I am truly one hundred years old."
The Patriarch said, "Are you skilled in the pivotal point? The youth replied, "The Buddha said:

'If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the pivotal point of the Buddhas, it would be better to live for a single day and attain definitive realization. The Patriarch asked, "What does that which is in your hand signify?"
The boy said, "The great perfect mirror of all Buddhas is without flaw or obscuration within or without; two people see it together, for their eyes and minds are alike.
When his parents heard these words from their son, they immediately relinquished him to allow him to leave the household life.

The Master took him to his original location and, having conferred the full precepts upon him, named him Gayāśata. Later, hearing the sound of wind blowing the temple bells, the Master asked, "Are the bells ringing?"
When a gale blew and the bells rang, She-t'o said, "It is not the wind or the bells that ring; it is my own mind that rings. The Patriarch asked, "And who, then, is this mind?
She-t'o replied, "Because all are utterly still and silent. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! He who shall continue my Way—if it be not you, then who?
He then transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; The ground arises from conditions. From conditions, seeds..."
They did not obstruct one another; the flowers and fruits were likewise. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he passed away while grasping the tree with his right hand.
The great assembly deliberated, saying, "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree; shall it provide shade for his descendants?

They intended to enshrine his entire body on a high plateau and erect a stupa there, but the multitude's strength could not lift him. Thus, they built the stupa directly beneath the tree during the tenth year of the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Former Han.
The third year was the year of Dingwei.
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His surname was Udrayana;
his father was Devavarma and his mother was Bhadra. She once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. After exactly seven days, she gave birth; his skin was—

His body was as translucent as lapis lazuli; he never washed or bathed, yet remained naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, he delighted in solitude and his speech was unlike that of ordinary children.
While out for a stroll carrying a mirror, he encountered the Venerable Nandī and received ordination. Later, leading his disciples, he traveled to the kingdom of Mahācīna.
Seeing that there was an unusual fragrance emanating from a Brahmin’s house, the Patriarch led his followers to enter it.

The master of the house, Kumāralata, asked, "What kind of assembly is this? The Patriarch replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, his mind and spirit were struck with awe.
He immediately closed the door. After a long while, Sengzhu knocked on the door. Luoduo said, "There is no one in this house. Sengzhu asked, "Who is it that says there is no one?

Upon hearing these words, Luoduo realized he was an extraordinary person; he hurriedly opened the bolt and invited him inside. Sengzhu said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy, saying:
'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mo-zhi (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and flourish [the Dharma]...'"

The profound transformation has now met you; you have encountered me at this auspicious juncture. Thereupon, Kumārajīva awakened to the wisdom of his past lives and devotedly renounced the household life.
Once he had received full ordination, the Dharma was entrusted to him with a verse which said: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, Through causes and conditions, a sprout can emerge.
If these conditions do not obstruct one another, Then birth will arise from that which was unborn. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, the Patriarch leaped into the void and manifested...

Having manifested eighteen kinds of supernatural transformations and entered the Samādhi of the Transformed Fire-Light, he spontaneously incinerated his own body. The multitude erected a stūpa for his relics;
this was during the twentieth year of the Chengdi era of the Former Han dynasty, the Wushen year.
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.

In a former life, he was a deva of sovereign power (the sixth heaven of the desire realm). Upon seeing the jeweled necklaces of a Bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the second heaven of the desire realm).
There, he heard Kauśika preach the Prajñāpāramitā; because the Dharma was supreme, he ascended [to a higher realm].
In the Brahma Heaven (the Realm of Form), because his faculties were sharp, he skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma. All the devas honored him as their teacher.
When the time came to succeed to the patriarchal lineage, he descended to the country of the Yuezhi, and later arrived at the kingdom of Central India. There was a Great Being named Jayata.
Question: "The parents of my household have long placed their faith in the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by illness and whatever they undertake never turns out as they wish.
On the other hand, the neighbors next door have long followed the occupation of *caṇḍālas*, yet their bodies are always vigorous and healthy, and all their undertakings are harmonious.
Why are they so fortunate while we are so guilty? The Patriarch said: "Why should you doubt this? Furthermore, regarding the retribution for good and evil—"

"There are three points here. Ordinary people, seeing only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, and that the rebellious meet with good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune, claim that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and retribution are empty.
Little do they realize that shadow and echo follow one another, without the slightest discrepancy;
even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they shall never perish. When Śāṇakavāsin heard these words, his doubts were instantly dispelled. The Patriarch said: "You..."

Although one has already gained faith in the three karmas, one has not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*), delusion exists because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*), and non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*).
The mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without creation or fabrication, without retribution or response, and without victory or defeat.
"Tranquil and still; numinous and alert. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas.
All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions. Jñānagupta (Shéyàduō) received these words and grasped their meaning;

his innate wisdom was immediately awakened, and he earnestly sought ordination. Once he had received full precepts, the Patriarch told him: "The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived. You should succeed me."

Having completed his tour of transformation and instruction, he then transmitted the Dharma-eye. He spoke in verse: "In the nature of things, there is fundamentally no birth; It is spoken only to respond to those who seek it.

Since nothing can be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts as to whether it is resolved or not? He further said: "These are the words of the Tathāgata Sublime Sound regarding the purity of seeing one's own nature.
You should propagate them for the sake of future students. Having finished speaking, he immediately scratched his face with his fingernails while seated upon the dais.
Like a red lotus in bloom, he emitted great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly before entering parinirvāṇa.
Śāṇakavāsa erected a stūpa for him in the fourteenth year of the Xinshi era, the *wuchen* (renwu) year.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep; he transformed and guided immeasurable beings.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the teachings of the sudden school (*tun-jiao*). Among the assembly of students there, they valued debate above all else.

Their leader was named Vaśu-bandhu (translated here as *Biànxíng*, "Universal Practice"), who constantly ate only one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day. Pure...

He was pure and free from desire, and was sought after by the multitude. When the Patriarch wished to deliver him, he first asked the assembly, "Can this Parivrajaka ascetic, who is able to cultivate the Brahma-faring, attain the Way of the Buddha?
The assembly replied, "Our teacher is diligent; why should he not be able to do so?
The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice austerities for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it would all be in vain."

"This is the fundamental principle. The assembly asked, "What virtues and practices does the Venerable One possess that you would disparage our teacher? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way, yet I am not deluded.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent."
"I do not eat but once a day, nor do I eat mixed foods. I am neither discontented nor greedy;
my mind harbors no expectations—this is what is called the Way. When Pūrvācārya heard this, he attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him.
The Master then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? It is because his resolve for the Way is so earnest. Now, consider a string..."
He immediately cut it off. Therefore, I do not praise [this method], but rather cause him to abide in the ground of peace and bliss and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He further addressed Viśvāmitra, saying: "I have just rebuked you, O Benevolent One, before this assembly; has it not caused distress in your heart? Viśvāmitra replied:
"I recall that seven kalpas ago, when I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss, my teacher and the wise Moon-Pure (Candraprabha) prophesied to me that it would not be long."
When I was realizing the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, there appeared in the world a Bodhisattva named Mahāprabha. Because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him.
The Master rebuked me, saying, "To honor the son and slight the father—how vulgar this is! At that time, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to show me where I had erred.
The Master said, "When you paid homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, you leaned your staff against the wall upon which a Buddha was painted."

[The Master] said: "Because of this arrogance (*adhimāna*), you have consequently lost two fruits [of the Path]. Since I began to reproach myself and repent my errors, when I hear various evil words, they are like the wind or an echo.
How much more so now that you have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar (*amṛta*); would you instead give rise to feverish affliction? He further said:
"I pray only that, with great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said: "You have long planted manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage. Listen to me..."

The verse says: "In the moment of speech, one accords with non-arising; this is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand it thus, one has fully mastered both phenomena and principle.
After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he did not rise from his seat and suddenly entered parinirvāṇa. His remains were cremated, the relics were collected, and a stupa was erected.
This occurred in the seventeenth year of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the Jiaxu year.
The twenty-first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha; his father was named Jyotiṣka and his mother, Śreṇikā.
Although his family was wealthy, they had no son. Consequently, his parents prayed at a Buddhist stūpa in their quest for an heir.
One night, his mother dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dark. Upon waking, she became pregnant.

After seven days had passed, an arhat named Bhadrayaśas arrived at her home. Guanggai offered him obeisance, and Bhadrayaśas sat upright to receive it; when Yan came forward to bow, the arhat remained seated.
The assembly of worthy ones rose from their seats and said, "We return our salutations to the Great Being of the Dharma-body. Guanggai (Light Canopy) could not fathom the reason for this;
he then took a precious jewel and knelt to offer it as a test of his sincerity. The worthy assembly immediately accepted it without the slightest show of modesty or thanks.
Unable to restrain himself, Guanggai asked, "I am a man, yet when I offered my respects, you paid me no heed. What virtue does my wife possess that you avoided her?"

The virtuous assembly said, "We accepted your prostrations and received your pearls merely to bestow blessings upon you. Your wife is pregnant with a holy son who, when born, shall become a lamp for the world and a sun of wisdom;
therefore, we avoided him, not out of any regard for women. The virtuous assembly spoke further, "Your wife shall give birth to two sons.
One shall be named Vasiṣṭha (this means 'dwelling in the highest'), whom I shall honor; the second shall be named Kātyāyana (which means..."
Regarding the Wild Magpie: Formerly, when the Tathāgata was practicing the path on Mount Himavat, a female magpie nested upon his head.
Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, the magpie received her retribution by becoming the King of Nadi.

The Buddha prophesied, saying, "In the second five-hundred-year period, you shall be born into the family of Viśākha in Rājagṛha as a sibling of a noble one; now this has not failed to come to pass. One month later, she indeed gave birth.
The two sons were Venerable Vaśpaṇḍita and Śāradvatīputra. When Vaśpaṇḍita reached the age of fifteen, he paid homage to the Arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life.
Moved by this, the Bodhisattva Vibhāṣa conferred the precepts upon him. Traveling to propagate the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Nadī.
Its king was named Nityeśvara, who had two sons: the first was named Mahāla, and the second was named Maṇḍala. The king asked his grandfather, "Rājagṛha..."
"What is the difference between the customs and climate of that city and this one? The Patriarch replied, "In that land, three Buddhas have appeared in the world.
Now, in your kingdom, two masters are guiding and transforming beings. The King asked, "Who are these two masters?

The Patriarch said, "The Buddha prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two great beings of supernatural power who would leave the household life to succeed the Sages; one of them is your second son, Maṇiratha."
"Although my virtue is meager, I dare to accept one of them. The King said, "Truly as the Venerable One has spoken, I shall renounce this son to become a śramaṇa.

The Patriarch said, "Excellent, Great King! You are able to follow the Buddha’s intent. He immediately conferred the full precepts upon him and bestowed the verse of the transmission of the Dharma, saying:
"Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded; why do you not realize this? To penetrate the Dharma within this—neither now nor in the future..."

This was not of antiquity. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the air to a height of half a *yojana* and remained suspended there, motionless. The fourfold assembly gazed up at him in reverence and earnestly requested that he return to his seat.
He then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His body was cremated, and *śarīra* relics were obtained for which a stupa was erected;
this occurred in the *ding-si* year, the twelfth year of Emperor Shang of the Later Han dynasty.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara, was the son of King Nitya-vaśavartin of the country of Naṭika.
At the age of thirty, he met the patriarch Vasu and left the household life to receive the transmission of the Dharma. He traveled to Western India, where the king was named Pradyota;
he belonged to the Gautama clan and had turned toward the Buddha Vehicle, practicing with diligent perseverance. One day, while at his place of practice, [he encountered the following].
A small stūpa appeared, and when he wished to take it to offer worship, the assembly was unable to lift it.

The King immediately convened a great assembly of the three groups—the practitioners of the Brahma-faring life, those in meditative contemplation, and those of incantations—with the intent to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Patriarch also attended this assembly;

none of these three groups were able to discern its origin. The Patriarch then explained to the King in detail the causes and conditions of the stūpa (the account of the stūpa being built by King Aśoka is not recorded here at length). Now it emerged...

[The Buddha] appeared. This was brought about by the power of the King’s merit. Upon hearing these words, the King said, "A Most Holy One is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not lasting.
He immediately transmitted the throne to his crown prince and went forth as a renunciant under the Elder. After seven days, he realized the fruit of Arhatship.

The Elder comforted him deeply and instructed him, saying, "While you reside in this kingdom, skillfully deliver others. Now, in a foreign land, there is one who is a great vessel of the Dharma; I shall [go there]."

He was about to go to convert them when they attained liberation and said, "The Master manifests traces throughout the ten directions; whenever you stir a thought, you shall arrive. Why trouble yourself with the journey? The Patriarch replied, "So be it.
Thereupon, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the Bhikṣu Huike (Hegelena) in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna): "You are in that kingdom..."
He instructed the flock of cranes, saying, "The Way and its fruits are about to be realized; you should know this for yourselves.
At that time, Hakena recited a sūtra verse for King Ratnamudrā. Suddenly, he beheld a wondrous fragrance forming into tassels. The king asked, "What omen is this?

He replied, "This is the precursor of the arrival of the patriarch Mañjuśrī, who transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal from the Western Land of India. First, he has descended with this fragrant token of faith."

[The King] said, "What is the supernatural power of this master like? [Bodhidharma] replied, "This master has received a distant prediction from the Buddha that he shall widely proclaim the profound transformation in this land.

At that time, the King and Helena together paid homage from afar. The Patriarch, having perceived this, immediately took leave of the bhikṣu De-du (Deduo) and departed for the kingdom of Mo-zhi (Mokṣa).
There he accepted the offerings of the King and Helena. Later, Helena questioned the Patriarch.
He said, "I have already dwelt among the forest trees for nine *śata* (in India, one year is counted as one *śata*). I have a disciple named Longzi (Dragon Son), who was intelligent from his youth.
Though I have investigated him through the three periods of time (*trikāla*), I could not discover his origin. His ancestor said:
'In the fifth eon (*kalpa*), this child was born into a Brahmin family in the Land of Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*). He once offered sandalwood to a Buddhist temple to serve as a mallet.'"

He struck the bell; his faculties were sharp and perceptive, and he was held in high esteem by the assembly. Again, [the Emperor] asked, "What karmic conditions do I possess that have caused this flock of cranes?
The Patriarch replied, "In the fourth eon, you were once a bhikṣu. When you were about to attend a gathering at the Dragon Palace, your disciples..."
All wished to follow him. You observed that among the five hundred followers, not a single person was capable of providing such exquisite offerings.
At that time, the disciples said, "The Master constantly preached the Dharma, saying that those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma.

Now, since this is not the case, what sanctity is there? You then immediately ordered them to attend the assembly. From the moment you relinquished this life to enter the next, you traveled through various kingdoms, transforming beings; as for those five...

There were one hundred disciples. Because their merit was slight and their virtue thin, they were born among the feathered tribes. Now, moved by your kindness, they have followed you as a flock of cranes.
Hele-na asked, "By what skillful means can they be brought to liberation? The Patriarch replied, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure;
you should listen and receive it so that you may transform beings until the end of time. Then he spoke this verse: "The mind follows the myriad objects..."
"Transformation! The place of transformation is truly profound. If one recognizes the nature within the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
When the flock of cranes heard this verse, they flew away with cries. The Patriarch sat in the lotus posture and passed away peacefully. Harelana and King Baoyin erected a stupa for him;
this was in the nineteenth year of Emperor Huan of the Later Han, the year of Yisi (469 CE).

The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hōrakana (Hōrakana is a Sanskrit term; *hō* is the Chinese word for "crane," so he was named thus because a flock of cranes constantly felt affection and longing for him).

He was a native of the country of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna). His clan was Brahmin; his father was Sāhasra-jaya and his mother was Kanakaprabhā. Because they had no son, they prayed before the golden pillar of the Seven Buddhas.
Thereupon, in a dream, a divine youth atop Mount Sumeru appeared holding a golden ring and saying, "I have come. Upon waking, [he realized this].
She became pregnant, and when he was seven years old, while traveling through the villages, he saw the people performing vulgar sacrifices.

He entered the temple and rebuked them, saying, "You falsely claim to bring about fortune and calamity, deluding the people. Year after year you expend livestock and victims; the harm you cause is extreme.

As soon as he finished speaking, the temple structure suddenly collapsed. Because of this, the local community called him the "Holy Child" (Shengzi). At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life.
At thirty, he met the Venerable Maṇḍarava, who transmitted to him the treasury of the Dharma-eye. He traveled to Central India to propagate the teachings.

There, the king was named Abhayasāgara; he held deep faith in the Buddha-way. After the Patriarch had expounded the True Dharma for him, the king suddenly saw two figures dressed in red and white garments bowing before the Patriarch.
The king asked, "Who are these people? The Patriarch replied, "These are the Sun and Moon Devas."
"I once preached the Dharma for you in the past; therefore, I have come to pay my respects. After a long while, he was not seen, and the king heard only a wondrous fragrance.

The king asked, "How many suns and moons are there in total throughout all the lands? The Patriarch replied, "In the worlds transformed by the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, there are billions of Mount Merus, suns, and moons each.
If I were to explain this extensively, I could never finish. Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy. At that time, the Patriarch...

He propagated the Unsurpassed Way and delivered those with whom he had a karmic connection. Because his elder brother, the Dragon Prince, had died young, he had a brother named Siṃha who was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory.
Siṇha served a Brahmin; when that teacher passed away, his younger brother (the Dragon Prince) also died. Siṃha then took refuge in the Venerable One and asked:
"I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind? The Patriarch said: "If you wish to seek the Way, there is nothing to be used."
[The student] said, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the Buddha-work? The Patriarch said, "If you have any application, it is not merit;
if you have no action, that itself is Buddha-work. As the Sūtra says: "The merit I have performed is such that there is no 'mine' in it."
Having heard these words, Shizi immediately entered the Buddha-wisdom. At that moment, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of atmospheric phenomenon is this?
Shizi replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth; furthermore, there are five paths of black vapor stretching across its midst.
The Patriarch asked, "What does this omen portend? He replied, "It cannot be known. The Patriarch said, "I shall pass away."
"Fifty years hence, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India. The infant [of the Dharma] shall reside within your person, and I shall pass into extinction.
I now entrust the Eye of the Dharma to you; guard and uphold it well. He then spoke this verse: "When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable.
When it is clearly understood, there is nothing to be attained; At the moment of attainment, one does not speak of knowing. —Śāriputra Bhikṣu"

Upon hearing the verse, they were filled with joy and satisfaction; however, they did not yet understand what kind of hardship was about to befall them. The Patriarch then secretly revealed this to them.

Having finished speaking, he manifested eighteen transformations and entered nirvana. After the cremation was completed and the relics were distributed, everyone wished to erect a stupa for their portion.

The Patriarch again appeared in the air and spoke a verse, saying: "One dharma encompasses all dharmas, and all dharmas are subsumed within one dharma. My body is neither existent nor non-existent; why [should there be stupas]?"
The stūpa was to be divided among all the great assembly; however, upon hearing this verse, they ceased further division and instead erected the stūpa at the site of the *dhātu* (relic) field.
This was precisely the year Jichou, the twentieth year of Emperor Xian of the Later Han dynasty.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, Bhikṣu Siṃha, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brahmin.
Having attained the Dharma, he traveled abroad and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was one named Parika who had originally practiced meditative contemplation; thus, there were five groups:

those with meditative concentration, those with intellectual insight, those attached to signs, those who had abandoned signs, and those who remained silent. The Patriarch interrogated them and transformed them; the four groups all fell silent.
They were all humbled in their hearts. Only the meditation master Dharmadatta, hearing that the fourfold assembly had been rebuked, arrived there in a state of indignation and agitation.
The Patriarch said, "Virtuous one, you practice meditation; why have you come here? Now that you have arrived here, how can you still claim to be practicing meditation?
He replied, "Though I have come here, my mind remains undisturbed. Meditation follows the practitioner; how could it depend on a particular location? The Patriarch said, "Since you, virtuous one..."
"Come," he said. "The practice has also reached you. Since there is no fixed location, how could it depend on human practice? He replied, "It is certainly the person who practices;
it is not that the person practices concentration. [Baizhang] said, "If it is the person who practices concentration, then when you come here in the future, who will be practicing that concentration?
He replied, "It is like a pure, bright pearl, with nothing obscuring it within or without—this is concentration."
"If one attains penetration, it must necessarily be like this. The Patriarch said, "If one were truly to attain penetration, it would be just like a bright pearl.

Now that I see you, sir, you are not of the class of pearls. The other replied, "That pearl is transparent and clear; both inside and out it is perfectly still. My mind is undisturbed, just as pure as this.
The Patriarch said, "That pearl has no interior or exterior; how can you, sir, be 'perfectly still'? A foul object does not waver."
This samādhi is not the pure [state]. Damodara received the patriarch’s awakening; his mind-ground became luminous.

Once the patriarch had gathered the fivefold assembly and his fame spread far and wide, he began to seek a Dharma heir. He encountered an elder who led forth his son and asked the patriarch, "This boy is named Sthira.
Since birth, his left hand has remained clenched in a fist; now that he is grown, he is still unable to open it. We pray that the Venerable One [will help him]."
This was to reveal his past causes. When the Patriarch saw him, he immediately reached out his hand and said, "Return my pearl to me.
The youth suddenly opened his hand and offered the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In a previous life, I was a monk named Vatsa.
Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea, I received this pearl as an offering and entrusted it to him. That he now returns my pearl to me is but natural."

The elder then renounced his son for the monastic life. The Patriarch immediately conferred the full ordination upon him; because of these prior circumstances, he was named Vasiṣṭha. The Patriarch then said to him:
"My teacher had a secret prophecy that you would encounter hardship before long. The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you.
You must protect it and universally moisten all beings until the end of time. He spoke in verse: "Know the true teaching..."
At the time of seeing, both knowing and seeing are the mind; when the mind arises, there is knowing and seeing, and knowing and seeing are right here and now.
Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Sthiramati, charging him to go to another country and transform beings according to their capacities.

Having received these instructions, Sthiramati traveled directly to South India. The Patriarch, however, felt that it was impossible to avoid the impending danger and remained alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, in his own country...
There were two non-Buddhist practitioners, one named Māmuta and the other named Durlabha. Having mastered various magical arts, they plotted together to incite a rebellion;
they then stole the appearance of Śākya-sons and secretly entered the royal palace. They said, "If we do not succeed, the guilt shall fall upon the sons of the Buddha.
Since the sorcery was their own doing, the calamity followed immediately. The King indeed became enraged and said, "I have long placed my heart's devotion in the Three [Jewels]..."
"O Treasure, why have you brought about such harm as this? He immediately ordered the destruction of the monastery and the expulsion of the Śākya community.

Furthermore, he personally took up a sword and went to where the Venerable was, asking, "Has the Master realized the emptiness of the aggregates (skandha-śūnyatā)? The Patriarch replied, "I have already realized the emptiness of the aggregates."

The King asked, "Have you transcended birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I have already transcended birth and death. The King said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head.
The Patriarch said, "This body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head? The King then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable One's head.
White milk surged upward several feet high. At the same time, the king’s right arm also fell to the ground, and he passed away after seven days.
Prince Prabhāśiras sighed and said, "Why has my father brought this calamity upon himself? At that time, there was a seer named Śvetaśaila who lived on Mount Elephant.

Having deeply understood the law of cause and effect, he became the foremost in radiance. He extensively proclaimed his past causes and conditions to unravel the net of doubts (the details of which are found in the *Shengzhou ji* and the *Baolin zhuan*).
Thereupon, a stupa was erected for the venerable Śrīmitra’s remains in the year Jīmōu (439 CE), the twentieth year of the reign of Emperor Qi of the Wei dynasty.
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Venerable Vasishṭha, was a native of Kaśmīra. He was of Brahmin lineage; his father was named Śāntacaryā and his mother Nityasukhā.
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently conceived. Upon his birth, he held his left hand in a fist.
Having met the patriarch Siṃha, his past causes were revealed, and he was secretly entrusted with the Heart-Seal (Cittamudrā). Later, he traveled to South India and arrived at Central India.

In India, there was a king named Kāśyapa who offered him hospitality and worship. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner known as Nirātma-guru (the Venerable Selfless One), who had previously been highly esteemed by the king.
Envious of Bodhidharma’s arrival, he wished to debate with him, hoping to defeat him and thereby consolidate his own position.
Thus, before the king, he said to Bodhidharma, "I understand the art of silent debate; it requires no spoken words. Bodhidharma asked, "Who knows this?"
[The Master asked: "Are you competing for victory or defeat? He replied, "I do not contend for victory or defeat; I only seek its meaning.
The Patriarch asked, "What do you take to be its meaning? He replied, "Taking no-mind as the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can you attain the meaning?

He replied, "When I speak of 'no-mind,' it is a designation, not the meaning itself. The Patriarch said, "When you speak of 'no-mind,' it is a designation, not the meaning. When I speak of 'non-mind,' it is..."
"Meaning is not name. He said, "If meaning is not name, who can discern meaning? The Patriarch said, "Your name is not meaning. What name is this name?

He said, "It is for the purpose of discerning what is not meaning; thus, this name is a nameless name. The Patriarch said, "Since the name is already not a name, and the meaning is also not meaning, who is it that discerns?
And what is there to be discerned? Thus they exchanged questions and answers fifty-nine times. [The outsider]—
The Daoist Du fell silent in submission. At that moment, the Master suddenly faced north, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying:
"My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, has encountered this calamity today; how tragic! He then took leave of the king and traveled south, reaching Southern India.

There he lived in seclusion among the mountain valleys. At that time, the king of that land was named Devaśrī (Tian-de). He welcomed and made offerings to him. The king had two sons; the first was named...
Devasena was fierce and his physical strength was robust; his other name was Amṛtodana. He was mild and gentle, yet had long suffered from chronic illness.
The Patriarch then explained the law of cause and effect to him, and the King immediately resolved his doubts. Furthermore, there was a master of incantations who envied the Patriarch’s Way;
he secretly placed poison in food and drink, but the Patriarch, knowing of it, ate it nonetheless, while the sorcerer instead suffered the consequences.
Fearing disaster, he then went to the Patriarch to leave the household life. The Patriarch immediately conferred the full precepts upon him. Sixty years later, Emperor De-sheng ascended the throne;
he again believed in non-Buddhist paths and brought trouble upon the Patriarch. Unlike Upagupta, who was imprisoned for offering remonstrance, the King suddenly questioned the Patriarch, saying:

"In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive teachings have long been eradicated. As for what you have transmitted, Master, to which school does it belong? The Patriarch replied: "In the kingdom of Your Majesty in the past..."

"In what has come to me, there is truly no heterodox teaching; that which I have attained is the very lineage of the Buddha. The King asked, "One thousand two hundred years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
From whom did you receive it, Master? The Patriarch replied, "The Mahāsattva Kāśyapa personally received the seal of the Buddha.
It was transmitted successively down to the twenty-fourth generation, the Venerable Siṃha, from whom I received it. The King said, "I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha..."
"One cannot escape execution; how could one possibly transmit the Dharma to future generations?

The Patriarch said, "When my teacher’s time of peril had not yet arisen, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the Dharma verses to manifest the lineage of transmission. The King asked, "Where is that robe?

The Patriarch immediately took the robe out from his bag and showed it to the King. The King ordered it to be burned; its five colors remained vivid, and even when the fuel was exhausted, it remained as it was before. The King then...
He felt remorse and paid his respects to the Lion (Śāṇavāsa). Once it was clear that he was truly the successor, he then pardoned Guptadatta. Guptadatta then requested to leave the household life.
The Patriarch asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so? Guptadatta replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not pursue those things.
The Patriarch asked, "What things will you not pursue? Guptadatta replied, "I shall not pursue worldly affairs. The Patriarch asked, "Then for what purpose will you do so?"
Guṇamati said, "This shall be performed as a Buddha-activity. The Patriarch replied, "The Prince’s wisdom is divinely supreme;

surely it is the descent of various sages. He then granted him permission to leave the household life. For six years he served [the Patriarch], and later received full ordination within the royal palace.

At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the earth shook violently, accompanied by many miraculous omens. The Patriarch then addressed him, saying, "I have already grown old and infirm; how could I remain for long?"
"You must well protect the treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma and universally deliver all sentient beings. Listen to my verse: "The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision;
Within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now awakened to true nature; There is neither Path nor Principle. Mudantuo (Mukta) then recited this verse.
He addressed the Patriarch once more, saying, "The Dharma robe should be transmitted to you. The Patriarch said, "This robe is for the sake of difficulty; it is a provisional..."

To prove this, he said, "Your body is free from affliction; why do you need his robe? Its transformative influence shall spread throughout the ten directions, and people will naturally have faith and turn toward it.

Then, as if in secret, he prostrated himself before Maudgalyāyana’s words and withdrew. The Patriarch manifested a supernatural transformation and, through the power of samādhi, burned himself with fire.

The śarīra on the ground was approximately one chi in height. King De-seṅ (Deśeng) first constructed a stūpa to enshrine it, which occurred in the third year of the Taíning era of Emperor Míng of the Eastern Jin, the year of Yǐyǒu.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was the second son of King Devaśrī of South India.
Having received ordination and attained the Dharma, he traveled to East India. There, the king was named Sthira; he followed non-Buddhist paths and held the Brahmin Dīrghanakha as his teacher.
When the Venerable Patriarch was about to arrive, the king and the Brahmin both beheld a white vapor piercing through from the zenith to the nadir. The king...

He asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Brahmin, having foreseen that the Elder [Mahāmaudgalyāyana] would enter the kingdom and fearing that the King might convert to the True Dharma, said, "This is merely a portent of Māra’s arrival;
what auspiciousness is there in it? He then gathered his disciples and deliberated, saying, "It would be better to keep him from entering the capital.
Who among us can defeat him? A disciple replied, "Each of us possesses various incantations and arts by which we can move [him]."

"Even if heaven and earth enter into water and fire, what cause for concern is there? When the Patriarch arrived, he first saw black vapors over the palace walls and said, "This is but a minor difficulty.
He went directly to the King's location. The King asked, "Master, why have you come? The Patriarch replied, "I have come to deliver sentient beings. The King said:
"By what means do you deliver them? The Patriarch replied, "I deliver each according to their own kind.

When the Brahmin heard these words, he could not contain his anger and immediately used his illusory powers to conjure a great mountain atop the Patriarch's head. The Patriarch pointed at it, and suddenly it appeared above the heads of the entire assembly.
The Brahmins were struck with terror and threw themselves at the Patriarch's mercy. The Patriarch, pitying their ignorance and delusion, pointed again, and the conjured mountain vanished instantly.
He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the king, leading him toward the True Vehicle (samyak-yāna). He said to the king, "In this kingdom, there shall be a sage who will succeed me.
At that time, there was a son of a Brahmin, about twenty years of age, who had lost both his parents in childhood and whose name and lineage were unknown;
as he sometimes called himself "Sragdharin" (The Garlanded One), people referred to him as the "Sragdharin Boy. He wandered through the streets and villages.
He begged for alms to sustain his daily life, much like the monk Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). When people asked him, "Why do you walk so hurriedly?
he would immediately reply, "Why do you walk so slowly? Or when they asked, "What is your surname? he would say, "It is the same as yours. No one knew the reason for this.
Later, when the King and the Venerable One were traveling in the same carriage, they saw the Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta bowing his head before them. The Patriarch said, "Do you remember the past?"
The Master asked, "Is this so? The boy replied, "I recall that in distant kalpas past, I lived together with you, Master.
You expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, while I turned the wheel of the profound *Sūtras*. Today’s events are surely in accord with our former causes.
The Patriarch further said to the King, "This boy is none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Following this holy one, two more shall appear."
One person was transformed in South India; one person’s karmic conditions lay in China. Within four or five years, he returned to this land.

Thus, based on his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra (般若多羅) and entrusted with the Dharma-eye Treasury. The verse says: "The treasury of the true nature of the mind-ground has neither head nor tail.
Responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom'. Having thus transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch passed away.

He then took leave of the King, saying, "My transformative karmic conditions have come to an end; I shall now return to nirvana. I pray that Your Majesty will not forget to provide external protection for the Supreme Vehicle.
He then returned to his original seat, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. A fire spontaneously emerged to cremate him, and his relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa.
This occurred in the year Wuzi, the thirteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to South India to propagate the teachings.
There, the king was named Gandhāra; he revered the Buddha-vehicle and honored it with offerings that surpassed those of all others.
Furthermore, he bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons: Candravairocana, Śrīcandra, and [the third son].
Tiduo (Devadatta) said, "Putiduo (Bodhidatta). He was the youngest of the bodhisattvas.
Their grandfather wished to test what they had attained, so he took the pearl he had been given and asked the three princes, 'This pearl is perfectly bright; is there anything that can equal it?
The first prince and the second prince both replied, 'This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures; certainly nothing surpasses it. It is not something for Your Honor [to possess].'"
"As for the power of the Way, who is able to receive it? The third prince said: "This is a worldly treasure, yet it is not supreme.
Among all treasures, the Treasure of the Dharma is supreme. This is a worldly light, yet it is not supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is a worldly clarity, yet it is not supreme. Among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme. This...
The radiance of a jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a jewel;
once it is known to be a jewel, its preciousness is clarified. If its preciousness were self-evident, the jewel would not be a jewel by itself;
if the jewel were self-evident, the jewel would not be a jewel by itself. That the jewel is not a jewel by itself means that it must rely upon the "wisdom-jewel" to discern the worldly jewel.
"A treasure is not inherently a treasure; it requires the treasure of wisdom to illuminate the treasure of the Dharma. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, that treasure manifests.
When sentient beings possess the Way, their mind-treasure is likewise so. The Patriarch praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what is signless? He replied, "Among all things, non-arising is signless. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the highest?
He replied, "Among all things, the person-self (pudgala-ātman) is the highest. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the greatest. The Patriarch knew that he was a true Dharma heir.
Since the time had not yet arrived, he remained silent and blended in with the crowd. When the incense reached the king, who was weary of the world, the assembly all wailed and fainted;
only the third son, Bodhidhara, entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days, whereupon he sought ordination.
Once he had received full precepts, his grandfather told him: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, just as..."
This was transmitted in succession, even unto me. I now entrust this to you; listen to my verse: "The mind-ground gives rise to all seeds;

Through conditions, they again produce principles. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; When the flower opens, the world arises. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, the Venerable One [passed away].
Immediately, he rose from his seat and extended his left and right hands, each emitting twenty-seven rays of light, brilliant with five colors.
He then leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and manifested fire to consume himself. Śarīras fell like rain from the sky;
these were collected and enshrined in a stupa. This occurred in the year Dingyou, the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, during which time [the Master] Zu...
The King of East India invited the Patriarch for a meal. During the meal, the King asked, "Everyone here recites the sutras; why alone do you not?
The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk’s exhalation does not follow external conditions, and his inhalation does not dwell within the aggregates or realms.
He constantly recites such a sutra as this—hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls—not merely one or two."
The First Patriarch of the Eastern Land, the Great Master Bodhidharma, was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. Later, he encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra.

Upon arriving in his own country, he received the royal offerings. Recognizing that his teacher was Guhyapada, [the king] tested him by having him distinguish between the precious jewels bestowed upon his two elder brothers, thereby illuminating the essential points of the mind.
Thereafter, the Venerable One said to him: "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery."
Now, "Dharma" is the meaning of "penetrating the Great. It was thus appropriate to name him Dharma; consequently, he was renamed Bodhidharma.

The Patriarch then addressed the Venerable One, saying: "Since I have attained the Dharma, to which country should I go to perform the work of a Buddha? I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Venerable One replied:
"Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet. Stay for a time in Southern India and wait until after my passing."
"In sixty-seven years, you shall go to China to administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior faculties.
Be careful not to travel too soon; there will be decline under the sun. The Patriarch asked again, "In that land, are there Great Beings capable of being vessels for the Dharma?
Will there be obstacles for a thousand years to come? The other replied, "In the regions where you will transform beings, those who attain Bodhi shall be beyond counting. As for me—"
More than sixty years after his parinirvāṇa, that country will face a crisis. Wenzhubu will naturally subdue it through his own virtue. When that time comes, do not remain in the south;
for there, people value only conditioned achievements and do not perceive the principle of the Buddha. Even if you should go there, [you must proceed with caution].
"This, too, cannot last long. Listen as I recite this verse for you: 'On the road one meets a man crossing water, then again a sheep;
All alone and weary, he secretly crosses the river. At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses! Two young cassia trees have flourished for a long time. He asked again:
"What further events will there be after this? The Master replied: "From now until one hundred and fifty years have passed, there will be a minor period of difficulty.

Listen to my prophecy: 'Though auspicious within the heart, it is ominous on the outside; a monastic dwelling by the river, its name ill-fated. Because of encountering a venomous dragon, a martial son is born;
suddenly meeting a small mouse, there is eternal stillness. Again he asked: 'What will be after this? The Master said:"
He said: "Two hundred and twenty years hence, a person beneath this forest shall attain the fruit of the Way. Listen to my prophecy: 'Though Zhendan is vast, there is no other path;
it must be traversed by the feet of one's descendants. A golden rooster knows how to hold a single grain of millet, providing sustenance for the arhat-monks of the ten directions.
He further recited various verses, all of which were prophetic premonitions regarding the rise and fall of the Buddhist teachings."

(The details are found in the *Baolin zhuan* and the *Shengzhou ji*). Master Sengzhu reverently received the teachings and served at [Buddhabhadra’s] side for nearly forty years without ever neglecting his duties.
When the Venerable One passed away, he subsequently propagated the teachings in his own country. At that time, there were two masters:
the first named Buddhajīva and the second named Buddhasānta. Originally, they had studied together with Master Sengzhu under Buddhabhadra in the practice of Hīnayāna meditation.
When Buddhadasa encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra, he abandoned the Hinayana and turned toward the Mahayana, coming to teach alongside the Patriarch;
at that time, they were known as the "Two Gateways of Ambrosia. However, Buddhadasa’s followers further divided into six schools:
first, the School of Characteristics; second, the School of Non-characteristics; third, the School of Samādhi and Wisdom; fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice; fifth...
The School of Non-Attainment and the sixth, the School of Quiescence, each clung to their own understanding and separately expanded the source of their conversion.

Their settlements were numerous and their followers were exceedingly vast. The Patriarch sighed deeply and said, "If even one of those teachers has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so for these fragmented and proliferating groups that have divided into six schools?
If I do not eliminate them, people will remain forever entangled in false views. Having spoken, he subtly manifested his spiritual power.
[He] proceeded to the place of the Saṃlakṣaṇavādins (the School of Characteristics). He asked: "What is called the 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas?
Among that assembly was a senior elder named Sarvala, who replied: "Among all marks, not mutually [confusing] the various marks—this is called the true mark."
The Patriarch said, "If all phenomena are such that they do not mutually exclude one another, yet you call this the 'true mark' (bhūtalakṣaṇa), how can it be fixed?
He replied, "Among all phenomena, there is truly nothing fixed. If one were to fix the nature of phenomena, how could it be called 'true'?
The Patriarch said, "That phenomena are not fixed is precisely what is called the true mark. Since you yourself are not fixed, how can you attain it? He replied, "I say that it is not fixed."

"One does not speak of the various marks; one should speak of the various marks. Their meaning is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Your statement is not definitive. It should be the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because it is both definitive and non-definitive, it is not the true mark. He replied, "Since the definitive is itself non-definitive, it is not the true mark."
[The Master] said, "I know that you are not the same as before; you are neither fixed nor unchanging. Zu said, "If you are now unchanging, why do you call it the 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?
That which has already changed and passed away is likewise of this nature. He [the Master] said, "Unchanging should exist; because of its existence or non-existence, the true mark changes."

He sought to establish the meaning of this through meditative concentration. Zuzi said, "The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is unchanging; that which changes is not the true mark. Within the realm of existence and non-existence, what can be called the true mark?
Sabaluo, knowing in his heart that the holy master had attained profound understanding and reached the depths of realization, pointed his finger at empty space and said:

"This is a worldly phenomenon with characteristics; yet it can also be empty. Might my own body become like this? The Patriarch said, "If you understand the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), you will see that which is non-characteristic.
If you comprehend that which is non-characteristic, its form is likewise so. You should look into the midst of form."
"Without losing the physical form, one does not obstruct existence within the realm of non-characteristics. If one can understand it thus, this is called the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
