When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it in faith. The Patriarch suddenly vanished from sight and went to the school of the Non-Characteristic (animitta) sect.
He asked, "You speak of the Non-Characteristic; how do you realize it? Among the assembly was one named Pratītya, who replied:
He said, "I clearly realize formlessness because the mind does not manifest. The Patriarch asked, "If your mind does not manifest, how can you clearly realize it?
He replied, "I clearly realize formlessness because the mind neither grasps nor rejects; at the very moment of clear realization, there is even no one who 'realizes'.

The Patriarch said, "If, regarding all existence and non-existence, the mind neither grasps nor rejects, and furthermore there is no one who realizes, then because all forms of clarity are absent... He replied, "I enter the Buddha's three..."

"If even in samādhi there is nothing to be attained, how much less can one know that which is signless? The Patriarch said: 'Since you do not know the signs, who says there is existence or non-existence?
If there is still nothing to be attained, what do you call this samādhi? He replied: 'I speak of non-attainment;
I realize that there is nothing to be realized because it is not [ordinary] samādhi. Therefore, I speak of samādhi. The Patriarch said: 'If it is not samādhi, what should it be called? You..."
"Since you have not realized it, what is there to realize if there is no realization? When Boluotidu heard the Patriarch’s analysis, he immediately awakened to his original mind.
He prostrated in gratitude to the Patriarch and repented for his past errors. The Patriarch prophesied, saying: "You shall attain the fruit; you will realize it before long.
There is a demon in this country; you shall subdue him before long. Having spoken, the Patriarch suddenly vanished. Boluotidu went to the abode of Dinghui Zong and asked: "What do you study?"
"Are concentration and wisdom one or two? Among the assembly was one named Bharanda, who replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two.
The Patriarch said, "If they are neither one nor two, why are they called concentration and wisdom? He replied, "In concentration, it is not concentration."
Abiding in wisdom is not wisdom. One is not one; two is also not two. The Patriarch said: "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two.
Since it is neither fixed wisdom nor insight, by what means can it be defined as wisdom or insight? He replied: "Neither one nor two—this is what wisdom and insight are able to know."
"It is the same for concentration and wisdom. The Patriarch said, "Because wisdom is not concentration, how can one know it? It is neither one nor two; who is concentrated and who is wise?
When Bharadvāja heard this, his doubts were completely dispelled like ice melting.

He then went to the abode of the fourth master, Śīlacāritra, and asked, "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? What is called 'conduct' (cāritra)? Regarding this precept and conduct, are they one or are they two?"
Within that assembly, there was a worthy man who replied: "One and two, two and one—these are all produced from that;

following the teaching without defilement is called the practice of precepts. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that 'following the teaching' implies there is still defilement. Since both 'one' and 'two' are shattered, how can you say you follow the teaching?
These two are contradictory and do not reach the true practice. When what is internal and external is not clear, how can it be called precepts? He [the worthy man]...
[The Master] said: "I have [the categories of] internal and external; he has already understood this thoroughly. Having attained such penetration, it is itself the practice of precepts (*śīla*).

If one speaks of 'contradiction' or 'both right and wrong,' or speaks of 'purity,' then that is precisely the precepts and the practice. The Patriarch said: "If they are both right and both wrong, how can you speak of purity?
Since penetration has been attained, why discuss internal and external? Upon hearing this, the worthy man felt ashamed and submitted. He then—

[The Master] said, "There is no place for the doctrine of 'non-attainment'. He asked, "You speak of non-attainment; how can there be attainment through non-attainment? Since there is nothing attained, there is also no attainment of attainment.
Among the assembly was one named Baojing, who replied, "When I speak of non-attainment, it is not that there is no attainment of non-attainment.

I shall explain that the attainment of attainment is precisely non-attainment; non-attainment is itself attainment. The Patriarch said, "Since attainment is already non-attainment, even attainment is not attainment. You have already spoken of attainment..."
"Attainment. "What does attainment attain? He replied, "Seeing attainment is non-attainment; non-attainment is attainment. If one sees non-attainment, it is called the attainment of attainment.
The Patriarch said, "Since attainment is non-attainment, the attainment of attainment is without attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, what is there to be attained by attainment?
Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt. He went to Jijing’s monastery and asked, "What is meant by 'quiescence'?"
"Within this Dharma, what is stillness and what is tranquility? A venerable one among the assembly replied, "This mind is unmoving;
this is called tranquility. To be unstained by phenomena is called stillness. The Patriarch said, "If the fundamental mind were not already tranquil, it would require the cultivation of tranquility.
Since it is tranquil from the very beginning, what need is there for further tranquility? The other asked, "All phenomena are fundamentally empty; because they are empty of emptiness..."
Because it is empty within that emptiness, it is called "quiescence. The Patriarch said, "Emptiness is already empty; all phenomena are likewise so.
Quiescent and signless—what is there to be quiescent, what is there to be still? Upon hearing the Master’s instruction, the Venerable One attained sudden enlightenment.

Thereafter, the six groups of followers all vowed to take refuge. From this, his transformation spread throughout Southern India, and his fame eclipsed that of the Five Indias. After sixty years had passed, he [passed away].
There was a vast multitude of people. Later, they encountered King Heterodox-View (Yijian), who disparaged and reviled the Triple Gem.
He would say every time: "My ancestors all believed in the Buddha-way, yet they fell into false views; consequently, their lifespans were not long and their reigns were brief.

Furthermore, I myself am a Buddha—why should I seek elsewhere for the retribution of good and evil? All such claims are merely fabrications devised by those of excessive cleverness. This continued until his kingdom...

Within the inner court, those who had been honored by previous kings were all dismissed and deposed. When the Patriarch learned of this, he sighed, lamenting their meager virtue and wondering how he might save them.

He then thought of two leaders within the School of Non-Form (Wuxiang zong): the first was named Poluotidi (Bhāradvāja), who shared a karmic affinity with the king and was on the verge of realizing the fruit of his practice;
the second was Zongshe (Saṃgha), who was not lacking in broad learning and eloquence, yet lacked the necessary past causes.

At that time, the six disciples also each thought to themselves, "The Buddha-Dharma is in peril; why does our Master remain so at ease? The Patriarch perceived their thoughts from afar and responded by snapping his fingers.
Hearing this, the six disciples said, "This is the sound of our Master, Bodhidharma’s faith.

We should proceed quickly to comply with his compassionate command. They immediately went to where the Patriarch was, prostrated, and inquired after his well-being. The Patriarch said, "A single leaf..."
"It obscures the sky. Who can clear it away? Zongsheng said, "Though I am shallow and insignificant, how could I dare shrink from the journey?

The Patriarch said, "Though you possess eloquence and wisdom, your power of the Way is not yet complete. Zongsheng thought to himself, "My Master fears that if I see the King and perform great Buddhist services, my fame and reputation will become so prominent that they will eclipse His Majesty’s majesty.
Even if he possesses such merit and wisdom as to be king, I am but a śramaṇa. He accepted [the command].
"The tenets of Buddhism—how could they not be difficult to oppose? Having finished speaking, he vanished.

He went to the king's location and extensively expounded upon the essential points of the Dharma, as well as matters such as the suffering and happiness of the world, and the good and evil of humans and devas. The king engaged him in a series of exchanges and interrogations; there was nothing that did not accord with principle.
The King said, “As for what you now understand, where does that Dharma reside? Zongsheng replied, “Just as Your Majesty governs and transforms the world, it should accord with the Way.
The King asked, “As for the Way You possess, where does that Way reside? The King said, “The Way I possess is intended to eliminate heterodox teachings.

As for the Dharma you possess, whom do you intend to subdue? Without rising from his seat, the Patriarch immediately perceived that Zongsheng’s meaning had fallen into error, and he suddenly addressed him:
Pralati said, "My doctrine is superior; he has not received my teachings, yet he has secretly influenced the King. In a moment, his arguments will be defeated. You must quickly save Pralati.
He respectfully received the Patriarch’s instruction and said, "I pray that you will lend me your divine power. Having spoken, clouds rose from beneath his feet.
They arrived before the Great King and stood there in silence. At that time, the King was in the midst of questioning Zongsheng when he suddenly saw Boluoti arriving by riding upon the clouds.
Startled, he forgot his line of inquiry and asked: "Is he who rides through the air a sage or a heretic? Boluoti replied: [The text continues with Boluoti's response.]
"I have not come from either the heterodox or the orthodox to convert the orthodox to the heterodox. If Your Majesty’s mind is orthodox, I shall be neither heterodox nor orthodox.
Although the King was struck with wonder, his arrogance was still burning fiercely; he immediately banished Zongsheng and ordered him out.

Pratītya said, "Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you banish this śramaṇa? Though I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me a question. The King, in a fit of rage, asked: "Who is the Buddha?"
Dizang said, "To see one's nature is to be a Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see your own nature? Dizang replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside?
Dizang replied, "It resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning? I do not see it now."
Dizang said, "The manifest functioning is right here; Your Majesty simply does not see it. The King asked, "Is it present within me?
Dizang replied, "If Your Majesty functions, there is nothing that is not it. If Your Majesty does not function, its essence is difficult to perceive. The King said, "When it is being used..."
"In how many places does it appear? Pāṭali replied, "When it appears, there shall be eight instances. The King said, "Tell me of these eight appearances.
Pāṭali then spoke in verse: "In the womb it is the body; dwelling in the world it is the person.
In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing. In the nose it discerns fragrance; in the mouth it is discourse. In the hand it grasps and seizes; in..."
The movement of the feet runs on; manifestations appear everywhere, encompassing all, yet the myriad realms are gathered within a single mote of dust.
Those who recognize this know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*jīva*). Upon hearing these verses, the King immediately attained awakening.

He repented his former errors and inquired after the essentials of the Dharma, forgetting weariness day and night until the ninety-day retreat was concluded. At that time, Zongsheng, having been expelled, withdrew into seclusion.
Shanshan said to himself, "I am now a hundred years old; for eighty years I have committed wrongs, and only in the past twenty years have I returned to the Way of the Buddha.

Though my nature is dull and ignorant, my conduct has been free from blemish. Unable to withstand this calamity, what is life compared to death? Having spoken these words, he threw himself off a cliff.
Suddenly, a divine being caught him with his hands and placed him upon a rock above, where he remained safe and uninjured. — Zongsheng.
The Master said, "I am but a humble śramaṇa who ought to be the guardian of the True Dharma; I was unable to suppress [the king's transgressions].

It is for this reason that the King has cast away his life and reproaches himself. What divine protection or assistance could have reached such an extent? I pray you grant me a word to preserve my remaining years.
Thereupon, the divine being spoke a verse, saying: "The Master’s lifespan shall reach one hundred years. At eighty, he committed a transgression. Because he drew near to [the end]..."
Because of my arrogance, I cultivated [practices] to enter the Path; yet though I possessed a modicum of wisdom, I was full of self and other.
Toward the various worthies I encountered, I never once gave rise to reverence or esteem. For twenty years, despite my meritorious deeds, my mind remained restless.
Because of my cleverness and disdain, I have come to this state. That I have attained this lack of respect from the King is precisely the fruit I should experience. From now on, I shall not—
Through diligence, he soon attained extraordinary wisdom; all the sages took him under their care, and the Tathāgata did likewise.
Upon hearing this verse, Zongsheng was delighted and immediately sat in meditative seclusion among the crags. Then the King asked Pratītya, "Virtuous one, you possess such wisdom and eloquence;
whom do you take as your teacher? Pratītya replied, "The one from whom I received the precepts of renunciation is the Tripiṭaka Master Uśanas of Śālā Monastery."
He served as his master for receiving the precepts. As for his master who appeared in the world, it was the Great King’s uncle, Bodhidharma.

When the King heard the Patriarch’s name, he was struck with awe for a long time and said, "In my baseness and unworthiness, I have been disgraced by inheriting the royal throne; I pursued the heterodox and turned my back on the orthodox, forgetting my venerable uncle.
He immediately commanded his close ministers to specially go out to welcome him. The Patriarch followed the envoys and arrived, whereupon he performed repentance for the King.
He repented of his past transgressions. Upon hearing these exhortations, the King wept and apologized to the Patriarch. He then issued an edict for Zongsheng to return to his own country.
A high minister reported, "Zongsheng was banished and threw himself off a cliff; he has already perished. The King said to the Patriarch, "The death of Zongsheng was entirely my doing.
How can your great compassion cause me to be exempted from this sin? The Patriarch replied, "Zongsheng is now among the cliffs, feasting."

"Rest. Simply send a messenger to summon me, and I shall arrive immediately. The King then dispatched a messenger into the mountains and indeed found Zongsheng sitting upright in meditative stillness.
Upon receiving the summons, Zongsheng said, "I am deeply ashamed of Your Majesty's intent. This humble monk has sworn to dwell among the crags and springs.
Furthermore, in Your Majesty’s kingdom there are virtuous men as numerous as a forest: Bodhidharma is Your Majesty’s uncle and the teacher of the Six Groups; there is also the *Prātimokṣa* Dharma..."
"O Elephant among Men! I pray that Your Majesty will revere and honor these two sages, thereby securing the foundation of the imperial throne.

Before the envoy had returned with his report, the Patriarch asked the King, "Do you know whether you have obtained the victory? The King replied, "I do not yet know. The Patriarch said, "One invitation has not yet arrived;

upon a second summons, he will surely come. After a long while, the envoy returned, and it was indeed just as the Patriarch had said. The Patriarch then took his leave of the King, saying, "You should cultivate virtue well."
Before long, he fell ill and said, "I shall depart. Seven days later, the king also fell ill. The court physicians examined and treated him, yet his condition worsened without any improvement.

The high-ranking relatives and close ministers recalled the Master’s previous prediction and urgently dispatched a messenger to inform Sengzu: "The King’s illness has reached a critical stage; he is at the point of death.
We pray that you, Venerable Sir, will come from afar to examine and save him. Sengzu immediately arrived to offer his condolences. At that time, Zongsheng [repeated his request].

Having received the King’s summons, he immediately took his leave from the mountain retreat. Pratītya also came to inquire after his illness and said to the Patriarch, “What should be done to enable the King to escape his suffering?
The Patriarch immediately instructed the Crown Prince to grant clemency for the King’s transgressions and bestow favor upon him, so that he might reverently uphold the Triple Gem.
He further performed repentance, vowing that his transgressions might be extinguished; he did this three times. The King’s illness subsequently improved.

The Master thought that the conditions in China were now ripe and the time had come to travel there to transform others. He first took leave of the ancestral stupa, then bid farewell to his fellow students, and finally went to the King’s presence.
He consoled and exhorted him, saying: "You should diligently cultivate pure deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem. My departure is not late; once the cycle of nine years has passed—"
[He] returned. When the King heard the Master’s words, his tears flowed profusely as he said, "What transgression has this kingdom committed? What auspiciousness does that land possess?

Since you, my younger brother, have such a karmic affinity there, it is not where I shall remain. I only pray that you will not forget your fatherland; once your mission is complete, return home at once.

The King immediately prepared a great ship, filled it with various treasures, and personally led his ministers and officials to escort him to the seashore. As the Master sailed across the vast deep, for...

After three cycles of winter and summer, he reached the South Sea. This was indeed on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the Gengzi year.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, received him with full state honors and submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu.

Upon reading the petition, the Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to welcome and invite him. (The cyclical characters for the year in the old edition were erroneous; the present version follows the *Continued Dharma Records* by Liang’s Seng Baochang and the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of Master Song Sengsong*.)

[The text] was revised as follows: On the first day of the tenth month, [Huineng] arrived at Jinling. The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting.
What merit and virtue do these bring? The Patriarch replied, "There is no merit or virtue whatsoever. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit or virtue?
The Patriarch replied, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas; they are causes subject to outflows (*āsrava*). They follow one like a shadow follows a form; though..."
"It is not real," [the Emperor] said. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still.
Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?"
The Patriarch said, "Vast and empty—there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not grasp this.
Realizing that their karmic conditions were not in accord, on the nineteenth day of that month, he secretly returned north of the Yangtze River.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Luoyang; this was the first year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty. He took up residence at Mount Song.
At Shaolin Temple, he sat facing a wall, remaining silent all day long; no one could fathom him, and thus he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin.
At that time, there was a monk named Shen Guang, a man of expansive talent who had lived for a long time in the region of Yi and Luo.

He had extensively studied various books and was skilled at discussing the profound principles of the Way. He often sighed, saying: "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi consist of ritual arts and social norms; the texts of Zhuangzi and the *I Ching*..."
The subtle principles had not yet been fully realized. Having recently heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma was residing at Shaolin, he thought, "The Sage is not far away;

I shall surely reach this profound realm. He then went there and attended upon the Patriarch morning and evening. The Patriarch constantly sat upright facing a wall, and no instructions were heard. Huiguan reflected to himself:
"In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their veins to provide nourishment for the hungry, and spread their hair to cover the mud. He then...
Feeding tigers from a cliff—ancients were already like this; what person am I to be otherwise? On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, there was a heavy rain and snow.
Huiguang stood upright without moving. By dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees. The Patriarch, moved by compassion, asked him, "You have stood for a long time in the snow;
what do you seek? Huiguang said with tears of sorrow, "I only pray that the Master, out of your great kindness, will open the gate of the sweet Dharma."
He opened the gates of the Dharma to extensively deliver all classes of beings. The Patriarch said: "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas was attained through diligent effort over vast eons;

it requires performing what is difficult to perform and enduring what is difficult to endure. How could one hope for the True Vehicle with meager virtue and meager wisdom, or with a frivolous and arrogant mind?"
In vain did he labor with diligent hardship. Upon hearing the Patriarch’s exhortation, he secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Patriarch.
The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma.
Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking may indeed be granted. The Patriarch then changed his name to Huike. Huike said: "The various..."
Huineng asked, "Can the Dharma-seal of the Buddhas be heard? The Patriarch said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
Huineng said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will bring it to rest for you.

Huineng remained silent for a long while and then said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Patriarch said, "I have brought your mind to rest. Nine years later, the Patriarch wished to return to India.
The Master commanded his disciples, saying: "The time is drawing near; why do you not each speak of what you have attained? At that time, Dao Fu replied:
"As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters, using them as the vehicle for the Way. The Patriarch said:
"You have obtained my skin," the Patriarch said. Niti Zongchi replied, "What I now understand is like the vision of Ānanda upon seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha;
having seen it once, he never saw it again. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates do not exist.
In my place of vision, there is not a single dharma to be obtained. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bones. Finally—
Huike prostrated himself and stood in his place. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my marrow. He then turned to Huike and told him:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa. It was passed down through successive entrustments until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also grant you this robe as a token of the Dharma. Each [of them]...

There is something indicated here; it should be understood accordingly. One may say: "I request that the Master point this out for me. The Patriarch said: "Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with and realize the mind;
externally, the *kāṣāya* robe is bestowed to establish the fundamental principle. In later generations, when people become shallow and insincere, doubts will arise in competition.
They will say: 'You are a man from the Western Heaven, while I am a son of this land. On what basis did you obtain the Dharma? By what do you certify it? You—"
Now, regarding the method for receiving this robe: in the future, difficulties will arise. Simply produce this robe along with my Dharma verses to manifest its meaning;
thus, your transformation of beings will be unhindered. Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the transmission of the robe shall cease, while the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra.

Those who understand the Way are many; those who practice the Way are few. Those who discourse on principle are many; those who penetrate principle are few. There are more than ten million who secretly accord with it and silently realize it;
you should propagate this teaching and not disparage those who have not yet awakened. A single thought that turns the mechanism of the mind is identical to original attainment.

Listen to my verse: "I have come to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower blooms and five petals unfold; The fruiting occurs spontaneously. [Old records state: "The Patriarch said:

'I have the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which I also entrust to you. This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter [it].

According to the *Rendian yimou* (Eye of the Human and Heavenly Eye), Da’guan Ying repeatedly debated and corrected these errors until they were most clearly established. I now follow this account and have therefore deleted the previous passage. Since I arrived here, it has been five...
I have already transcended these poisons. I once came forth myself to test this by placing a stone [upon it]; the stone split.

Because I originally departed from South India to come to this Eastern Land, I beheld that the land of Shen-zhou possesses the majestic air of the Mahāyāna. Consequently, I crossed the seas and traversed the deserts to seek those who would uphold the Dharma;
yet our meeting was not yet harmonized, and I remained as if foolish and mute. Now that I have received your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled.

(A separate record states: When the Patriarch first resided at Shaolin Temple for nine years, he preached the Dharma for the Second Patriarch, teaching only that one should externally cease all conditions and internally remain without the panting of thought, making the mind like a blank wall so as to be able to enter the Way.

Although Huike spoke variously about the nature of the mind, he never once realized the principle. The Patriarch merely refuted his errors and did not explain the essence of the non-conceptual mind. Huike suddenly said, "I have already ceased all conditions. The Patriarch asked, "Have you not fallen into annihilationism? Huike replied, "I have not fallen into annihilationism.

The Patriarch said, "This is what has been transmitted by all Buddhas; do not harbor further doubt regarding the essence of the mind. Having spoken these words, he went with his disciples to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen, where they stayed for three days.

There was a man named Yang Xuanzhi, the Prefect of Chengzhou, who had long admired the Buddha Vehicle. He asked the Patriarch, "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, those who serve as teachers are called 'Patriarchs' (Zu).
What is the nature of their Way? The Patriarch replied, "One who clarifies the mind-source of the Buddha and whose practice corresponds with understanding is called a Patriarch.
Yang Xuanzhi asked again, "What about beyond this? The Patriarch said, "One must clarify the minds of others and know both the present and the past, without ever wearying of existence."
There is nothing. Regarding all phenomena, there is no grasping; one is neither wise nor foolish, neither deluded nor awakened. If one can understand in this way, they are called a Patriarch.
He further said, "I, your disciple, have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom remains clouded and dull, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle.
Having just heard your words, Master, I do not know how to proceed. I pray that you will show me compassion and reveal the essential teaching. The Patriarch, knowing [his intent]...
He spoke earnestly, immediately uttering this verse: "One does not harbor aversion upon seeing evil, nor does one strive diligently upon observing good.
One does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, nor does one cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment. To realize the Great Way is to transcend all measure."
Penetrating the Buddha-mind, he emerged to deliver others; not sharing the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages, he transcended them all and was thus named a Patriarch.
When Xuanzhi heard this verse, his grief and joy mingled together, and he said, "I pray that you, Master, will remain long in this world to transform and guide all living beings.

The Patriarch said, "I shall depart immediately and cannot stay long. The capacities of sentient beings differ by ten thousand degrees, and many encounter the obstacles of ignorance and folly. Xuanzhi said, "I do not yet understand..."

"Is it permissible for a disciple to remove [the master's] attainment for the sake of his teacher? The Patriarch said, "I have transmitted the Buddha’s secrets to benefit those on the path of delusion.
To harm him for one's own peace is certainly contrary to reason. Xuanzhi said, "If you, Master, persistently refuse to speak, how can you manifest the power of your transformative observation?
The Patriarch, having no other choice, uttered a prophecy: "The raft on the Yangtze divides the jade waves; the bamboo torch opens..."
The Golden Locks: five mouths moving together, ninety years without "self" or "other. Hearing these words, Xuanyan could not fathom their origin;
he silently committed them to memory, paid his respects, and departed. Although the prophecies made by Sengzhu were not understood at the time, they were later all proven true.
At that time, the Wei dynasty honored Buddhism, and eminent Chan masters were as numerous as a forest. Among them were Master Guangtong and Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci.

He was truly a phoenix among the sangha. Upon witnessing the Master expound the Way—rejecting external forms and pointing directly to the mind—he would frequently debate doctrine with him, and arguments of right and wrong arose like swarms of bees.
While the Patriarch widely propagated the profound wind and universally bestowed the rain of Dharma, [the other] possessed a narrow and biased capacity that could not endure this;

he competitively gave rise to malicious intent and repeatedly administered poison. When this reached the sixth instance, [the Master realized] his transformative conditions were exhausted, and he... transmitted [the teaching].

Fada obtained [the power of] human [longevity], and consequently no longer saved others. He passed away while sitting upright on the fifth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Yong’an era of Emperor Zhuang of the Wei dynasty, which was the year Wushen (498 CE).
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that same year, he was buried at Mount Xiong’er.
A stupa was erected at Dinglin Temple. Three years later, Wei Songyun, returning from a mission to the Western Regions, encountered Huizang on the Pamir Mountains.
He saw him carrying a single shoe, walking gracefully and alone toward the west. Songyun asked, "Where are you going, Master? Huizang replied, "I am going to the West.
When Songyun returned and related these events in detail, his disciples opened the tomb; there was only an empty coffin, with a single leather shoe remaining.
The entire court was struck with wonder and admiration. By imperial decree, his cast-off sandals were retrieved from Shaolin Temple for veneration.
In the fourteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty (the Dingmao year), they were stolen by a seeker of the Way at Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai; their current whereabouts are unknown.

Initially, when Emperor Wu of Liang met the Patriarch, their karmic conditions had not yet harmonized; however, upon hearing that the Master’s transformation was spreading throughout the Wei kingdom, he [sent envoys].
I wished to compose an inscription for my master’s stele, but lacked the leisure to do so. Later, upon hearing the account of Song Yun, I finally completed it.

Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Yuanguo (Perfect Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Kongguan (Contemplation of Emptiness). (The reign titles follow the *Jinian tongpu*.)

(The General Discussion states: *The Transmission of the Lamp* records that Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty admired the Master’s extraordinary traces and thrice issued imperial edicts inviting him; yet the Master ultimately did not descend from Shaolin. When the Master passed away, Song Yun was returning from the Western Regions and encountered him on the Pamir Mountains.

Emperor Xiaozhuang issued an order to open the tomb, as recorded in the *Southern History*. The eighth year of the Putong era is the same as the first year of the Datong era. Emperor Xiaoming died on the day of Guichou in the fourth month of this year. The Master arrived in Liang in the tenth month;

thus, by the time the Master reached Wei, Emperor Xiaoming had already passed away. His son ascended the throne shortly thereafter but was assassinated by Er Zhu Rong. Consequently, Emperor Xiaozhuang was established, from which point the Wei state fell into great chaos. Three years later, Emperor Xiaozhuang died, and five years after that, the realm was divided into East and West.)

Wei: That being so, when my ancestor was at Shaolin, it was precisely during that period of chaos. By the time Song Yun returned, Emperor Xiaozhuang had already passed away for five or six years; his kingdom had long since been partitioned. How could there have been such a thing as Emperor Xiaozhuang ordering the opening of the tomb?

According to the *History of Tang*, toward the end of the Later Wei, there was a monk named Bodhidharma who came by sea. After he died, the Wei envoy Song Yun encountered him while returning from the Pamir Mountains.
His disciples opened the grave, and there was nothing there but a single shoe. This is indeed a factual record.
The Second Patriarch, Grand Master Huike, was a native of Wulao. His surname was Ji, and his father’s name was Ji.

Before he had a son, the father often thought to himself, "My family has honored the good; how could we be left without an heir? After praying for a long time, one night a miraculous light appeared, illuminating the room.
Consequently, his mother became pregnant. When the child grew up, they named him after this auspicious sign of the light illuminating the room.

Daokuang was from childhood possessed of an extraordinary spirit. He read widely in the *Shi* and *Shu* classics and was particularly proficient in the profound principles of the *Xuanxue* (Dark Learning) school;

yet he did not concern himself with family property and delighted in wandering through mountains and rivers. Later, upon reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a state of transcendent self-realization and immediately traveled to Mount Xiangshan at Longmen in Luoyang.

Relying on Master Baojing, he left the household life and received full ordination. At Yongmu Temple, he wandered among the lecture halls, studying extensively the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
At the age of thirty-three, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he sat in meditative seclusion all day long.

After another eight years had passed, while in a state of profound silence, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him: "You are about to receive the fruit of enlightenment; why do you linger here? The Great Way..."
"It is not far; you shall go south. Zu perceived that this was divine assistance and consequently changed his name to Shenguang (Divine Light).

On the following day, he felt a pain in his head as if it were being pierced with needles. His master wished to treat him, but a voice from the air said, "This is the transformation of the bones; it is no ordinary pain."
The Patriarch then reported his encounter with the deity to his master. The master examined the bone of his cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), which was as prominent as five peaks rising up.
He then said, "Your marks are auspicious; you shall surely attain realization. As for the deity who directed you to the south, this is none other than the Great Being Bodhidharma of Shaolin;
he will certainly be your teacher. Following these instructions, the Patriarch traveled to Shaoshi Mountain, where he received the Dharma and transmitted it.

Regarding the history of his vestments, it is fully detailed in the chapter on Bodhidharma. After the Patriarch entrusted his transformation at Shaolin and returned to the West, he succeeded in propagating the profound wind of the Dharma and extensively sought a dharma-heir.
In the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, there came a lay practitioner over forty years of age who did not disclose his name or lineage;

he arrived to pay his respects and asked: "My disciple’s body is afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment. I pray that you—" The Patriarch said: "Disciple, your body is entangled in the malady of wind. I pray that you..."

The Master was repenting his transgressions. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall repent them for you. After a long while, the layman said, "I have searched for my transgressions, but they cannot be found.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for your transgressions. You should now abide by the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The layman said, "Now I see the Master."

"I already know what the Sangha is, but I do not yet understand what is called the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. Dharma and Buddha are non-dual;
the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. The scholar said, "Today I have finally understood: the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma—they are non-dual. The Patriarch held him in high esteem and immediately—
He shaved [Huike’s] hair and said, "This is my treasure; you should be named Sengcan.

On the eighteenth day of the third month of that year, he received full ordination at Guangfu Temple. From then on, his illness gradually improved. After serving him for two years, the Patriarch told him:
"Bodhidharma came from afar from India, and he secretly entrusted to me the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye along with the robe of faith. I..."
I now bestow this upon you; you must guard it and ensure that it is not severed. Listen to my verse: "Originally there was ground due to conditions;
from the ground, seeds and flowers grew. Originally there were no seeds; the flowers likewise never grew. Having thus transmitted the robe and the Dharma, the Patriarch said:
He further said, "You have received my teaching; you should dwell in the deep mountains and must not yet go forth to transform others. There will surely be national calamities.
Huìcǎn said, "Since the Master already knows this in advance, I pray that you will deign to grant me instruction. The Patriarch replied, "It is not that I know it.

This is what was recorded as a prophetic prediction by Prajñātāra, whom Bodhidharma transmitted: 'Though auspicious within the mind, there is misfortune on the outside. I have calculated the years, and it is precisely..."
"It rests with you. You should reflect carefully upon my previous words so as not to encounter worldly calamities. However, I too have karmic debts from past lives that must now be repaid.

Depart well and act virtuously; wait for the time to transmit the Dharma and entrust the lineage. Having finished these instructions, he immediately departed for the capital city of Ye, where he preached the Dharma as appropriate.
With a single voice he expounded the teachings, and the fourfold assembly took refuge in him. In this manner, thirty-four years passed, at which point he finally withdrew [into seclusion].
Huineng blended his traces with the common crowd, altering his appearance and demeanor. At times he entered wine shops; at times he passed by butcher stalls;
at times he engaged in street chatter; and at times he followed along with common laborers. When people asked him, "Master, you are a man of the Way; why do you act like this?
the Patriarch replied, "I am merely disciplining my own mind; what concern is it of yours? Furthermore, beneath the triple gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County, he spoke of non-existence.
Regarding the "Higher Path": The listeners gathered like a forest. At that time, there was a Dharma Master named Bianhe who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the monastery.

When the students heard their master expounding the Dharma, they gradually drifted away. Bianhe could not overcome his indignation and instigated a slander against the district magistrate, Zhi Zhongkan.

Zhi was deluded by these heterodox arguments and subjected Huizhu (Sengzu) to unlawful treatment. Huizhu remained serene and submitted to his fate with equanimity; those who recognized him [praised him].

"True" refers to what is called "repaying one's debts. At the age of one hundred and seven, on the sixteenth day of the third month in the *guichou* year, the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, he was buried seventy li northeast of Fuyang County in Cizhou.

Emperor Dezong of the Tang posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Ancestor Chan Master. (Hao Yue, an Imperial Attendant, questioned Master Chen of Changsha: "An ancient worthy said: 'If one has realized it, karmic obstacles are originally empty; if one has not yet realized it...')"

"One must repay past debts. [The Master asked: "As for Venerable Siṃha and the Second Patriarch, the Great Master, why were they able to repay their debts? Sanda said, "Virtuous One, you do not recognize original emptiness. Yue said, "What is original emptiness? Sanda said, "Karmic obstructions are it.

[Yue] asked, "What are karmic obstructions? Sanda said, "Original emptiness is it. Yue was speechless. Sanda showed him the meaning through a verse: "Provisionally existent, yet fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, yet fundamentally not non-existent. The principle of repaying debts through nirvāṇa— In its single nature, there is no further distinction."
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, was a man of unknown origins. Initially, he approached the Second Patriarch as a layman (*avadātavasana*).
Having received ordination and the transmission of the Dharma, he lived in seclusion on Mount Wangong in Shuzhou.

During the period when Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddhist teachings, the Patriarch traveled between Taisu County and Mount Sikong, dwelling in no fixed location for more than ten years. At that time...

No one was able to understand him. In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the year of Renzi, there was a novice monk named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came to pay his respects to the Patriarch and said, "I pray that the Master will show me compassion and grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Daoxin attained realization.

He attained great enlightenment. He served [his master] with diligent labor for nine years. Later, he received the full precepts in Jizhou and attended upon him with even greater reverence. The Patriarch repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle mysteries;

knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma verse, saying: "Though the seed of the flower depends on the earth, it is from the earth that the flower grows.
If no one sows the seed, neither flower nor earth will ever come to be. The Patriarch further said: "In the past, Master Ke transmitted..."
"My Dharma was previously propagated in the capital of Ye for thirty years before I finally passed away. Now that I have found you, why do you linger here?

He then departed for Mount Luofu, where he stayed at leisure for two years. Upon returning to his former site, more than a month later, the local officials and commoners rushed there in great numbers.

A grand offering of *dāna* was prepared. Having extensively proclaimed the essentials of the mind to the fourfold assembly, he stood with palms joined beneath a great tree at the site of the Dharma assembly and passed away.
This was on the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Daye era of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, the Bingyin year.

Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jianzhi and erected a stupa named Jueji. The Master’s *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Believing in the Mind) states: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult."
Simply loathe discrimination; merely do not harbor hatred or love. Then all will be transparently clear. A difference of even a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth.

If you wish to attain realization before you, do not maintain compliance or resistance. To contend with compliance and resistance is the disease of the mind; it shows that one does not recognize the profound essence.

To strive in vain for stillness is to become like the great void—perfectly complete, lacking nothing and having no excess. This failure stems precisely from grasping and rejecting; therefore, it does not equal the Way.
Do not pursue conditioned objects, nor dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of even-mindedness, all things subside of their own accord. Cease movement and return to stillness.

The more one attempts to still it, the more it moves; one merely stagnates within the two extremes. How can one know the single principle? If this single principle is not penetrated, effort is lost at both ends.

To dispel existence while clinging to existence, or to follow emptiness while turning one's back on emptiness—through much talk and much deliberation, one becomes increasingly inconsistent. Only by cutting off words and cutting off deliberations can one attain it.

There is nowhere it does not penetrate. Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning; following after illumination, one loses the source. If you reflect back for even a moment, this surpasses the previous emptiness.
That previous emptiness underwent transformation entirely due to deluded views. Do not seek the truth; simply cease your views. When these two views do not abide, [the mind is liberated].
Be careful not to pursue them; as soon as there is right and wrong, confusion arises and the mind is lost. Two arise from the existence of one; do not even cling to that one.

When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. Without fault, there are no dharmas; when there is no arising, there is no mind. When the capacity [to perceive] ceases through the extinction of objects, [the mind is liberated].

The object follows the subject into submergence; the object exists because of the subject-object relationship, and the subject exists because of the object-subject relationship. If you wish to know these two aspects, they are fundamentally one emptiness.
This one emptiness encompasses both, equally containing the myriad phenomena. When neither the refined nor the coarse is seen, how could there be partiality? The essence of the Great Way is vast.

There is neither ease nor difficulty. A slight glimpse gives rise to doubt; the more one strives, the slower one becomes. To grasp it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path.

To let it go naturally, its essence has neither departure nor abiding. To follow one's nature is to accord with the Way; to roam at ease is to be free from affliction. To fixate the mind is to deviate from the truth.

Laxity is not good; it is not good to weary the spirit. What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

If you do not loathe the six sense-objects, you will be identical to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). The wise act without striving; the foolish bind themselves. In the Dharma, there is no separate dharma.
To falsely harbor self-attachment and to employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error? Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes.
All dualistic extremes arise from one's own deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—why labor to grasp them? As for gain and loss, right and wrong...
At once let go. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of themselves. If the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are as one.
This oneness is profound in its essence; in its stillness, it forgets conditions. Viewing all dharmas equally, one returns to spontaneity. Thus, that which is the cause of all things is extinguished.
It cannot be compared by analogy. Stillness and movement are without movement; movement and stillness are without stillness. Since both are not established, how could there be a single [reality]?
Reaching the ultimate limit, no fixed rules remain. The mind accords with equality, and all activities cease. Doubt is completely purified.

With right faith, one becomes harmonious and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. Luminous emptiness reflects itself spontaneously, requiring no exertion of mind or power, and existing in a realm beyond discursive thought.
Consciousness and emotion cannot fathom it. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. One must urgently seek resonance with this.

The word "only" (*kevala*) signifies non-duality. In this non-duality, all things are identical; there is nothing that it does not encompass. All wise ones of the ten directions enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor expansive:
in a single thought-moment there are ten thousand years. Neither existing nor non-existing, it is present before the eyes of those in the ten directions. The smallest is identical to the greatest.
Forget and sever all boundaries; the ultimate is great, yet it is identical to the small. One sees no limits or perimeters. Existence is itself non-existence; non-existence is itself existence.
If it were not thus, there would certainly be no need for guarding. The one is all, and all is the one. It is sufficient simply to be able to act in this way.
What concern could there not be brought to completion? The mind of faith is non-dual; this non-dual mind of faith cuts off the path of words and is neither past, future, nor present.

As for the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, his secular surname was Sima. His family had resided in Henei for generations before later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou. From birth he was extraordinary and transcendent;
from childhood he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the various gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) were as if already familiar through prior cultivation. Once—

Successing the tradition of his ancestors, he restrained his mind and did not sleep; for sixty years, his side never touched his mat. In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Jizhou.
There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city, which remained besieged for seventy days without resolution.

The multitude was terrified, but the Master took pity on them and instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, from among the rebel ranks, it appeared as if there were [a vision] between the battlements...
The divine soldiers then said to one another, "There must be an extraordinary person within this city; it is not possible to attack. They gradually withdrew.
In the Jia-shen year of the Wu-de era of the Tang dynasty, the Master returned to Qichun and resided at Mount Pòtóu. Disciples gathered there like clouds.

One day, he went to Huangmei County and encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and extraordinary compared to ordinary children. The Patriarch questioned him.
The Master asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I do have a surname, but it is not a permanent one.
The Master asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Master asked, "Do you have no surname? He replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none.

The Master silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately ordered his attendant to go to the boy's mother to request that she allow him to leave the household life. Because of past karmic conditions, the mother had no objection whatsoever.
Feeling abashed, he finally surrendered and became his disciple. Upon the transmission of the Dharma and the entrustment of the robe, he spoke in verse:
"The nature of the lotus seed exists; Because of the ground, the lotus grows. When the great condition unites with this nature, Birth itself becomes non-birth.
He then entrusted his students to him. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "During the Wude era, I traveled to Mount Lu and climbed to its summit. From there, I gazed toward Mount Pòtóu."
He saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors divided horizontally into six paths. "Do you understand? he asked. The assembly remained silent.
Hui-ren said, "Could this not be the Dharma-branch that the Master will produce later on? The Patriarch replied, "It is well.

Later, in the year of Kaimao during the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, having heard of the Master’s flavor of the Way and wishing to behold his dignified bearing, issued an imperial decree for him to come to the capital. The Patriarch ascended [to the palace].
He submitted his humble refusal three times in succession, ultimately declining on the grounds of illness. On the fourth occasion, the Emperor issued a command to a messenger, saying:

"If he does not rise, then take his head and bring it here. When the messenger arrived at the mountain to convey the imperial decree, the Master extended his neck toward the blade; his countenance remained solemn and composed.

He sent someone to investigate this. Wei Hui reported the circumstances to the Emperor, who became even more deeply moved by his reverence and admiration. He personally bestowed precious silks upon him so that he might fulfill his aspirations.
On the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month in the *xinhai* year of the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong, he suddenly addressed his disciples, saying:
"All dharmas are entirely liberation. You each must protect and mind yourselves, spreading this transformation to future generations. Having spoken these words, he passed away peacefully.

He passed away while seated. He was seventy-two years of age. His stupa was erected at his original mountain. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord for no apparent reason;

his physical features were as if he were alive. Thereafter, his disciples did not dare to close it again. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Physician Chan Master and named his stupa "Cloud of Compassion."
The Great Master Wuzu Hongren was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou.

Previously, while serving as the "Pine-Planting Wayfarer" at Mount Poutou, he once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "You are already old."
"If I were to hear that you have been able to widely transform the heterodox and the common folk, even if you were to return, I could still wait for you.
He then departed and went to the water's edge, where he saw a woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman said, "I have father and brothers."
"You may go and seek him. She replied, "Yes. I shall venture to do so. The girl nodded her head in agreement and, turning her horse, departed.
This girl was the youngest daughter of the Zhou family. Upon returning home, she immediately became pregnant. Her parents detested this greatly and expelled her.

Having nowhere else to turn, she spent her days spinning for hire in the village and stayed at the foot of the public hostel at night. Later, she gave birth to a son; because they considered it an ill omen, they... [text ends]

He was cast into a turbid harbor. When [the mother] saw him the next day, he had already swum upstream; his physical appearance was bright and clear. She was greatly astonished and subsequently picked him up.
As a young child, he followed his mother to beg for food, and the villagers called him "The Child Without a Surname. He encountered a man of wisdom who sighed and said:
This son lacked seven characteristics and had not yet attained the level of a Tathāgata. Later, he encountered the Great Master [Hongren] and received the Dharma;

he succeeded to the lineage and propagated the teachings on Mount Pótóu. During the Xiánhéng era, there was a layman surnamed Lú and named Huìnéng who came from Xīnzhōu to pay his respects to the Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from? Lú replied, "From south of the Ling Mountains. The Patriarch asked, "What do you seek? Lú said:
“I seek only to become a Buddha. The Patriarch said, “The people of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you hope to attain Buddhahood?

Lu replied, “People may be from the north or the south, but how could the Buddha-nature be like that? The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary man and rebuked him, saying, “Go and work in the fodder shed!
Lu prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the rice-hulling room, where he performed manual labor at the pestle and mortar without ceasing day or night. After some time had passed—
In the eighth month, the Patriarch knew that the time for the transmission had arrived. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The True Dharma is difficult to understand;

it must not be left as mere memorization of my words. You must take this as your own responsibility. Each of you, according to your own inclination, compose a verse. If the meaning of your words accords with the profound essence, [I shall transmit the Dharma to you]."
Then he entrusted both his robes and the Dharma to him. At that time, there were over seven hundred monks in the assembly.

Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both internal and external teachings, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to. They all commended him, saying, "If it were not for the Venerable Shenxiu, who else would dare to receive this?
Hearing the public acclaim, Shenxiu no longer reflected further; instead, he inscribed a verse upon a wall in the corridor, which said: "The body is the Bodhi tree."
"The mind is like a bright mirror-stand; from time to time, diligently wipe it clean. Do not allow it to gather dust.

When the Patriarch was walking about, he suddenly saw this verse and knew it had been composed by Shenxiu. He then praised it, saying, "If future generations practice according to this, they too shall attain the supreme fruit.
The wall was originally intended for the scholar Lu Zhen to paint the *Lengqie* transformation scenes; however, upon seeing the inscription...
The verse was inscribed on the wall. [Huineng] then stopped painting and had everyone recite it. Lu was at the mortar house when he suddenly heard the recitation of the verse.

He asked his fellow students, "What are these lines? His fellow students said, "You do not know. The Master sought a successor to the Dharma and ordered each of us to compose a verse expressing our realization.
This is the one composed by Upāsaka Xiu; the Master has praised it with deep admiration and will certainly transmit the Dharma to him."
[This refers to] the transmission of the robe. Hui Lu asked, "What is that verse? His fellow student recited it for him.
After a long while, Hui Lu said, "It is beautiful, yet it is not yet fully realized. The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could a commoner like you know this?

Do not utter such mad words. Hui Lu said, "Do you not believe me? I wish to compose a verse in response. The fellow student did not answer, but they looked at one another and laughed. That night, Hui Lu...
He secretly informed a young boy, who led him down to the corridor. Lu himself held a candle and requested Zhang Riyong, the Vice Governor, to write a verse beside Xiu’s poem, which read:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is likewise not a stand.
Fundamentally there is not a single thing— Where could dust and grime settle? Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he asked, "Who wrote this? It is also not yet..."

[The Master] saw into their nature. When the assembly heard the Master’s words, they paid them no heed. When night fell, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet?
Lu said, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the mortar three times with his staff. Lu immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room.
The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one great matter; therefore, according to the capacity of beings, [they teach] the Great..."

He guided them by means of simplified [teachings], and thus there arose the principles of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the sudden and gradual [approaches] as gateways for instruction.
Nevertheless, he entrusted the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmaparyāya*—the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye—to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted successively through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived in this land and attained [it].
"It is well, Great Master. This lineage has been inherited down to the present day. I now entrust to you the Dharma-treasure and the robe transmitted from me.
Protect them well yourself; do not allow them to be severed. Listen to my verse: When sentient beings come to plant seeds, The fruit arises again according to the ground.
Since insentient things have no seeds, That which lacks nature also does not arise. The Practitioner Lu knelt and received the robe and the Dharma.
Dafu said, "The Dharma has now been received; to whom shall the robe be entrusted? The Patriarch replied, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him.

Therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a cause for contention. It shall end with your person and no longer be transmitted.
Furthermore, you should remain hidden in seclusion for a time until the moment comes to travel and transform others. This is what is meant by 'the one who receives the robe receives the mandate.'"
"It is like a hanging thread. Lu asked, "Where should you hide? The Master said, "Stop when you encounter Hui; conceal yourself when you meet Hui.
After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed. That night he traveled south, and the assembly knew nothing of it.
Thereafter, the Fifth Patriarch no longer ascended the hall. When the assembly grew suspicious and questioned him, the Master said, "My Way has gone forth; why ask further?"
He asked again, "Who shall receive the robe and the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "The capable one shall receive them. Thereupon, the assembly deliberated;
since the name of Practitioner Lu was known to be capable, and as he had been sought but lost, they secretly learned that he had received them and immediately set out to pursue him.

After the Fifth Patriarch had transmitted the robe and the Dharma, another four years passed until the second year of the Shangyuan era, when he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now finished; it is time for you to depart."
He immediately entered his room, sat down peacefully, and passed away at the age of seventy-four. A stupa was erected on East Mountain in Huangmei;
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title "Great Fulfillment Chan Master Fayu" (Dharma Rain) Stupa.
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was of the secular surname Lu. His ancestors were from Fanyang.

His father, Xingtao, was transferred to an official post in Xinzhou, Nanhai, during the Wude era and subsequently registered his residence there. He lost his father at the age of three; his mother remained steadfast in her resolve to raise him.
Upon reaching adulthood, the family was particularly impoverished, and the Master provided for them by gathering firewood. One day, while carrying a load of wood, he arrived at—

While in the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he experienced a profound realization and asked the guest, "What teaching is this?
From whom did you obtain it? The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*."

Having attained [the Dharma] from Master Ren at Huangmei, the Patriarch suddenly informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the sake of the Dharma and set out directly for Shaoshan Prefecture.
There he met the man of noble conduct Liu Zhilüe, with whom he formed a friendship. A nun named Wujinzang was the aunt of Zhilüe;
she regularly recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and when the Master briefly listened to it, he immediately explained its meaning to her.

The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I would ask you about their meaning. The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters, how can you comprehend the meaning?
The Patriarch replied, "The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has no concern with written words. The nun was struck with wonder and marvel at this.

He announced to the elders of the village, "This man is one who possesses the Way; you should invite him to receive our offerings. Thereupon, the local inhabitants vied with one another to come and pay their respects.

It so happened that there was a former site for the ancient Bao Lin Temple nearby; the community deliberated and decided to restore it, thereby providing him with a place to reside as his ancestral home.

The fourfold assembly gathered like a mist, and in an instant, a precious monastery was established. One day, the Master suddenly thought to himself, "I have sought the Great Dharma; how could I stop midway?
The next day, he set out and reached a stone grotto in the western mountains of Changle County, where he met Chan Master Zhiyuan.
The Master then requested instruction from him. Zhiyuan said, "Observing your spiritual bearing, you are exceptionally refined; you are surely no ordinary man. The Master...
Hearing that Bodhidharma of the Western Regions had transmitted the Mind-Seal at Huangmei, you should go there to seek his instruction and resolve your doubts.
The Patriarch took his leave and traveled directly to Mount Dongshan in Huangmei; this was the second year of the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty.
Upon seeing him, Master Ren recognized him in silence. Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma, instructing him to remain hidden between Huaiji and Sihuai. When the Yixi...
On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Fengyuan era (the *bingzi* year), he arrived at Nanhai.

There he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong, who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Faxing Temple. The Patriarch took up residence among the corridors and eaves. One evening, as the wind blew the temple banner atop the pagoda, he heard two monks debating one another.
One said, "The banner moves," while the other said, "The wind moves. They exchanged arguments back and forth, yet neither had grasped the underlying principle. The Patriarch said:
"Is it appropriate for those of the secular world to rashly participate in such lofty discourse? [Huineng] replied simply, "The wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind alone.
Upon hearing these words, Yinzong was struck with awe and marveled at them. The following day, he invited Huineng into his chambers and inquired about the meaning of the wind and the banner.
The Patriarch explained the matter in detail according to the truth. Master Yin Zong rose unconsciously and said, "The practitioner is certainly no ordinary person. Who is your teacher?

The Patriarch, without any concealment, directly recounted the circumstances of how he had attained the Dharma. Thereupon, Yin Zong assumed the etiquette of a disciple and requested instruction in the essentials of Chan.
He then addressed the fourfold assembly, saying, "Yin Zong was formerly a complete ordinary man, but now I have encountered..."
The Bodhisattva of the Body then pointed to the layman Lu beneath his seat and said, "This is the very person.

He then requested that the robe of transmission be brought forth so that everyone might gaze upon and pay homage to it. On the fifteenth day of the first month, he gathered various eminent and virtuous monks to shave [Lu's] hair.
On the eighth day of the second month, I received the full ordination from Dharma Master Zhiguang at Faxing Temple.
This ordination platform was established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty. The Tripiṭaka Master’s record states:

"In the future, there shall be an incarnation Bodhisattva who will receive the precepts upon this platform. Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally [marked] the side of the platform with his hand...

He planted two Bodhi trees and addressed the assembly, saying: "One hundred and twenty years hence, there will be a Great Bodhisattva who, beneath these trees, shall expound the Unsurpassed Vehicle and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
After the Patriarch had received full ordination, he opened the Dongshan Dharma-gate beneath these very trees, as if fulfilling a long-standing covenant.
On the eighth day of the second month the following year, he suddenly said to the assembly: "I shall no longer..."
Wishing to return to his former hermitage, he resided there for a time. Subsequently, Master Yin Zong and over a thousand monastics and laypeople escorted the Patriarch back to Baolin Monastery.
Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou, invited him to the Dafan Temple to turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma and receive the formless Mind-Ground Precepts.
His disciples recorded these teachings, titling them the *Platform Sutra*, which became widely circulated throughout the world. Later, the Patriarch returned to Caoxi.

He rained down the great rain of the Dharma. Those who studied under him numbered no fewer than a thousand. In the first year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng, an imperial edict was issued stating:

"I have invited the two masters An and Xiù to provide offerings within the palace. In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle. Both masters declined, saying:
'In the south there is Master Nénghuì, who secretly received the robe and dharma of the Great Master (Bodhidharma). You may go to him and inquire.'"
I have now dispatched the Inner Attendant Xue Jian to ride with this imperial decree to invite you. I pray that you, Master, will look upon me with compassion and proceed swiftly to the Capital.

The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, wishing to spend his final years among the forest slopes. Xue Jian said, "The virtuous Chan masters of the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It has never been the case that liberation can be attained without relying on Chan and *samādhi*. Unfinished.
The Master asked, "How do you understand the Dharma as taught by the Teacher? The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? A sutra says:
'If one sees the Tathāgata as either sitting or lying down, this is practicing a deviant path. Why is this? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata. That all dharmas are empty and still—this is the purity of the Tathāgata."
"Seated, there is ultimately nothing to realize; how much less so 'sitting'? Jian said, "I am returning to the capital. Your Majesty will surely question me.

I pray that you, Reverend, will out of compassion point out the essential core of the mind. The Patriarch said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of alternation."
Brightness and darkness are inexhaustible, yet they are also exhaustible; these names are established in mutual dependence. Thus, a sutra says:
"Dharmas have no peer, for they do not depend on one another. Jian said: "Brightness is a metaphor for wisdom, and darkness is an illustration of affliction (*kleśa*).

If a practitioner of the Way does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means can they escape the cycle of birth and death that has no beginning? The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are precisely..."

Bodhi is neither dual nor differentiated. If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those with the faculties of sheep, deer, and so forth.
Those of great wisdom and superior roots do not act in this way. [The questioner] asked: "What is the perspective of the Mahāyāna? The Patriarch said:
"Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature. This non-dual nature is itself the true nature. True...
As for "nature" (*xing*): it does not diminish when dwelling among the ordinary and ignorant; it does not increase when among the worthy and holy. It is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions;

it is not quiescent while residing in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes. It is not in between, nor within or without. It is neither born nor extinguished; its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), eternally abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way (*mārga*). To summarize: The nature does not decrease among the foolish, Nor does it increase among the sages. It is not chaotic amidst afflictions, Nor is it silent in meditative absorption.

Neither severed nor permanent, Neither coming nor going, Not in the middle, nor within or without, Unborn and undying— Its nature and characteristics are suchness, Eternally abiding and unchanging: This is named the Way. Briefly stated:
The Master said, "To speak of 'neither arising nor ceasing'—how is this different from the non-Buddhists?

The Patriarch replied, "What the non-Buddhists call 'neither arising nor ceasing' involves using cessation to stop arising, or using arising to manifest cessation; thus, though they speak of cessation, it is not truly ceased, and though they speak of arising, it is said to be non-arising.
What I call 'neither arising nor ceasing' is that which is fundamentally unborn and, even now, unceasing. This is why it differs from the non-Buddhists. If you..."
"If you wish to know the essence of the mind, simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever.

You will naturally enter the body of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet possesses wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Having received this instruction, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.

He paid his respects and took leave to return to the capital, where he submitted a memorial reporting the Master’s words. An imperial edict was issued to thank the Master, and he was granted a *mò-nà* (sand-cleansing) *kāṣāya* robe, five hundred bolts of silk, and precious jewels.
One alms bowl. On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, by imperial decree, the ancient Baolin [Monastery] was renamed Zhongxing Temple.

On the eighteenth day of the eleventh month of the third year, there was again an imperial decree for the Prefect of Shaoyang Prefecture to further embellish and adorn it, granting it the name Faquan Temple.
The former residence of the Master in Xinzhou was designated as Guoen Temple. One day, the Master said to the assembly: "All you virtuous ones..."
"Knowledgeable ones, each of you should purify your minds and listen to my preaching of the Dharma. All of you, your own minds are the Buddha;
do not harbor further doubts. There is not a single thing outside that can be established; all are produced from the fundamental mind as the myriad kinds of phenomena."
Therefore, a sutra says: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.

If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā), one must attain the samādhi of the single characteristic and the samādhi of the single practice. This means not dwelling upon any characteristics whatsoever.
Within those signs, one does not give rise to hatred or attachment, nor is there any grasping or rejecting. One does not dwell on matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure.
Serene, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and pure—this is called the Samādhi of the Single Sign.
