If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind, remaining unmoved within the site of enlightenment, this truly constitutes the Pure Land; this is called the Samādhi of the Single Practice. If...
When a person possesses two or three samādhis, it is like the earth having seeds, which can contain and nurture them until their fruit is fully realized.
One mark and one practice are also like this. My current preaching of the Dharma is like timely rain that thoroughly moistens the great earth;
your Buddha-natures are like various seeds, and upon meeting this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain [enlightenment].
"Bodhi. Those who rely on my practice will certainly realize the wondrous fruit. In the first year of the Tianxian era, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:

"I have humbly received the robe and the Dharma from the Great Master of Endurance. Now I preach the Dharma for you, yet I do not transmit the robe. This is because your roots of faith are pure and mature;
you are resolute and free from doubt, capable of undertaking this great task. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all...'"
All seeds, when rained upon universally, will sprout. Once the essence of the flower of sudden awakening is realized, the fruit of Bodhi is naturally attained.
Having spoken these verses, he said again: "The Dharma is non-dual; the mind is likewise so. The Way is pure and devoid of all marks.
You must be careful not to contemplate purity, nor to empty the mind. This mind is fundamentally pure; there is nothing to be grasped or abandoned. Each of you must exert yourselves accordingly."
"Go on your way with good fortune. Once, a monk recited the verse of Chan Master Wo-lun, saying: "Wo-lun has skill; he can sever a hundred thoughts.
When facing objects, his mind does not arise; thus Bodhi grows day by day. Upon hearing this, the Patriarch said, "This verse does not clarify the mind-ground.
If you follow it in practice, it will only add further fetters. He then showed him a verse, saying: "Huineng has no skill..."
"Artful skills! Never ceasing the hundred thoughts; when encountering objects, mental states arise. How can Bodhi grow? (Wolun was not his name; this refers to his place of residence.
The Patriarch preached the Dharma to benefit sentient beings for forty years.

On the sixth day of the seventh month of that year, he instructed his disciples to go to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou to construct a memorial pagoda, ordering them to redouble their efforts. There was also a monk from Shu named Fangbian.
He came to pay his respects and said, "I am skilled at modeling clay. The Patriarch looked at him with a stern expression and said, "Try modeling something for me to see.

Fangbian did not grasp the meaning of this instruction, so he proceeded to model a portrait of the Patriarch himself, seven feet in height, capturing every detail with exquisite skill. When the Patriarch observed it, he said, "You are skilled in the nature of form, but not in the Buddha-nature.
He rewarded him with clothing and other goods, and Fangbian bowed in thanks and departed. On the first day of the seventh month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era, [he] said:
The disciples said, "I wish to return to Xinzhou; you must quickly prepare the boats. At that time, the great assembly was filled with grief and longing, entreating the Master to remain.
The Patriarch said, "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest nirvana. That there is a coming must entail a going; this principle is likewise constant."
"As for this physical frame of mine, upon its return, it must have a destination. The assembly asked, "When the Master departs from here, when will you return?
The Patriarch said, "Leaves fall and return to their root; when one comes, there are no words. They asked again, "To whom did your Dharma-eye transmission pass? The Patriarch said:
Those who possess the Way attain it; those without a [discursive] mind penetrate it. He asked again, "Will there not be difficulties after my passing?

The Patriarch said, "Five or six years after my extinction, there shall be a man who comes to take my head. Listen to my prediction: 'On his head he supports his parents; from his mouth he must eat his food.
He will encounter the calamity of Man; Yangliu shall become an official. Furthermore, seventy years after I depart, there shall be two..."

The Bodhisattva came from the east; one was a householder and the other had left the household life. Simultaneously they arose to transform the world, establishing our school, restoring monasteries, and causing the lineage of the Dharma to flourish.
Having finished speaking, he went to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou, bathed, sat in the lotus position, and passed away.
A rare fragrance pervaded the air, and a white rainbow stretched across the ground. This was on the third day of the eighth month of that year. At that time, Shao—
The two new prefectures each constructed a spirit-stupa for him, and neither the clergy nor the laity could decide where he should be enshrined.

The Prefectural Governors of both prefectures burned incense together and prayed, saying, "Wherever the smoke of the incense leads shall be the place where the Master wishes to return. At that moment, the incense in the burner surged upward and pierced straight through to Caoxi.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he was placed into the stupa; his age was seventy-six. At that time, Wei [was the] Prefectural Governor of Shaoyang.

According to the inscription composed [for the stele], the disciples recalled their master’s instructions regarding the preservation of his remains; they therefore first secured his neck with iron plates and lacquered cloth.
Within the stupa were the robe of faith transmitted by Dharmatrāta (a *kucīna* cloth from the Western Regions, woven with the heart of *mukūya* flowers;

later generations used green silk as its lining), the *mona* robe and precious alms bowl bestowed by Emperor Zhongzong, and the implements for fashioning the true likeness [of the Master]. The attendant in charge of the stupa was Shi... (Note: The final character appears to be incomplete in the source text.)

In the eighth month of the year Renxu, the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era (742 CE), at midnight on the third day, there was suddenly heard from within the stupa a sound like that of dragging iron chains.
The monks rose in alarm and saw a filial son emerge from the stupa. They immediately discovered that the Master’s neck had been wounded.
They reported the matter of the robbery in full to the local prefecture and county authorities. County Magistrate Yang Kan and Prefectural Governor Liu Wutian received the official notification.
All were arrested. In the fifth month, at Shijue Village, the thieves were captured and sent to Shaoyang Prefecture for interrogation.
They stated that their surname was Zhang and their name was Jingman; they were natives of Liang County in Ruzhou.

At Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou, they had received twenty thousand coins from the Silla monk Kim Daebi (Jin Dabeicheng), who ordered them to take the head of the Sixth Patriarch Master back to the Eastern Sea for veneration. Liu...

Upon hearing the circumstances, the Protector did not immediately impose the punishment. He then went in person to Caoxi and asked the Patriarch’s senior disciple, Lingtao, "How should this be adjudicated?
Lingtao replied, "If judged according to the laws of the state, the principle requires that he be executed; however, based on the compassion of the Buddha-dharma..."
"Between enemies and kin, one must be impartial; how much more so when they seek to offer worship? Their offense may be forgiven.

Liu Shou sighed in admiration, saying, "Only now do I realize the vastness of the Buddha-dharma," and he subsequently pardoned him. (Thereafter, there were many famous worthies who praised and recorded his offerings of rare treasures; these texts are too numerous to be recorded here. The first year of the Shangyuan era.
Emperor Suzong dispatched an envoy to request the Master’s robe and alms bowl to bring back for veneration within the palace.

On the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yongtai era, Emperor Daizong dreamed that the Great Master Huineng requested his robe and bowl. On the seventh day, he issued an edict to the Regional Inspector Yang Jian, stating:
"In my dream, I was moved by the Chan Master’s request to return the Dharma-robe to Caoxi. I now dispatch the State Protector General..."
The military commander Liu Chongjing received it upon his head and escorted it back. I have declared this to be a national treasure.

You may install it in your temple according to the Dharma, and you must strictly command those among the monastic community who have personally inherited the essential tenets to guard it with the utmost care so that it does not fall into ruin.
Should it later be stolen by someone, it shall be recovered before long. This has happened several times. Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Dajian (Great Mirror).

The Chan Master’s stupa was titled "Yuanhe Lingzhao. At the beginning of the Kaibao era of the Imperial Dynasty, when the Imperial Army pacified the remnants of the Liu clan in Nanhai, their rebellious forces reduced the patriarch’s stupa and temple to ashes.
Yet his physical remains were protected by a monk guarding the stupa and suffered no damage at all.
Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued for reconstruction, though the work remained unfinished when Emperor Taizong ascended the throne.
He paid close attention to the Chan school, greatly enhancing its magnificence.
*Wudeng Yantong*, Fascicle One;
*Wudeng Yantong*, Fascicle Two.
The first generation of the collateral lineages of the Fourth Patriarch, Great Physician Chan Master [Daoxin], was Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou.
He was a native of Yanling in Runzhou, surnamed Wei. At the age of nineteen, he...
His learning encompassed the Confucian classics and histories. Upon examining the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained a profound understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

One day, he sighed and said, "The secular texts of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma; the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he entered the monastic order under a master and shaved his head.
Later, he entered Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou and dwelt in a stone chamber on the northern cliff, where hundreds of birds would bring him offerings.

Regarding the marvel of this flower: during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric signs from afar and knew there was a person of extraordinary character on that mountain.

He went in person to seek him out and questioned the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way here? They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, which one is not a practitioner of the Way?
The Patriarch said, "Which one among them is the practitioner of the Way? The monks were speechless. Another monk said, "This—"
About ten *li* into the mountains, there was one named Lanrong. He would not rise when seeing people, nor would he join his palms in greeting.

"Could this be a man of the Way? the Patriarch thought, and so he entered the mountains. There he saw the Master sitting upright and composed, completely unconcerned with his surroundings. The Patriarch asked:
"What are you doing here? the Master asked. The Teacher replied, "I am contemplating the mind. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this mind? The Teacher was speechless.
He then rose and paid his respects, saying, "Where does the Great Virtuous One dwell?
The Patriarch said, "This poor monk has no fixed abode; I go either east or west. The Teacher asked, "Do you know Meditation Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him?"
The Master said, "I have long admired your virtue and have hoped to pay my respects. The Patriarch said, "I am that very Daoxin, the Chan Master.
The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. The Master then asked, "Is there perhaps another place where you might rest?"

The Master pointed behind him and said, "There is another small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the site of the hermitage; as they circled it, they saw nothing but tigers, wolves, and other such beasts.
The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this [fear] remaining. The Patriarch replied:
"What is this? The Master remained silent for a moment. Then the Patriarch took his seat upon the stone where the Master was sitting in meditation and wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛).
Upon seeing it, the Master stood in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining. The Master did not yet understand and bowed his head, requesting an explanation of the essential truth.
The Patriarch said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all converge in the single square inch of the mind; the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all..."
Within the source of the mind, all gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and spontaneously complete;
they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty and still. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions.
There are no three realms from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be sought. Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics. Great!
The Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma you have now attained; it lacks nothing.

How does it differ from that of the Buddha? There is no other separate Dharma. You need only allow the mind to be at ease and free. Do not engage in contemplative practices, nor do you need to clarify the mind.
Do not give rise to greed or anger; do not harbor sorrow or anxiety. Be expansive and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions, and do not perform any [artificial] acts.
"Excellent! To refrain from all evil and to act, walk, sit, or lie down—whatever one encounters through the senses or meets with conditions—is entirely the wondrous function of the Buddha.
To be joyful and free from sorrow is therefore called 'Buddha'. The Master asked: "Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha?

And what is the mind? The Patriarch said: "If it is not the mind, do not ask about the Buddha; if you ask about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind. The Master said: "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplation..."
When an object arises within the field of experience, how does the mind counteract it? The Patriarch said: "The conditions of objects have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind.
If the mind does not apply forced designations, from where can deluded sentiments arise? Since deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind functions as universal cognition.
You need only follow the mind with ease and freedom; there is no further need for counteraction. This is what is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya. There is nothing more to it.

[The Master] said, "I have received the Dharma-gate of Sudden Enlightenment from Master Huicán. I now entrust it to you. You must now receive my words with careful attention and remain on this very mountain.
Hereafter, there shall be five men who attain realization and will carry forward your profound transformation.

Having finished transmitting the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng and spent the remainder of his life there. From that time on, the master’s Dharma seat flourished greatly. During the Yonghui era of the Tang Dynasty, his disciples...
Lacking grain, the Master went to Danyang to seek alms. Traveling eighty *li* from the mountain, he personally carried one *shí* eight *dǒu* of rice;

going in the morning and returning by evening, he provided for three hundred monks without fail at the two meal times for three years. The local magistrate, Xiao Yuanshan, invited him to the Jianchu Monastery to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Listeners gathered like clouds. When he reached the "Chapter on Cessation and Tranquility," the earth shook because of it.

[The mountain] shook. Having finished his lecture, he returned to the mountains. Prince Boling asked the Master, "When an object-condition arises from form, you do not say that it arises from the condition of form.
How can one know the condition, such that one wishes to still its arising? The Master said, "When the objective form first arises, both the nature of form and the nature of the object are empty.
Fundamentally, there is no knower of the condition; the mental measure (citta-mātra) is identical with the knowing. When illuminating the source, there is neither arising nor non-arising."

At that time, arising occurs spontaneously from cessation. Embracing darkness gives rise to the conditions for perception; yet when the mind encounters these conditions, it does not pursue them. This is like the state prior to the arising of phenomena:

form and mind are not nurtured [by external causes]. From emptiness, there is fundamentally no thought; it is through ideation (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) that verbal thoughts arise. Since their origination has never truly originated, how could one employ the Buddha’s teachings to command them?
Question: When the eyes are closed and forms are not seen, mental objects and deliberations nevertheless abound. Since form is no longer involved, why do these thoughts persist?
"Where does the mind and its objects arise? The Master said: "When the eyes are closed, forms are not seen; yet the inner mind stirs with manifold deliberations.

These illusory consciousnesses form provisional functions; though names are given to them, they ultimately do not transcend [the source]. When one knows that forms do not concern the mind, the mind likewise does not concern the person.

As one acts, there are shifting appearances, like a bird flying away into the empty sky—this is the truth. He asked: "If objects arise from no fixed location, how does the awakened one perceive their birth?"
When the object passes away, awareness returns; awareness then transforms into an object. If one uses the mind to pull at the mind, it is again what is perceived by awareness.

Following it, following it as it goes, one does not leave the boundary of arising and ceasing. The Master said: "In the beginning, middle, and end of form and mind, there is truly no realm of dependent origination.
When a single thought spontaneously forgets its own doubt, who can calculate movement and stillness? This knowing is itself without knowing; knowing and knowing are conditions."

It will not. When you examine your own fundamental form, why must you seek it beyond this realm? The preceding object does not change or pass away; the subsequent thought does not come from the present.
To seek the moon by grasping its dark reflection, or to trace a path by pursuing a flying bird—to wish to know the nature of the mind is like looking at a dream.
It is likened to ice in the sixth month: everywhere it is the same. One cannot escape emptiness by avoiding it; yet to seek emptiness is likewise [futile].

This is not established. Let us inquire about the reflection in a mirror: from where does the mind arise? Question: When one applies the mind with exactness (*zhèzhè*), how can it be peaceful and secure?
Master: When one applies the mind with exactness, it is precisely the non-application of mind. To discuss names and characteristics in a circuitous way is wearisome;
to speak directly is free of redundancy. Non-mind is applied with exactness; constant application is precisely non-existence. Now I speak of non-mind.
[The Master said: "In their locus, they do not differ from the mind. Question: "The wise cite sublime words; when these accord with the mind, they are appropriate.

But if the words and the path of the mind diverge, then even if they coincide, they will be a hundred thousand times more discordant. Master: "Sublime words are spoken as skillful means to shatter the illnesses [of the mind]; this is the Mahāyāna path."

This does not concern the discussion of original nature; it is rather produced through transformation from emptiness. Taking non-thought as the true constant, one shall ultimately sever the path of the mind.
When detached from thought, the nature is immovable; arising and ceasing are free from contradiction or error. Just as the echo in a valley possesses sound, the reflection in a mirror can look back.

Question: When the practitioner’s essence perceives the object, the object perishes due to that awareness. There are three mental states: the preceding awareness, the subsequent awareness, and the object itself.

The Master said: The function of the object is not its essence; once awareness has ceased, one should not dwell on it. Because the object perishes due to the awareness of it, the object does not arise at the time of awareness.
There are three delays: the preceding awareness, the subsequent awareness, and the object itself. Question: In abiding in meditative concentration, both [object and subject] are absent.
It turns; it shall become the true samādhi, which no karmas can drag away. Not knowing subtle ignorance, one slowly follows after its traces. The Master said:
"Furthermore, I have heard of others who falsely grasp at the arising of mental constructs (*cittamātra*). In these three matters, they do not achieve success;

they do not turn back from their delusions, and their minds are bound by what they take to be right reception. They thereby create obstacles to pure karma. Even a ten-thousandth part of the dust of the mind is not understood."
I speak of ignorance: it arises from subtle and subtle habitual causes; names and forms gradually emerge. When the wind comes, the waves turn;

when one desires stillness, the water returns to its natural level. I wish to speak further of the path ahead, yet I fear that later minds may be startled. The great beast of non-thought roars; the emptiness of nature lets fall frost and hail.
Stars scatter, foul weeds are crushed; birds fall, flying hither and thither. The five paths are surely in turmoil; the four Māras...

It neither advances nor retreats; it is like a fierce fire blazing, and yet it is like a sharp sword cutting. Question: "I rely on awakening to know the myriad dharmas, for the myriad dharmas are thus from the beginning.
If one relies on illumination to employ the mind, one can only obtain the employment of the mind through illumination; this should not be a matter within the mind."
The Master said: "One relies on the awakening awareness of the myriad dharmas, yet the myriad dharmas ultimately have nothing to rely upon.

If you employ the mind through provisional illumination, it should not exist outside the mind. A questioner asked: "If one follows along with everything without making any discernment, the luminous mind will not manifest before one. Furthermore, fearing that the mind may become dark and dull, one applies effort while remaining within the mind;
yet even so, the obstacles of wisdom remain difficult to eliminate. The Master said: "There is this which must not be, and there is that which must not be sought."

Investigation: Non-discrimination is itself true discernment; it is the mind that emerges from darkness into light. Those who harbor anxieties have minds that are obscure and dull; they rely on mental cultivation and entrust themselves to meritorious practices.

How could they discuss the difficulty of the obstacle of wisdom? It is only upon reaching Buddhahood that this becomes a sickness. Question: In the midst of adjusting and pacifying [the mind], it is truly difficult to find stability.

Unless one is a practitioner who applies this in action, this difficulty will ultimately remain unseen. The Master said: "In desiring to adjust and pacify through 'breaking the middle,' [one must realize]..."
The transmission of the message is neither difficult nor easy. First, observe the mind within the locus of the mind; next, infer wisdom within wisdom. Third, illuminate that which infers;
fourth, penetrate the indeterminate. Fifth, it is called liberation; sixth, it equalizes the true and the false; seventh, one knows the fundamental nature of all phenomena.

The eighth is the unconditioned of loving-kindness; the ninth is the pervasive emptiness of the aggregates. The tenth is that which is covered by clouds and rain; it is the ultimate exhaustion of that which is without perception.
Fundamental wisdom arises from ignorance; the mirror-image manifests the three karmas. Like an illusory person appearing at the crossroads, one does not abide in the limit of emptiness.

When one illuminates that which exists within existence, it does not emerge from within emptiness or existence; yet, since emptiness and existence have not been joined together, this is termed "the Middle Way.
This Middle Way is not a verbal expression; how can it be established where there is no place for establishment? How then can its application be determined? Question:

There is another kind of person who well understands emptiness and signlessness. They claim in speech that stillness and distraction are one, and further say that non-existence within existence is the same realization as functional application.

Eternally quiescent, knowing and perceiving through the function of quiescence, one employs the mind to realize the True Principle. Furthermore, it is said that function is non-function; wisdom and skillful means are manifold.
Though words may seem chaotic, they accord with the Principle. Suchness is the Principle itself, abiding as it is; it is not realized through the conscious mind.

Since one knows that realization by the mind is erroneous, mind after mind dissolves into one another. Such a dharma difficult to know cannot be known even throughout eternal kalpas; it functions in this very way.
"A person of the mind cannot be transformed by dharmas. The Master said: "There is another who realizes emptiness, yet it is still as discussed in the previous verse:

'Practicing emptiness and guarding quiescence, the perception of consciousness is momentarily overturned; though one meets with true reality as the measure of the mind, in the end one knows that the source has not been fully understood.

Furthermore, regarding the function of ceasing the mind: 'Though possessing much wisdom, one suspects what is similar; this is truly because the nature is not clear, and seeking emptiness merely fatigues oneself forever.'"
Consciousness remains hidden for eons; though it embraces all forms, it knows nothing of them. When light is emitted, the earth trembles—what could one possibly do about that? Question:

Regarding the aforementioned practice of "observing the mind," there is further the difficulty of the "floating net" (luohun). The Master said: "If observing the mind involves a floating net, why wait to observe a delusory mind?
Furthermore, for one who has no delusory mind, it is difficult to speak with ease. Question: "For a long time there has been a great foundation."
In the midst of the shifting and conflicting paths of the mind, one may perceive subtle obstacles; thus one reaches the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Were it not for a skillful teacher, none could resolve this principle. I look up to our Great Master, who shall surely open the essential gate for those who apply their minds, guiding them along the way.
"Do not allow them to lose the true path. The Master said: "The Dharma-nature is the fundamental basis; within the dream-like realm, discrepancies arise.
The subtle body of true reality—form and mind—are constantly unrecognized. Suddenly encountering a man of primordial chaos, he takes pity on sentient beings in their suffering and lamentation.

Entrusting his doubts, he poses extensive questions; though harboring the Principle within, he is ever-luminous. Having penetrated the dark paths of birth and death, he is unperturbed by praise or blame. Thus the Wild Elder reveals himself."
He replied in installments: "I am humbled by your visit. Having received the medicine for all sentient beings, I shall act as if it were my own nature.
In the first year of the Xianqing era, the district magistrate Xiao Yuanshan requested that he establish a monastery at Jianchu. The Master declined, but could not avoid the request;

he consequently entered the room and entrusted the Dharma seal to his chief disciple, Zhiran, ordering him to transmit it in succession. As he was about to descend the mountain, he said to the assembly: "I..."
He once again visited this mountain. At that time, the birds and beasts wailed in lamentation for over a month without ceasing. Before his hermitage stood four large paulownia trees;
in the middle month of summer, they suddenly withered and fell. On the twenty-third day of the first month of the following year, he passed away without illness.
He was interred at Mount Jilong.
The Second Generation under the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral line):
Chan Master Niu-t’ou Shan-chung-yung, Dharma heir of Chan Master Niu-t’ou Shan-chung-yung of Chin-ling, was a native of Ch’ü-ā.
His surname was Hua. At the age of twenty, his wisdom and courage surpassed [those of others].
This man was seven chi and six cun tall. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as a *langjiang* (colonel).

He habitually carried a water-strainer suspended from his bow wherever he went, drawing water for use at every stop. He repeatedly followed great generals on military expeditions and frequently achieved martial success.
In the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of forty, he requested ordination and entered Mount Wangong in Shu Prefecture to study under Chan Master Baoyue.
After becoming a disciple, one day while sitting in meditation, he beheld a strange monk over ten feet tall, with a spirit that was refined and noble, and a voice that was clear and resonant.
The monk said to the Master, "You have left the household life after eighty births; you ought to apply yourself with even greater diligence. Having spoken, he vanished.
Once, while he was in meditative absorption within a valley, the mountain waters suddenly surged. The Master remained serene and unmoved, and the water receded of its own accord.

A hunter encountered him there and subsequently reformed his ways to cultivate virtue. Later, two men who had formerly served with him in the military heard that the Master had retired to live in seclusion;
they entered the mountains together to seek him out. Upon finding him, they said to the Master, "Was the General mad? Why did you do this?"

He stayed there. The Master said, "My madness is about to subside, while yours is now fully manifest. As for those who indulge in lustful sights and lewd sounds, or who covet glory and seek favor, they wander through birth and death;
by what means can they emerge from this on their own? The two men were moved to realization and departed with a sigh. Later, the Master went to visit Chan Master Rong to clarify the Great Matter.
Rong said to him, "I have received the true instructions of the Great Master Xinxing. What he had attained was as follows:
"All have perished. Even if there were a single dharma superior to Nirvana, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.

A single speck of dust flying can obscure the sky; a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth. You have now transcended such views—what more need I say? The guidance of this mountain gate shall be entrusted to you.
The Master received this command and became the second patriarch. Subsequently, he transmitted the True Dharma [to his successor].
Master Fang resided at both Bai Ma and Xi Xuan monasteries, and later moved to Shi Tou City.

On the tenth day of the first month in the second year of the Yifeng era, he manifested his passing; his countenance remained unchanged, and his body could be bent and extended as if alive. A wondrous fragrance filled his chamber, which did not cease for ten days.
His final instruction was that he be buried in water.
The Chan Master Tancui of Mount Zhong in Jinling was a native of Wu Commandery. His surname was Yan.
He first went to visit Chan Master Rong, who looked at him and marveled at his extraordinary character. The Master then told him: "Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising;
sensation and perception are the pitfall of the supreme person. Do you understand this? The Master pondered these words in silence and attained a great awakening to the profound principle. Thereupon—
He concealed his traces on Mount Zhong for many years, spending his final days in a thatched hut with earthenware vessels.
On the sixth day of the second month in the third year of the Tiānshòu era of the Tang dynasty, he entered meditative absorption with serene composure; seven days later, he passed away.
The Fourth Patriarch’s third and fourth generations (those who branched out are not listed in the formal sequence).
The Fourth Patriarch’s fifth generation (branched out):
Dharma heirs of Chan Master Chi of Niu-tou Mountain in Jinling.
Chan Master Zhìwéi of Niutou Mountain was a native of Jāngníng. His secular surname was Chén.

He left the household life under Dharma Master Tǒng of Tiānbǎo Monastery and visited Chan Master Fǎchí, from whom he received the transmission of the True Dharma. Thereafter, disciples from the region east of the Yangtze River all flocked to his gate.
One named Huìzhōng was regarded by him as a vessel for the Dharma. The Master once showed him a verse, saying: "Do not bind..."
[The Master said: "Thought. Thought forms the river of birth and death; one wanders through the ocean of the six realms, seeing no way out from its long waves.
Zhong replied: "Thought and perception have always been illusions; their nature is inherently without beginning or end. If one grasps this meaning, the long waves shall naturally cease.

The Master further showed him a verse: "My original nature is empty and void; Due to delusion, the notions of self and other arise. How can these deluded feelings be stilled? Return [to the source]..."
He returned to sit in a secluded place. Zhong replied: "Emptiness is the true substance; where do 'self' and 'others' exist?
There is no need to extinguish deluded sentiments; simply board the boat of Prajñā. The Master, knowing that he had attained realization, entrusted him with the affairs of the monastery.
He traveled about to transform and guide others according to conditions, passing away at Yanzuo Temple.
The Sixth Generation after the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral line):
Zen Master Wei of Mount Niutou in Jinling, successor to the Dharma of Zen Master Huizhong of Mount Niutou.
He was a native of Runzhou and surnamed Wang. At the age of twenty-three, he received [the precepts].

While at Zhuangyan Monastery, Yuanjue heard that Chan Master Wei had appeared in the world, so he went to visit him. As soon as Wei saw him, he said, "The master of the mountain has arrived. Yuanjue was thus enlightened to its subtle meaning and subsequently attended upon him.

Later, taking his leave, he traveled to various regions to pay his respects to teachers; while on pilgrimage, he visited Chan Master Wei at Jujie Monastery and saw that the *lingxiao* vine had withered during the summer.

When people wished to cut it down, Wei spoke to them, saying: [...]* *Note: The source text provides the context for the encounter but does not contain the full dialogue attributed to Wei. The translation reflects the narrative structure provided.*
He said, "Do not cut it down. When Huizhong returned, the vine had grown back. When the Master came back, it was indeed as he had said.

He then entrusted the mountain gate to him and departed to reside at Yanzuo Temple. Throughout his life, the Master wore only a single robe and never changed his utensils; he possessed only a single cauldron.
Once, there were two storehouses of grain provided for the monks, which thieves sought to plunder, but a tiger guarded them. The County Magistrate Zhang...
Xun went to the summit of the mountain to pay his respects. He asked the Master, "How many disciples do you have? The Master replied, "There are three or five. Xun asked, "How may I see them?
The Master struck the meditation seat, whereupon three tigers roared and emerged. Startled and terrified, Xun withdrew.

Later, the assembly requested that he enter the city, where he resided at the Old Temple of Adornment (*Zhuāngyán Jìusì*). The Master intended to construct a separate Dharma Hall to the east of the main hall.
There was an ancient tree there upon which a colony of magpies had built their nest. When the craftsmen were about to cut it down, the Master said to the magpies, "A hall is to be built on this site;
why do you not depart quickly? As soon as he finished speaking, the magpies moved their nest to another tree. When the foundation was first being laid, there was...
Two divine beings determined the four corners [of the site] and secretly assisted with labor at night; thus, it was completed in no time.
Consequently, disciples from the four quarters gathered like clouds, and thirty-four people attained the Dharma. Each settled in a different region and converted many followers.
The Master had a verse on settling the mind which says: "When person and dharmas are both purified, good and evil are forgotten. With a direct mind of true reality, bodhi..."
At the Daochang Monastery, in the third year of the Dali era, the bell-hanging tree and the robe-hanging vine in front of the stone chamber suddenly withered and died during the height of summer.
On the fifteenth day of the sixth month of the fourth year, after the assembly of monks had completed the *poṣadha* ceremony, he commanded his attendant to shave his hair and bathe his body.
At night, auspicious clouds appeared, covering his vihāra, and the sound of celestial music was heard from the sky. At dawn, he sat peacefully and passed away.
At that time, wind and rain broke out violently, shaking and breaking the trees and forests; furthermore, a white rainbow pierced through the cliffs and valleys.
In the spring of the fifth year, his body was cremated, and śarīras were obtained in incalculable numbers.
When Chan Master Xuántíng of Ān-guó Temple in Xuānzhōu first visited Master Wéi, he stood in attendance.

At that time, a monk who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asked, "What is the meaning of 'true nature arising through conditions'? After Master Wéi had remained silent for a long while, Master Xuántíng suddenly called out, "Virtuous One! (Dàdé).
At the very moment he raised this single thought as a question, it was an arising-by-conditioning within true nature. The monk attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words.
Someone asked, "From where did the Southern School establish itself? He replied, "The Dharma of the Mind has no north or south."
Chan Master Chonghui of Mount Tianzhu in Shu Prefecture was a native of Pengzhou. His surname was Chen.
At the beginning of the Qianyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he went to Mount Tianzhu in Shu Prefecture and founded a monastery. In the first year of the Yongtai era, it was granted an official plaque.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Tianzhu? The Master said, "At Mount Zhubushan, the sun is difficult to see; before Mount Yujing Peak, people are easily enlightened. The monk asked again.
"When Bodhidharma had not yet come to this land, was there still the Buddha-dharma or not? The Master said, "Let us set aside for a moment what will be in the future;
as for the matter at hand right now, how is it? [The monk] said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "Ten thousand ages, the eternal void."

"In a single morning breeze and moonlight. The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again, "Ācārya, do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "How is it from your own side?
What does it have to do with whether Bodhidharma came or did not come? His coming here was much like a fortune-teller;
seeing that you did not understand, he broke open the lines of the divination for you. As soon as good or bad fortune arises, it is all contained therein."
[The Master said: "It is up to you; look for it all within yourself. A monk asked, "What is one who understands divination?
The Master said, "The moment you step out the door, you have already missed it. He asked, "What is the family style of Tianzhu? The Master said, "At times white clouds come to close the door;
there is no more wind or moon flowing through the four mountains. He asked, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?"
[The monk] departs. The Master says: "The peaks of Mount Shui are high, ever accumulating emerald green; the bright moonlight of the Shu River shines with radiant splendor.
[The monk] asks: "What is the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū? The Master says: "Since vast kalpas past, it has never been obstructed.
If it were not the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, what would it be? [The monk] asks: "Why do the Buddha-dharma and dharmas not manifest before me? The Master says: "Precisely because..."
"You do not understand. That is why it remains unmanifest before you. If you were to understand, there would likewise be no Buddha to be realized.
Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "White clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies dote on the courtyard flowers. Question: "What have the sages of the past ever said?
The Master said: "Look at me now; what have I said? Question: "I ask about the matters of the School Gate (Zongmen). The Master said: [Silence] (or, as the text implies, he did not speak).
The Master raised his voice and sang: "The stone ox bellows beyond the void; when the wooden horse neighs, the moon hides behind the mountain.
A monk asked, "What is the Master’s way of benefiting others? The Master said, "A single rain nourishes all; the thousand peaks display their exquisite beauty.
A monk asked, "Who is the person within the Tianzhu Mountains? The Master said, "Walking alone atop a thousand peaks, strolling leisurely by the nine-bend spring. [Question: ...asked.
"What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master replied, "A white monkey carries its young to the green cliffs; bees and butterflies carry blossoms among the green stamens.
In the fourteenth year of the Dali era, he passed away into stillness. His stupa was erected to the north of the mountain.
Chan Master Xuansu of Helin in Runzhou was a native of Yanling. His surname was Ma. Later, he studied under Chan Master Wei and attained enlightenment into the essence of the nature.
He subsequently resided at Helin Temple. One day, a butcher came to pay his respects and requested that the Master come to his residence to partake in a meal offering.
The Master went with joyful composure. The assembly all looked on in astonishment, but the Master said, "The Buddha-nature is equal; it is the same for the worthy and the foolish."
They are identical. However, as for those who can be saved, I save them immediately. What difference, then, could there be? A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Master said, "If you understand, it is not understanding; if you doubt, it is not doubting. He further said, "That which does not understand yet does not doubt;
that which does not doubt yet does not understand. A monk knocked on the door. The Master asked, "Who is there? The monk replied, "I am a monk. The Master said—

[The Master] said, "It is not only the Sangha; even if the Buddha were to come, he would not find a place to stay. [The other] asked, "Why would he not find a place to stay? The Master said, "Because there is no place for you to lodge.
(A collateral branch under the seventh generation of the Fourth Patriarch.)
Chan Master Weize of Fuku Yan on Mount Tiantai was a successor of Chan Master Zhong of Niuhead Mountain in Jinling. He was a native of Jingzhao and bore the surname Changsun.

Having first visited Chan Master Zhong, he attained a great awakening to the profound principle, whereupon he declared: "Heaven and earth are devoid of things; things and the self are devoid of things."
"Though there is no thing, it has never been that there was no thing. Thus, the sage is like a shadow and the common people are like a dream;
who then can speak of life and death? The Perfect Man, by means of this, is able to shine alone and is able to be the lord of the myriad things—I have understood this.
Thereupon, he traveled south to Mount Tiantai and lived in seclusion on the western cliff of the waterfall. During the Yuanhe era, those who admired the Way...
When the Master arrived, he had a disciple named Kesu. He subsequently built a hermitage, and gradually it became a center for the Dharma.
The designation "Buddha Cave" originated with this Master. A monk asked, "What is the Nārāyaṇa arrow? The Master replied, "It hits the mark.
One day, he suddenly told his disciples, "You must all exert yourselves. Two days later, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. Three years later, his stupa was completed.
Regarding his remains at Mount Ben (the stele was composed by Han Yu of the Tang dynasty and currently exists at Guoqing Temple):
Chan Master Daoqin of Jingshan in Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Sushan Su of Helin, was a native of Kunshan in Suzhou. His surname was Zhu. Initially, he donned...
Having been a follower of Confucianism, at the age of twenty-eight he met Master Su. The master said to him, "Observing your spirit and temperament, you are truly a vessel for the Dharma-treasure.
He was moved to realization and requested to become his disciple. Master Su personally shaved his head and instructed him, saying, "Follow the current as you travel;
stop whenever you encounter a path. Thereupon, the master journeyed south and arrived at Lin’an, where he saw [a mountain] to the northeast.
At Mount Yi, he questioned a woodcutter, who replied, "This is Mount Jing. Thereupon, he halted his journey and took up residence there.

A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "There are carp on the mountain; there is dust and weeds at the bottom of the sea. Mazu sent someone to deliver a letter to him; inside the letter was a circle.
Upon opening the seal, the Master placed a single dot within the circle and then sealed it back and returned it.
When National Teacher Zhong heard of this, he remarked, "Master Qin was still being deluded by Master Ma. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Your question is improper. The monk asked, "How can one ask properly? The Master said, "Wait until after I have passed away, and I shall tell you.
Later, Mazu sent Zhizang to ask him, "In the twelve hours of the day, what do you take as the objective realm? The Master said, "I will tell you when you return."
Xin Zang said, "I shall return right now. The Master said, "When you deliver my message, you must ask about Caoxi.
When Duke Cui Zhao asked, "Disciple, may I now leave the household life? the Master replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man;

it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. At this, the Duke attained realization. In the third year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree summoning him.
At the foot of the palace steps, he personally paid his respects. One day, while sitting in the inner court together with National Teacher Zhong, they saw the Emperor’s carriage approaching.
The Master rose to his feet. The Emperor asked, "Why have you risen? The Master replied, "How can you, O Donor, perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment?
The Emperor was pleased and said to the National Teacher, "I wish to bestow a name upon this master. The National Teacher joyfully agreed.

Having received the imperial decree, he was granted the title Guoyi (National One). Later, he took leave to return to his native mountain. In the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era, he manifested illness;
after preaching the Dharma, he passed away. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Da jue (Great Enlightenment).
The Eighth Generation (a collateral branch) under the Fourth Patriarch:
Chan Master Yunku Zhe, a successor of Chan Master Fokuze of Mount Tiantai.
Once, a monk named Jizong from Huayan Monastery asked: "Regarding the realization of nature..."
"What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? The Master replied, "The nature of purity is fundamentally serene and without fluctuation;

it does not belong to existence or non-existence, purity or defilement, long or short, nor to grasping or rejecting. Its essence is naturally free and easy. To perceive this clearly is called 'seeing one's nature.

Nature is the Buddha, and the Buddha is nature; therefore, it is said that 'seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. [The questioner] asked: 'If nature is already pure and does not belong to [any category]...'"
[The student asked: "Regarding existence and non-existence, by what cause does seeing arise? The Master said: "Seeing is the absence of anything seen. [The student] said:
"If there is nothing seen, how can there still be seeing? The Master said: "Even the locus of seeing is non-existent. [The student] said: "When seeing occurs in this way, who is it that sees?

The Master said: "There is no one who is able to see. [The student] said: "Ultimately, what is the nature of this principle? The Master said: "Do you know? To falsely conceptualize [it] as existing is precisely..."
When there is subject and object, one is said to be deluded. Following what is seen to produce interpretations, one falls into birth and death.

For one who sees with clarity, it is not so: though seeing all day long, one has never truly seen. Even when seeking the name, location, essence, or characteristics, they cannot be found; both subject and object are utterly transcended.
[The student] said, "This is called 'seeing one's nature. Does this nature pervade all places? The Master said, "There is nowhere it does not pervade.
[The student] asked, "Do ordinary beings possess it? The Master said, "I have just stated that there is nowhere it does not pervade; how could ordinary beings not possess it?
[The student] asked, "For what reason are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by birth and death, while ordinary beings alone are entangled in this suffering? When has it ever been..."
[The student] said, "I have attained universal penetration. The Master said, "Ordinary people, within the nature of purity, conceptualize subject and object; they thus fall into birth and death.
The Buddhas and Great Beings well know that within the nature of purity there belongs neither existence nor non-existence, so that subject and object do not arise.

[The student] said, "If it is as you say, then there must be persons who can realize this and those who cannot. The Master said, "Since even 'realization' itself cannot be found, how could there be one who realizes?"
[The student] asked, "What about one who realizes [the truth]? He said, "As for the ultimate principle, how is it? The Master said, "I shall tell you the essential point:

you should immediately reflect that within the pure nature, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor is there anyone who realizes or fails to realize. Both 'ordinary' and 'sage' are merely names.
If you give rise to understanding based on these names, you will fall into birth and death; if you know that these are provisional names lacking reality, then there is nothing to attain."
Regarding "names," it is further said: This is the ultimate point of consummation. To say, "I can comprehend this, but that one cannot," is a great illness.

To perceive distinctions between the pure and the defiled, or the ordinary and the sage, is also a great illness. To form the understanding that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages belongs to the negation of cause and effect.
To perceive a pure nature as a place where one may dwell is also a great illness; to form the understanding that there is no such place to dwell [is the correct view].
This too is a great illness. Yet, although there is no movement within the nature of purity, one does not destroy the application of skillful means nor the arousal of compassion and pity.
Where such arousal occurs, it is precisely the entirety of the pure nature; this may be called "seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha.
Jizong leaped for joy, bowed in gratitude, and withdrew.
Chan Master Daolin of Niaoke, in Hangzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Guoyi Qin of Jingshan.
He was a native of Fuyang in his home prefecture. His secular surname was Pan, and his mother’s surname was Zhu.
She dreamed that the light of the sun entered her mouth, and consequently she became pregnant. Upon her birth, an extraordinary fragrance filled the room;
she was thus named Xiangguang (Fragrant Light). At the age of nine, she left home to become a nun. At twenty-one, she received full ordination at Guoyuan Temple in Jingzhou.

Later, she went to Ximing Temple in Chang’an to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith* under Master Fuli. Fuli showed her the "Verses on Reality and Delusion" (*Zhenwang song*) and instructed her to practice them.

Regarding Chan meditation, the Master asked, "How do you first contemplate? How do you apply the mind? Zhi Li prostrated for a long time without speaking; the Master performed three prostrations and withdrew.
Later, when Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree summoning National Teacher Guoyi to the capital, the Master went to pay his respects to him and thereby attained the True Dharma.
Upon returning south to Yongfu Temple on Mount Gushan, there was a stupa of a Pratyekabuddha; at that time, both monastics and laypeople together established a dharma [commemoration] for it.
The assembly gathered. The Master entered, shaking his monk’s staff. Dharma Master Taoguang of Lingyin Temple asked, "Why is there a sound at this dharma assembly?
The Master replied, "If there were no sound, who would know it is an assembly?
Later, seeing a tall pine tree on Mount Qinwang with lush foliage and branches curling like a canopy, he took up residence upon it; thus, people of the time called him "The Bird Nest" (Niaoke).
Zen Master. Furthermore, there was a magpie’s nest beside him that naturally became tame and familiar with people; thus he was also called "The Magpie Nest Zen Master.
He had an attendant named Huìtōng who, one day, suddenly wished to take his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going now? He replied, "Huìtōng has left home for the sake of the Dharma.
Since the Master does not deign to grant me compassionate instruction, I shall now go to various quarters to study the Buddha-Dharma."
"Go," the Master said. "If it concerns the Buddha-dharma, I too have a little here. Baotong asked, "What is the Master’s Buddha-dharma?
The Master plucked a tuft of cloth from his robe and blew upon it. Baotong thereupon attained realization of the profound principle.

During the Yuanhe era, Bai Juyi, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was appointed to govern this prefecture. He entered the mountain to visit the Master and asked, "Master, you reside..."

"Your position is extremely perilous," the Master said. Baizhang replied, "The Governor’s position is even more perilous. Baizhang asked, "My rank stabilizes the mountains and rivers; what peril could there be?
The Master said, "When fuel and fire intersect, the nature of consciousness does not remain still—is this not perilous? Baizhang asked again.
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good.
Bai said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say this. The Master said, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it.
Bai paid his respects and withdrew. On the tenth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Changqing era, the Master announced [his passing].
The attendant said, "I have now reached the end of my karmic retribution. Having spoken these words, he sat and passed away (some say his name was Yuánxiū; this is likely a posthumous title).
As for the first-generation Dharma heir of Wǔzǔ Dàmǎn Chánshī, Chánmaster Běiān Shénxiù (Yèshē Sānzàng’s inscription states:

"The profound principle arises from the earth of Qian; both the honored and the lovely are likewise honored. He stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the three and nine clans; a single hair on his foot divides them").

He was a native of Kaifeng and surnamed Li. In his youth, he devoted himself to Confucian studies and became widely learned in many fields. Soon thereafter, he renounced worldly attachments to enter the monastic life, seeking out teachers and inquiring after the Way.
He arrived at Dongshan Temple on Shuangfeng Mountain in Qizhou, where he met the Fifth Patriarch; there, he made the practice of seated meditation his primary endeavor.
He then sighed in admiration and said, "This is truly my teacher. He vowed to practice with austere discipline, employing himself to gathering firewood and drawing water while seeking the Way.
Huizang perceived this silently and held him in profound esteem. After Huizang passed away, Xiu went to reside at Mount Dangyang in Jiangling.
When Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty heard of him, she summoned him to the capital to receive offerings at the Inner Palace Chapel, treating him with exceptional honor.

The Emperor issued a decree at Mount Jiùshān to establish Duōmén Monastery in order to commemorate his virtue. At that time, the princes, dukes, officials, and commoners all prostrated themselves upon seeing even the dust raised by him.
When Zhōngzōng ascended the throne, he honored him with even greater reverence. The high minister Zhāng Shuō once heard the essentials of the Dharma from him.

He observed the rites of a disciple. His teacher had a verse for the assembly that said: "All Buddha-dharma is inherently present within one's own mind; to seek it elsewhere with the mind is to abandon one's father and flee.
In the second year of the Shenlong era, he entered nirvana at Tiangong Temple in the Eastern Capital. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Datong.
With ceremonial insignia and ritual objects, his funeral procession was sent to Longmen. The Emperor escorted him as far as the bridge, as did the princes, dukes, officials, and commoners.
All arrived at the burial site. Zhang Yue and the retired scholar Lu Hongyi each composed a stele inscription and a eulogy.
His disciples, including Pujì and Yifú, were both highly esteemed by those in court and the commonalty.

National Teacher Huian of Mount Song (recorded by Tripiṭaka Master Yashas: "Nine daughters left the human realm; eight daughters severed marriage ties. An old bed with added legs; the Heart-ancestors, most honored among the multitude") was a native of Zhiyang in Jingzhou. His surname was Wei.
In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, when a census was conducted across the empire to register privately ordained monks and nuns, the Master was investigated.
He replied, "I originally have no name," and subsequently fled into the mountain valleys. During the Daye era, a large number of conscripts were mobilized.
When the Tongji Canal was opened, the people were so famished that they lay upon one another like pillows. The Master begged for food to rescue them, and many were saved.

Emperor Yang summoned the Master, but he did not go; instead, he secretly entered Mount Dahuo. Later, when the Emperor traveled to Jiangdu and the realm was in turmoil, the Master took up his staff and ascended Mount Heng, where he practiced the dhūta austerities.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he went to Huangmei to visit the Patriarch Huineng, and subsequently attained [enlightenment].
The Essentials of the Mind. In the first year of the Linde era, he traveled to the stone cliffs of Mount Zhongnan and settled there.

Emperor Gaozong once summoned the Master, but he did not comply with the imperial decree. Thereupon, he traveled extensively through famous sites until he reached Mount Songxiao, saying, "This is the place where I shall spend my final days."
From that time on, practitioners flocked there. Two monks, Tanran and Huairang, came to seek instruction and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Why do you not ask about the meaning of your own self? They asked, "What is the meaning of my own self?"
The Master said, "You should contemplate my secret function. He asked, "What is the secret function? The Master indicated it by opening and closing his eyes.
Thus, under these words, Rāhula knew where to return. He then went to pay his respects at Caoxi. Emperor Wu summoned him to the capital and treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He was held in equal high esteem as Zen Master Xiu. The Empress once asked the Master, "How old are you? The Master—
He replied, "I do not record it. The Master asked, "Why do you not record it? The teacher said, "The body of birth and death is like a revolving cycle.

Since the cycle has neither beginning nor end, what use is there for recording? Furthermore, within the continuous flow of this mind, there is no interval. To perceive the arising and ceasing of bubbles is merely deluded thought.
From the first consciousness until the moment the signs of movement cease, it is exactly like this. What need is there for years, months, [days, or hours]?"

Could this be recorded? Later, he heard [of the teachings], prostrated himself in reverence, and accepted them with faith. In the second year of the Shénlóng era, Emperor Zhōngzōng bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* and ordained fourteen disciples.
He was subsequently invited into the imperial palace to receive offerings. In the third year, he was again granted a *mona* (patchwork robe). Taking his leave, he returned to Mount Sōng.
On the third day of the third month of that year, he addressed his disciples, saying: "After my death, take my corpse toward the forest."

In the midst [of this], he waited for a wild fire to consume him. Suddenly, Master Wanhui arrived; seeing the Teacher acting in such a frantic manner, he took his hand and engaged him in conversation.

Those attending by his side strained their ears to listen, yet none could comprehend a word. On the eighth day, he closed his door, lay down, and passed away peacefully at the age of one hundred twenty-eight (born in the second year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the Renyin year;
died in the third year of the Jinglong era of the Tang dynasty, the Jiyou year; he was then known as National Teacher Lao’an). His disciples followed his instructions and carried him out.
He was placed among the trees; there, a wild fire spontaneously cremated him. Eighty grains of *śarīra* were obtained, five of which were purple in color.
These were kept within the palace until the second year of the Xiāntián era, when his disciples constructed a stūpa for them.
Chan Master Daoming of Mount Meng in Yuanzhou was a native of Poyang. He was a descendant of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty. After the fall of his kingdom, he settled among the common people;
because he was a great-grandson of a king who had once held official rank, he was given the title of General. In his youth, he left the household life at Yongchang Temple.
His aspiration for the Way was most earnest, and he went to rely upon the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch, where he investigated with total dedication. At first, there was...

Upon gaining understanding and hearing that the Fifth Patriarch had secretly entrusted the robe and Dharma to Lu the Layman (Huineng), he immediately led several dozen companions to track his footsteps in pursuit.
They reached Mount Dayu, where the Master was the first to see him; the others had not yet arrived.
Seeing the Master rushing toward him, Lu immediately cast the robe and bowl onto a flat rock, saying, "This robe represents the seal of faith; can it be contested by force? It is yours to keep."

As he was about to leave, the Master [Nanquan] reached out and lifted him up; [Huangbo] remained as immovable as a mountain. Hesitating and trembling with awe, he said, "I have come to seek the Dharma, not for the sake of robes.
I pray that the Practitioner will reveal it to me. Lu said, "At this very moment, when you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—right now, what is the true face of Elder Ming?
At that moment, the Master attained great enlightenment. He... [repeated the verse].

His body broke into a sweat and he wept as he performed several prostrations. He asked, "Aside from these secret words and secret meanings you have given me thus far, is there any further underlying intent?
Lu said, "What I am telling you now is not a secret. If you turn back and reflect upon your own true face, the secret will reside within you.
The Master said, "Although I have been among the assembly at Huangmei, in truth I have not yet—"
"Examine your own true face. Now that you have received my instruction on the point of entry, it is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
"The practitioner here is now my teacher," [Nanquan] said. Lu said, "If this is so, then you and I share the same teacher at Huangmei. Guard and uphold this well yourself.
The Master asked again, "Where should I go in the future? Lu said, "When you encounter..."
Yuan Kezhi encountered [the Master] while he was staying at Mengjiu. The Master bowed and expressed his thanks, then suddenly turned back and reached the foot of the ridge.
He said to the crowd, "Just now I ascended the high peak and looked far into the distance; there was no trace of him whatsoever. We should seek him by another path. Everyone agreed that this was so.
Once the Master had returned, he went alone to Bushuitai on Mount Lu. After three years had passed, he finally went to Mount Meng in Yuanzhou. Great...
He propagated the profound transformation. Originally named Huiming, he changed his name to Daoming to avoid the first character of the Sixth Patriarch’s name.
He sent all his disciples away to cross the mountain ridges to the south to pay their respects to the Sixth Patriarch.
The second generation under the Fifth Patriarch (a collateral branch):
Chan Master Jufang of Mount Wutai, successor to Chan Master Xiu of the Northern School, was a native of Anlu. His surname was Cao. In his youth, he received his training at Mingfu Temple.

Chan Master Yuanlang initially lectured on the sutras and śāstras, but later joined a Chan assembly. Upon visiting Xiu of the Northern School, he asked, "What is it like where the white clouds disperse?
The Master replied, "It is not obscured. Xiu asked again, "And what is it like after arriving here? The Master replied:
"From the single branch of Right View, five leaves grow. Xiùmò approved of this. He entered the master’s chamber to attend him, responding to his teachings without fail.
Soon thereafter, he went to reside at Hángǐng in Shàngdǎng. Within a few years, his followers numbered over a thousand. Later, he was at Mount Wútaí.
He propagated the teachings for over twenty years before passing away; his stupa was erected at his home mountain.

Chan Master Zhifen of Mount Zhongtiao in Hedong Prefecture was surnamed Wu. Initially, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), but he became mired in conceptual designations (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
When he was cross-examined by a learned master, he resolved to abandon his lectures and travel abroad. There, he met Chan Master Xiu, and his doubts were resolved.
Dunshi then took his leave and resided at Anfeng on the Pujin River. For ten years he did not descend from the mountain, subsisting on wild fruits and drinking from mountain streams.
The regional governor, Wei Wensheng, established Jianguo Monastery for him to dwell in. Monastics and laypeople alike sought refuge with him, their arrival never ceasing.
The Prefect asked, "What will it be like after today? The Master replied, "The sun rises from the Mongsu [the western ocean], yet when it shines upon the trees, they are entirely without [shadow]."
The Prefect could not initially understand him and withdrew with a bow. After a short while, he was enlightened; his doubts were cleared away and he attained a sense of realization.
Master [Dao]ying traveled back and forth through Mount Zhongtiao for over twenty years. Those who attained the Way under him were beyond counting.
After his passing, his disciples erected a stupa to the north of the city.
Chan Master Jiangmo Zang of Yanzhou was a native of Zhaojun. His surname was Wang, and his father served as a clerk in Bo. The Master entered the monastic life at the age of seven.

At that time, the countryside was infested with many malevolent spirits who deluded and bewitched people; the Master, however, subdued them alone through his physical presence, never showing even the slightest fear.
Thus, he acquired the name "Jiangmo" (Subduer of Demons). He subsequently received the tonsure under Chan Master Mingzan of Guangfu Monastery. Later...
Encountering the flourishing propagation of the Northern School, he vowed to follow them as a disciple. Huixiu asked him, "Your name is 'Subduing Demons' (Jiangmo).
Here there are no mountain sprites or forest monsters; why then do you act like a demon? The Master replied, "There are Buddhas and there are demons.
Huixiu said, "If you are a demon, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm. The Master replied, "Even a Buddha is empty; what realm could there be? Huixiu then made a prophetic prediction.
He said, "You have a karmic affinity with the ruins of Shao Hao. The Master then entered Mount Tai and remained there for several years.
Students gathered like clouds. One day he told his disciples, "I am now old and infirm; when things reach their limit, they return to their source. Having spoken, he passed away.
Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou was a native of Tangzhou. His surname was Wen. In his youth, he explored the classics and scriptures.

When he was nearly fifty years old, he encountered a high monk who exhorted and instructed him; he subsequently vowed to leave the household life. He paid homage to Huiben of Mount Mingyue in his own region as his teacher.

The master felt ashamed that Daoshu was advanced in years and that his pursuit of the Dharma had been so delayed. Consequently, Daoshu resolved to travel abroad, visiting every place without exception. Later, he returned...
In Eastern Luo, he met Master Xiu. Upon hearing the Master’s words, he realized the subtle truth. He then chose Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou to build a thatched hut and dwell there.

There was always a rustic man there, whose clothing was simple and plain, and whose speech was strange and unconventional. Beyond his joking and laughter, he would manifest the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, celestial immortals, and so forth.
At times he emitted divine light, and at other times he produced sounds and voices. [The Master]— (Note: The source text ends abruptly with "師之" (the Master's), indicating it is likely a fragment.)
The disciples beheld him, yet none could fathom him. This continued for ten years. Thereafter, he became silent, leaving no trace of form or shadow. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"The rustic man employs many-colored arts and wiles to dazzle and delude people; it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them.
His wiles are finite, while my non-seeing and non-hearing are inexhaustible. In the first year of the Baoli era of the Tang dynasty, he manifested illness.
He passed away there.
Chan Master Renjian of Fuxian Monastery in Luojing was a successor of National Teacher An of Mount Song.
Having ceased his inquiries at Mount Song, he lived in carefree abandon amidst the suburban markets; thus he was known as—
During the Tiānchè Wànsuì era of the Tang dynasty, the Empress Dowager summoned Monk Téngténg to appear before her in the palace hall.

He gazed up at the Empress for a long while and asked, "Do you understand? The Empress replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This old monk observes the precept of silence," and having finished speaking, he departed.
The following day, he presented nineteen short songs. When the Empress read them, she praised him and bestowed upon him generous gifts and rewards.
The Master would not accept them at all. He further ordered that the lyrics be transcribed and disseminated throughout the world;
these verses all expounded upon the ultimate truth to admonish the common people. Of these, only the single song by Liaoyuan became widely popular in the world.
The Monk Pòzào Duò of Mount Song did not disclose his name or lineage; his words and deeds were unfathomable.

He lived in seclusion on Mount Song, where there was a temple of great efficacy in a mountain valley. Within the hall stood only a single hearth, upon which offerings were made by people from near and far without ceasing, and many living beings were slaughtered for cooking.
One day, the Master led an attendant monk into the temple and struck the hearth with his staff three times, saying: "Tut! This—"
The hearth is merely composed of clay and tiles; from where does the "sage" come, and from where does the "spirit" arise? Yet you thus slaughter living beings!
[He] struck it three more times, whereupon the hearth collapsed and fell apart. In a moment, there appeared a man dressed in green robes and wearing a tall cap.
He prostrated himself before the Master. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am the hearth god of this temple.

Having long endured the retribution of my karma, today I have been fortunate enough to hear the Master preach the Dharma of non-arising; thus I have escaped this place and been reborn among the devas. I have come specifically to express my gratitude.
The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature; it was not my words that brought it forth. The spirit bowed once more and vanished. A short while later—
An attendant monk asked, "We have served the Master for a long time, yet we have not received his instruction.

What essential principle did the stove god obtain that he was able to be reborn in heaven? The Master said, "I simply told him that it is composed of clay and tiles. There is no other principle or doctrine to impart to him.
The attendant monk remained silent. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It is originally present."
[The Master asked: "What is the nature of this? Why does it not [arise]? The attendant monks then prostrated. The Master said, "Falling! Falling! Broken! Broken!
Later, Chan Master Yifeng recounted this to National Teacher An, who sighed and said, "This man has fully realized it."
The identity of things and self is one; it may be said to be like the bright moon in the sky—there is no one who does not see it.
It is difficult to grasp the pulse of his speech. Feng asked, "I do not yet understand: what kind of person can grasp the pulse of his speech? An said, "One who does not know.
At that time, he was known as "Puo-zao-duo" (The Oven-Breaker). A monk asked, "When every single thing is formless, how is it? The Master said, "As for ritual, it belongs only to you—it is not me."
"I do not prostrate; it is simply I, not you. The monk then bowed in apology. The Master said, "That which is originally present is neither a thing nor a non-thing.
Therefore it is said: 'If the mind can turn things, one is identical to the Tathāgata. A monk came from the school of Niutou;
the Master asked him, "From whose Dharma assembly have you come? The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, and circumambulated the Master once.
He went out. The Master said, "There should not be such a person among the disciples of Niutou. The monk then turned back.
The Master stood with his hands folded over his shoulder and said, "As expected, as expected. The monk then asked, "How is it when responding to things without depending on another?"
The Master said, "How could it not be due to him? The monk said, "If that is so, then one follows the correct path back to the source. The Master said, "What need is there to follow the source?
The monk said, "Had it not been for you, Master, I would have nearly committed a transgression. The Master said, "That is still the principle before you saw the Fourth Patriarch.
Try saying it after you have seen him. The monk then circled the Master once and departed. The Master said, "Following the correct path."
This is the Way; it has been so from antiquity to the present. The monk prostrated. After the monk had stood in attendance for a long time, the Master said:

"Patriarch after patriarch and Buddha after Buddha have spoken only of the original nature and original mind of human beings; there is no other principle. Understand this! Understand this! The monk bowed in thanks.
The Master then struck him with his whisk and said, "It is so in one place; it is likewise in a thousand places.
The monk then joined his palms, stepped forward, and gave a single response of assent. The Master said, "I do not believe you further! I do not believe you further!
The monk asked, "What is the person of great icchantika? The Master said, "To pay respect and prostrate. [The monk] asked, "What is the person of great diligence? The Master said, "To revile..."
He was humiliated and filled with anger. Thereafter, nothing was known of his final end.

Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song was a native of Yique. His surname was Li. He entered the monastic life in his youth and received full ordination in the second year of the Yongchun era of the Tang dynasty.
He was registered at Xianju Monastery and studied the Vinaya without slackening. Later, he went to visit National Teacher An. Suddenly—
Having realized the profound essence of the Way, he subsequently chose to build a hermitage at Pangwu on the mountain.

One day, a strange man arrived, wearing a high cap and trousers with leggings (tújié), accompanied by a vast retinue. Moving with lightness and composure, he announced that he came to pay his respects to the Great Master.

The Master, observing that the man’s appearance was extraordinary and magnificent beyond the ordinary, addressed him, saying: "Welcome, O benevolent one! For what purpose have you come? He replied: "Master..."
"Do you perhaps recognize me? The Master said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye. How could I make such distinctions?
The spirit said, "I am the mountain deity of this peak, capable of bringing life and death to others. How can you, Master, treat me with such a single eye?"
The Master said: "I am fundamentally unborn; how could you cause me to die? I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you.
Can you destroy space and yourself? If you could indeed destroy space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished.
