Since you cannot even do this, how could you possibly bring about my birth or death? Shen bowed his head and said: "I too—"
"You are wise, sagacious, and upright compared to other deities; how could you not know that your Master possesses vast wisdom and eloquence?
I pray that he may bestow upon you the true precepts, so that you may transcend the world. The Master said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them. Why is this?"

"Outside of the precepts there are no precepts; what precepts, then, could there be? The deity said, "This is the principle. I have heard it, yet it remains obscure and dim to me; I seek only the Master’s precepts.
The Master then prepared a seat for him, lit the incense burner, and set out the ritual table, saying, "I shall confer the Five Precepts upon you.
If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you should say 'No'. [The deity] replied, "I respectfully receive your instruction. The Master said:
"Are you able to refrain from sexual misconduct? He replied, "I am married. The Master said, "That is not what I mean. I mean being free from lustful desire. He replied, "I can.
The Master said, "Are you able to refrain from stealing? He replied, "What would I lack that I should steal? How could I take anything by theft?"
The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that one brings blessings upon the licentious by making offerings, and brings calamity upon the virtuous by failing to offer.
[The official] said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from killing? He replied, "In truth, I hold the authority over it. The Master said, "I do not mean this.
I mean that there may be errors, mistakes, or confusions. He replied, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from falsehood? He replied, "I am indeed upright."
"Is it not straightforward? How could there be any delusion? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that what precedes and follows does not accord with the Will of Heaven.
[The student] said, "I am able. The Master said, "Are you not ruined by alcohol? [The student] said, "I am able. The Master said, "As for the above, these constitute the Buddha-precepts."
Furthermore, it is said that one upholds with a mind, yet is without a mind that clings; one acts for the sake of others with a mind, yet has no thought of a self.
If one can be thus, then though born before heaven and earth, one does not become a vital essence; though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become old.
Throughout the day one undergoes transformations, yet does not become stirred; throughout the night one remains in total silence, yet does not come to rest.

To believe this is to realize that though one marries, it is not for the sake of a wife; though one partakes in feasts, it is not for the sake of acquisition; though one holds office, it is not for the sake of power; though one acts, it is not for the sake of habit; though one is intoxicated, it is not for the sake of delusion.

If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then even if one is ensnared by desires, it shall not constitute lust. As for blessings for the licentious and calamities for the virtuous—[this is the natural order].

To not commit theft out of goodness; to not commit killing through negligence, error, doubt, or confusion; to not speak falsely by violating the Way of Heaven through prior or subsequent contradictions;
and to not become intoxicated through delusion, negligence, or inversion—this is called being "without mind. Without mind, there are no precepts; without precepts, there is no mind.
"There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is no you and no self. What, then, would constitute precepts? The spirit said, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha.
The Master said, "Of your ten supernatural powers, you can perform five and cannot perform five. Of the Buddha's ten, he can perform seven and cannot perform three.
The spirit was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat. Kneeling, he asked, "May I hear them? The Master said, "You can fly upward."
[The Emperor asked: "Can the Emperor travel eastward through the heavens while the Seven Luminaries move westward?
He replied, "No. The Master said, "Can you seize the Earth Deity, melt the Five Peaks, and bind the Four Seas? He replied, "No. The Master said, "This is called the 'Five Inabilities.
The Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of the myriad dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. The Buddha can know all that exists..."
The nature [of phenomena] exhaustively encompasses the events of billions of kalpas, yet it cannot transform or guide those for whom there is no affinity.
A Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings. These are the three "incapacities. Even fixed karma is not eternal;

even the lack of affinity is but a single lifetime. The realm of sentient beings fundamentally has neither increase nor decrease. Throughout all time, not a single person can preside over this Dharma. There is...
“The Dharma has no master; this is what is meant by ‘the non-existence of dharmas. That there is no dharma and no master is what is meant by ‘no-mind.
As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, there is likewise no supernatural power (*abhijñā*); it is simply that one can penetrate all dharmas through no-mind.

The deity said, “I am indeed shallow and ignorant, and have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). I shall faithfully observe the precepts you have bestowed upon me. Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue; please grant me [your instruction].”
The Master said, "I contemplate the body as being without substance; I contemplate all phenomena as impermanent. Being but a lump of flesh, what further desires could I have?

The spirit said, "The Master must surely command me to perform a worldly task to display my minor divine powers, so that these five types of people—those who have already resolved their minds, those who have first resolved their minds, those who do not yet believe, and those who will certainly come to believe—may behold my spiritual traces and know that [the Way] exists."
"The Buddha possesses spiritual power (*śakti*). There are things he can do and things he cannot; there are things that are spontaneous (*svabhāva*) and things that are not.
The Master said, "Non-action is non-action; this is it. The Spirit said, "The Buddha also commands spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, rebel against the Buddha?
I pray that you will grant me instruction as you please. The Master, having no choice, spoke: "At Dongyan Temple, the surrounding barriers are vast and treeless. To the north..."
"The mountain clefts possess them, yet their backs are not shielded by barriers. Can you move the northern trees to the eastern ridge? The spirit replied, "I have received your command.
However, there will surely be clamor and commotion during the dark night; I pray that you, Master, do not be alarmed. He then performed a prostration and took his leave.
The Master saw him off at the gate and watched him depart; he saw the ceremonial guards winding along like the retinue of a king, amidst mists, vapors, smoke, and clouds.
Amidst a profusion of intermingled wonders, banners and streamers, and tinkling jade pendants, vanished into the air. That evening, indeed, there was a violent wind and thunderous peals;
clouds rushed by and lightning flashed, causing the buildings to tremble and the nesting birds to clamor. The Master said to the assembly, "Do not fear, do not fear!

The deity has entered into harmony with me. At dawn the next day, when the weather had cleared and become bright, all the pine and cypress trees from the northern cliff had been moved to the eastern ridge, standing in dense array.
However, Xingzhi’s master said to his disciples, "After my death, do not let outsiders know; if they have something to talk about, people will treat me as a supernatural being.
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Bingchen year, he instructed his door-disciples, saying, "I originally resided on the eastern ridge of the temple.
When I pass away, you must place my remains there. Having finished speaking, he was like one casting off a sloughed skin.
The Third Generation under the Fifth Patriarch (a collateral line):

Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain, successor to Chan Master Ji of Songshan, was a native of Pingyuan. His surname was Zhou. He received his monastic training at [the monastery] in his home prefecture.
The Dharma Master Shuandeng of Heshi Temple received the Dharma from Chan Master Pují of Mount Song. He subsequently entered Mount Taiyī, where his disciples filled his chambers.
During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Wenzong was fond of eating clams; officials along the coast had previously been required to present them to him in succession.
The people were also weary from their labors. One day, while the Emperor was partaking of his midday meal, there was among the dishes a [lotus] that had been split but did not open.

The Emperor, considering it a marvel, immediately burned incense and prayed to it. It then opened to reveal the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the marks of a Brahma-like appearance.

The Emperor subsequently placed it in a casket of gold-dusted sandalwood, covered it with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Monastery, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and worship it. He then questioned his ministers.

"What kind of auspicious omen is this? Someone then memorialized the Emperor regarding Chan Master Weizheng of Mount Taiyi, stating that he had a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma and was widely learned with a powerful memory.
The Emperor requested that an imperial decree be issued to summon him for questioning. The Emperor immediately issued the decree. When the Master arrived, the Emperor questioned him about the matter.

The Master replied, "Your servant has heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause; this is intended to awaken Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, the Sūtras state: 'One should [regard] this body...'"

"To those who are ready for deliverance, he manifests this body and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed appeared, yet we have not yet heard him preach the Dharma.
The Master replied, "Your Majesty, as you behold this, is it permanent or impermanent? Is it real or unreal?"
The Emperor said, "This is a most rare and marvelous matter; I believe it deeply. The Master replied, "Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma to its conclusion.

The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy and delight, such as he had never experienced before. He issued an edict for all monasteries throughout the realm to establish an image of Avalokiteśvara in order to repay this extraordinary grace.

He invited the Master to remain in the inner palace chapel, but the Master repeatedly declined and requested to return to the mountains. The Emperor then commanded him to reside at Shengshou Temple until the reign of Emperor Wuzong.
Upon his accession to the abbacy, the Master suddenly retired to live in seclusion in Mount Zhongnan. When people asked him the reason for this, the Master said, "I am avoiding my enemies.
After his death, he was cremated; forty-nine śarīras were collected, and a stupa was erected over them.
A monk asked National Teacher Pózuòduò of Mount Sōng, "What is one who practices good? The Master said, "Carrying a cangue and wearing shackles.
The monk asked, "What is one who commits evil? The Master said, "Practicing dhyāna and entering samādhi. The monk said, "My faculties are shallow."
"Please, Master, point directly. The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good; if you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil.
After the monk had been silent for a long while, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "An evil person has no thoughts of goodness."
"A good person has no evil mind. This is why it is said that good and evil are like floating clouds; both have no place of arising or ceasing.
Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Later, when Puzhuo heard this account, he remarked, "This man has realized that all dharmas are ultimately unborn."
The Fourth Generation under the Fifth Patriarch:
Chan Master Wuxiang of Yizhou and his Dharma heir, Chan Master Wuzhu of Baotang Temple in Yizhou. Having first received the Dharma from Master Wuxiang, he then resided in the South.

At Mount Yangbaiya, he devoted himself exclusively to the tranquility of meditative stillness. After several years had passed, students gradually began to arrive; as their earnest requests did not cease, he thereafter began to bestow his instructions.
Although he extensively expounded upon verbal teachings, he took "non-thought" (amanasikāra) alone as his fundamental principle.

When Du Hongjian, the State Councilor of the Tang Dynasty, was dispatched to govern the region of Shu, he heard of the Master’s reputation and desired to pay him homage. He sent an envoy to the mountain to extend an invitation. At that time—
Cui Ning, the Regional Inspector, also ordered the monks of various temples to travel a great distance to welcome him, leading him to Konghui Temple.

At that time, Lord Du and the military commander summoned eminent masters of the Three Studies to assemble within the temple. After the formal greetings were concluded, the Lord asked, "I have heard, Master, that you now teach the Dharma-gate of the three phrases:
'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not be deluded. Is this so? The Master replied:

The Duke said, "Are these three phrases one or three? The Master replied, "'No recollection' is called precept; 'no thought' is called concentration; 'do not delude' is called wisdom. When the single mind does not arise, it possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom—it is neither one nor three. The Duke asked, "In the last phrase, the character for 'delusion' (妄), is it the 'wàng' that is written with the radical for 'heart' (心)? The Master said, "It is the one written with the radical for 'woman' (女). The Duke said, "Is there a source for this? The Master said, "There is. The Duke said, "I have heard of it before, but I did not know its meaning. The Master said, "That which is written with the 'heart' radical is 'to forget' (忘); that which is written with the 'woman' radical is 'delusion' (妄). To forget is to lose oneself; delusion is to lose the Way. Therefore, the former is used when referring to the mind, while the latter is used when referring to the Way. The Duke said, "I am fortunate to have encountered such a person today. The Master said, "This is not due to my virtue, but because you have long cultivated the roots of goodness. The Duke said, "I have been ill for some time and have not yet recovered. I pray you will visit me again. The Master bowed and withdrew. The Duke sent someone to escort him back to the monastery. That night, the Duke’s illness was suddenly cured. He went to the monastery to thank the Master, saying, "Last night I dreamed of a divine man who told me, 'The Master has come to save you. I now know that this was indeed you. The Duke then had a portrait of the Master painted and enshrined it in his residence. He also composed a hymn of praise, which read: "Vast and boundless is the ocean of the Dharma, The myriad phenomena are all within it. When the single mind does not arise, The threefold nature is naturally extinguished. If one can attain this state, One is truly a Buddha. The Duke also wrote a letter of recommendation for the Master, which he presented to the Emperor. The Emperor granted him the title of "Great Master of the True Principle" (真如大師). The Duke further requested that the Master reside at the Xiangshan Monastery. The Master accepted. Subsequently, the Duke built a hall and a pavilion for the Master at the monastery. One day, the Duke visited the Master and said, "I have heard that the ancients spoke of 'the Way being near and yet people seek it afar. I wonder what this means. The Master replied, "The Way is originally near; it is only because people seek it outside themselves that they consider it distant. If one simply returns to the source and rests in the fundamental, the Way is right here. The Duke said, "How can one return to the source? The Master said, "To cease all seeking and let go of all grasping—this is returning to the source. The Duke said, "I am deeply grateful for your instruction. The Master remained at the monastery for several years, teaching and transforming sentient beings. His reputation spread throughout the realm, and disciples from all quarters came to study under him. Later, the Duke passed away, and the Master returned to Mount Huangmei. There, he lived in seclusion, practicing meditation and cultivation. One day, he ascended the mountain peak and gazed toward the east. Seeing the rising sun, he smiled and said, "The light of the Dharma is about to shine upon the world. He then composed a verse: "The great matter is already settled, The heavy burden is finally cast off. The thousand sages and ten thousand Buddhas All enter through this single gate. Having finished the verse, he sat upright and passed away. He was seventy-four years old. The local authorities reported this to the Emperor, who issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of "Great Master of Universal Wisdom" (普濟大師). His remains were interred on the mountain, and a stupa was erected. His teachings continue to benefit the world to this day.
"No," the Master replied. He said, "The *Dharmapada* states: 'If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence.

If one can ensure the mind is not deluded, diligence will be boundless. Upon hearing this, the official’s doubts were completely dispelled. The official asked again, 'Does the Master still instruct people by means of three phrases?
The Master said, 'For a beginner practitioner, one must first cause them to cease discursive thought and settle the waves of consciousness, so that the water becomes clear.'"

Manifesting as reflections, one awakens to the essence of non-thought (*amanyana*), and quiescent extinction (*śānti*) appears before one; even "non-thought" no longer stands. At that time, a crow cawed in the trees of the courtyard.
The Master asked, "Did you hear it, Teacher? The Teacher replied, "I heard it. After the crow had gone, he asked again, "Teacher, did you hear it? The Teacher replied, "I heard it.
The Master said, "The crow has gone and there is no sound; why do you say you heard it? The Teacher then addressed the assembly at large: "In the Buddha’s world..."
It is difficult to encounter; the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Each of you listen attentively. To hear is to have no hearing;
it is not related to the nature of hearing. It is originally unarisen; how could it ever cease? When there is sound, that is merely the auditory object arising of itself.

When there is no sound, that is merely the auditory object ceasing of itself. Yet this nature of hearing does not arise following the sound, nor does it cease following the sound. Realize this nature of hearing.
Then one is liberated from being turned by the dust of sound. You should know that hearing is without arising or ceasing; hearing is without coming or going.

The Duke, together with his officials and the great assembly, bowed their heads and asked again: "What is called the primary truth (paramārtha)? From what sequence does one enter the primary truth? The Master said:
"The primary truth has no sequence, nor does it have entering or exiting. All things of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti) exist."

"The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in all phenomena; this is designated as the ultimate truth. The Buddha said, "The existence of phenomena is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
the absence of intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth. The Duke said, "As you have elucidated it, Master, this is truly inconceivable.

The Duke further said, "My own faculties and understanding are dull and shallow. Previously, during my leisure time, I composed two fascicles of commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*."
"Can it be called the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Now, the composition of commentaries and treatises all employs the consciousness-mind to deliberate and discriminate;
they involve conditioned activity and effort, arising from the stirring of thought and intention, and thus can be brought to completion.

However, according to the *Śāstra* (Treatise), one should know that all dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately level."
It is thus: there is no change or alteration; there is only the single mind, and for this reason it is called *tathatā* (Suchness).

Now, you, sir, are attached to the characteristic of verbal expression, attached to the characteristic of names, and attached to the characteristic of mental objects. Since you are attached to such various characteristics, how can this be the Buddha-dharma?
The official rose, prostrated, and said: "I, your disciple, have also asked [these questions] before. All the venerable masters in attendance praised me, saying that I am inconceivable."

[The Master] deliberated: "You should know that those [others] merely follow worldly sentiments. My teacher now explains from the perspective of understanding; this Dharma which accords with the mind is truly the inconceivable ultimate truth.
The Duke asked again: "What is non-arising? What is non-extinction? How does one attain liberation? The Master said:
"When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called non-arising. Non-arising is itself non-extinction. Since there is neither..."
Arising and ceasing—this is precisely not being bound by external objects. Liberation in the very place [of arising] is what is called "non-thought" (*amanyanā*).
Where there is no thought, there is no cessation; where there is no thought, there is no bondage; where there is no thought, there is no liberation. To state the essentials:

when the consciousness-mind is detached from thought, one sees the nature. Apart from detaching from the consciousness-mind and seeing the nature, there is no further dharma-gate for realizing the Unsurpassed.
"Bodhi" means that there is no such place [to be found]. The Official asked, "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing one's nature'?

The Master said, "All practitioners of the Way wander about following their thoughts, precisely because they do not recognize the true mind. As for the true mind: when thoughts arise, it does not follow them in arising;
when thoughts cease, it does not rely on stillness. It neither comes nor goes; it is neither fixed nor chaotic; it neither grasps nor abandons."
Sinking, yet not floating; non-active and signless; lively and agile; ordinary and sovereign. This essence of mind is ultimately ungraspable;
there is nothing to be known or perceived. Everything met by the eye is thus; there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the nature.
The Master and the great assembly prostrated themselves in praise and departed with joyful leaps. Later, the Master resided at Baotang Temple until his passing.
The First Generation of Dharma Heirs branching from the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Mirror Chan Master:
The Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions was a native of India. He attained realization upon hearing the words of the Sixth Patriarch.

Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he saw a monk sitting in meditation within a hermitage. The Master asked him, "For what purpose do you sit alone? The monk replied, "I am practicing the contemplation of stillness. The Master [said]:...
[The Master] said: "Who is it that observes? What is it that is still? The monk prostrated and asked:
"What is the principle of this? The Master said: "Why do you not observe yourself and bring yourself to stillness? The monk was bewildered. The Master said: "Whose lineage do you come from?
He replied: "From Zen Master Xiu. The Master said: "Even those of the lowest seed among the heterodox paths of the Western Regions do not fall into such views; [you are] utterly deluded."
"Sitting empty-handed like this, what benefit is there for the Path? The monk then asked, "Who is your teacher? The Master said, "My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch.
Why do you not go quickly to Caoxi to resolve the essential truth? Thereupon, the monk went at once to visit the Sixth Patriarch.
The Sixth Patriarch’s instruction accorded perfectly with that of the Master [Nanyue Huairang]. The monk immediately attained realization. As for the Master, his final whereabouts were unknown.
As for Chan Master Fahai of Shaoshan, he was a native of Qujiang. When he first met the Sixth Patriarch, he asked, "Regarding 'the very mind is Buddha,' I pray you will grant me an illustration.
The Patriarch said, "When the preceding thought does not arise, that is the mind; when the succeeding thought does not cease, that is the Buddha. Thus it was accomplished.
All phenomena are identical with the mind; being free from all phenomena is itself the Buddha. Were I to explain this in full detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
Listen to my verse: "That which is the mind is called wisdom; that which is the Buddha is concentration. When concentration and wisdom are held in equal balance, the mind becomes pure.

To awaken to this Dharma-gate is due to your own habitual nature; by realizing that [all things] are fundamentally unborn, you cultivate both correctly. The Master accepted this with faith and spoke in verse:

The eulogy says: The mind is originally the Buddha; failing to awaken to this, one remains self-subdued. I know that through the causes of concentration and wisdom, one cultivates both and leaves behind all phenomena.
Master Zhicheng of Jizhou was a native of Tahe in that same province. Initially, he studied under Chan Master Xiu, and later...
As the two schools flourished, the disciples of Xiu frequently derided the Southern School, saying, "Master Neng cannot recognize a single character;
what excellence does he possess? Xiu replied, "He has attained teacherless wisdom and deeply realized the Supreme Vehicle; in this, I am not his equal.
Furthermore, my master, the Fifth Patriarch, personally entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma—how could that have been for nothing? What I regret is that I am unable to travel far [to see him]."
"I have left my kin to receive the country's bounty in vain. You all should not remain stagnant here; you may go to Caoxi to resolve your doubts.

When you return another day, you must explain it for me. Upon hearing these words, the Master paid his respects and took his leave. Arriving at Shaoyang, he joined the assembly for formal inquiries, yet did not mention where he had come from.
At that time, the Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "There is currently a thief of the Dharma who is secretly staying among us."
Huike emerged from the assembly and prostrated himself, recounting the matter in detail. The Patriarch said, "How did your teacher instruct the assembly?

Huike replied, "He used to exhort the great multitude, commanding them to settle the mind and contemplate stillness, sitting for long periods without lying down. The Patriarch said, "To settle the mind and contemplate stillness is a sickness, not dhyāna;
to sit for long periods and constrain the body—what benefit is there for the principle? Listen to my verse: 'Since birth, sitting and never lying down.'"
"Dead and lying down, not sitting; a single set of stinking bones. Why establish merit or fault? The Master said, "I do not yet understand. With what Dharma does the Abbot instruct people?
The Patriarch said, "If I were to say that I have a Dharma to give to others, I would be deceiving you.
I simply follow the occasion to untie their bonds, provisionally calling it 'samādhi. Listen to my verse: 'When the mind-ground is free from transgression, it is the precept of self-nature.'"
"The mind-ground is free from delusion; its self-nature is wisdom. The mind-ground is free from distraction; its self-nature is concentration.

Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the original vajra. The coming and going of the body is fundamentally samādhi. Upon hearing this verse, the Master repented and apologized, immediately vowing to take refuge [in him].
He then presented his own verse, saying: "The illusory body of the five aggregates—what is the ultimate end of such illusion? Turning toward True Suchness, the dharmas still do not return to purity."
Regarding the biography of Chan Master Xiaoliao of Biandang Mountain, it is not recorded in [standard] historical accounts;

however, a stele inscription for his pagoda composed by Chan Master Hulei Cheng of the Northern School is widely circulated in the world. Its brief summary states: "The Master resided at Mount Biandang and was styled Xiaoliao."
He was the direct successor of the Sixth Patriarch. The Master attained the mind that is without mind and realized the appearance that is without appearance.

That which is without appearance is the myriad phenomena dazzling the eyes; that which is without mind is the blazing of discrimination. Beyond every word and every sound, no sound can be transmitted.

The transmission has been passed on; words cannot exhaust it. To exhaust it would be an error. You, Master, have attained the "non-existence" of non-existence, yet you do not remain fixed in that non-existence.
I, for my part, now employ the "existence" of existence, yet I do not remain fixed in that existence. This existence that is not existent means that coming and going do not increase [reality].
This non-existence that is not non-existent means that *nirvāṇa* is not annihilation. Alas! Master, may you remain in this world, and may Caoxi shine bright!
The Master has entered nirvana; the Dharma-boat has capsized. The Master’s discourse on the ineffable fills the universe. To the deluded disciples, he revealed the vehicle of ultimate meaning.
The mountain colors of Bian Mountain hang down their hues here; in the empty valley, the name "Xiaoliao" remains.
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou was a native of Fengcheng in Hongzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of seven and recited the Lotus Sūtra.

After receiving full ordination, he went to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch, yet his head did not touch the ground. The Patriarch rebuked him, saying, "If your prostration does not reach the ground, how is it any different from not prostrating at all?
There must be something within your mind; what have you been habitually practicing? The Master replied, "I am mindful of the Dharma."

After he had finished reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and three thousand other sections, the Patriarch said: "If you can reach ten thousand sections and grasp the meaning of these scriptures without regarding it as a source of superiority, then you may walk with me.
You are currently burdened by this task, yet you do not recognize your own transgression.

Listen to my verse: "Reverence is fundamentally for breaking the banner of pride; why does your head not touch the ground? When 'self' exists, fault arises; when 'merit' is absent, there is blessing."
The Master said, "Peerless One. He asked again, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Fada.
The Master said, "Your name is Fada; when have you ever mastered the Dharma? He then spoke a verse: "You now bear the name Fada, Diligently reciting without ceasing.
You recite in vain, merely following the sound; To understand the mind is called a Bodhisattva. Because you now possess the necessary conditions, I shall now speak for your sake. Simply believe..."
The Buddha remained silent, and lotus flowers issued forth from his mouth. Hearing the verse, the Master repented and said, "From this day forward, I shall treat all with humility and respect.
I only pray that the Preceptor’s great compassion will briefly explain the meaning and principles within the sutras.

The Patriarch asked, "As you recite this sutra, what do you take as its central tenet? The Master replied, "I am a dull-witted student; heretofore I have merely recited it according to the literal text. How could I have known..."
Regarding the fundamental purport, the Patriarch said, "Try reciting it once for me, and I shall explain it to you.

The Master then recited the sutra aloud. When they reached the "Expedient Means" chapter, the Patriarch said, "Stop. This sutra fundamentally takes the appearance in the world through causes and conditions as its central theme.
Although it employs many kinds of parables, none exceed this point. Why? Because the cause and condition is solely the One Great Matter."
The "One Great Matter" is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra.

If you see others say that "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong solely to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that we have no share in it—if you interpret it thus, you are slandering the sutra and defaming the Buddha.
Since he is already a Buddha, he has already perfected knowledge and vision; why would he need to "open" them further? You should now believe that the Buddha...
As for this "knowledge and vision," it is simply your own mind; there is no other essence.

It is because all sentient beings obscure their own radiance, greedily clinging to sensory objects, and being disturbed internally by external conditions that they willingly submit to being driven about. Thus, you have toiled to cause him to arise from samādhi.
With various bitter words, he exhorted him to rest and cease, telling him not to seek outwardly, for he is no different from the Buddha. Thus it is said: "He opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If you merely weary yourself with clinging thoughts, claiming them to be your daily practice, how is this any different from a yak that loves its own tail?

The Master said, "If that is so, then you need only understand the meaning; is there not no need for the labor of reciting the sutra? The Patriarch said, "What fault is there in the sutra? How could it obstruct your mindfulness?
It is simply because delusion and awakening depend on the person, while benefit and harm depend on yourself. Listen to my verse: When the mind is deluded, the Lotus Sutra revolves [around it];
When the mind is awakened, it revolves the Lotus Sutra. To recite for a long time without clarifying oneself Is to become an enemy to the meaning. Non-thought..."

"Mindfulness is itself correct; yet there are instances where mindfulness becomes perverse, and others where one does not even reckon with existence or non-existence. Thus one forever drives the white ox-cart.

Upon hearing this verse, the Master replied again: "The Sūtra states that even the great Śrāvakas and even the Bodhisattvas, though they exhaust their thoughts and measure with their intellects, cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Yet now you say that if an ordinary person merely awakens to their own mind, it is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

Unless one possesses superior faculties, one cannot avoid doubt and slander. Furthermore, the Sūtras speak of three vehicles: the Great Ox Cart and the White Ox Cart—how are these to be distinguished?
I pray that the Master will deign to explain this further. The Patriarch said: "The intent of the Sūtra is clear; it is you who are deluded and turn your back on it.
That those of the Three Vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom lies in their habit of measuring it with their own limited intellects. Even if they were to exhaust..."
As we reflect together upon this, it becomes increasingly remote and distant. The Buddha originally taught for the sake of ordinary beings; he did not teach for the sake of Buddhas.
If you are unwilling to believe this principle, then withdraw from the assembly. Little do you realize that you have already boarded the White Ox Cart, yet you seek the three carts outside the gate.
Furthermore, the sutra text clearly says to you: "There are neither two nor three. Why do you fail to understand this? Three.
The carriage is provisional, for it pertains to the past; the One Vehicle is real, for it pertains to the present. I am merely instructing you to abandon the provisional and return to the real.
Once you have returned to the real, even "reality" has no name. You should know that all precious wealth belongs entirely to you.
"Because you have received and utilized [this teaching], you no longer harbor the thought of him as a father, nor the thought of him as a son, nor even the thought of utility;
this is called 'upholding the Lotus Sutra. From kalpa to kalpa, your hand shall not let go of the scroll; from day to night, there shall be no moment when you do not keep it in mind.
Having received this inspiration, the Master leaped for joy and praised him with a verse: "I have recited three thousand sections of the sutra... Cao...
A single phrase from the *Xi* [Sutra] was lost; I had not yet clarified the intent of appearing in the world. How could I have ceased my lifelong delusion?

The provisional teachings of the sheep, deer, and ox were established; the excellence of the beginning, middle, and end was proclaimed. Who would have known that within the burning house there was originally the Dharma King?

The Patriarch said, "From now on, you may truly be considered a monk who recites the sutras. From this point on, the Master understood the essential meaning and never ceased his recitation and upholding of the scriptures.

Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu was a native of Ānfēng. Initially, he studied the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* more than a thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
He went to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies..."
The pure *dharmakāya* is your nature. The perfect *saṃbhogakāya* is your wisdom. The thousands of millions of *nirmāṇakāyas* are your practice.
If one departs from the original nature and speaks of the three bodies separately, this is called having bodies but lacking wisdom.
If one realizes that the three bodies have no inherent self-nature, this is called the four wisdoms of *bodhi*. Listen to my verse: "The original nature is endowed with..."
The three bodies manifest and give rise to the four wisdoms; without departing from seeing and hearing conditions, one transcends and ascends to the stage of Buddhahood.
I shall now explain this for you: believe it with earnest faith and you will never again be deluded. Do not follow those who run about in pursuit, speaking of *bodhi* all day long.
The Master asked: "May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms? The Patriarch said: "Since you have already understood the three bodies, you naturally comprehend the four wisdoms. Why ask further?"
Incorrect. If one were to speak of the four wisdoms separately from the three bodies, this would imply having wisdom without a body;
yet such wisdom would, in turn, become non-wisdom. Furthermore, a verse is spoken: The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; The Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in its mind;
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. Five, eight, six, and seven...

The transformation of cause and fruit consists merely of conventional designations and lacks any substantial nature. If one leaves no lingering attachment toward that which undergoes transformation, then amidst all profuse activity, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*.

(Regarding the transformation of consciousness into wisdom, the teachings state: the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done; the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality; and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Although the sixth and seventh are transformed during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are transformed at the level of fruition, this is merely a transformation of their names, not a transformation of their essence. The Master bowed in gratitude.

He praised it with these verses: "The Three Bodies are fundamentally my own essence; The Four Wisdoms are originally the luminosity of the mind. Body and wisdom are fused without obstruction, Responding to things according to their forms.

To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; To dwell in fixed maintenance is not the true quintessence. Through the Teacher, I have understood the wondrous principle; At last, the name of defilement has vanished."
Chan Master Zhiche of Jiangxi was surnamed Zhang and named Xingchang. In his youth, he was a man of chivalrous spirit.
Since the division of the Northern and Southern schools, although the two Patriarchs had ceased all notions of "self" and "other," their disciples vied with one another to favor their own masters.

At that time, the followers of the Northern school established Chan Master Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch, yet they resented that the transmission of the robe to Dajian (Huineng) was known throughout the world. However—
The Patriarch had foreknowledge of this matter and immediately placed ten taels of gold in the abbot’s quarters.

At that time, Xingchang, acting upon the instructions of a follower of the Northern School, entered the Patriarch’s room with a blade hidden about him, intending to do him harm. The Patriarch extended his neck for Xingchang to strike;
though the blade was swung three times, it caused no injury at all. The Patriarch said, "A true sword is not crooked; a crooked sword is not true. You have merely brought [this] upon yourself."

"Gold," [Huineng] said. "I will not take your life. Startled, Xingchang fell prostrate; only after a long time did he regain consciousness. He begged for mercy and repented his transgressions, immediately vowing to leave the household life.
The Master then gave him gold, saying, "Go for now; I fear that your fellow monks might instead harm you. You may come back another day in a different guise, and I shall accept you.
Following these instructions, Xingchang fled under the cover of night, entered the monastic order as a monk, and received full ordination.

With great diligence, one day he recalled the words of the Patriarch and traveled a long distance to pay his respects and seek an audience. The Patriarch said, "I have long been thinking of you; why did you come so late?
He replied, "Yesterday I received the Master’s pardon of my offenses. Although I have now left the household life and practice asceticism, it will be difficult to repay your profound kindness.

Is there not only the transmission of the Dharma and the saving of sentient beings? Your disciple has often read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I do not understand the meaning of 'permanence' and 'non-existence'."
[The monk] said, "Master, I pray that you will compassionately explain this briefly for me. The Patriarch said, "'Constant' refers to the Buddha-nature.
'Inconstant' refers to the discriminating mind regarding all phenomena, both good and evil. [The monk] said, "What the Master has said greatly contradicts the scriptures.
The Patriarch said, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how would I dare to contradict the Buddha’s scriptures? [The monk] said, "The scriptures state that the Buddha..."
"Nature is eternal, yet you, Preceptor, say it is impermanent. All dharmas, whether good or evil, up to and including the bodhicitta, are all impermanent, yet you, Preceptor, say they are eternal.
This is contradictory and causes students to become increasingly confused.
The Patriarch said, "In the past, I heard the nun Wujinzang read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* once, and I immediately gave a lecture on it."
"There is not a single word or a single meaning that does not accord with the scriptural texts; even for you, I have never given two different teachings.
The student said, "My capacity for understanding is shallow and dim. I pray that the Master will explain this to me in detail. The Patriarch replied, "Do you know? If Buddha-nature were permanent..."
What more need be said of good and evil dharmas? Even until the end of kalpas, not a single person would have given rise to the Bodhicitta.
Therefore, when I speak of impermanence, it is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the Way of True Permanence.
Furthermore, if all dharmas were merely impermanent, then every individual thing would possess its own self-nature that accommodates birth and death; yet, the nature of True Permanence exists.
Because it is not present in all places, what I call "permanent" is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.

The Buddha [taught this] because ordinary people and non-Buddhists cling to false permanence, while those of the two vehicles conceive of the permanent as impermanent; together, these constitute the eight inversions.
Therefore, within the definitive teachings on Nirvāṇa, he refutes those biased views and clearly expounds true permanence and true [emptiness].
The True Self is joyful, true, and pure. You now rely on the words while turning your back on the meaning;

by taking the cessation of impermanence as the certainty of eternal death, you have misinterpreted the Buddha’s perfectly wondrous and final subtle words. Even if you were to read them a thousand times, what benefit would there be?
Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor. He then spoke this verse: "Because I guarded against impermanence, the Buddha taught the nature of permanence.
Those who do not know the skillful means are like those picking up pebbles from a spring pond. Now, without applying effort, the Buddha-nature appears before me."
"It was not transmitted to me by a teacher, nor did I myself attain anything. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration; you should be named Zhiche (Voluntarily Penetrating).
The Master bowed in gratitude and departed.
Chan Master Zhichang of Xinzhou was originally from Guixi in that province. Having entered the monastic life at the age of seven, he was determined to realize the nature of his own being.
One day, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? What do you seek?

The Master replied, "I recently paid my respects to Chan Master Datong and received his instruction on the principle of realizing one's nature to attain Buddhahood; however, I have not yet resolved my doubts. Upon arriving in Ji... [text continues]
On the way, he encountered a man who pointed out his confusion and directed him to seek out the Abbot. He prostrated himself, praying: "I beseech you to bestow your compassion and accept me.

The Patriarch asked, "What words did he say? Try reciting them for me; I shall provide testimony for you. The Master replied, "When I first arrived there, three months had passed and I had not yet received any instruction.

Because my longing for the Dharma was so intense, I entered the abbot’s quarters alone during the middle of the night. I prostrated myself and entreated him with deep sorrow, saying: 'Great Penetration (Dàtōng)..."* *Note: The text here ends abruptly with "Dàtōng" (Great Penetration), which refers to Mazu Daoyi, the future master of this disciple.*
He then said, "Do you see empty space? He replied, "I see it. He asked, "Do you see empty space as having any form or appearance?
He replied, "Empty space is formless; what form or appearance could it have? He said, "Your own fundamental nature is like empty space."
Turning back to contemplate one's own nature, one realizes that not a single thing can be seen; this is called right view. Not a single thing can be known;

this is called true knowledge. There is no blue or yellow, long or short; seeing only the fundamentally pure essence of awakening, perfectly bright and luminous, is what is called "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.
It is also called the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and it is also called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. Although the student...
Having heard these words, he was still not fully resolved and requested instruction from the Master so that he might no longer be hindered by lingering doubts.

The Patriarch said, "The teacher’s explanation still retains a reliance on views and intellectual knowledge; that is why you have not yet attained understanding. I shall now show you a verse, which says:

'To see not a single dharma while maintaining the view of non-existence is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun. Not knowing a single dharma while guarding a knowledge of emptiness—'" [The text continues: "...is likewise obscured."
Like a flash of lightning arising in the great void, this knowing-and-seeing arises in an instant. How could such a mistaken recognition ever understand the skillful means?
You should, in a single thought, know for yourself that it is wrong; your own spiritual radiance is constantly manifest.

Upon hearing this verse, the Master’s mind was suddenly enlightened. He then composed a verse of his own, saying: "Groundlessly giving rise to conceptual understanding, One clings to marks in the pursuit of Bodhi. If one harbors such sentiments..."

I reflect on this awakening: how could it be that I am still lost as I was in the past? The source-body of self-nature is the wellspring of enlightenment; yet by following appearances, I have wandered through the flux of change.
Failing to enter the chamber of the Patriarchs, I remain bewildered, pursuing the two extremes.
Chan Master Zhidao of Guangzhou was a native of Nanhai.

Initially, he went to attend upon the Sixth Patriarch and asked, "Since I left the household life, I have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for over ten years, yet I have not yet clarified its great meaning. I pray that the Master will grant me instruction.
The Patriarch said, "What is it that you do not understand? He replied, "'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased...'"
"Quiescent extinction is bliss. Regarding this, he harbored doubts. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt it?
He replied, "All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the form-body and the dharma-body. The form-body is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing;
the dharma-body is permanent, without cognition or awareness. The Sūtra says, 'When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. I do not yet understand [this]."

What kind of body is this that is in nirvana? What kind of body experiences bliss? If it were the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then at the time of its extinction, the four great elements would disperse;
being entirely suffering (*duḥkha*), it could not be called bliss. If it were the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) in nirvana, it would be the same as grass, trees, tiles, or stones.

Who, then, would experience pleasure? Furthermore, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the essence of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the function of arising and ceasing.

The essence and its five functions constitute a single reality; thus, arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the essence; when there is cessation, the function is withdrawn back into the essence.

If one allows for further rebirth, then the class of sentient beings is neither interrupted nor extinguished. If one does not allow for further rebirth, then they would forever return [to extinction].
"Quiescence is identical to insentient matter. If this were so, then all dharmas would be suppressed by nirvana;
since they could not even arise, what joy would there be? The Patriarch said, "You are a son of the Śākyas.

Why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism, and discuss the Supreme Vehicle? According to your understanding, you believe that apart from the physical body, there exists [a separate self]."

The Dharmakāya is free from arising and ceasing; seek quiescence therein. Furthermore, regarding the words "Nirvana is eternal and blissful," if one claims there is a body that experiences them, this is merely clinging to birth and death and being addicted to worldly pleasures. You should now know that the Buddha [speaks thus] for the sake of all who are deluded.
They recognize the aggregation of the five aggregates as their own self-nature and discriminate all phenomena as external objects.
They take birth as good and death as evil, drifting through the flux of every thought-moment. Unaware that things are like dreams and illusions—empty and false—they undergo saṃsāra in vain.

Consequently, they perceive the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa as a state of suffering, spending their days in constant pursuit [of worldly things]. Out of compassion for them, the Buddha reveals the true bliss of nirvāṇa. Kṣetra...
That which has no characteristic of arising possesses, in each moment, no characteristic of ceasing; furthermore, there is nothing further to be extinguished through arising and ceasing.
This is quiescent extinction manifest before one. At the time it is manifest before one, there is also no measure of its being manifest before one.

This is called eternal bliss. This bliss has no recipient, nor is there anyone who does not receive it. How could there even be the names of "one substance" and "five functions," let alone anything more?
To say that *nirvāṇa* restrains and subdues all phenomena so that they never arise again is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse:
The unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa* is perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating. The ignorant and foolish call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation.
Those seeking the two vehicles regard it as non-action (*akṛta*). All these belong to the conceptualizations of the mind—the sixty-two views.
Fundamentally, one falsely establishes empty and provisional names; what, then, is the meaning of reality? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate this without grasping or rejecting.

By knowing that the phenomena of the five aggregates, as well as the "self" within the aggregates, and all external manifestations of forms and individual sounds and appearances, are equal to dreams and illusions, they do not give rise to views of ordinary or holy beings, nor do they form a conceptual understanding of nirvana. Regarding the two extremes and the three periods of time...
Severance. Constantly employing the functions of the sense-faculties, yet not giving rise to the notion of "functioning. Discerning all phenomena, yet not giving rise to the notion of "discernment.
When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and the winds strike the mountains together, the bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—the mark of *nirvāṇa*—is like this.
I now speak these words by force, so that you may abandon false views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you only a small portion [of the truth].
The Master heard the verse and leaped for joy; he paid his respects and withdrew.

The Chan Master Zhenjue of Yongjia, whose name was Xuangjue, was the son of the Dai family of that prefecture. He left home to become a monk at the age of seven and extensively explored the Tripiṭaka.
He mastered the perfect and subtle Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) and constantly practiced meditative contemplation in accordance with the four postures.
Later, inspired by the exhortation of Chan Master Zuo Xi Lang, he traveled together with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang to Caoxi.

Upon first arriving, he shook his monk’s staff, circumambulated the Patriarch three times, and stood there upright. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices.
From what direction have you come, Great Virtue, that you give rise to such great arrogance? The Master replied, "I have come."

"The matter of death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? To understand non-arising is to understand swiftness. The Master said, "Realizing is itself non-arising;
understanding is fundamentally without swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment.
The Master then assumed his formal demeanor and paid his respects. After a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Your return is very swift."

The Master said, "Fundamentally, there is no movement; how could there be speed? The Patriarch asked, "Who knows that there is no movement? The Master said, "You, O Benevolent One, yourself give rise to discrimination.
The Patriarch said, "You have truly grasped the meaning of non-arising. The Master said, "In non-arising, how could there be any meaning?

The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination? The Master said, "Even discrimination is not a matter of meaning. The Patriarch sighed in admiration and said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent! Excellent! Stay for one night. This is why he was called "The One-Night Enlightenment" (Yi-xiu-jue). The Master descended the mountain the following day and returned to Wenzhou.

Students gathered there like spokes converging at the hub. He composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) in one chapter, as well as the *Profound Meaning of Awakening and Cultivation in the Chan School*, which proceeds from the shallow to the profound.
Wei Jing, the Regional Inspector of Qingzhou, compiled these and wrote a preface, forming ten chapters, which were titled the *Yongjia*.

Collected and circulated together in the world. Chapter One: The Aspiration for the Way and the Ritual for Serving the Teacher. Now, one who wishes to practice the Way must first establish their resolve.

Furthermore, the ritual for serving the teacher clarifies the standard of training; therefore, this chapter is titled "The First: Clarifying the Ritual for Aspiring to the Way. Chapter Two: Guarding Against Arrogance and Extravagance.

Although one may initially establish the resolve to cultivate the Way and properly understand the ritual standards, if the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) are characterized by arrogance and extravagance, [the practice will fail].

When the mind is agitated, how can one attain meditative concentration? Therefore, secondly, the arrogance regarding ethical discipline (*śīla-mada*) is clarified. Thirdly, the purification of the three modes of action (*trikarma-pariśuddhi*) is explained.

While the previous section on the arrogance regarding ethical discipline provided a brief outline of the essential principles, this section now conducts a detailed examination and reproof so that coarse transgressions do not arise;
thus, thirdly, the purification of the three modes of action is clarified. Ethical discipline pertains to body, speech, and mind. *Śamatha-gāthā*.
Fourth: Having already examined and restrained body and speech so that gross transgressions do not arise, one must next enter the gate of the path of cultivation through its gradual stages.
This involves the five ways of arising the mind and the six types of discernment within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, the fourth section clarifies the verses on *śamatha*. The verses on *vipaśyanā* constitute the fifth. Without ethical discipline (*śīla*), there is no meditation; without meditation, there is no wisdom. Since the former [section] has already explained the practice...

Concentration (*samādhi*). When concentration is long-sustained, wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes clear; therefore, the fifth verse clarifies *vipaśyanā*. The sixth verse clarifies *yuganaddha* (the yoked pair).
If one practices concentration exclusively, it leads to sinking after a long duration; if one studies wisdom exclusively, the mind becomes restless due to an excess of wisdom.

Therefore, the sixth verse clarifies *yuganaddha*, bringing about equanimity between concentration and wisdom so that they do not sink or become restless, thereby making concentration and wisdom equal.

Abandoning the two extremes, one proceeds through the gradual stages of the Three Vehicles. When concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced, there is stillness while constantly illuminating.

With the three contemplations unified within a single mind, what doubt remains unremoved? What illumination remains incomplete? Although one’s own understanding is clear, one feels compassion for others who have not yet awakened.
Because there are varying depths of awakening, the seventh stage next clarifies the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles. Eighth, the non-duality of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*). Three.
Riding upon the awakening to principle, there is no principle that is not exhausted. The exhaustion of principle resides in phenomena; when phenomena are understood, they are themselves principle.
Therefore, the ninth section clarifies the non-duality of phenomena and principle, showing that phenomena are themselves the truth, in order to eliminate inverted views.

In the ninth "Letter of Exhortation to a Friend," since phenomena and principle have already been harmonized, the inner mind naturally becomes clear. Furthermore, one laments those who study afar and waste their precious moments; thus, the ninth section clarifies this.

This is a letter of exhortation to a friend. It is the tenth [section] of the *Pranidhāna-vākya* (Text on the Vow). Although the exhortation to a friend involves compassion for others, its focus is concentrated on a single object;
thus, the sentiment has not yet become universal. Therefore, the *Pranidhāna-vākya* follows next, clarifying the ten stages and vowing to deliver all beings.

The *Utpatti-śloka* (Verses on Origination) states briefly: "Furthermore, there are ten gates for contemplating the mind. The first describes its natural state (*dharmatā*); the second reveals its..."
1. Contemplating the essence; 2. Explaining the nature of reality; 3. Describing their mutual correspondence; 4. Warning against overweening pride; 5.

Admonishing negligence and indolence; 6. Reiterating the essence of contemplation; 7. Clarifying right and wrong; 8. Distinguishing the purport of the teachings; 9. Realizing contemplation in every encounter;
10. Wondrously acceding to the profound source. Regarding the first point, "the nature of things" (*dharmatā*): the nature of the mind is empty.
Pervasive. The source of movement and stillness is non-dual. True Suchness transcends thought; the conceptualizations of conditioned deliberation are not distinct from it.
When deluded views race about in confusion, one who exhausts them finds only a single tranquility. The spiritual source has no form; when reflected upon, it appears in a thousand differences.

Because these thousand differences are not the same, the name "Dharma-eye" is established. Because this single tranquility is not different [from the source], the title "Wisdom-eye" persists. Thus, principle and cognition are both present.
The merit of the Buddha-eye is fully realized. Thus, the three truths are one realm; the principle of the Dharmakāya is eternally pure. The three wisdoms are one mind;
the brilliance of Prajñā is eternally illuminating. Realm and wisdom merge in profound stillness, while the response of liberation accords with capacities.

It is neither vertical nor horizontal; the Way of the circular *i* (the character for "three") is a profound convergence. Therefore, know that the wondrous nature of the three virtues is perfectly harmonious and without discrepancy.
The mind is profound, vast, and inconceivable; what path of departure could possibly not be its way?
Therefore, those who take the mind itself as the Way may be said to have found the source by tracing the current. Second, regarding the essence of this contemplation:

one simply knows that a single thought-moment is both empty and non-empty, neither empty nor non-empty. Third, regarding its correspondence: when the mind corresponds with emptiness, then [criticism]—

When disparagement, praise, and fame are [seen as] empty, what is there to worry about and what is there to rejoice in? When the body corresponds with emptiness, then whether it is cut by a blade or smeared with incense, what suffering is there and what pleasure is there?
When the circumstantial retribution corresponds with emptiness, then whether there is giving or plundering, what is gained and what is lost?

When the mind corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, then attachment and views are entirely forgotten, and one universally saves through compassion. When the body corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, then...

Internally like withered wood, externally manifesting dignified deportment, when one’s conditioned environment corresponds to both emptiness and non-emptiness, craving and seeking are forever severed, and resources are provided for the relief of others.

When the mind corresponds to that which is neither empty nor non-empty, and neither not-empty nor not-not-empty, the true mark (dharmatā) is first clarified, and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened.
When the body corresponds to that which is neither empty nor non-empty, and neither not-empty nor not-not-empty, then [the path] is unified.
The sensory objects enter into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and from the various objects, one arises in samādhi.

When the conditioned environment corresponds with that which is empty, non-empty, neither empty nor non-empty, then the fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions adorn the land for those born through transformation. Fourth, this warns against those who harbor arrogance;
if it were otherwise, there would be no such correspondence. Fifth, this admonishes those who are negligent; however, to cross the sea, one must necessarily ascend.
A boat: if it were not a boat, how could one cross over? Cultivating the mind must involve entering into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); without contemplation, there is no means to clarify the mind.

As long as the mind is not yet clarified, when will you achieve realization (*yoga*)? Reflect on this and do not rely on your own conceit. This is the sixth section, which further elucidates the essence of emerging from contemplation.

One merely knows that a single thought is both empty and non-empty, neither existent nor non-existent; yet one does not know that this very thought is both empty and non-empty, neither "not-existent" nor "not-non-existent.
The seventh point clarifies what is correct and what is incorrect: the mind is not existent, the mind is not non-existent, the mind is not "not-existent," and the mind is not "not-non-existent.
To hold that it is existent or non-existent is to fall into the error of affirmation; to hold that it is neither existent nor non-existent is likewise to fall into the error of negation.

This immediately falls into "non-being. Thus, this is merely the "non" of being and non-being; it has not yet reached the "is" that is neither being nor non-being, nor the "is" that transcends both being and non-being.

Now, by means of the double negation (ubhayābhāva), one destroys both forms of "being," whereby "being" itself is destroyed as "non-being. Furthermore, by means of the double negation, one destroys both forms of "non-being."
It is neither negation nor non-negation; it is precisely "is. Such an "is" is merely the "is" that is neither "is" nor "non-is.

It has not yet reached the state of being neither "non-is" nor "not non-is," nor the state of being neither "not is" nor "not not is. This delusion regarding "is" and "non-is" is subtle and difficult to perceive;

only when the spirit is clear and the mind is tranquil can one examine it minutely. Regarding the eighth section, which clarifies the essential meaning: although the ultimate truth is wordless, it is provisionally expressed through written words.

Words are used to clarify the intent; the intent, however, is the fundamental principle (*zong*), not the contemplation itself. One relies upon the practice of contemplation to realize that fundamental principle.
If the intent is not clarified, then the words are not precise; if the fundamental principle is not realized, then the contemplation is not profound.

Only through profound contemplation does one realize the fundamental principle, and only through precise words can the intent be clarified. Once both the intent and the fundamental principle have been clarified and realized, how could words and contemplation still persist?

[Response: It is false. As for the ninth point, "forming contemplation wherever one encounters [phenomena]": to restate the words and re-emphasize the essence of contemplation is intended to clarify that the fundamental principle (*zong*) is no different;

it is merely that the expression of "contemplation" shifts according to the direction. To shift the words does not mean the principle differs; to change the term "contemplation" does not mean the essence of contemplation changes.

This non-different essence is precisely the principle, and this undifferentiated principle is precisely the fundamental principle (*zong*). Thus, the fundamental principle and its essence are one, though expressed as two.
The title: "Contemplating Clarity" serves merely as an introductory prelude. Regarding the tenth section, "Miraculously Accordance with the Profound Source":

Now, a practitioner who has awakened to the mind would never cling to contemplation while remaining lost to the ultimate meaning; how could one who has mastered the teachings remain stagnant in words while being deluded about the principle?

When the principle is clarified, the path of speech is severed—what words can possibly discuss it? When the meaning is realized, the sphere of mental activity ceases—what contemplation can possibly conceive of it?
That which cannot be conceived by mind or expressed in words may be called a wondrous resonance with the center of the circle.

On the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Tianxian era, he sat peacefully and manifested his passing. He was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of West Mountain. He was posthumously titled Great Master Wuxiang (Formless), and his stupa was named Jingguang (Pure Light).
The nun Xuanji of Jingju in Wenzhou received the full precepts during the Jingyun era of the Tang dynasty. She frequently practiced meditative concentration within a stone grotto on Mount Dayi.

One day, she suddenly thought to herself: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly still; fundamentally, there is neither going nor staying. To loathe clamor and seek quietude is [a delusion]."
Could this be considered attaining realization? He then went to visit Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "From Dayu Mountain. Xuefeng said, "Has the sun risen yet? The Master said, "If it had risen, it would have melted away Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "What is your name?"
The Master said, “The profound mechanism. Xuefeng asked, “How much do you weave each day? The Master said, “Not a single thread hangs [upon me]. He then bowed and withdrew.

After he had walked only three or five paces, Xuefeng called out, “The corner of your *kāṣāya* is trailing on the ground! The Master turned his head; Xuefeng said, “Truly excellent—‘not a single thread hangs [upon you]’!

(Tradition holds that Xuanyi was the younger sister of the Great Master of Yongjia and once traveled with him; this is confirmed by examining the dates of the Jingyun era. However, the Xuefeng she encountered was not [the same one as the one in the current record].)
The True Awakening still exists. Once Yongjia arrived at Caoxi, he was surely a snow peak atop the ridge. His dharma lineage is not detailed; therefore, he is appended here).
Chan Master Benjing of Mount Sikong was a native of Jizhou. His surname was Zhang. Having donned the black robes at a young age, he received a prediction of enlightenment in the hall of Caoxi.

He was affiliated with Wuxiang Monastery on Mount Sikong. In the third year of the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Xuanzong dispatched the palace messenger Yang Guangting into the mountains to gather evergreen vines;
he subsequently constructed a hall for the master. Upon paying his respects and inquiring after him, the Emperor said: "Your younger brother..."

"You have pursued the Way for such a long time. I pray that the Venerable One will, out of compassion, grant me a brief instruction. The Master said, "The eminent scholars of the Chan school throughout the empire have all assembled in the capital.
Since you are returning to court as an imperial envoy, you should consult them there for resolution. This poor monk dwells by the mountains and beside the waters."

He had no intention of using his mind [for formal ritual]. Guangting prostrated himself in tears. The Master said, "Cease your worship of this poor monk. Does the celestial messenger seek the Buddha, or does he seek the Way?
He replied, "Your disciple’s intellect and knowledge are dark and dull; I do not yet understand the meaning of 'Buddha' and 'the Way'."
The Master said, "If you wish to seek the Buddha, the very mind is the Buddha. If you wish to realize the Way, no-mind is the Way. [The student] asked, "In what sense is the very mind the Buddha?
The Master said, "The Buddha is realized through the mind; the mind is manifested by the Buddha. If one realizes no-mind, even the Buddha does not exist.
[The student] asked, "In what sense is no-mind the Way? The Master said, "The Way is fundamentally no-mind; no-mind is called the Way."

"If one realizes there is no mind, no-mind is itself the Way. Guangting prostrated himself and accepted this with faith. Upon returning to the imperial court, he reported in detail all that he had encountered in the mountains.
The Emperor immediately issued an edict for Guangting to summon the Master to the capital and commanded him to reside at Bailian Pavilion.

On the fifteenth day of the first month of the following year, the Emperor summoned the eminent monks and great scholars of the two monastic districts to attend the Inner Sanctuary (Neidaochang) to join the Master.

As he was expounding the Buddha’s principles, there was a Chan Master named Yuan who raised his voice and said to him, “Now that we are before His Majesty to deliberate upon our fundamental tenets, we ought to ask and answer directly without resorting to flowery language. According to what you, Master, perceive, what do you take to be the Way?
The Master replied, “A mindless state is the Way. Yuan said, “The Way arises because of the mind; how can you say it is mindless?”
“This is the Way. The Master said, “The Way is fundamentally nameless; it is because of the mind that the Way is named. If the name ‘mind’ were real, then the Way would not be empty.
Since the mind, when investigated to its limit, is non-existent, upon what could the Way be established? Both are equally illusory; they are all merely provisional names.
Yuan said, “Does the Chan Master see that body and mind are already the Way? The Master said, “This mountain monk’s body and mind have been the Way from the very beginning. Yuan said, “...”
"Previously you said that 'mindlessness is the Way. Now you say again that 'body and mind are originally the Way. Are these not contradictory? The Master said:
"Mindlessness is the Way because when the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent. Mind and the Way are one and the same; therefore, it is said that 'mindlessness is the Way.
That 'body and mind are originally the Way' means that the Way is also originally body and mind. Since the original nature of body and mind is empty, the Way is likewise exhausted."
Yuan said, "There is no source. Yuandong remarked, "Master Guan’s physical form is quite small, yet he understands this principle.
The Master said, "Virtuous One, you see only my physical appearance; you do not see my formlessness. To see the appearance is what you, Virtuous One, perceive.
As the Sutra says: 'All that has appearance is entirely illusory. If one sees all appearances as non-appearance, then one sees the Way. If...
"Taking marks as real, one cannot see the Way even after the exhaustion of kalpas. Dàoyuán said, "I now request that the Chan Master explain the markless upon the basis of marks.
The Master replied, "The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: 'The four great elements have no master; the body likewise has no self. To be free from the view of 'mine' is to be in accord with the Way.
Venerable Sir, if you hold that the four great elements have a master who is the 'self,' and if you possess the view of a self, then even after the exhaustion [of kalpas]..."
"Kie (Jiaye) could not comprehend the Way. Upon hearing the words from afar, he turned pale with fear; hesitating, he rose from his seat to withdraw. The Master had a verse that said:
"The four elements have no master and are like water; Meeting curves or encountering straightness, there is neither 'self' nor 'other. In both the pure and the defiled, the mind does not arise."
"Blocking or diverting [the flow] has never had two intentions; when touching objects, it is merely like water being without mind. Moving freely through the world, what matter is there?
It further says: 'The one great element is thus; the four great elements are likewise. If one understands that the four great elements have no master, one immediately awakens to the state of no-mind.
If one realizes no-mind, one naturally accords with the Way. Master Zhiming asked: "If you say that no-mind is the Way..."

"Even mindless rubble should be the Way," he said. Furthermore, he said, "Body and mind are fundamentally the Way. Since all four modes of birth and ten classes of beings possess body and mind, they too should be the Way.
The Master said, "If you, Great Virtue, understand this through the conceptualization of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing..."
This is far removed from the Way; it is the pursuit of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, rather than the pursuit of the Way itself. As the Sutra says:
"If one lacks the six sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—there is still no seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Upon what, then, could these be established?"
When one exhaustively investigates the root and finds it does not exist, where can the mind abide? How could one not be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles?
Ming Du’kou withdrew. The Master had a verse that said: “Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction; Sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena are always in samādhi.
Like a bird flying through the air, simply so it goes; Without grasping or rejecting, without hatred or love. If you understand that at the very point of response there is fundamentally no mind,”
