Seeing that the first seat was unoccupied, the King asked for the reason. Venerable Sāgaramati replied, "This is the seat of Piṇḍola;
this man has recently come to see the Buddha. The King asked, "Where is he now? The Venerable replied, "Wait a moment."
"Yū. Having finished speaking, Piṇḍola descended from the sky. The king invited him to take a seat and paid him homage, but he did not look back.
The king then asked, "I have heard that you personally saw the Buddha come; is this true? The elder raised his eyebrows with his hand and said, "Do you understand?
The king said, "I do not understand. The elder said, "The Nāga King of Lake Anavatapta once invited the Buddha for a meal. At that time, I—"
He was also included among their number.
For a thousand years, the Obstructing Demon King (Māra), leading his retinue, followed the Bodhisattva Vajrasama, searching for the place where he had arisen, but could not find it.
Suddenly one day, he saw him and asked: "Upon what do you rely for your dwelling? I have followed you for a thousand years..."
When he sought the place from which you arise, he could not find it. Qi said, "I do not abide by abiding in existence, nor do I abide by abiding in non-existence;
I abide in this manner."

Prince Naci dismembered his flesh to return it to his mother and his bones to return them to his father; thereafter, manifesting his true form, he exercised his great supernatural powers to preach the Dharma for his parents.
Chan Master Qin Baotuo asked Dharma Master Sheng, "Which sutras or treatises do you lecture on? Sheng replied, "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The Master asked, "How do you explain the meaning of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? Sheng said, "'Form' refers to the aggregation of many atoms; 'emptiness' refers to those atoms having no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Master asked, "Before the atoms have aggregated, what would you call them? Sheng was at a loss for an answer. The Master asked again, "What other [scriptures] do you lecture on?"
The scripture says, "The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. The Master asked, "How do you explain the meaning of nirvāṇa?
He replied, "'Nir' means non-arising; 'vāṇa' means non-extinction. Because it is neither arising nor extinction, it is called nirvāṇa.
The Master asked, "Which of these is the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, and which is the Dharma-master’s nirvāṇa? He replied, "As for the meaning of nirvāṇa, how could there be two? [I am] Somaka."
"It is exactly like this. I do not yet understand how you, Master Chan, explain nirvana. The Master picked up his *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) and asked, "Do you see it?
The monk replied, "I see it. The Master said, "What do you see? The monk replied, "I see the *ruyi* in the Master's hand.
The Master threw the *ruyi* to the ground and asked, "Do you see it? The monk replied, "I see it. The Master said, "What do you see? The monk replied, "I see the Master's hand."
As he was about to drop the gong, the Master rebuked him, saying, "Judging by your understanding, you have not yet emerged from the common stream.

How can you claim your fame shall resound throughout the universe? He then brushed his sleeves and departed. His disciples remained in doubt and pursued the Master to question him, saying, "Our teacher’s explanation of form, emptiness, and nirvana did not accord with our understanding;
we do not know how the Chan Master explains the meaning of form and emptiness. The Master replied, "I did not say..."

"What your teacher says is incorrect. Your teacher only understands the emptiness of form within the fruit [of enlightenment], but he does not understand how to explain the emptiness of form within the cause.
His disciples asked, "What is the emptiness of form within the cause? The Master said, "Because a single atom is empty, many atoms are empty;
because many atoms are empty, a single atom is empty. Within the emptiness of a single atom, there are no many atoms; within the emptiness of many atoms..."
Wu-yiwei. At the beginning, Master Baozhi was the son of Zhu, the wife of a commoner in Dongyang, Jinling. On the Shangsi festival day, she heard a child crying in an eagle’s nest;
she climbed the tree and retrieved him, raising him as her own son. At the age of seven, he followed the śramaṇa Seng at Mount Zhongshan.

Jian left the household life and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation. In the second year of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he shaved his hair and went barefoot, wearing a brocade robe, as he traveled back and forth beneath Mount Xuan and the Jian River.
He carried a pair of scissors, a whisk, and a staff, slinging them over his head as he walked.

In the second year of the Tianjian era, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an edict asking him: "I, your disciple, have not yet eliminated my afflictions and delusions; how should I treat them? He replied: [text missing]
12. The Emperor asked what its meaning was. He replied, "It is within the time-measurements and the divisions of the day recorded in the written characters.

The Emperor understood this even less. Once, the Emperor issued an edict for the painter Zhang Sengyou to paint the Master’s likeness. Whenever Zhang Sengyou set his brush to the work, he could not determine how to proceed.
The Master then used his finger to scratch across his face, revealing the wondrous and exquisite features of the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara.
Whether it was his benevolence or his majesty, Lu Tanwei could not capture it in painting. On another day, while he and the Emperor were gazing out over the river, an object came floating upstream.
The Master pointed his staff toward it, and it followed the direction of the staff; it was a piece of purple sandalwood.

He immediately entrusted it to the court official Yu Shao, ordering him to carve a statue of the Master. It was completed in an instant, its spirit and countenance appearing as if alive. The Master asked:
A certain Brahman monk said, "I have heard that the Venerable One calls me a butcher. Have you ever seen me kill a living being? The Master replied, "I have.

The monk asked, "Was it a seeing with seeing, a seeing without seeing, or a seeing that is neither existent nor non-existent? If it was a seeing with seeing, that is the vision of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

If it was a seeing without seeing, that is the vision of a *śrāvaka*. If it was a seeing that is neither existent nor non-existent, that is the vision of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). I do not yet understand, Venerable Sir..."
"How do you see it? The Indian monk replied, "Do you have such a view as this? [Fenyang] said, "It was not in vain that he came from the West. The Master gave these turning words:
"All day long one picks up incense and selects firewood, yet one does not realize that the body itself is the site of enlightenment (dōjō).

He further said, "The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet for all its importance, it is difficult to behold within the immediate presence. If you wish to recognize the true substance of the Great Way, it is not apart from sound, form, and speech. Furthermore:
He said: "The capital and the city of Ye—this vast expanse is indeed the Great Path of Bodhi. (Fayan said: "The capital and the city of Ye—this vast expanse is not the Great Path of Bodhi.")
The Great Being Shanhui was a native of Yiwu County in Wuzhou.

On the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty (the Dingchou year), he descended at Shuanglin Village. He was originally named Xi, according to the tradition of the Cixi family.
At the age of sixteen, he took as his wife a woman of the Liu clan named Miaoguang, with whom he fathered two sons, Pujian and Pucheng. At twenty-four, together with a fellow villager from Jiting...

He was fishing by straining the water through a net. Having caught some fish, he submerged a basket in the water and made this vow: "Those who wish to go, may they depart; those who wish to stay, may they remain. Some people called him foolish.
Later, a monk from India named Sthūlamata said to him, "I and you both made a vow before the Buddha Vipaśyin.
The robes and alms bowl in the Tuṣita Heaven still exist there. On what day shall we return? He then ordered [the fisherman] to look at his reflection in the water, whereupon he saw—
Yuan Guang held up a jeweled canopy and the Great Being smiled, saying to him: "The forge produces many pieces of dull iron; the gate of a skilled physician is filled with the sick.
Saving sentient beings is the urgent task—why dwell on that pleasure? Sheng pointed to the summit of Mount Song and said, "This is a place where one may dwell.
The Great Being personally tilled the soil and lived there. When someone stole beans, wheat, melons, or fruit, the Great Being immediately...
He took [the offerings] away in a basket. During the day he engaged in manual labor; at night he practiced the Way (*caryā*).
He saw the three Tathāgatas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—emanating light that enveloped his body. The Great Being then said, "I have attained the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.
In the second year of the Tianjia era, seven Buddhas appeared following him: Śākyamuni led the way and Vimalakīrti followed behind; only the World-Honored One Śākyamuni looked back repeatedly.

They conversed together. [The Master said: "I am the one who shall succeed me. Atop that mountain, yellow clouds swirled like a canopy; thus it was named Mount Yellow Clouds (Yunhuang Shan). Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty invited him to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As soon as the Master ascended the seat, he struck once with his staff and immediately descended. The Emperor was astonished. The Holy Master asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. The Holy Master said: *The Dharma is not something that can be grasped by the mind or intellect; it is beyond words and speech. It is like empty space—vast, boundless, and without form. To seek it through conceptual thought is to miss its true nature.* [The Master then recited:

"Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. Emptiness is no other than form; form is no other than emptiness. The same is true for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The Emperor, having heard this, attained great realization. He bowed deeply and withdrew. The Master remained seated, silent and unmoving. The Emperor departed, his heart filled with profound reverence. The Master then returned to his quarters.

This was the first time the Emperor had witnessed such a direct manifestation of the Buddha's teaching. From that day forward, the Emperor’s devotion to the Way deepened immeasurably. He subsequently issued an edict throughout the realm to propagate the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings and to provide support for the Sangha. Thus, the influence of the Master spread far and wide, benefiting both the state and the Dharma. His legacy remains a testament to the power of sudden enlightenment and the ineffable nature of ultimate reality.

When the Great Being had finished preaching the sutra, on another day while he was in the midst of preaching, the Emperor arrived. The entire assembly rose, but the Master alone sat upright and did not move.
An attendant reported, "The Imperial carriage is here; why do you not rise? The Master replied, "If the ground of the Dharma were to move, [then I would move]."
Everything was in a state of unrest. One day, the Great Being (Daisō) appeared for an audience with the Emperor, wearing his patched robe (*nāṃha*), a crown upon his head, and slippers on his feet.
The Emperor asked, "Is this a monk? The Great Being pointed to his crown. The Emperor said, "Is this the Way (*dō*)? The Great Being pointed to his slippers. The Emperor said, "Is this a layman?
The Great Being pointed to his patched robe. The Great Being’s *Mind-King Inscription* (*Shin'ōmei*) says: "Contemplate the Mind, the Empty King; it is profound and mysterious."
It is unfathomable. Formless and signless, it possesses great spiritual power capable of extinguishing a thousand calamities and accomplishing ten thousand virtues.

Although its essential nature is empty, it can bestow the Dharma-ordinances. When observed, it has no form; when called upon, it has sound. It acts as the Great General of the Dharma, transmitting the scriptures through the mind-precepts.
Like the taste of salt in water or the presence of blue pigment within lacquer, it is definitively existent, yet its form is not seen. This is the Mind-King.
It is likewise so. Dwelling within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face, it responds to objects and follows conditions with sovereign unimpededness;

all that is done is accomplished. One realizes the fundamental consciousness-mind (*ālayavijñāna*); the consciousness-mind sees the Buddha. This mind is the Buddha, and this Buddha is the mind. In every thought-moment, there is the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.
If you wish to achieve success early, let the mind of precepts discipline itself; purify the precepts and purify the mind. The mind is...
This is the Buddha. Apart from this mind-king, there is no other Buddha. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Upon entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood by sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way should observe their own mind; knowing that the Buddha is within, they do not seek him outwardly. This very mind—

This is precisely the Buddha; this is precisely the Buddha, which is precisely the mind. When the mind clearly recognizes the Buddha, it thoroughly understands the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind.
That which is not the Buddha cannot be fathomed; it is incapable of any function. To cling to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence is to drift and sink within this state.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace of mind in this. The Great Being who clarifies the mind awakens to this profound resonance. The nature of body and mind is wondrous; its functioning is without limit.
It changes. Therefore, the wise let the mind rest in its natural freedom; do not say that the "King of the Mind" is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
It is that which can cause the physical body to act either wrongly or rightly; it is neither existent nor non-existent, appearing and disappearing without fixed certainty.

The nature of the mind transcends emptiness; it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely. For this reason, I urge you: guard yourself well. Every moment of action leads once again to drifting and sinking. [Only through] purity...
The mind-intellect is like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind. This unconditioned jewel of the Dharma is neither shallow nor deep.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized this original mind; those with the karmic affinity to encounter it do so beyond the categories of past, future, and present.

As a verse says: "Night after night, one sleeps embracing the Buddha; Morning after morning, one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, they are ever in attendance; In speech and silence, they dwell together."
"Cease! Not even a hair’s breadth apart; they are like a shadow and its form. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech.
He also said: "Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; walking, one rides a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge;

the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. And he said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally still and vast. It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena."
It does not wither along with the four seasons. The Verse on the Four Marks says: Birth, aging, illness, and death.
Consciousness rests upon the rising of floating bubbles; birth comes from craving and desire. In former times one was once grown, yet today one is again an infant.

Star-like eyes follow people as they turn; vermilion lips open toward the breast. Out of pity for those who lose their awakened nature, one returns once more to undergo saṃsāra. Beholding one’s own reflection in the mirror...
Alas! My strength has failed as I ascend the steps. How lamentable that I have now grown old; my bowing and prostrations are no longer perfect.
My body is like a tree on a precipice; my mind is like a tortoise longing for water. Yet I still indulge in outflows (*āsrava*), refusing to study the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Suddenly struck by a deep-seated malady, I have thus become one who lies ill in bed. My wife and children grieve in silence; my friends weary of my presence. A thousand piercing pains tear at me.
The pulse falters; groans resound through the four neighboring houses. Unaware of the perils of the path ahead, one still indulges in greed and anger.
The vital spirit follows the road of birth, while the wandering soul enters the barrier of death. One hears only of millions departing, yet sees not a single person returning.
The fine steed stands neighing in vain; the flowers of the courtyard can never again be plucked. Seek the Unsurpassed Way early, and you shall surely escape the mountains of the four quarters.
Chan Master Huisi of Nanyue was the son of Li of Wujin. Because Master Zhigong sent someone to deliver this message to him, saying:
"Why do you not go down the mountain to transform sentient beings? Why do you merely gaze at the clouds and the Milky Way? The Master replied:

"The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all been swallowed by me in a single mouth; where else could there be any sentient beings to be transformed? He addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of the Way is not..."
Far? The ocean of nature is not distant; simply seek it within yourself and do not look for it elsewhere. To seek it is to fail to find it; even if found, it would not be real. A verse says:
Sudden awakening to the source of the mind opens the treasure-store; The hidden and the manifest, with spiritual penetration, reveal the true aspect.
Walking alone or sitting alone, one is eternally majestic; A hundred billion transformation bodies are beyond measure. Even if they were to fill the void of space, when looked upon—
Not a trace of even a speck of dust is seen; this laughable thing is beyond all comparison. From the mouth it emits a bright pearl, its light shimmering and radiant.
What is commonly seen and spoken of is inconceivable. A single word marks the name, falling directly upon the ground. It is further said: "Heaven cannot cover it, nor can earth support it.
There is no going and no coming, no obstruction. There is no long and no short, no blue and no yellow. It does not abide in the middle."
Regarding both the internal and external, he transcends the multitudes and stands out from the crowd in the vast, profound void. Pointing to objects to transmit the mind, people do not understand.
The Zen Master Zhizhe of Xiuchan Temple on Mount Tiantai was named Zhiyi; he was the son of the Chen family of Huarong in Jingzhou.
While at Mount Nanyue, he was reciting the Lotus Sūtra. Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Medicine King," it said: "This is true diligence;
this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. Thereupon, he awakened to the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and attained the Dhāraṇī of Revolving.
He beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as solemnly present as if it had never dispersed.
When someone asked the Great Sage Sengqie of Sizhou, "What is your surname? the Master replied, "The surname He. [The questioner] asked, "What country are you from?
The Master replied, "The country He.
Zen Master Fenggan of Mount Tiantai was once asked by Hanshan: "How can an ancient mirror illuminate when it has not yet been polished?"
The Master said, "An ice pitcher has no reflection; a monkey reaches for the moon in the water. They replied, "This is not illuminating.
"Please speak further," the Master requested. The Master said, "Since you do not bring forth the myriad virtues, what am I to teach you?
Hanshan and Shigede both paid their respects and withdrew. The Master wished to travel to Mount Wutai and asked Hanshan and Shigede, "Will you go with me to visit?"
"Mount Wutai is where my fellow practitioners reside. If you do not go with me to travel to Mount Wutai, you are not one of my fellow practitioners.
The mountain said, "What would you do by traveling to Mount Wutai? The Master said, "To pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The mountain said, "Then you are not one of my fellow practitioners.
Thereupon, the Master entered Mount Wutai alone. He encountered an old man who stepped back and asked, "Are you not Mañjuśrī?"
He asked, "How can there be two Mañjuśrīs? Before the Master had finished his prostration and risen, [Mañjuśrī] suddenly vanished. Zhaozhou spoke on his behalf, saying, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī."
While the monks at Mount Tiantai were roasting eggplants, Hanshan took a skewer of eggplants and struck one monk on the back.
As the monk turned his head, Hanshan held up the skewer and asked, "What is this? The monk replied, "This madman!
Hanshan then said to a nearby monk, "Tell me, how much salt and vinegar did this monk cost me? This was because of Zhaozhou.
While traveling on the road to Mount Tiantai, they met by chance. The mountain monk saw the footprints of an ox and asked National Teacher Zhou, "Does the Venerable recognize this ox?
Zhou said, "I do not recognize it. The mountain monk pointed to the ox tracks and said, "These are the tracks of five hundred arhats traveling through the mountains.
Zhou said, "If they are arhats, why have they turned into oxen? The mountain monk cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! Zhou laughed heartily.
[Zhaozhou] laughed. Shanshan asked, "What are you doing? Zhaozhou said, "Heaven! Heaven! Shanshan said, "This fellow truly possesses the bearing of a great man."
One day, Shide was sweeping the floor at Mount Tiantai. The Abbot asked him, "Your name is Shide, which means 'Picked Up.
When Fenggan picked you up and brought you here, what exactly was your surname? Shide dropped his broom and stood with his hands joined in a gesture of respect.
The Abbot asked again; Shide picked up his broom and swept the floor as he left. Hanshan beat his breast and cried out, "Heaven!"
"O Blue Heaven! Shide said, "What are you doing? Shan replied, "Has it not been said that when a member of one household dies, the members of another household offer their condolences?
The two men danced, laughing and weeping, as they departed. At Guoqing Temple, the assembly gathered for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts.
Shide clapped his hands and said, "You all sit together with your minds on thoughts; what is that matter? The Rector (Weina) rebuked him. Shide said, "Great Virtue!"
Furthermore, abiding in non-anger is itself the precepts; a pure mind is itself the renunciant life. My nature merges with yours;
all dharmas are without distinction.
The monk Pùtòu of Fènghuà County in Míngzhōu called himself Qìchǐ. His physical form was stout and fleshy... (nuózuì/núzuì).
With a furrowed brow and a protruding belly, his speech was erratic and he slept wherever he happened to be. He constantly carried a cloth bag and a tattered mat upon a staff.
All his personal belongings were stored within that bag. When entering markets or villages, he would beg for whatever he saw;

even when receiving items such as vinegar, fish sauce, or pickled fish, he would take only a small portion into his mouth before casting the rest into his bag. At that time, he was known as Changting.
One day, a monk was walking in front of the Master. The Master patted him on the back, and as the monk turned his head, the Master said, "I beg of you one wen of coin.
The monk replied, "If you can speak it, I will give you one wen. The Master then set down his cloth bag and stood with his hands crossed.
When Monk Bailu asked, "What is this cloth bag? the Master immediately set down his cloth bag. [Bailu] asked, "What is this? (The Master remained silent.)
"This is the business of a sack-carrying monk," the Master said, and he departed carrying it. Previously, when Master Baofu asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
the Master dropped his sack and stood with palms joined. Baofu said, "Is it only this? Or is there something further beyond this?
The Master then departed carrying it. While the Master was standing on the street, a monk asked, "Master, why are you standing here?"
"What are you doing? The Master said, "I am waiting for someone. [The monk] said, "He has come! He has come! (Master Niu-tou Huai-jang said, "Go back! Go back! The Master said:
"You are not this person. [The monk] asked, "What is this person? The Master said, "Beg me for a single coin.
The Master had a song which said: "This very mind, mind is the Buddha; The most spiritual thing in the worlds of the ten directions.
Its wondrous functions, manifest in all ways, are truly pitiable; Nothing compares to the reality of the mind. Leisurely and self-possessed, there is nothing to do; At ease..."
Tranquil is the ultimate state of one who has left the household life. If you behold the true Great Way before your eyes, not seeing even a hair’s breadth of it is truly marvelous.
How can the myriad dharmas differ, and how can the mind be otherwise? Why trouble yourself further to seek the meaning of the scriptures? The King of Mind is fundamentally beyond manifold knowledge;
the wise person simply clarifies the stage of no-learning. Being neither sage nor ordinary—how could it be otherwise? Do not force yourself to discriminate between the sacred and the profane.

Lonely in spirit. The priceless jewel of the mind is fundamentally perfect and pure; all that appears as diverse forms is but empty delusion. It is man who can propagate the Way, for the Way is clearly manifest.
Infinite purity and loftiness are what the Way’s nature is called. If you carry your staff and ascend the roads of your former kingdom, do not worry that the sound will not be heard in every place.
Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "In this world, likes, dislikes, attachments, and aversions abound. If one reflects upon them carefully..."
What can I do? I shall broaden my capacity and practice patience; I shall open my heart and let things take their course.
If I encounter a kindred spirit, I shall accord with them; even if I meet an enemy, I shall dwell in harmony.

If one can resolve these matters of the mind, one will naturally realize the six *pāramitās*. I have a cloth bag, as vast and unobstructed as space; when spread out, it pervades the ten directions. Enter!
At that time, Avalokiteśvara, I have a Hall of the Three Jewels. Its interior is empty and devoid of form or appearance; it is neither high nor low, neither obstructed nor hindered.
Those who study it find no likeness within themselves, and those who come find its model difficult to replicate. Only one in a thousand craftsmen possesses the wisdom to arrange it.
From its four gates, the four fruits arise, and all throughout the ten directions offer worship. I have a single image of the Buddha, which exists in the world...
No one recognizes it. It is neither molded nor adorned; neither carved nor engraved. There is not a single drop of plaster, nor a speck of color.
A person may try to paint it but cannot succeed; a thief may try to steal it but cannot take it. Its physical form is inherently natural; its purity requires no wiping away.
Though it is but a single body, it manifests in hundreds of thousands of millions of forms. Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "A single bowl..."
A meal from a thousand households; a solitary body wandering ten thousand *li*. With azure eyes beholding few people, he asks the way at the head of white clouds.

In the third month of the Bingzi year, the third year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty (916 CE), the Master was about to manifest his passing. At the eastern corridor of Yue-lin Temple, he sat upright upon a flat rock and spoke this verse:
"Maitreya, the true Maitreya, Manifests himself as hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies. From time to time, he reveals the time."
People of the time did not recognize him themselves. When the verse was finished, he passed away peacefully through transformation.
Subsequently, he reappeared in another province, likewise walking while carrying a cloth bag. The fourfold assembly vied with one another to paint his image.
Fahua Zhi was the son of the Xu family of Shouchun. In his early twenties, he traveled to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang), where he subsequently received full ordination at Qijuzhi Monastery.
He remained there for a long time attending lectures. One day, while reading the *Record of Yunmen*, he suddenly attained awakening. Before long, his past lives became clear to him;
he would speak to himself and laugh alone, his lips moving as if in conversation, never ceasing throughout the day. It was said that he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He was named accordingly. When Prime Minister Lü Xǔgōng asked about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, the Master said:
"Originally there is not a single thing; in this single flavor, one attains perfection. When Jíxiān Wángzhèn asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
the Master said: "Within the shadows of the green mountains, a deep blue surge rises; the precious pagoda chants aloud, shaking in the morning breeze. He also said: "Please recite the *Lotus Sūtra*."
[The Master] was burning incense. The Master said, "Do not seek it through the observance of precepts; do not seek it from the Buddha.
Xu Yue, Assistant Instructor at the National Academy, asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "That which is on the eastern side of the street.

Xu said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Three kinds of people cannot understand it. A monk asked, "Does the Buddha exist in this world? The Master said, "Wen-shu is in the temple. There he is.
A questioner asked, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? He then raised his hand and said, "I do not dwell here.

On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of the Wuzi year of the Qingli era, as he was about to pass away, he said to those around him, "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have perfected the land of Jetavana and manifested my body to propagate the teachings.
Now I am returning south. Having finished speaking, he passed away lying on his right side.

Koubing Zaoxian was a son of the Weng clan of Xin’feng in Jian’ning, who was a descendant of ancient Buddhas. His mother dreamed of a bhikṣu with a radiant and majestic countenance, carrying a *khakkhara* staff and seeking lodging.
People pointed him out and said, "This is a Pratyekabuddha. Shortly thereafter, she became pregnant. He was born in the fourth year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong;
a fragrant mist filled the room and did not dissipate for days. At the age of thirteen, he requested to leave the household life, but his parents...
He granted permission. He took Xingfu Temple on Mount Wu as his home and took Xingquan as his preceptor. In the year of Yiyou during the Xiantong era, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

Initially, he was sought after by the assembly for his lecturing; however, he abandoned that path to visit Xuefeng. Carrying a bundle of *fuzi* (tuberous roots) and a jar of sauce in his hands, he presented them to him.
Xuefeng asked, "What is in this bundle? The Master replied, "Fuzi. Xuefeng asked, "Where did you get these?"
The Master said, “I found it in the mud. Feng asked, “How deep is the mud? The Master said, “It is several *zhang* deep. Feng asked, “Is there anything else besides this?
He replied, “The more one goes, the deeper it becomes. Feng then asked, “What is in the vessel? He replied, “Soy sauce. Feng asked, “Where did you get it from?
He replied, “I made it myself. Feng asked, “Is it still hot? He replied, “Not by much. Feng marveled at him, saying, “You...”
"He will surely become a king in the future. Later, the Master returned from Ehu to settle in a hermitage at Wenzhiling (now the Yongfeng Temple).
He subsequently resided at Jiangjun Rock, where two tigers attended him by his side. A divine being offered the land, and it became Ruiyan Monastery, where students gathered in great numbers.
He once said to the assembly, "The ancient sages practiced their cultivation by relying on rigorous austerity. Now, in summer I wear paper garments, and in winter I bathe by striking the ice.
Therefore, the people of the world call me the 'Ancient Buddha Who Strikes the Ice. Later, while residing at Lingyao, he ascended the hall; the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds.
He asked, "What shall I, an old monk, say? and immediately descended from the seat. There was a monk who was burning charcoal and piling it into a fire.
Kān said, "I invite the Master to enter here and practice. [The Master] said, "True jade does not change by following flowing water;
lapis lazuli vies with the multitude of stars for its brilliance. [Kān] said, "Is it not simply this? [The Master] said, "Do not mistake the servant for the lord.

[Kān] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? [The Master] said, "The plum blossoms bloom in the twelfth month; heaven is accomplished. In the *wuzi* year, he responded to the summons of the ruler of Min and was invited to reside within the palace.
In the hall, he paid his respects, saying, "Thank you for descending from afar. During the serving of tea, the Master held up a small bag and asked, "Does the Great King understand?

He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The King of Men and the Dharma King each illuminate one another. He remained for ten days, after which he took leave on account of illness. Upon his arrival, he departed.

On the second day of the twelfth month, he bathed, ascended the hall, and passed away while addressing the assembly. The King, along with the monastics and laypeople, prepared fragrant wood, ghee, oil, and tea for his cremation.
A radiant auspicious light filled the mountains, and five-colored śarīra relics were obtained. He was enshrined in a stupa at the main chamber of Saeok Mountain.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Miaoying Fawei Ciji.

Upādhyāya Baozhang of the Thousand Years was a native of Central India. In the twelfth year of the Weili reign of Emperor Wuliang of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Dingmao, he descended in spirit to receive his physical form.

He was born with his left hand clenched in a fist; it was only when he received the tonsure at the age of seven that the fist opened. Consequently, he was named Baozhang (Precious Palm). This occurred during the Wei and Jin periods.

He traveled east to this land and entered Shu, where he paid homage to Samantabhadra and remained at Daci Monastery. He never ate food, reciting over a thousand scrolls of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras daily.
One who praised him said: "His weary jade teeth are cold, like rushing rock springs;
sometimes sitting in the middle of the night, the gods and ghosts weep before his steps. One day he said to the assembly: "I have a vow to remain in the world for a thousand..."
This year marks his six hundred and twenty-sixth. Thus, he is honored with the title of "One of a Thousand Years.
Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Wutai, then moved his residence to Huayan on Mount Zhurong, Shuangfeng at Huangmei, and Donglin on Mount Lu.

Eventually, he arrived in Jianye, where he encountered Bodhidharma’s arrival in the Liang dynasty. The Master approached him to inquire about the essential meaning of the Dharma and attained awakening. Emperor Wu, highly regarding his years of practice and realization, invited him [to court].
He entered the inner court. Not long after, he went to Wu, where he composed a verse: "In the city of Liang I met the Teacher; through Zen practice I realized the mind-ground.
Drifting and wandering, I traveled through the two Zhe regions, exhausting the finest mountains and waters. Following the current downstream, he traveled from Qianqing to Tianzhu.
He traveled to Maofeng and ascended Taibai. He traversed Yandang, lingering among the seventy-two hermitages on the emerald peaks.
Returning to Chicheng, he rested at Yunmen, Fahua, Zhujia, Yupu, Chifu, Dayan, and other locations. Upon returning to Feilai, he took up residence in Shidou.
There is a verse by him that reads: "Having traveled to the end of the four hundred prefectures of China, everywhere here one praises the wandering monk."
This was during the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era. Later, he resided at Baoyan Monastery in Pujiang, where he maintained a close friendship with Chan Master Lang.
Whenever he sent a messenger to inquire after him, a white dog would gallop there; Master Lang likewise employed a green monkey as his messenger.
Thus, he inscribed upon Lang’s wall: "The white dog brings the letter; the green monkey returns with the bowl washed. In all places the Master passed through, they later became monasteries (baofang).
In the first month of the second year of the Xianqing era, he fashioned a statue by hand. When the ninth day arrived, the image was completed.

He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble? Yun replied, "It is no different from you, Master. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus posture. Addressing Yun, he said:
"I have remained in this world for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years. Now I am about to depart from the world. Listen to my verse: "Fundamentally..."
"In coming, there is no birth-and-death; now, he likewise manifests birth-and-death. I have attained the mind that comes and goes; having been born on earth, I return once more to this place.

After saying this for a short while, he gave a final instruction, saying: "Sixty years after my passing, there will be a monk who comes to take my bones; do not refuse him. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Fifty-four years after his entry into *parinirvāṇa*, the Elder Cifu came from Yunmen to the site of the stupa and paid his respects, saying:
He hoped that the stupa would open of its own accord. After a short while, the door of the stupa indeed opened; his bones were linked together like golden rings.
He immediately took them to Mount Qinwang and erected a *stūpa* to enshrine them.

Calculating from the *dingmao* year of the reign of Emperor Weile of the Zhou dynasty to the *dingyi* year of the Xianqing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, it was exactly one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years. From that time until this present year, four hundred years have elapsed.
The rest has been lost from the monastic histories (*saṃgha-śāstra*). During the Kaiyuan era, Zongyi, a disciple of Huiyun, once had it engraved on stone to commemorate it.

The Chan Master Nanyue Huairang, Dharma heir of the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Mirror Chan Master, was surnamed Du and was a native of Jinyou. He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty.
A white vapor was perceived in response to the celestial signs in the region of Ankang; thus did the Grand Astrologer record it.

Upon beholding this, he reported it to Emperor Gaozong. The Emperor then asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied, "This is a vessel of the state’s Dharma that remains unstained by worldly glory.
The Emperor issued an imperial decree for Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, to go in person to offer condolences and comfort to the family.
The family had three sons, of whom the Master was the youngest; he was radiantly extraordinary, and his nature was solely one of kindness and deference. His father then—
His name was Huairang. At the age of ten, he took pleasure solely in Buddhist scriptures.

At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuánjìng visited his home and told his parents, "If this child leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle and extensively deliver sentient beings.
In the third year of the Chuígǒng era, when he was fifteen, he took leave of his kin and went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu to rely upon Vinaya Master Hóngjǐng.
He left the household life in the second year of the Tongtian era and received the full precepts. Subsequently, he studied the Vinaya Piṭaka.

One day, he sighed to himself, saying, "As for one who has left the household life, it is for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma). Among all things in heaven or on earth, there is nothing superior to this.

At that time, his fellow student Tanran, recognizing that his teacher’s aspirations were lofty and far-reaching, urged him to visit Master An of Mount Song. Master An enlightened him, and [Huineng] was then directly pointed out [to the Truth].
He went to Caoxi to attend upon the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song.
The Patriarch said, "What thing comes in such a manner? The Master was speechless. Thus he remained for eight years until, suddenly, he attained realization.
He then addressed the Patriarch, saying, "I have reached a point of understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so? The Master said, "To describe it as a single thing is not correct. The Patriarch—
The Master asked, "Is it still necessary to rely on cultivation and realization? The Teacher replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, one must not be defiled by them.
The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied of you:
'From beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. The illness lies here."
"My mind need not be expressed in haste. For fifteen years, he attended to his master at his side.
In the second year of the Xiāntiān era, he went to Mount Heng and resided at Pánruò Monastery. During the Kāiyuán era, there was a śramaṇa named Dàoyī (who is Mázǔ) on Mount Heng.
He constantly practiced seated meditation. The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you intend to achieve by sitting in meditation?
The other replied, "I intend to become a Buddha. The Master then took a brick and began rubbing it on a stone in front of the hermitage.

The other asked, "What are you rubbing that for? The Master said, "I am rubbing it to make a mirror. The other said, "By rubbing a brick, how can one possibly make a mirror? The Master replied, "Rubbing a brick..."
"Since you have not yet become a mirror, how can you hope to become a Buddha through sitting meditation? One asked, "How is it so? The Master said, "It is like an ox pulling a cart.
If the cart does not move, do you strike the cart, or do you strike the ox? The man was at a loss for a reply. The Master spoke again:

"You study sitting meditation; are you studying to sit as a Buddha? If you study sitting meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study to sit as a Buddha, the Buddha is not a fixed form.
Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as a Buddha, that is precisely to kill the Buddha."
If you cling to the form of sitting, you do not penetrate its principle. Upon hearing this instruction once, it was as if he had drunk the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*).

He prostrated and asked, "How should I apply my mind so that it accords with the signless samādhi? The Master said, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is like sowing seeds in the earth;

"The Way is not a form or appearance; how, then, can it be seen? The Master said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way;
the same is true for the signless samādhi. The first disciple asked, "Is there arising and ceasing?

The Master said, "If one sees the Way through the lens of arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing, that is not seeing the Way. Listen to my verse: 'The mind-ground contains all seeds; When meeting with moisture, they all sprout.'"
All sprout forth. The flower of samādhi is signless; what is there to destroy, and what is there to establish? Once they were enlightened, their minds transcended the mundane.
They attended him for ten autumns, and day by day he became more profound and mysterious. He had six入室 (入室) disciples in total. The Master individually certified them, saying:
"You six people have collectively realized my person. Each of you has attained one aspect. One of you has attained my eyebrows—he excels in majestic authority."

The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Nanyue Huairang (First Generation):
Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi was a native of Shifan County in Hanzhou. His surname was Ma. He left the household life at Luohan Temple in his home district.
His appearance was extraordinary: he had the gait of an ox and the gaze of a tiger; his tongue could extend past his nose, and beneath each of his feet were two wheels.
Wen was tonsured at a young age by Master Tang of Zizhou. He received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Yuzhou.

During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he practiced *dhyāna* concentration on Mount Heng. There he met Master Rang; among the six who studied under him together, only Wen secretly received the seal of the Mind.

(Master Rang was the first successor of Huineng, just as Shenxiu was the first successor of Daoxin. Since they shared the same source but followed different lineages, the flourishing of the Chan method began with these two masters. Liu Ke said: "In Jiangxi, Mazu Daichi is the master.")

In Hunan, the master [Huineng] presided over Shitou; though people came and went in constant throngs, they did not see the two Great Beings, which was due to their ignorance. The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied of Bodhidharma, saying: "Though China is vast, there is no other path; one must rely on the feet of the descendants to travel."

The golden rooster unclasps its beak to offer a single grain of millet as an offering to the Arhat Saṃgha of the ten directions. Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch said to Master Rang: "In the future, the Buddha-dharma shall proceed from you; this 'horse colt' will trample the people of the world.

Subsequently, his lineage of dharma transmission in Jiangxi spread throughout the land, and he was then titled Mazu. He first moved from Mount Foji in Jianyang to Linchuan, and next to Mount Gonggong in Nankang.
During the Dali era, he registered his name at Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling. At that time, Lu Sijing was the regional commander.
He listened to the teachings with longing and personally received the essential principles. Consequently, scholars from the four quarters gathered at his seat like clouds.
One day he said to the assembly, "All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha; this mind is itself the Buddha-mind.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle, the single mind."
You all must awaken to this. Furthermore, I cite the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the ground of the minds of sentient beings, fearing that you might be deluded and lack self-confidence.
This Dharma of the one mind exists within each and every person; therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its essence and "no-gate" as its Dharma-gate.
Now, those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek; outside of the mind, there is no separate Buddha.

Outside the Buddha, there is no separate mind. It does not grasp at good, nor does it reject evil. It relies upon neither of the two extremes of purity or defilement. It realizes that the nature of offenses is empty;
they cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, the three realms are mind-only, and the myriad phenomena of the universe are sealed by this single dharma. Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind. The mind is not the mind itself; it arises in dependence upon form.
Therefore, it exists. You merely speak according to the occasion; whether in terms of phenomena or principles, there is no obstruction whatsoever. It is the same with the fruit of the path to Bodhi:
that which arises in the mind is immediately termed "form" (rūpa). Because one knows that form is empty, arising is itself non-arising.
If you understand this intent, then you may dress and eat according to the occasion, nourishing the sacred embryo and passing the time with effortless spontaneity.
What further matters would there be? You have received my teaching; listen to my verse: "The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion; Awakening is likewise only peace.
When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, That which is born is, in truth, unborn. A monk asked: "Why does the Master speak thus?"
“It is the very mind that is Buddha. The Master said, “This was only to stop a child’s crying. The monk asked, “When the crying has stopped, what then? The Master said, “Neither mind nor Buddha.
The monk asked, “Setting aside these two types of people, how would you instruct one who comes before you? The Master said, “I would tell him, ‘It is not a thing.
The monk asked, “If someone who truly belongs to this [inner] category should suddenly come, what then? The Master said, “First, have him realize the Great [Function].”
Dao asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Right now, what is this meaning?
Layman Pang asked, "The person of original nature is not obscured; I ask the Master to cast his eyes high. The Master looked straight down. The Layman said, "This is a single-stringed lute;
only the Master can play it with such mastery. The Master looked straight up. The Layman bowed. The Master returned to his quarters, and the Layman followed.
Later, [the Master] said, "Just now, you used cleverness and ended up with clumsiness. He asked again, "It is said that water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-hu boat.
What is the principle behind this? The Master replied, "In this place, there is neither water nor boat; what talk can there be of sinews and bones?
One evening, while Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan were attending him as he enjoyed the moonlight, the Master asked, "At this very moment, how is it? Xitang—

[Daoyuan] said, "This is precisely the time for making offerings. Baizhang said, "This is precisely the time for practicing cultivation. Daoyuan shook his sleeves and departed. The Master [Yunmen] said, "The Sutras have entered the Canon;
Chan has returned to the sea. Only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world. Baizhang asked, "What is the essential purport of the Buddha-Dharma?
The Master said, "It is precisely where you lay down your body and life. The Master [Yunmen] asked Baizhang, "By what Dharma do you instruct others?"
A monk stood up, and the Master held his whisk upright. The Master said, "Is it only this, or is there something else?

The monk threw down the whisk. A monk asked, "How can one attain accord with the Way? The Master said, "I have long been out of accord with speaking. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Master struck him and said, "If I did not strike you, people everywhere would laugh at me. There was a junior disciple named Danyuan.
Returning from his travels, he drew a circle before the Master, prostrated himself upon it, and stood up. The Master said, "Do you not wish to become a Buddha?
He replied, "I do not know how to rub my eyes. The Master said, "I am not as good as you. The junior monk remained silent.

Rest from all affairs—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane—from all phenomena whatsoever. Do not recall them; do not attend to them.

All objects of perception are transcended; greed, anger, craving, and grasping, as well as all defilements and purities, are exhausted.

One remains unmoved by the five desires and the eight winds, is not bound by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is not deluded by any external objects. Thus, one naturally becomes fully endowed with supernatural powers and wondrous functions.
Such a person is one who has attained liberation. Facing all objects, their mind is neither still nor distracted; it is neither gathered nor dispersed.
Penetrating through all sounds and forms without obstruction, they are called a "person of the Way. Regarding good and evil, right and wrong, they employ neither;
they do not cherish a single dharma, nor do they reject a single dharma. They are called a person of the Mahāyāna. They are not defiled by any good, evil, or emptiness.
That which is bound by the merit and wisdom—whether defiled or pure, conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane—is called the Buddha-wisdom.
It is neither good nor ugly, neither principle nor non-principle; when all sentiments of knowledge and views are exhausted, it can no longer bind.
To attain mastery everywhere is called a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening ascending directly to the stage of Buddhahood.

Question: Facing all objects of perception, how does one attain a mind that is like wood or stone? The Master said: "All dharmas fundamentally do not say of themselves that they are empty, nor do they say of themselves that they are form.
They do not speak of right or wrong, nor of defilement or purity. Nor is there a mind that binds people; it is only that people themselves are deluded."
They falsely conceptualize and cling, forming various interpretations and giving rise to various cognitions and views, as well as various attachments and fears.
They simply fail to realize that all phenomena do not arise of themselves, but exist solely through the grasping of signs by one's own single thought of deluded, inverted imagination.
Knowing that the mind and its objects fundamentally do not reach one another, they are liberated in their very place; each and every phenomenon is liberated in its own place.
It is quiescent extinction; it is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) right where one stands. Furthermore, this originally existing nature cannot be named or designated.
From the beginning, it is neither ordinary nor holy, neither defiled nor pure, neither empty nor existent, and neither good nor evil.

When it is associated with various defiled phenomena, it is called the realm of humans, devas, and the two vehicles. If the mind of both defilement and purity is exhausted, one abides neither in bondage nor in liberation.
There is no mind-measurement (*cittamātra*) bound by or liberated from any conditioned or unconditioned phenomena. Abiding within birth and death, its mind is sovereign;
it ultimately does not conjoin with delusions, false illusions, worldly afflictions, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, or the cycle of birth and death.
It stands aloof and without dependence, unrestrained by anything; its coming and going are unhindered, and its passage through birth and death is like the opening of a door. As for one who studies...
A practitioner of the Way, when encountering various circumstances of suffering or joy, whether agreeable or disagreeable, remains without retreat or dejection in mind.
They do not dwell upon fame, profit, gain, food, or clothing; they do not crave merit or benefit; they are not obstructed by the various phenomena of the world.

Having neither kin nor attachment, they maintain an even disposition toward both suffering and joy. Wearing coarse garments to ward off the cold and taking simple food to sustain life, they remain steadfastly resolute.

Like one who is foolish or deaf, there may be a slight degree of correspondence. However, if within the mind one extensively studies for knowledge and understanding, seeking merit and seeking wisdom—all of these belong to birth and death and are of no benefit to the Principle.
Instead, one is drifted and drowned by the winds of the realm of knowledge and understanding, returning once more to the ocean of birth and death.
The Buddha is one who seeks nothing; to seek him is to deviate from him. The Principle is a principle that is sought after nothing; to seek it...
To do so is to lose it. If one clings to non-seeking, that is the same as having a seeking mind. If one clings to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), that is the same as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Moving and abiding with freedom, one is not bound by the causes and effects of any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). One is not struck down by outflows (*āsrava*).

The Master said: "Do not seek the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; do not even seek merit, wisdom, knowledge, or understanding.

In hell, there is no obstruction to bondage or liberation; thus, body, mind, and all places are all termed "liberation. Do not say that because your body, speech, and mind are pure, you have thereby attained realization.

You do not know that among the gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*) in which you have not yet entered even a single hair’s breadth. Strive forward and investigate with vigor; do not wait.
The ears grow deaf and the eyes grow dim; the face wrinkles and the hair turns white. The suffering of old age overtakes the body; one is entangled by the grief of attachment.
Tears flow from the eyes, and the heart is filled with terror and alarm. With nothing whatsoever to rely upon, one knows not where to go.

When such a time arrives, one can no longer manage one's own hands or feet. Even if one possesses merit, wisdom, fame, or gain, none of these can provide rescue, for the eye of the mind has not yet opened.
The eyes open, yet one merely perceives various objects without knowing how to reflect back upon oneself; furthermore, the Buddha-way is not seen.

All the karmic conditions of good and evil from one’s entire life appear before one. One experiences either joy or fear as the six realms and the five aggregates manifest simultaneously, all arrayed in magnificent splendor—houses, boats, ships, carriages, and palanquins, their radiance brilliant and dazzling—all of which are manifested by the greed and attachment of one's own mind.
All evil environments are transformed into sublime realms. However, wherever one’s craving is most intense, there the *karmic consciousness* leads one;
following that attachment, one takes birth, possessing no freedom whatsoever. Whether as a dragon or a beast, noble or lowly, these states are likewise entirely undetermined.

Regarding acceptance and rejection: when stinginess, envy, greed, and attachment, as well as the sentiment of "mine," are exhausted, both defilement and purity vanish.
Like the sun and moon in the sky, they illuminate without depending on external conditions; the mind is as firm as wood or stone, yet every thought-moment is like saving one's head from fire.
It is also like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, cutting through the current without hesitation. Such a person cannot be encompassed by either heaven or hell. Indeed,
When reading scriptures and examining the words of the teachings, you must in every instance turn them back upon yourself.
All verbal instructions merely clarify the self-nature of present-time discernment; it is simply that one must not be swayed by any objects of existence or non-existence.
This is your guide. That which can illuminate and shatter all objects of existence and non-existence is adamantine wisdom (*vajra-prajñā*); this is immediate, autonomous, and solitary.
Establishing the divisions: if you cannot understand it in this way, then even if you can recite the twelve Vedas, it will only result in arrogance;

it is rather slandering the Buddha and not practicing cultivation. Simply to be detached from all sounds and forms, yet not dwelling in that detachment, and not dwelling in intellectual understanding—this is cultivation.
As for reading scriptures and studying the teachings, if judged by worldly standards, this is...
This is a good matter. If you approach those who understand the principle, these [conceptualizations] are seen as obstructions;
even a person of the tenth stage would not escape them, but would flow into the river of birth and death. All teachings of the Three Vehicles treat diseases such as greed and anger;

therefore, if at this very moment, moment by moment, there is the disease of greed, anger, and so forth, you must first treat it. There is no need to seek out meanings, phrases, or intellectual understanding.

Cognitive understanding belongs to craving; craving turns into illness. Simply now, by merely distancing yourself from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and further distancing yourself from that very distancing—transcending beyond the three propositions—you will naturally be no different from the Buddha. Since you are already the Buddha yourself, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your words?
I only fear that you are not the Buddha, being bound by the dharmas of existence and non-existence so that you cannot attain freedom. For this reason...
If principle has not yet been established, one first possesses merit and wisdom; carried away by this merit and wisdom, one is like a lowly person being elevated to nobility.

This is not as good as first establishing principle and subsequently possessing merit and wisdom. If one wishes to produce merit and wisdom at the last moment, one could grasp soil and turn it into gold, take gold and turn it into soil, transform the waters of the ocean into ghee and curd, shatter Mount Sumeru into fine dust, and draw the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore.
The pores of the skin. To take a single meaning and make it immeasurable meanings; to take immeasurable meanings and make them a single meaning. I pray you, hold this in high esteem.

Once, when the Master had finished preaching the Dharma and the great assembly was descending from the hall, he called out to them. The assembly turned their heads, and the Master asked, "What is this?

(Yaoshan later referred to this as "Baizhang’s sentence for descending from the hall"). When the Master was a child, he accompanied his mother to a temple to pay homage to the Buddha. Pointing to a Buddhist image, he asked:
"Mother, what is this? His mother replied, "This is the Buddha. The Master said, "His appearance is no different from that of a human being; I too shall become like him in the future.
Whenever the Master performed manual labor or took up tasks, he was invariably the first among the assembly. The overseer could not bear it and secretly gathered up his tools, requesting him to rest.
The Master said, "I have no virtue; why should I compete with others for labor? Having searched everywhere for his tools, [he found them].
He did not obtain [food], yet he ate it nonetheless; thus, the saying "if one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day" spread throughout the world.
On the seventeenth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he entered nirvana. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dazhi.
The stupa is named "Great Jewel Victorious Wheel.
As for Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of Chizhou, he was a native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou. His surname was Wang. From childhood, he admired the school of emptiness.
In the second year of the Zhide era of the Tang dynasty, he received his monastic training under Chan Master Dahui of Mount Dawei and subsequently proceeded to Mount Song.
He received full ordination and initially studied the ancient texts of the Xiangbu school, thoroughly investigating the *Vinaya* sections on the *piṇḍa* and *āpatti*.

Subsequently, he traveled among various lecture halls, attending lectures on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and entering the contemplations of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra* to refine his mastery of their profound meanings.
Later, he sought out Mazu Daoci; suddenly casting aside the trap, he attained the Samādhi of Play. One day, while serving rice gruel for the assembly of monks, Mazu—
Question: "What is that in the bucket? The Master said, "Shut your mouth, you old fellow, and talk like this! The Patriarch then ceased speaking.
Among the rest of his fellow practitioners, none dared to question him further. In the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he rested his staff at Chiyang and established a Zen retreat;
for over thirty years, he did not descend from Nanquan. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, the official Lian of Xuancheng...
Lord Lu Gongxuan, having long admired the Master’s spiritual style, subsequently requested him to descend from the mountain along with the military supervisor to pay the rites of a disciple.

Thereupon, the esoteric principles were greatly revitalized; from this time on, his disciples numbered no fewer than several hundred, and his reputation filled all quarters, earning him the title of "the Master-Carpenter of Ying.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way of Dīpaṃkara Buddha is already complete. If one gives rise to various phenomena through the conceptualizations of the mind, they are merely false and illusory."
It is not real. Why? Because the mind itself does not exist; how then could it give rise to all phenomena?

It is like a shadow following a form, or discriminating within empty space; it is like a person trying to capture sound and place it inside a box, or like blowing into a net, wishing to fill it with air.
Therefore, the ancient masters said: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing. This is merely to teach you brothers how to practice. According to this—
It is taught that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds, dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, attain the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
they spontaneously acquire all meditative concentrations, liberations, and the wondrous functions of supernormal powers, and manifest form-bodies throughout all worlds.
Or manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, turning the great wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvana; causing immeasurable [beings] to enter a single pore,

wherein one recites a single verse of a sutra for immeasurable eons without its meaning being exhausted, thereby teaching and transforming immeasurable billions of sentient beings so that they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas—
even this is still called the extreme of ignorance regarding the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), the subtle ignorance regarding the knowable, which is entirely at variance with the Way.
"A great difficulty, a great difficulty! Take care! The Master ascended the hall and said: "Since my youth, Old Man Wang has raised a water buffalo.

If I intend to pasture it on the east bank of the stream, I cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass; if I intend to pasture it on the west bank of the stream, I likewise cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass.
It would be better to simply accept things as they are—yet even this is not seen. The Master then asked:
The monk said, "A fine wind last night. [The Master] said, "A fine wind last night. The Master said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate.
[The monk] said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate. Next, he asked another monk, "Was there a fine wind last night? [The monk] said, "What kind of wind was it?
The Master said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate. [The monk] said, "What kind of pine tree was it? The Master said, "One who has attained."
The first failure: The Master sent a letter to Zhuyou (Zhu Daoming) saying, "Principle follows the transformation of phenomena;
vastness is not external. Phenomena attain the fusion of principle; stillness is not internal. When Sengda finished reading the letter, he asked Zhuyou, "What is meant by 'vastness is not external'?
Zhuyou said, "To one question, answer a hundred; there is no harm in that. He then asked, "What is meant by 'stillness is not internal'? Zhuyou said, "Beholding the opposite."
"Sound and form are not the work of a master. The monk then asked Changsha, who stared at him with wide-open eyes.

When the monk repeated his previous question, Changsha closed his eyes to show him. The monk then asked Zhaozhou, who made a gesture of eating. When the monk again repeated his previous question, Zhaozhou made a gesture of wiping his mouth with his hand.
Later, when the monk reported these encounters to the Master (Linji), the Master said, "These three men are not..."
[The Master] said, "Wrong! You are my disciple. Beneath the mountain of Nanquan there is a hermitage master. People say to him, 'Recently, the Monk of Nanquan has appeared in the world;
why do you not go to pay him a visit? The master says, 'Not only would I not go to see Nanquan appear in the world, even if the thousand Buddhas were to arise, I still would not go.
When the Master heard this, he ordered Zhaozhou to go and investigate him. Zhaozhou went and immediately prostrated himself."
The Master did not look back. As Zhou went from west to east and again from east to west, the Master still did not look back.
Zhou said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated," whereupon he pulled down the curtain and departed. He reported this to the Master, who said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
The next day, the Master took a novice monk and, carrying a bottle of tea and three cups, went to the hermitage; he threw them to the ground.
The Master said, "Yesterday’s thing, yesterday’s thing. The Head asked, "What is 'yesterday’s thing'?
The Master struck the novice on his back once and said, "You’ve led me astray! You’ve led me astray! Then he shook out his sleeves and turned back.
Later, ascending the hall, he said, "To speak of 'suchness' (tathatā) is already to have changed it. These days, monks must walk among the heterodox. — From Guizong.
[The monk] said, "Even though one performs the actions of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal. The Master said, "Alas, you fellow Meng! You have gone off in that way again.
He ascended the hall and said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra fought each other last night at the third watch; I gave each of them twenty blows with my staff."

Taking advantage of his discharge from the hospital, he departed. Zhaozhou asked, "Whom did the Master intend for the staff to strike? The Master said, "Tell me, where exactly was Old Teacher Wang's fault?
Zhaozhou bowed and withdrew. The Master then went to a manor estate. The master of the estate had prepared a formal reception in advance.
The Master said, "I usually enter or leave this place without letting anyone know. Why have you made such elaborate preparations? The master of the estate...
The Master said, "Last night the Local Deity (Tǔdì) reported that the Abbot would come today. The Teacher said, "Old Wang lacks the power of cultivation;
he was spotted by ghosts and spirits. The attendant then asked, "Since the Abbot is a true spiritual friend (śāstr), why was he spotted by ghosts and spirits?
The Teacher said, "Serve another portion of rice before the Local Deity. (Xuánjué said: "Where is the Local Deity?")

Before the ground [of realization], he further set down one portion of rice. Yunju Xi said, "This is both rewarding him and punishing him. It is just like when the Land Deity saw this as Nanquan; it was not Nanquan.
The Master once said, "In Jiangxi, Mazu taught 'this very mind is Buddha. Old Wang does not speak thus; I say, 'It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
In speaking thus, is there any fault? Zhaozhou bowed and departed. At that time, there was one...
A monk, following the inquiry, asked Zhaozhou, "When the Senior Monk (Sengzuo) bowed and immediately left, what was his intention? Zhaozhou said, "You should ask the Abbot instead.
The monk then asked, "What was the intention of the Senior Monk Shen just now? Zhaozhou said, "He indeed grasped my meaning.
Once, when Huangbo served as the Head Seat (Prathama-śrāvaka) under the Master, he one day held out his alms bowl toward the Master’s seat.
The Master entered the hall, saw [Huangbo], and asked, "In what year did you begin practicing the Way, Elder? Huangbo replied, "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.
The Master said, "That is still the lineage of Old Teacher Wang; go sit down below. Huangbo then moved to the second seat and sat there.
The Master then desisted. One day the Master asked Huangbo, "If the world were made of gold and the ground of silver..."
[The Master] looked at the wall and said, "What kind of person lives here? Huangbo replied, "A sage lives here.
The Master said, "There is yet another person; in what land does he dwell? Huangbo then stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. The Master said, "You cannot say it. Why not ask Old Teacher Wuzhuo?
Huangbo then asked, "Where does that other person dwell? The Master said, "What a pity! The Master then questioned [Huangbo].
Huangbo said, "The equal training of concentration and wisdom leads to clearly seeing the Buddha-nature. What is the principle of this?

Huangbo replied, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, one does not rely upon or depend on a single thing. The Master asked, "Is this your own realization, Elder? Huangbo replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "..."
"Let us set aside the money for the gruel; who will repay the cost of the straw sandals? The Master saw a monk hewing wood and struck the wood three times.

Seeing the monk sitting beneath his robes and bowl, the Master said, "He has deceived me to death. [The monk] asked, "Master, having returned to your quarters..."
"What is the guiding principle? The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, I had lost my fire.

"What are you mumbling about? The monk had no reply. Later, as the Master entered the vegetable garden, he saw a monk and struck him with a tile.
The monk turned back to look at him, and the Master stood on one foot. The monk remained speechless.
The Master then returned to the abbot’s quarters, followed by the monk, who paid his respects and said, "Master, just now you threw a tile and struck me; was that not so?"
He alerted someone by name. The Master said, "What about when one stands on tiptoe? The monk had no reply. (Later, a monk asked Shishuang, "What was the meaning of Nanquan standing on tiptoe?

is there anyone who will buy him? A monk stepped forward and said, "I will buy him. The Master said, "Neither as something expensive nor as something cheap—how will you do it?"

"Buy. The monk had no reply. (Wolong [Dongshan Liangjie] said in his stead: "It belongs to such-and-such a person, who has gone away. Heshan [Shouchu] said in his stead: "What kind of principle is this? Zhaozhou said in his stead: "Next year, I will sew a robe of cloth for the Master.

"Why did Nanquan instead call him back? Tell me, what was the meaning of the ancient? While the Master was performing manual labor on the mountain, a monk asked, "Where does the road to Nanquan lead?

After finishing his meal, he went from the east corridor down to the west corridor; he did not ask everyone whether they had received their portions or not.

He suddenly broke off his household affairs at once and lay down on the bed. The Master waited, not seeing him return, and went back to the hermitage.
Seeing the monk lying there, the Master also lay down beside him. The monk then got up and left.

"The earth shares the same root as I; all things and I are one body. The Master pointed to the peony flowers in the courtyard and said, "Great Officer, when people of this age see this single stalk of flowers, it is like being in a dream.

Lu took his leave and returned to the administrative seat of Xuancheng. The Master asked the Grand Officer, "Once you have departed for that place, how will you govern the people?"
[The Master] said, "I govern the people with wisdom. The teacher said, "If that is so, then the living beings there must all be suffering in misery.
The teacher entered Xuanzhou. When Governor Lu came out to welcome him, he pointed to the city gate and said, "Everyone calls this the 'Gate of Yong.

Regarding the transformation of customs, [Lù] asked, "When bandits suddenly arrive, what then? The Master said, "It is the fault of Old Wang.

The Master asked, "In what land do you dwell? Qin remained silent. The Master asked, "The patriarchs have transmitted to one another;

"What object do you take as your focus during these two periods? The Master asked. The student said, "Why not ask the Venerable Wang? The Master said, "I have already asked you.

National Teacher Qian’an of Haichang Monastery in Yanguan, Hangzhou, was a native of Haimen Commandery. His surname was Li.

"Zhao—could this not be you? You have long relied upon Chan Master Yunzong of your native district to shave your head and receive full ordination.

The One Who is Without Obstruction is called the One Who Responds to Conditions. The One Who Responds to Conditions is called the One Who Manifests Forms.
