When the monk arrived to wait upon Master Baizhang, as the Master was ascending the hall, the monk spread his sitting mat and prostrated.
Having finished, he stood up, took one of the Master’s sandals, brushed the dust from it with the sleeve of his robe, and turned it upside down toward the ground. The Master said, "Old..."
[The Master] said, "This is the fault of the monks. Someone asked, "The Patriarchs transmitted the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground.
Is this the True Suchness mind, the deluded mind, or the mind that is neither true nor deluded? Or is it a mind established separately outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles?

The Master said, "Do you see the empty space before you? He replied, "I know with certainty that it is always present before me; it is only people who do not see it. The Master said, "Do not mistake the reflection for the reality."
Xiang asked, "How about you, Master? The Master struck the air three times with his hand. Xiang asked, "What does this mean? The Master said, "You will understand it later.
A monk came and circumambulated the Master three times, then stood there shaking his staff.

The Master said, "Right! Right! (Changqing spoke on his behalf, saying: "Where are the Master’s Buddha-dharma, body, and mind? That monk then went to Nanquan and likewise circumambulated Nanquan three times.

[The monk] circumambulated [Nanquan], shook his mendicant’s staff, and stood there. Nanquan said, "It is not so, it is not so. This is turned by the power of the wind; in the end, it will fall into ruin.
The monk asked, "Zhangjing says it is so; why does the Master say it is not? Nanquan said, "Zhangjing is indeed right; you are not.

*Changqing* (Longqing) spoke on his behalf, saying: "Master, what kind of mental activity is this? *Yunju Xi* said: "Zhangjing did not necessarily say it was so; Nanquan did not necessarily say it was not. He further said:
It happened that just as this monk was leaving with his staff, the junior attendant returned from his travels. The Master asked, "How many years has it been since you left here?
He replied, "I have been away from the Master’s presence for nearly eight years. The Master asked, "What have you accomplished? The junior attendant drew a circle on the ground.
The Master said, "Is there anything more than just this? The junior attendant then drew a line through it.
Yuanxiang then prostrated. The Master said, "It is not so, it is not so. A monk asked, "Within this body of the four elements and five aggregates, which one is the original Buddha-nature?
The Master called the monk by his name; the monk responded. After a long silence, the Master said, "You have no Buddha-nature.
He entered nirvana in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty and was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajue.
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou was the son of the Zhu family of Jianzhou. He received his training under Venerable Zhi of Dayun Monastery in Yuezhou.
When he first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Monastery in Yuezhou.
Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He replied, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "In my place, there is not..."
"Things do not exist. What Dharma is there to seek? You neglect your own precious treasury; why do you abandon your home and wander about?
He asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Haima? The Patriarch said, "That which is asking me right now—this is your precious treasury."
Everything was complete; there was nothing lacking. He possessed mastery over all functions, so why should he seek anything outside himself?

Upon hearing these words, the Master immediately recognized his own original mind, not through intellectual cognition. He leaped for joy and prostrated in gratitude. He served the Master for six years, after which, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned home abruptly to provide for him.
Thereupon, he concealed his traces and hid his capabilities, outwardly appearing dull and mute. He then composed the *Wuwei Rudao Yaomen* (The Essential Gate of Sudden Enlightenment).
The *Treatise on the Essential Gate of the Way* (Dàoyào mén lùn), one fascicle. His Dharma-nephew Xuanyan secretly brought it out beyond the Yangtze River and presented it to Mazu.

After Mazu had finished reading it, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a Great Pearl, perfectly round and bright; its light penetrates with ease and freedom, leaving no place unilluminated.
Among the assembly was one who knew the Master’s surname was Zhu; they recommended him to come to Yuezhou to seek him out and rely upon him (at that time he was called Master Dazhu). The Master said:
He said, "I am not a Chan master; I do not understand Chan. I have no single dharma to show to people. Do not trouble yourself by standing here so long; please go rest for now.
At that time, the number of students gradually increased, and they pressed him with questions day and night. Having no other choice, he answered each question as it was asked.
His eloquence was unimpeded. At that time, several Dharma masters came to visit him and said, "We intend to pose a question.

Will you respond to us, Master? The Master replied, "The moon's reflection in a deep pool may be grasped at will. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "In this clear conversation face-to-face, who else could it be but the Buddha?
The assembly was all at a loss. (Fayan said: "If it is so, there is no connection. After a long while, the monk asked again, "Master..."
"What Dharma do you teach to save people? The Master said, "I, this poor monk, have never had a single dharma to save people. [The other] said, "This is the way of all Chan masters.
The Master then asked in return, "Virtuous One, what Dharma do you teach to save people? He replied, "I lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master said:
[The Master] asked, "How many lectures have you given? He replied, "More than twenty. The Master said, "Who preached this sutra? The monk raised his voice and said, "Master, you are mocking me!
Do you not know that it was preached by the Buddha? The Master said, "If one says that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, they slander the Buddha;
such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have preached. If one says this sutra is not..."

The Master said, "If you say this was spoken by the Buddha, then you are slandering the sutra. I request the Venerable One to speak upon it. The monk had no reply. After a short while, the Master asked again, "The sutra says:
'If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Venerable One, tell me: which of these is the Tathāgata? The monk replied, "When I reach this point, I am lost. The Master said, "... (The text ends here).
[The monk] said, “I have never awakened from the beginning; how can you speak of being deluded? [The monk] said, “Please, Master, explain this for me.

The Master said, “You, Virtuous One, have lectured on the sutras more than twenty times, yet you do not recognize the Tathāgata. The monk prostrated himself and said, “I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Master said:
"The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas. How could you forget this? He replied, "It is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas.
The Master said, "Virtuous One, even this is not yet it. He asked, "The scriptural text is clear; how can it be 'not yet'? The Master said, "Virtuous One, are you such?
He replied, "I am such. The Master said, "Are wood and stone such? He replied, "They are such. The Master said, "Virtuous One, are you such as wood and stone are such?"

"No," he said. "I have no duality. The Master asked, "What distinguishes you, Venerable One, from wood or stone? The monk had no reply. After a long silence, he asked again, "How does one attain Great Nirvana?
The Master replied, "By not creating the karma of birth and death. [The monk] asked, "What is the karma of birth and death?"

The Master said: "Seeking great nirvana is the karma of birth and death. Abandoning defilement to grasp purity is the karma of birth and death. Having attainment and realization is the karma of birth and death.
Not being free from the gates of counteraction is the karma of birth and death. [The student] asked: "How, then, can one attain liberation? The Master said:
"Originally there has been no bondage; there is no need to seek liberation. To proceed directly and act directly—this is the peerless equality."
He said, "A meditation master such as you, O Venerable One, is truly rare. Having paid his respects and departed, a practitioner asked, "'The very mind is Buddha.
Which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "Which one do you doubt is not the Buddha? Point it out to me. The practitioner had no reply.
The Master said, "To penetrate it, the entire realm is it; if you do not awaken, you will remain forever estranged. The Vinaya Master Faming addressed the Master:

[The Master] said, "In the houses of Chan masters, there is much falling into emptiness. The Master [Yunmen] replied, "On the contrary, it is in the houses of the Dharma Masters that one falls into emptiness.
Mingda was greatly startled and asked, "How can one fall into emptiness? The Master said, "The sutras and śāstras are but paper and ink characters;

since paper, ink, and characters are all empty, even if one establishes dharmas such as names and phrases based upon sounds, they are none other than empty. The Dharma Master clings to the teachings."
"Does your essence not fall into emptiness? Ming asked. The Master said, "It does not fall into emptiness. Ming asked, "How is it that it does not fall into emptiness?
The Master said, "All things, such as words and letters, arise from wisdom. When the great function manifests before one,"
"Then you have fallen into emptiness," the Master said. Ming replied, "Therefore, I know that if one does not master even a single dharma, one cannot be called Siddhārtha.
The Master said, "The Vinaya Master has not only fallen into emptiness; he has also misunderstood the terminology. Ming flushed with indignation and asked, "Where is the point of error?
The Master said, "If you have not yet distinguished between the sounds of China and India, how can you lecture and explain? Ming said, "I beg the Chan Master to point out the specific error."
The Master said, "Do you not know that 'Siddhārtha' is a Sanskrit term? (In full, it is *Viparīta-siddha*;

in the Central Kingdom [China], it is translated as 'One by Whom All Meanings are Accomplished. The old translation 'Siddhārtha' is merely a corrupted abbreviation of the Sanskrit. Ming, though he recognized his error, remained inwardly indignant. The Master said again, "The Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras are the words of the Buddha.
You recite them and follow their teachings in practice; why then do you not see your nature? The Master continued, "It is like a mad dog..."
"A lion chasing a clod of earth bites people. The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are the function of the nature; those who read and recite them are the phenomena of the nature.
Ming asked, "Does Amitābha Buddha have parents and a clan? The Master said, "Amitābha’s clan is Kauśika;
his father’s name is Candrottarā, and his mother’s name is Viśiṣṭamukhā. Ming asked, "In which scriptural text does this appear? The Master said, "It appears in the *Dundubhisvara*."
In the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra*, Dharmaprabhā paid his respects, offered thanks, and withdrew after offering praise. A Tripiṭaka Master asked, "Does True Suchness undergo change?
The Master replied, "It does. The Tripiṭaka Master said, "Zen Master, you are mistaken. The Master then asked the Tripiṭaka Master in return, "Does True Suchness exist? He replied, "It exists.
The Master said, "If it were without change, it would certainly be the state of an ordinary monk. Have you not heard the verse on 'Good'?"
"One who possesses true knowledge can transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts; transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers;
transform afflictions into bodhi; and transform ignorance into great wisdom.

If suchness were devoid of transformation, then the Three Pitakas would truly be the teachings of the naturalists. Zang said, "If that is so, then suchness must possess transformation. The Master replied:
"If one holds that True Suchness undergoes change, one is also a non-Buddhist.
[The student] asked, "Just now you said that True Suchness undergoes change, and now you say it does not change. How can this be the definitive truth?
The Master said, "If one clearly perceives one's nature, it is like a *maṇi* jewel manifesting colors; one may say it changes, and one may also say it does not change. If one does not..."
One who has seen their nature, upon hearing it said that True Suchness undergoes transformation, immediately understands it as undergoing transformation;

upon hearing it said that it does not undergo transformation, they immediately understand it as not undergoing transformation. Baizhang said: "Thus we know that the Southern School is truly unfathomable. There was a practitioner who asked:
"Is there any dharma in the world that surpasses spontaneity (*ziran*)? The Master said, "There is. [The student] asked, "What dharma can surpass it?
The Master said, "One who is able to know spontaneity. [The student] asked, "Is the primal qi (*yuanqi*) the Way (*dao*)? The Master said, "The primal qi is the primal qi; the Way is the Way.
[The student] said, "If this is so, then there must be two. The Master said, "In knowing, there are not two people. [The student] asked again, saying:
"What is the perverse? What is the correct? The Master said, "The mind pursuing external objects is perverse; objects following the mind is correct.
Vinaya Master Yuan asked, "When you, Reverend, cultivate the Way, do you still apply effort? The Master said, "I apply effort. [Yuan] asked, "How do you apply effort?"
The Master said, "When hungry, one eats; when tired, one sleeps. [The student] asked, "Do all people do this? Do they apply themselves to practice in the same way as you, Master?
The Master said, "They do not. [The student] asked, "Why do they not? The Master said, "When others eat, they are unwilling to eat;
they demand a hundred things. When they sleep, they are unwilling to sleep; they harbor a thousand schemes. That is why they are different. — *Lü* (Vinaya) [Section]
The Master remained silent. The Great Virtue Yun Guang asked, "Does the Chan Master know where he will be reborn? The Master said, "I have not yet died; why discuss being born?
To know birth is itself the dharma of non-birth (*anutpāda*). There is no dharma of non-birth apart from the dharma of birth.
The Patriarch [Wuzhuo] said, "At the very moment of birth, there is no birth. [Yun Guang] asked, "Can those who have not seen their nature also attain this? The Master said, "If one does not..."
Seeing-nature is not the absence of nature. Why is this? Seeing is itself nature; that which lacks nature cannot see. Consciousness is itself nature;

therefore it is called the "nature of consciousness. Awareness is itself nature; thus it is called the "nature of awareness. That which can give rise to the myriad dharmas is called the "dharma-nature," and is also named the "Dharmakāya.
The Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa said: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings. If...
Because the mind arises, all phenomena arise; if the mind does not arise, phenomena have no source from which to arise, nor do they possess names.
Deluded people do not understand that the Dharma-body has no form, yet it manifests forms in response to things.

Consequently, they declare that every verdant bamboo shoot is the Dharma-body, and that every lush yellow flower is none other than Prajñā. If yellow flowers were Prajñā, then Prajñā would be identical to nothingness.

How lamentable! If green bamboo were the Dharma-body, then the Dharma-body would be identical to grass and trees. If a person eats bamboo shoots, they would consequently be eating the Dharma-body as a whole.
How can such talk be worthy of being recorded? Facing the Buddha and yet remaining deluded, one seeks him for long kalpas;

within the totality of the Dharma, one is lost and searches for it externally. Therefore, for those who understand the Way, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are none other than the Way itself.

"One who awakens to the Dharma" is one for whom there is nothing—not even the horizontal and vertical dimensions—that is not the Dharma. Guang asked again: "Can the great void give birth to spiritual wisdom?
Does the true mind condition itself by means of good and evil? Is a person of greedy desires on the Way?

Will a person who clings to 'is' and 'is not' attain penetration of the mind hereafter? When encountering objects, does a person have a fixed [mind]? Does a person dwelling in stillness possess wisdom? He harbored...
Those who treat others with arrogance—do they have a self? Those who cling to emptiness or cling to existence—do they possess wisdom?

Those who seek verification through texts; those who seek the Buddha through ascetic practices; those who seek the Buddha apart from the mind; those who cling to the mind as being the Buddha—is this wisdom called the Way?
Please, Master, explain each of these for me. The Master said: "The vast void does not give birth to spiritual wisdom; the true mind does not engage with good or evil."

Those with deep cravings have shallow spiritual capacity; those for whom right and wrong contend have not yet attained penetration. Those who give rise to thoughts upon encountering objects lack stability;
those who dwell in silence and forget their mental mechanisms have sunk into dullness. Those who are arrogant toward things and hold themselves in high esteem are puffed up with self-importance;

those who cling to emptiness or cling to existence are all deluded. Those who seek verification through texts become increasingly mired in stagnation; those who seek the Buddha through asceticism are equally lost. To seek the Buddha apart from the mind—[is this not the way?]
"Non-Buddhists who cling to the mind as being the Buddha are possessed by Māra. [The monk] said, "If it is thus, then ultimately there is nothing at all.
The Master said, "Ultimately it is so; it is you, Venerable One, who are not so. Ultimately there is nothing at all. Kō leaped for joy, prostrated in thanks, and departed.
Question: What are the similarities and differences among the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism? The Master said: "For those of great capacity, they function as one;
for those of limited faculties, they are grasped as different. They all arise from the single nature, yet through the differentiation of faculties and views, they become three.
Delusion and enlightenment depend on the person; it does not lie in whether the teachings are the same or different."
The Chan Master Weizheng of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou was once visited by an elderly practitioner who saw a shaft of sunlight piercing through a window.
He asked the Master, "Does the window move toward the sun, or does the sun move toward the window? The Master replied, "Elder, there is a guest in your room; it would be best for you to leave.
Later, the Master asked Nanquan, "Do the virtuous teachers of all quarters have any teaching that they do not explain to others? Nanquan said, "There is. The Master [pressed further].
[The monk] asked, "How is it? [The Master] said, "It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have already explained it to people.
[The monk] said, "I am just like this; how about you, Teacher? The Master said, "I am not even a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend);
how could I know whether there is a teaching that is spoken or one that is not? [The monk] said, "I do not understand. I beg the Teacher [to explain]."
The Master said, "I have already explained it to you quite thoroughly. A monk asked, "What is the state where the Buddhas and the Way are equal? The Master said, "It is settled.
While on the road to the capital, the Master encountered an official who was eating. Suddenly, he heard a donkey bray. The official called out, "Head-taoist!
The Master raised his head, and the official pointed at the donkey. The Master, however, pointed back at the official. (Fayan commented: "Just do as...")
[The sound of] a donkey braying).
Chan Master Hetan Fahui of Hongzhou asked Mazu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Mazu said, "Lower your voice and come closer; I will tell you. The Master then drew near, and Mazu gave him a slap, saying, "Six ears!"
"Do not plot together; go now, and come back tomorrow. The next day, when the Master arrived, he entered the Dharma Hall alone and said, "I request the Abbot to speak.
The Patriarch said, "Go for now; wait until I have ascended the hall, and I will come out to question you and provide testimony for you.
The Master suddenly attained realization and said, "Thank you, Great Assembly, for your testimony. He then circumambulated the Dharma Hall once and departed.
When Chan Master Zhijian of Shanshan in Chizhou was first traveling as a mendicant with Guizong and Nanquan, they encountered a tiger on the road.
Each passed by the tiger. Nanquan asked Guizong, "What did that tiger just now look like to you? Guizong replied, "It looked like a cat.
Guizong then asked the Master (Zhijian), and the Master said, "It looked like a dog. He then asked Nanquan. Nanquan—
He said, "I see this as a great tiger. While the Master was eating his rice, Nanquan gathered up some raw rice and said, "Raw?
The Master replied, "Non-arising. Nanquan said, "Non-arising is still the secondary. After Nanquan had walked several paces, the Master called out, "Elder!"
Nanquan turned his head and asked, "What is it? The Master said, "Do not say that this is merely the secondary.

While they were all being asked to gather and select bracken shoots, Nanquan picked up a single stalk and said, "This one is excellent for making an offering. The Master said, "Not only this one; even a hundred flavors of exquisite delicacies [are likewise offerings]."
He also did not heed it. Quan said, "Even so, each and every one must taste it before they can attain it. (Xuánjué remarked: "These are words spoken after meeting;
they are not words spoken before meeting. A monk asked, "What is the primordial body? The Master said, "In all the world, there is nothing like it."
One day, Chan Master Ledu Weijian of Hongzhou was sitting in meditation behind the Dharma Hall.
When Mazu saw him, he blew twice on the Master’s ears. The Master rose, and upon seeing it was Mazu, he returned once more to his meditative absorption.
Mazu went back to his quarters and ordered an attendant to bring a bowl of tea to the Master; the Master paid no heed and simply returned to his hall.
Chan Master Daoheng of Mingxi in Lizhou once said, "I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world.

Later, a monk asked Caoshan, "The ancients said, 'I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world. I wonder what kind of illness this is? Caoshan replied, "It is the illness that cannot be gathered together. The monk asked, "Do all sentient beings also have this illness? Caoshan said, "Everyone has it. The monk asked, "Does the Master also have this illness?

Caoshan said, "I am searching for its point of origin and cannot find it. The monk asked, "Why do all sentient beings not fall ill? Caoshan said, "If all sentient beings were to fall ill, they would no longer be sentient beings. [The monk asked,] "Not yet..."

[The monk] examined whether the Buddhas also have this illness. Deshan said, "They do. [The monk] asked, "Since they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), why are they not ill? Deshan said, "It is because they are alert and aware (*jāgrat*). A monk asked, "How does one practice cultivation? The Master said, "What a fine master you are;
do not act like a hired laborer. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "Even to try to settle it would be inadequate."
Question: "What is the path of correct cultivation? The Master said: "It exists after nirvāṇa. Question:
"What is it that exists after nirvāṇa? The Master said: "Not washing one's face. Question: "I do not understand, Master. The Master said: "If there is no face, what is there to wash?"
Chan Master Huizang of Shigong in Fuzhou originally made his living as a hunter. He detested seeing śramaṇas.
Once, while pursuing a deer, he passed in front of Mazu’s hermitage. Mazu went out to meet him, whereupon the Master asked, "Did you see the deer pass by?
Mazu said, "Who are you? He replied, "A hunter. Mazu said, "Are you skilled at archery? He replied, "I am skilled at archery. Mazu said, "You..."
"How many can one arrow shoot? he asked. "One arrow shoots one," [the monk] replied. The Patriarch said, "You do not understand how to shoot.
"Does the Master understand how to shoot? he asked. "I do understand how to shoot," the Patriarch replied. "How many can one arrow shoot? "One arrow shoots a whole flock," the Patriarch said.
[The Master] said, "This is life and that is life. Why use this to shoot at that flock? The Patriarch said, "Since you know it is thus, why do you not shoot yourself?
He replied, "If you were to command me to shoot myself, there would truly be no place to apply my hand.

The Patriarch said, "This man's ignorance and afflictions (*kleśa*) from kalpas past have today been suddenly stilled. The Master cast down his bow and arrows and entered the Patriarch’s community to leave the household life. One day—
While he was working in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked him, "What are you doing? He replied, "I am herding an ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you herd it?
He said, "Whenever it goes into the grass, I pull it back by the nose. The Patriarch said, "You truly herd an ox. The Master then ceased [speaking].

After the Master took up residence, he constantly used the bow and arrow as a means of testing others (as recorded in the *Sanping Zhang*). The Master asked Xitang, "Do you understand how to capture the void?"
"Is it empty? Xitang said, "I have caught it. The Master asked, "How do you catch it? Xitang reached out his hand and grasped at empty space.
The Master said, "You do not know how to catch it. Xitang then asked, "How does my elder brother catch it? The Master seized Xitang’s nostrils and pulled them.
The Hall Attendant made a cry of agonizing pain, saying, "You are pulling at my nostrils far too hard; I feel as though they will come right off!
The Master said, "You must grasp empty space in this very manner before you can succeed. As the assembly was in session for inquiry, the Master asked, "Where has that which was just now gone?"
A monk said, "It exists. The Master asked, "Where does it exist? The monk snapped his fingers once. The Master asked, "How can one escape birth and death?
The Master said, "Why use 'escape'? The monk asked, "How then can one escape? The Master said, "This very thing does not undergo birth and death."

When paying respects to the true image of the former master, Huilang said, "For what reason did he teach that one should not pay respects? The Master replied, "How could there ever have been an error?

Chan Master Daoming of Nanyuan in Yanzhou ascended the hall and said, "A swift horse requires but a single whip; a swift man requires but a single word. If you have something to say, why do you not step forward?
If you have nothing to say, each of you should take care of yourselves. A monk asked, "What about that 'single word'? The Master then—
He stuck out his tongue and said, "When I possess the mark of a broad and long tongue, I shall speak to you.
When Dongshan went on a pilgrimage and ascended the Dharma Hall, the Master said, "I have already met you. Dongshan then descended.
The next day, he ascended again and asked, "Yesterday, I was already graced by the Master’s compassion; I do not know in what place we met. The Master—
The Master said, "Mind after mind, without interruption, flows into the ocean of nature. Sanshan said, "How many times have you let this pass? Sanshan took his leave.
The Master said, "Study the Buddha-dharma extensively and bring great benefit to others. Sanshan said, "I do not ask about studying the Buddha-dharma extensively;
what is meant by 'bringing great benefit'? The Master said, "Do not oppose a single thing. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Not..."
"You may say it is you. Zen Master Ziman of Licun in Xin Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Past and present are no different; the Dharma is naturally so. What more is there to say?
Even so, there are many who are at a loss regarding this matter. A monk asked: "Without falling into the ancients..."

"Now, I request that the Master speak directly. The Master said, "I knew well that you would be at a loss. The monk was about to offer a word when the Master said, "I thought for a moment that the old monk had fallen into the trap of 'the ancient' and 'the modern' [conventional logic].
The monk asked, "How is it so? The Master said, "A fish leaping into the azure sky—its flight is difficult to scale step by step.
The monk asked, "How can one avoid this fault? The Master said, "If one has the form of a dragon, who would discuss high or low? The monk prostrated.

[The disciple] prostrated. The Master said: "How bitter! How unjust! Who else is like me? He ascended the hall and said: "Setting aside the brightness of day and the darkness of night, what more could be said?
Take care! A monk asked: "What is the phrase of non-contention? The Master said: "It resounds through the heavens and shakes the earth."
Whenever Master Hong’en of Zhongyí in Lǎngzhōu saw a monk approach, he would snap his fingers and make a "he-he" sound.

When Yǎngshān was receiving the precepts, the Master likewise snapped his fingers and made the "he-he" sound. As Yǎng passed from west to east, the Master again snapped his fingers and made the "he-he" sound;
as Yǎng passed from east to west, the Master again snapped his fingers and made the "he-he" sound; when Yǎng stood in the center, the Master...
He stood up and then offered his apologies for the transgression of the precepts. The Master asked, "Where did you obtain this samādhi?
Nanquan Yang replied, "I brought it out from the seal at Caoxi. The Master asked, "Tell me, who did Caoxi receive with this samādhi? Nanquan Yang replied:
Jieyisujue looked up and asked, "Where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Great Master Mazu.
Jieyisujue asked, "How does one realize the principle of seeing Buddha-nature? The Master said, "I will give you a parable.
Suppose there is a room with six windows and a monkey inside. Outside, there is another monkey. From—"
From the east he called, "Singing-sing! and Singing-sing responded. He did this at all six windows, calling and receiving responses from each.
Yangshan bowed in thanks and rose, saying, "I have now fully understood through the Master’s parable. Yet there is one further matter:
if the inner monkey has fallen asleep while the outer monkey wishes to meet him, what then? The Master descended from his rope-corded seat and took hold of [Yangshan].
Yangshan gestured with his hand and performed a dance, saying: "The *xingxing* has met you.
It is like a tiny gnat building a nest upon the eye-lashes of a mosquito, then shouting at the crossroads: 'The land is vast and the people are few; those who meet are scarce. (Yunju Xi said:

"If Zhongyi had not received this single phrase from Yangshan at that time, where would there be a Zhongyi? Chou of Chongshou asked: 'Is there anyone who can definitively settle this principle? If one were to settle it...')"

"It is not so. This is merely a display of restless spirit. Where, then, lies the meaning of Buddha-nature? Xuangjue said, "If it were not for Yangshan, how could one have seen Zhongyi? But tell me, where exactly was it that Yangshan saw Zhongyi?"
A monk asked Master Lètán Chángxīng of Hongzhou, "What is it like to be a guest under the gate of Caoxi?

The Master said, "A swallow coming from the south. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Feathering its wings, waiting for the autumn wind. The monk asked, "What is the ultimate matter of the School’s transmission?
The Master said, "Autumn rain, the grass falls in disarray. When Nánquán arrived and saw the Master sitting with his face against the wall, he patted him on the back.
The Master turned his back. He asked, "Who are you? He replied, "Puyuan. The Master said, "How so? He replied, "It is just as usual.
The Master said, "Why do you make such a fuss?"
Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou was the son of the Du family of Shangluo in Shangzhou; his mother was Lady Li. She heard a voice from the air asking, "May I take up residence here?
and immediately became aware that she was pregnant. On the night of his birth, a divine light filled the room. He had barely reached the age of childhood when—

When walking, he always kept his gaze straight ahead; when sitting, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). At the age of nine, he relied upon Master Zhiben of Kaiyuan Temple to receive the Mahāyāna sūtras.
He could read five lines at once, reciting them all without omission. At twelve, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master You of Xiangzhou.
He studied the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shu*), and as soon as he finished reading it, he was able to expound upon it. He frequently [taught] for the assembly of monks.

He lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* without ceasing during either winter or summer. Later, hearing that the Chan school under Master Ma was flourishing, he went specifically to pay his respects.
Upon seeing that the Patriarch’s appearance was majestic and his voice resonant like a bell, he remarked, "Aloft is the Buddha-hall, yet within it there is no Buddha.
The Master prostrated himself and knelt to inquire, saying, "I have roughly exhausted the principles of the literature of the Three Vehicles. I have often heard of 'Chan'..."

"The gate is precisely the mind that is Buddha. [The Master] truly did not yet understand this. The Patriarch said, "It is precisely this very mind that has not yet been understood; there is nothing else besides it.
The Master asked, "What is the Mind-Seal that the Patriarch secretly transmitted when he came from the West?

The Patriarch said, "Virtuous One, you are quite busy right now. Go for now and come back at another time. As soon as the Master had stepped out, the Patriarch called out, "Virtuous One! The Master turned his head, and the Patriarch said:
"What is this? Upon hearing this, the Master attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "Why does this dull-witted fellow prostrate?
(Yunju Xi said: "Where is the real hubbub at Fenzhou? Having received this instruction, he traveled to Caoxi to pay respects at the Patriarch’s stupa, as well as to Mount Lu and Tiantai.
He traveled extensively to seek out sacred sites and later resided at Kaiyuan Jingshe. When students came to question him, he frequently replied to them: "Do not engage in false conceptualization.
Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty summoned the Master several times, but each time he declined on the pretext of illness and did not attend.

Upon the accession of Emperor Muzong, who longed to pay his respects in person, he dispatched Lingfu, the Monastic Registrar of the Two Streets, along with others, carrying an imperial edict to invite him. Upon arriving there, the Emperor paid his respects, saying: "The Emperor..."
"His Majesty’s decree of grace is unlike those of ordinary times; I pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will comply with the Heavenly Will and not speak of illness.
The Master smiled and said, "What virtue do I, this poor monk, possess to trouble the Sovereign so often? Please proceed ahead; I shall take another path.
He then bathed his body and shaved his hair. At midnight, he addressed his disciples, including Huìyīn, saying, "You all..."
The nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is coeval with the great void; it is neither born nor extinguished.

All realms of experience are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended. Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus bewildered by objects; once they are moved by an object, they become attached to it.
The cycle of transmigration is inexhaustible. You should know that the nature of the mind exists inherently from the beginning; it is not produced through artificial construction.
It is like a diamond, indestructible. All phenomena are like shadows and echoes; they possess no substantial reality. As the Sūtra says:
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Constantly realize that all things are empty, so that not a single object remains within the sphere of the mind.
This is the place where all Buddhas apply their minds; you disciples should practice it with diligence. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.

On the day of his cremation, auspicious clouds appeared in five colors and a wondrous fragrance permeated the four quarters. The śarīra relics obtained were as brilliant as pearls and jade. His disciples...
He was enshrined in a golden jar and interred within a stone stupa. In the third year of the Changqing era, he was posthumously titled National Teacher Dada.
A monk asked Chan Master Guangcheng of Datong in Lizhou, "How can the six sense faculties be extinguished?
The Master said, "A wheeling sword cast into the air does not harm anything. The monk asked, "What is the person of original nature? The Master said, "Sitting together, we do not [see one another]."
The student said, "If that is so, then I, this student, take my leave with gratitude. The Master said, "In secret, one writes of a sorrowful heart; to whom can it be sent?
Chan Master Dayi of Goose Lake in Xingzhou was the son of the Xu family of Xujiang in Quzhou.

During the reign of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang Dynasty, he was once summoned to the palace to debate doctrine at Linqide Hall. A Dharma Master asked, "What are the Four Noble Truths? The Master replied, "The Sage..."
[The Emperor] said, "There is one emperor; where are the other three emperors? He asked again, "The desire realm has no dhyāna, and dhyāna abides in the form realm.
Upon what basis does this land establish dhyāna? The Master replied, "The Dharma Master knows only that the desire realm has no dhyāna; he does not know that the realm of dhyāna has no desire."
[The Emperor] asked, "What is Chan? The Master pointed at the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master was speechless.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master lectures on infinite sutras and treatises, yet he cannot even manage this single point.

The Master then asked the eminent scholars, "In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, what ultimately constitutes the Way? One replied, "Knowing is the Way. The Master said, "One cannot [use] intellect."
“Know that it cannot be known by consciousness; how then can one know the knower? It is found in the presence of opposition yet without discrimination. The Master said:
“One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena without wavering from the ultimate truth—how can such a person be without discrimination?

It is found in the presence of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis. The Master said: “The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories. How [can it be defined]?”
When the Master mentioned that Emperor Shunzong had asked Chan Master Śrī how all sentient beings in the great earth might see their nature and attain Buddhahood, the assembly fell silent.
Śrī replied, "Buddha-nature is like the moon reflected in water."
"It can be seen, yet it cannot be grasped. He said to the Emperor, "The Buddha-nature is not something seen by means of sight;
how can one seize the moon in the water? The Emperor then asked, "What is this Buddha-nature? The Master replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty is currently asking.

The Emperor understood this in silence, and the True Lord (Emperor Zhenzong) thereafter held him in even greater esteem. There was a monk who requested permission to erect a stupa. Minister Li Ao asked him:
The teachings do not permit carrying a corpse beneath a stupa. Furthermore, what would you say? The monk had no reply.
The monk then questioned the Master, who said, "He has attained great icchantika-hood. He passed away in peace in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huijue.
Chan Master Zizai of Mount Funiu at Ique was the son of the Li clan of Wuxing.

Initially, he relied upon National Teacher Guoyi to receive full ordination; later, he visited Mazu Daoyi and realized the mind-ground. Mazu ordered him to deliver a letter to National Teacher Huizhong.
The National Teacher asked, "With what Dharma does Master Ma instruct his disciples? He replied, "It is 'mind is Buddha. The National Teacher asked, "What is that?"
After a long silence, he asked again, "Beyond this, what further words of instruction are there? The Master said, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
Someone remarked, "It is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing. The National Teacher said, "That still leaves something remaining. The Master said:
“Master Ma was exactly like that. I wonder, how is it here at your place, Venerable Sir? The National Teacher replied, “The three dots are like flowing water;

the curve is like a sickle for reaping grain. Later, when the Master resided at Mount Funiu, he ascended the hall and said, “‘This very mind is Buddha’ is a phrase of seeking medicine when one is not ill.
‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ is a phrase of counteracting the disease with medicine. A monk asked, “How about...”
This is a phrase of liberation. The Master said: "It has been transmitted from ancient times beneath Mount Funiu. He passed away at Kaiyuan Temple in Suizhou.
Chan Master Weikuan of Xingshan Temple in Jingzhao was the son of the Zhu family of Xin’an in Quzhou. At the age of thirteen, he saw...
Regarding the taking of life: [the Master] could not bear to eat it with such distress, and thus sought ordination. Initially, he studied the *Vinaya* and practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Later, he attended upon Mazu Daoyi (Daji), whereupon he attained the essential point of the mind. In the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he began his missionary travels among the regions of Wu and Yue.

In the eighth year, he arrived at Poyang, where a mountain deity requested to receive the eight precepts. In the thirteenth year, he resided at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. [The text ends here. Monk.
Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "A most fine mountain. The student said: "I am asking about the Way; why do you speak of a fine mountain? The Master said:
"You recognize only the fine mountain; when have you ever attained the Way? Question: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? The Master said: "It has. The student asked: "Does the Master have it?
The Master said: "I do not. The student asked: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature..."
“Nature—why does the Master alone lack it? The Master said, “I am not any sentient being. He asked, “If you are not a sentient being, are you perhaps a Buddha?
The Master said, “I am not a Buddha. He asked, “Ultimately, what kind of thing are you? The Master said, “I am also not a thing. He asked, “Can you be seen or conceived?
The Master said, “It is beyond the reach of thought and cannot be grasped through deliberation; therefore, it is called ‘non-’.”
This is inconceivable. In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital.
The Court Gentleman Bai Juyi once asked him, "Since you are called a Chan Master, why do you preach the Dharma? The Master replied, "Supreme Bodhi—when it is applied to the body, it is the Vinaya;
when spoken from the mouth, it is the Dharma; when practiced by the mind, it is Chan. These three are its applications, yet their ultimate aim is one. It is like..."
Just as the Yangtze, the Huai, the Han, and the Jiang rivers each receive their names according to their location, though the names differ, the nature of water is one and the same.
The Vinaya is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is not separate from dhyāna. Why, then, do you falsely give rise to discrimination within it? [The questioner] asks:

"If there is no discrimination, why is it necessary to cultivate the mind? The Master says: "The mind is fundamentally without injury or harm; why then must it be cultivated? In principle, there is neither defilement nor purity. One.
"Do not give rise to thoughts. [The student] asked, "If defilement is not to be thought of, may purity be free from thought?
The Master said, "It is like the surface of a person's eye: not even a single thing can remain there. Though gold dust is a precious treasure, when it is in the eye, it becomes an affliction.

[The student] asked, "If there is neither cultivation nor thought, how does this differ from an ordinary person? The Master said, "Ordinary persons are characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*), while those of the Two Vehicles are characterized by attachment. To be free from these..."
These two illnesses—this is called true cultivation. One who truly cultivates neither exerts effort nor forgets. To exert effort is to approach attachment; to forget is to fall into ignorance.
This is the essential point of the mind, and that is all. A monk asked, "Where does the Way reside?
The Master said, "It is right before your eyes. The monk said, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Because you have a self, you do not see it. The monk said, "My..."
"If there is 'self,' one does not see. Does the Upādhyāya still see? The Master said, "If there is you and there is me, we will miss each other in our mutual pursuit.
[The monk] asked, "If there is no self and no you, do you still see? The Master said, "If there is no you and no me, who is there to seek seeing?

On the final day of the second month in the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, having finished preaching the Dharma from the hall, he passed away. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dache (Great Penetration).
Chan Master Wudeng of Ezhou was a native of Wei County. He left the household life at Mount Gonggong and secretly received the essential points of the mind-transmission.
Later, he went to reside at Tumen in Suizhou. One day, he went to visit the Provincial Governor, Chief Attendant Chang. As he was about to leave, the Governor called out, "Master!
The Master turned back; the Governor struck the pillar three times. The Master made a circular gesture with his hand and then struck it three times.
He brushed [the question] aside and departed. Later, he resided at Daji Temple in Wuchang.

One day, during the evening assembly, as each person came before the Master and said, "We hope you are well," the Master addressed the assembly, saying, "Where has the sound of the assembly just now gone?
A monk raised one finger. The Master said, "Take care. The next morning, that monk went up [to the hall].
"Param. The Master then turned his body around, lay down facing the wall, and feigned groaning, saying, "I have not been very well for these past few days.
Great Virtue, do you have any medicine by your side? Give me a little.
The monk struck the *jingping* (purification pitcher) with his hand and said, "From where did you get this purification pitcher? The Master replied, "This is..."
"Where is the old monk’s? Where is the Great Virtuous One’s? He replied, "It is also the Master’s; it is also mine.
A monk asked Chan Master Zongyin of Sanjiao Mountain in Tanzhou, "What are the Three Jewels? The Master said, "Rice and wheat."
Doubting, he said, "I, a student, do not understand. The Master said, "The assembly will joyfully receive and uphold this.
He ascended the hall and said, "If one discusses this matter, by the time you raise your eyebrows, you have already missed it. Magu then asked, "I do not ask about raising the eyebrows."
"What is this matter? The Master said, "You have missed it. Gu then overturned the meditation seat. The Master then struck him.
(Changqing spoke on his behalf: "Silently.")
A monk asked Chan Master Baoyun of Luzu Mountain in Chizhou, "What is the teacher of all Buddhas?
The Master said, "It is not he who has a jeweled crown upon his head. The monk asked, "Who then is it? The Master said, "He who has no jeweled crown upon his head. Dongshan came to visit him;
having prostrated, he stood in attendance for a short while and then went out. He entered once more, and the Master said, "Just like that..."
"Ma. Just so. That is why it is like this. Shan said, "There are many who would not agree with this. The Master said, "How can you use your verbal cleverness to take [the measure of] me?
Shan then bowed. A monk asked, "What is 'speaking without words'? The Master said, "Where is your mouth? The monk said, "I have no mouth.
The Master said, "With what do you eat your meals? The monk was speechless. (Dongshan spoke on his behalf, saying: "He does not eat when hungry.")
"What kind of rice? Whenever the Master saw a monk coming, he would simply turn his back to the wall.
Nanquan heard of this and said, "I have always told the monks to try to understand it before the Buddha appeared in the world; yet I still cannot find even one or half of one who succeeds.

For him to act like that—when will he ever get there? (Xuanjue said: Was this a response in kind, or was it a refusal to speak? Baofu asked Changqing, 'As for Luzu, where does the crux lie in being spoken of by Nanquan in such a way? Changqing—"

Yunmen said, "To withdraw for oneself and yield to others—there is not one such person in ten thousand. Luoshan said, "Teacher Chen, had you seen his back at that time, you would have given him five strokes with the fire-brush. Why did you let him go instead of taking him in? Xuansha said, "Had I been there at that time, I too would have given him five strokes with the fire-brush. Yunju Xi said, "Luoshan and Xuansha both speak in this way; are they identical, or is there a distinct principle? If you can discern this, I will grant that the Dharma has a place for you, Venerable One. Xuanjue said: [The text continues: "If you can see through this, you will understand the meaning of 'the fire-brush. If you cannot see through it, you will fall into the pit of the 'five fires. If you can see through it, you will know that the 'fire-brush' is not something external; it is the very function of your own mind. If you cannot see through it, you will mistake the 'fire-brush' for a physical object. If you can see through it, you will realize that the 'fire-brush' is the total freedom of the Way. If you cannot see through it, you will be trapped by the traces of words. If you can see through it, you will find that the 'fire-brush' is the very source of all phenomena. If you cannot see through it, you will remain bound by the duality of letting go and taking in. If you can see through it, you will attain the state where there is neither letting go nor taking in. If you cannot see through it, you will be lost in the confusion of gain and loss. If you can see through it, you will transcend all calculations. If you cannot see through it, you will be caught in the net of conceptualization. If you can see through it, you will realize that the 'fire-brush' is the ultimate reality itself. If you cannot see through it, you will remain within the realm of delusion. If you can see through it, you will awaken to the fact that there is no 'fire-brush' to be found anywhere. If you cannot see through it, you will continue to chase after shadows. If you can see through it, you will understand that the 'fire-brush' is the unobstructed functioning of the Great Function. If you cannot see through it, you will be hindered by the limitations of form and substance. If you can see through it, you will enter the gate of the Unborn. Chan Master Taiyu of Fuyong Mountain in Changzhou was the son of the Fan family of Jinling. Once, while serving food, he arrived before Layman Pang.
As the Layman was about to receive it, the Master withdrew his hand and said, "To give rise to a mind to accept offerings—Vimalakīrti already rebuked such a thing long ago."

The Master said, "I have not yet seen him; how can you know his point of ultimate reality?

Chan Master Daotong of Ziyu Mountain in Tangzhou was the son of He [surname] from Lujiang.

Seeing a stone that was square and brilliant purple, he sighed and said, "This is indeed purple jade; it is merely the prophetic prediction of my former master.
He then trimmed the thatch to construct a hut and took up residence there. Later, disciples gathered from the four quarters. A monk asked, "How can one escape the three realms?
The Master said, "How long have you been inside them? The monk asked, "How does one achieve liberation?"

When the Master arrived at Nanquan, he observed the assembly of monks in the midst of their practice. Nanquan pointed to a water pitcher and said, "The copper pitcher is an object.

Later, the Master arrived at Mt. Gui and entered the hall; there, at the head of the upper platform, he unpacked his robes and bowl.

Hearing that his "uncle" had arrived, Guishan first assumed a formal demeanor and descended into the hall to meet him. Upon seeing him coming, the Master made a gesture of lying down. Guishan then returned to his quarters.
Shortly thereafter, Guishan asked his attendant, "Is my uncle still here? The attendant replied, "He has already left."
Yangshan said, "When you left, what did you say? The Master replied, "I said nothing. Yangshan said, "Do not say you said nothing; your voice was like thunder.
The Master resided at Mount Heng during the winter and stayed at Qingliang during the summer. During the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled repeatedly to Mount Wutai.

On his way, he passed through Huaisi, where it happened that Wu Yuanji had raised troops in rebellion and defied the imperial mandate. The government forces and the rebel army were engaged in combat. Not yet...
The two sides were engaged in combat. The Master said, "I shall go and resolve this calamity. He then cast his mendicant’s staff into the air and flew across it.
The generals and soldiers of both armies looked up in wonder; the event corresponded exactly with their prior dream, and their fighting spirit was instantly extinguished.

Having manifested such supernatural wonders, the Master feared he might delude the masses, so he entered Mount Wutai. Before the Vajra Cave, intending to manifest his final passing, he first asked the assembly: "All of you..."

When he was about to pass away, he sat down and departed; when he was about to lie down, he did so and departed—this I have personally witnessed. "Is there also such a thing as departing while standing? he asked. "There is," they replied.

The Master said, "Has anyone ever reached the point of departing while standing on their head? "I have never seen such a thing," they replied. Thereupon, the Master turned upside down and passed away, remaining perfectly upright.

His robes clung to his body as if they were naturally aligned with it. At that time, the assembly discussed carrying him to the cremation pyre, but he remained motionless and firm. Those from near and far gazed upon him in wonder.
They marveled at this beyond measure. The Master had a younger sister who was a nun; she was also present there at the time.

She stroked him and rebuked him, saying, "Brother, you did not follow the laws and precepts in your past life, yet even in death you continue to delude people. She then pushed him with her hand, and he fell down dead.
Thereupon, his body was cremated, and his relics were collected to build a stupa.
A monk asked Chan Master Dasha (also known as Longshan Da-shan) of Tanzhou, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "The rooster crowing on a spring day. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The dog barking on the Mid-Autumn festival.
He ascended the hall and said, "Come forth, come forth, everyone! This old man has a vital teaching; after my passing, it shall not trouble you. The assembly said, "We ask for it at once."
The Master said, "It does not take more than a single pile of fire.
Chan Master Wuliang of Guiyang in Quanzhou was the son of the Shen family of that prefecture. At the age of seven, his father took him to Baizhang Monastery;
he regarded it as his own home and consequently renounced worldly attachments. At eighteen, he received the tonsure and was fully ordained at Lingyan.

Later, he visited Daji (Mazu), whereupon he fully realized the ancestral vehicle (*zucheng*). He immediately returned to the north of his original monastery, a place where the paths for gathering firewood had long been cut off.

One day, the Master set out with his staff, pushing through the thickets, when he encountered a giant six-eyed tortoise; in an instant, it vanished. He then built a hermitage on this peak, which consequently came to be called Guiyang (Tortoise Pond).
One day, a tiger chasing a deer entered the hermitage; the Master warded off the tiger with his staff, and thus [the deer] was saved.
Lüming, as he was about to manifest his passing into nirvana, composed a verse, saying: "For eighty years I have distinguished east from west;
Now I no longer need this white-haired old man. Neither long nor short, neither large nor small— It is identical in nature to that of all people.

Without coming, without going, and likewise without abiding, I have realized that the original self-nature is empty. Having finished the verse, he passed away peacefully and was interred at [the site].
The main hall had stood for nearly twenty years when it was submerged by mountain waters. A disciple opened the stupa and saw the entire body floating in the water.
Upon hearing this, the King of Min sent an envoy to carry the remains into the palace courtyard for veneration. Suddenly, a foul odor spread far and wide.

The King burned incense and prayed, saying, "May you return to your former site at Guiyang to have a stupa built. As soon as he finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance pervaded everywhere. The entire population...

He went to the city to pay his respects. The local governor memorialized the Emperor for the posthumous title "Great Master Zhenji" (True Tranquility), and his stupa was named "Lingjue" (Numinous Enlightenment).
Later, his disciple Huizhong was buried to the left of the stupa; today, the two *dharmakāya* (true bodies) remain at Guiyang. Huizhong received the Dharma from Master Yiyu of Ca’ān.
Chan Master Tanchang of the West Garden Hermitage on Mount Nanyue received the seal of mind from Daji. Later, he visited Shitou, where his realization became brilliantly clear and penetrating.

He went forth to reside at the West Garden, and his circle of dharma companions flourished daily. One day, while the Master was bathing by himself, a monk asked, "Why do you not have a novice attend to this?
The Master clapped his hands three times. (The monk reported this to Caoshan, who said, "In one sense, it is the same to clap or strike the palms; however, among them, [the Master of] Xiyuan... )

"How strange! Both [Zhaozhou and Caoshan] were practitioners of the 'one-finger Zen. This was because their way of taking responsibility was not thorough. A monk then asked Caoshan, 'When Xiyuan clapped his hands, was that not the business of slaves and servants? Caoshan said, 'Yes. The monk asked, 'Is there anything further above this? Caoshan said, 'There is. The monk asked, 'What is the matter above this?
Caoshan rebuked him, saying, 'You slave and servant! The Master kept a dog. Whenever he would practice walking meditation at night, [the dog would follow him].
The dog bit the Master’s robe, whereupon the Master immediately returned to his quarters. Furthermore, it would often lie down and guard by the side of the gate;
suddenly one night, it barked repeatedly, leaping up and assuming the posture of a fierce bite. At dawn the following day, there was a great python in the eastern kitchen, several *zhang* in length.
The snake opened its mouth and hissed; its poisonous flames blazed fiercely. An attendant requested that he move away from it, but the Master said, "Can death be escaped?
It comes with poison, yet I receive it with compassion. Poison has no inherent nature; it becomes potent only when provoked.

If there were no conditions for compassion, then enemies and kin would be one and the same. Having spoken, the python lowered its head and moved slowly away, suddenly vanishing. Again, one night, a group...
The thieves arrived, and the dog likewise bit at their clothes. The Master said to the thieves, "In this thatched hut there is whatever you may desire;
feel free to take it all. I have no regrets whatsoever. Moved by these words, the thieves all bowed their heads and dispersed.
Chan Master Zhentou of Yangqi Mountain in Yuanzhou ascended the hall and said: "The myriad spirits share a single source; they are provisionally named 'Buddha.

Though their substance is exhausted and their forms dissolve, they do not perish; though the metal melts and the raw ore disperses, they remain eternally present. When the ocean of nature is windless, the golden waves surge forth spontaneously.
When the spiritual mind is free from duality, the ten thousand phenomena are simultaneously illuminated. One who realizes this principle traverses the sands of all worlds without speaking."
Without effort, his merit further deepened the mysterious transformation. How could he turn his back on awakening and instead conform to worldly toil?
Within the aggregates and realms, he falsely imprisoned himself through attachment. Chan Yue asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master held up his rosary. Chan Yue was at a loss. The Master asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "I have come to study under Shitou. [Chan Yue] said, "I see."
Shitou. "What was his realization? The Master pointed to a deer in the courtyard and asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "He has attained freedom.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he passed away. Upon cremation, seven hundred śarīras were obtained.
A pagoda was built at the foot of East Peak.
Zen Master Shenzang of Maitou Peak in Cizhou ascended the hall and said: "To know while being without knowing—this is not a state of ignorance;

yet it is called 'being without knowing. He then descended from his seat. (Nanquan said, "If one follows the Master’s words in this way, one has only spoken half of it. Huangbo said, "It is not that Nanquan is refuting him; he wishes to complete the previous statement.")
Chan Master Shanjue of Hualin in Tanzhou constantly carried a *khakkhara* staff. At night, he would go out among the forest thickets;

every seven paces he would strike the staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara once. Jia Shan asked him, "I have heard from afar that you, Master, recite the name of Avalokiteśvara—is this true?"
The Master said, "Indeed. Shanshan asked, "What is it like when one has already mounted the head? The Master said, "If you put your head out, I will let you mount it;
if you do not put your head out, what is there to mount? Shanshan was speechless. When a monk came for an interview, he spread out his sitting cloth.

The Master said, "Slowly, slowly. The monk asked, "What did you see, Preceptor? The Master said, "What a pity—that you should smash the bell tower! From this, the monk attained awakening. (Observation)
The Censor-in-Chief Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Do you have any attendants? The Master replied, "There are one or two, but they cannot see guests.
