The protuberance on his forehead was raised like a pearl; his voice and speech were clear and resonant, and his disposition was profound and serene.

Later, while traveling at Mount Tiantai, he encountered a monk who spoke and laughed with him as if they were old acquaintances. Upon looking closely, however, the monk’s gaze pierced people; the Master then traveled with him.

When they reached a mountain stream that had suddenly swollen, the Master cast aside his rain hat, set down his staff, and stopped. The monk urged the Master to cross together, but the Master said, "Brother, you must..."
The ferryman was crossing himself. He immediately lifted his robes and stepped upon the waves as if treading on level ground.
Looking back, he called out, "Come across! Come across! The Master said, "Tsk! You self-enlightened fellow. Had I known earlier, I would have cut off your shins.
The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I am not his equal. Having spoken, he vanished. Later, the Master traveled to the capital, where he was awakened by another person.
He then went to visit Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Majestic and imposing, from where have you come? The Master replied, "Majestic and imposing, I have come from Lingnan.

Baizhang asked, "Being so majestic and imposing, for what purpose do you come? The Master replied, "Being so majestic and imposing, I do not come for any other purpose," and he immediately prostrated himself.
[Baizhang] asked, "How is the ancestral Dharma-transmission (zongcheng) indicated? Baizhang was pleased.

After a long silence, the Master said, "I cannot allow this to be cut off for future generations. The Staff-bearer said, "I thought you were someone after all. He then rose and entered the abbot’s quarters.
The Master followed him in, saying, "I have come specifically for this purpose. The Staff-bearer said, "If that is so, you must not let yourself be deceived by me in the future.
One day, the Staff-bearer asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Mount Daxiong."
[The Master] went down to gather mushrooms. Baizhang asked, "Did you see the tiger? The Master then made the sound of a tiger.
Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike; the Master then struck Baizhang with a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned.
He ascended the hall and said, "At the foot of Mount Daxiong there is a great tiger. You all must watch out for it. Old man Baizhang has now [seen it]."
Riqin encountered Mazu Daoyi. Later, while serving as an attendant under Nanquan Puyuan, during a communal work period of selecting vegetables, Nanquan asked, "Where are you going?
Riqin replied, "I am going to select vegetables. Nanquan asked, "With what will you select them? Riqin held up his knife. Nanquan said, "You only know how to act as a guest."
Not understanding how to act as the host, the Master (Nanquan) pricked him three times with his knife. Nanquan said, "Everyone, go pick the vegetables.
One day, Nanquan said, "I have a 'Song of Herding an Ox'; I ask you, Elder, to provide a response. The Master replied, "I already have my own teacher.
When the Master took his leave of Nanquan, Nanquan saw him off at the gate and held up his straw rain hat, saying, "Elder, your physical stature is of vast capacity; [is this] your rain hat?"
"Great and small beings are born. The Master said, "Even so, the great trichiliocosm is entirely contained within this. Yuanquan asked, "What about you, Master Wang?

The Master put on his rain hat and walked away. While the Master was prostrating before the Buddha in the hall of Yanguan, Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, who was then a śrāmaṇera, asked him, "The Elder does not seek the Buddha, does not seek the Dharma, and does not seek the Saṃgha."
"When prostrating, what should one seek? The Master said, "Do not seek it by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek it by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek it by clinging to the Sangha.
Always perform your prostrations in this manner. Zhao Mi said, "What is the use of performing prostrations? The Master then struck him with his palm. Mi said, "That was quite crude.
The Master said, "What kind of place is this for you to speak of 'crude' or 'refined'? He struck him again. (Later, when) Prime Minister Pei was stationed [there]...

In Wanling, a great Zen monastery was established and the Master was invited to preach the Dharma. Because the Master had a deep affection for his former mountain, he named it Huangbo after returning there.
One day, the Duke (Pei Xiu) set up a statue of the Buddha before the Master and knelt, saying, "I request the Master to bestow a name upon it.

The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! The Duke responded, "Yes. The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you. The Duke prostrated himself. Thereupon, the Master spoke these six [verses]:...
A man newly arrived; the five men paid their respects. One of them lifted up his sitting mat and drew a circle.
The Master said, "I have heard there is a very fierce hunting dog. The monk said, "It comes seeking the sound of the ewe.
The Master said, "The ewe makes no sound for you to seek. [The monk] said, "It comes seeking the tracks of the ewe. The Master said, "The ewe leaves no tracks for you to seek."
The monk said, "I have come following the tracks of the ewe. The Master said, "The ewe leaves no tracks; you have come here searching for them.
The monk said, "If that is so, then it is a dead ewe. The Master then ceased speaking. The next day, he ascended the hall and said, "Yesterday, the monk who was searching for the ewe—come forward!"
The monk then departed. The Master said, "Yesterday’s case was not yet resolved; I have retired for now. What do you say to this? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "I took you for a genuine patch-robed monk, but it turns out you are merely a scholar-monk.
He then struck him and drove him out. One day, the Master clenched his fist and said, "All the old monks of the world are here. If I..."

"I allow one thread of freedom. From this, you may move freely in all directions—up, down, across, and through. "If I do not grant this freedom, it will not take more than a single squeeze," [the Master] said.
A monk asked, "What is it like when you allow one thread of freedom? The Master replied, "Moving freely in all directions.

The monk asked, "What is it like when there is no granting of freedom and not even a single squeeze? The Master replied, "Universal. Once, Prime Minister Pei invited the Master to the prefecture and presented his own understanding.

The Master showed it to the teacher [Pei Xiu]. The teacher took it and placed it on his seat, not even glancing over it for a moment. After a long while, he asked, "Do you understand? Pei replied, "I have not fathomed it.
The Master said, "If you could understand it in such a way, you would still be somewhat close;

but if it were expressed in ink and paper, what would remain of our school? Pei then presented a poem, one chapter of which read: "Since the Great Being transmitted the Mind-Seal, a circle has appeared upon my forehead..."
With a body seven feet tall like a precious jewel, he hung his staff for ten years while dwelling by the waters of Shu. Today, floating his bowl, he crosses the banks of the Zhang River.
A thousand dragons and elephants follow his lofty steps; ten thousand miles away, incense and flowers form a cause for supreme merit.

Those who wish to serve the Master as disciples do not know to whom the Dharma will be entrusted. The Master showed no sign of joy. From that time on, the tradition of Huangbo flourished throughout the Jiangnan region.
This was manifest. One day he ascended the hall; the great assembly had gathered like clouds. He then said, "What do you all seek?
He drove them away with his staff, yet the assembly would not disperse. The Master sat back down and said, "You people are all nothing but wine-dregs eaters.
To travel on pilgrimage in such a manner is to invite ridicule from others. You only see where there are eight hundred or a thousand people."

He then departed. One must not seek to stir up a scene of clamor. When I was traveling on pilgrimage, if I encountered a man beneath the roots of a grass, I would strike him with a goad right between his brows.
If he had known how to feel pain or itch, I could have filled a cloth bag with rice and provided for him;
but since everyone is as easygoing as you are, where else would there be a day like today?
This is a matter of fact. Since you all call yourselves "wandering monks," you ought to apply some measure of spirit. Do you know that within the Great Tang there are no Chan masters?
At that time, a monk asked, "The venerable elders of all quarters gather crowds to teach and transform them;
why then do you say there are no Chan masters? The Master said, "I do not say there is no Chan; it is simply that there are no teachers. You, O Kalyāṇamitra..."
It is seen that beneath Master Mazu, there were eighty-four people sitting in the place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), yet those who attained Mazu’s True Dharma Eye were only two or three;
Master Guizong of Mount Lu was one of them. Now, a renunciant must know the matters transmitted from of old before they can truly succeed.
For instance, under the Fourth Patriarch, Niutou spoke horizontally and vertically, yet he had not yet [attained it].
To know the pivotal point that leads upward and to possess such an eye—only then can one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

Yet, if you cannot personally realize the appropriate application of these matters, but merely know how to study words and phrases, tucking them away in your leather bag and claiming everywhere, "I understand Chan," will this ever avail you against birth and death?
To treat the venerable elders with such contempt is to enter hell as if it were your own home.
"An arrow! As soon as I saw you enter the gate, I recognized you immediately. Do you understand? You must exert yourself with urgency;
do not let this life pass in vain, wearing a mere patchwork robe and subsisting on the food of others.
Those with clear eyes will laugh at you; in the end, you will be reckoned among the common folk. You should examine for yourself how far you have come and whose face this matter concerns. If...
If you understand, then you understand; if you do not understand, then disperse. Take care. [A monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master struck him.

All other pedagogical devices were intended for those of superior capacity; those of middling or inferior faculties could not fathom their depths. In the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, he passed away at his mountain seat.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Duanjì (Severing the Boundary).
Chan Master Changqing Da'an of Fuzhou (also known as Lanyan) was the son of the Chen family of that prefecture.

He received his monastic training at Huangbo Mountain, where he studied the Vinaya and the Mahāyāna teachings. He once reflected to himself, "Though I have practiced with diligent hardship, I have not yet heard the principle of the profound ultimate.

Thereupon, he traveled with his staff alone to seek out teachers elsewhere, intending to go to Hongjing. On his way, he passed through Shangyuan and encountered an old man who said to him, "Master..."

"I am going to Nanchang; I shall surely gain something there. The Master then went to Baizhang, paid his respects, and asked, "A student wishes to seek the realization of the Buddha—what is it that is the Buddha?
Baizhang said, "It is very much like riding a cow while searching for the cow. The Master said, "Once it has been realized, what then?
Baizhang said, "It is like a person riding a cow back home. The Master asked, "I do not yet understand how to maintain this from beginning to end. Baizhang...

[The Master] said: "It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over them, not allowing them to trample upon the crops. From this point on, the Master understood the essential meaning and no longer wandered in pursuit of it.
He joined Chan Master You, with whom he shared the same realization, and when they first settled at Mount Gui, the Master personally plowed the fields to assist in the Way.
When Master You passed away, the assembly requested him to succeed him as abbot. He ascended the hall and said: "All of you have come here to seek peace; what exactly is it that you are seeking?"
Ma. If you wish to become a Buddha, you are yourself already a Buddha. Yet you carry this "Buddha" about with you, running from house to house, just like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage;

when will you ever attain correspondence [with reality]? If you wish to become a Buddha, simply be free of all these inverted,攀缘 (pān-yuan), delusive thoughts, and evil perceptions—the defiled and pure mind of a sentient being—and that itself is the initial awakening of the right enlightenment. What further Buddha could there be?
To investigate this according to its specific context: for over thirty years he lived at Mount Gui, eating Mount Gui’s rice and defecating Mount Gui’s dung, yet he did not study Mount Gui’s Chan;
he simply watched a single water buffalo. If it strayed onto the path or entered the grass, he would pull its nose back;
as soon as it encroached upon the crops, he would whip and subdue it. Having been tamed through long practice, it was truly pitiable.
The words spoken by others have now been transformed into a white ox in the open air. It is always before you, manifest and vivid throughout the day;
though you try to chase it away, it will not go. Each of you possesses a priceless great treasure:
from the gateway of the eyes, light is emitted, illuminating the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; from the gateway of the ears, light is emitted, perceiving all sounds, whether good or evil.
These six gates constantly emit radiance day and night; this is also called the Samādhi of Emitting Light.
You yourself do not recognize that which you grasp as a reflection within the body of the four elements, which supports it from both within and without, preventing it from tilting.
It is like a person carrying a heavy burden crossing a single-plank bridge, yet never losing their footing. Tell me, what is the thing that sustains it? Speak!
"It is so. Yet, there is not even a hair’s breadth to be seen. Do you not see? Master Zhigong said: 'Searching within and without, nothing at all is found;
yet the functioning upon the objective realm is entirely present. Take care! A monk asked: "All functioning is the activity of the Dharmakāya.
What is the Dharmakāya? The Master said: "All functioning is the activity of the Dharmakāya. The monk said: "Apart from..."
[The monk] set aside the five aggregates and asked, "What is the primordial body? The Master said, "Earth, water, fire, wind, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

[The monk] said, "These are the five aggregates. The Master said, "These are distinct from the five aggregates. [The monk] asked, "When this aggregate has already passed away and that aggregate has not yet arisen, what is it then?

The Master said, "This aggregate has not yet passed away. Who is the Venerable One? [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said: *Note: The final response by the Master is left as a rhetorical challenge, indicating that the true nature of reality transcends the conceptual framework of arising and ceasing.*
"If you comprehend this aggregate (*skandha*), you will clearly understand that aggregate. A monk asked, "When the Great Function manifests before one and no fixed rules remain, what then?
The Master said, "You have used it; use it! The monk then bared his shoulder and circumambulated the Master three times.
The Master said, "Why do you not speak of the matter beyond [this]? As the monk prepared to open his mouth, the Master struck him and said, "You wild fox spirit, get out! There was another monk...
He ascended the Dharma Hall and looked east and west, but did not see the Master. He then said, "What a fine Dharma Hall! It is simply that there is no one here.
The Master came out from within the door and asked, "What is it? The monk had no reply.
Later, Xuefeng went into the mountains and found a branch of wood shaped like a snake; he inscribed upon its back: "Originally natural, requiring no carving," and sent it to [the Master].
The Master said, "A man who dwells in his true nature leaves no trace of axe-blows. A monk asked, "Where is the Buddha?
The Master said, "Not apart from the mind. The monk asked again, "What has the Venerable One of Double Peak attained? The Master said, "In the Dharma, there is nothing to be attained."
"If there is anything attained, it is fundamentally non-attainment. [A monk] asked, "When Huang Chao’s army arrives, where will the Master go to avoid it?
The Master said, "Into the mountains of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). [The monk] asked, "What if he suddenly catches you? The Master said, "I would disturb the General.
The Master extensively propagated the Dharma in Min and Gan. In the third year of the Zhonghe era of the Tang dynasty, he returned to Huangbo and passed away. His stupa was erected at Lengyan.
At Mount Jia, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Yuanzhi.
Chan Master Huanyong of Daci Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of the Lu clan from Puban. His cranial protuberance was rounded and prominent, and his voice was like that of a bell.

At a young age, he encountered the mourning for his mother; while at her grave, he served out the period of bereavement. Having fulfilled his obligations, he reflected on how to repay his mother’s boundless kindness, and thus went to Bingzhou.
He left home at Tongzi Temple and ascended Mount Song to receive full ordination, where he studied the various Vinaya teachings. Later, he visited Baizhang and received the seal of the mind.
Taking his leave, he went to Changle Temple on Mount Nanyue, where he thatched a hut atop the mountain.
One day, Nanquan arrived and asked, "What is the master of this hut? The Master replied, "Heaven! Heaven! Nanquan said, "Setting aside 'Heaven' for a moment, what is the hut?"
Zhongzhu asked, "Master, if you understand, then understand; do not be so talkative. Quan shook his sleeves and left.

Later, while presiding at Daci, he ascended the hall and said, "This mountain monk cannot answer questions; I can only recognize the illness. At that time, a monk stepped forward, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.

(Fayan said, "The assembly calls this 'the illness,' yet they fail to recognize it right before their eyes. Xuangjue said, "Tell me, did Daci recognize the illness or not? When this monk came forward, was it an illness or not? If you say it was an illness..."
"Every day, whether walking or sitting, one cannot be entirely ill. If you say it is not illness, then what is this when you come out? Zhaozhou asked, "What is the essence of Prajñā?
The Master replied, "What is the essence of Prajñā? Zhaozhou laughed loudly and went out. The next day, while Zhaozhou was sweeping the floor, the Master said:
"What constitutes the essence of Prajñā? A monk placed a broom down and clapped his hands, laughing loudly. The Master then returned to his quarters.
As the monk took his leave, the Master asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "To Jiangxi. The Master said, "May I borrow a portion of your labor for a while?"
The monk asked, "What business do you have with the Abbot? The Master said, "Can you take this old monk away?
The monk replied, "There are those even more eminent than the Abbot whom one cannot take away either. The Master then desisted. Later, the monk related this to Dongshan, who said:

The Acharya asked, "Why do you speak thus? The monk said, "How would you, O Master, speak? Sanshan said, "Attained. (Fayan offered an alternative: "If the Master were to go, I would carry his rain-cloak.
Sanshan then asked the same monk, "What other words or phrases did Daci have? The monk replied, "At times he addressed the assembly, saying:
'To speak for ten feet is not as good as practicing for one foot; to speak for one foot is not as good as practicing for one inch.'"
Yi-cun asked, "Master, why do you not speak in that way? Sanshan said, "I do not speak in such a manner. Yi-cun asked, "How then would you speak, Reverend?

Sanshan said, "Speak that which cannot be practiced; practice that which cannot be spoken. (Yunju said: "When practicing, there is no path of speech; when speaking, there is no path of practice. When neither speaking nor practicing, what path should one follow? Luopu said:

'If both practice and speech reach their destination, then the fundamental matter is absent; if neither practice nor speech reaches their destination, then the fundamental matter remains. Later, during the reign of Emperor Wuzong, the Buddhist teachings were suppressed. The Master [Sanshan] passed away.)

He lived in seclusion as a layman. During the Dazhong era, he was re-ordained and extensively propagated the fundamental tenets [of his school]. In the third year of the Xiantong era, he passed away without illness.
Emperor Xizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Xingkong.

Chan Master Puan of Tiantai Pingtian was a native of Hongzhou. Having attained the essential meaning under the guidance of Baizhang, he later heard that Tiantai possessed magnificent scenery and that sages and worthies had emerged there in succession.
Desiring to transcend the mundane world and follow in their distant footsteps, he cleared away the weeds and tied up his thatched hut beneath the trees to dwell in silent meditation.
As the months and years passed, he became known to the fourfold assembly, who established the monastery of Pingtian.

He resided at Chan Yuan Temple. Ascending the hall, he said: "The divine light is not obscured; it is a glorious legacy for all ages. Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.
He then descended from his seat. A monk came to pay his respects; the Master struck him with a staff. The monk stepped forward and seized the staff.
The Master said, "I was a bit hasty just now. The monk struck the Master with a staff. The Master said, "An adept! An adept! The monk bowed.
The Master seized him and said, "It was you, Dharma brother, who were hasty. The monk laughed heartily. The Master said, "This monk has been thoroughly defeated today.
Later, when Linji visited the Master, he first encountered an older sister-in-law working in a field at the entrance to the road.
Ji was driving the ox when he asked his sister-in-law, "Which way does the road to the level fields go? His sister-in-law struck the ox with a staff and said, "You beast!
You have wandered everywhere, yet you do not even know this road. Ji spoke again, saying, "I am asking you for the road to the level fields."
"Where are you going? His sister-in-law replied, "This beast is not yet five years old and cannot yet be used.
Jie thought to himself, "If one wishes to observe a person, one should first observe what they employ; this already suggests the intent to pull out nails and extract wedges.
When he saw the Master, the Master asked, "Have you seen my sister-in-law yet? Jie replied, "I have already taken her under my care. The Master then asked, "Lately..."
"From where have you come? Mazu replied, "From Huangbo on the West River. Mazu said, "I knew well that you would come to see a master.

Mazu said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master. Mazu said, "We have already met. Mazu said, "According to the etiquette between guest and host, I ought to offer three prostrations.
Mazu said, "Since it is the etiquette between guest and host, then prostrate yourself. He then spoke a verse to the assembly, saying: "The Great..."

The Way is vast and empty; it is the constant, singular true mind. Do not contemplate good or evil; let the spirit be pure beyond all things. Following conditions, drink and eat; what else is there to do?
He passed away at this very monastery, and his stupa remains there to this day.
A monk asked Chan Master Changguan of Wufeng in Ruizhou, "What is the realm of Wufeng?

The Master said, "Precipitous. The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Obstructed. When the monk took his leave, the Master asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to Mount Tai.
The Master held up a finger and said, "If you have seen Mañjuśrī there, come back here and I will meet with you. The monk—[departed].
[The monk] was speechless. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the village. The Master said, "Did you see the ox? He replied, "I saw it.
The Master said, "Did you see its left horn? Did you see its right horn? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke on his behalf: "I saw that there is no left or right."
[Yangshan spoke differently, saying: "Do you still distinguish between left and right? Another monk took his leave.
The Master said, "When you go to various regions, do not slander me by saying I am here. The monk said, "I do not say that the Master is here.
The Master asked, "Where do you say I am? The monk held up one finger. The Master said, "You have already slandered me."
A monk asked Chan Master Xingkong of Shishuang Mountain in Tanzhou, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master said, “Suppose there were a person in a thousand-foot well who could emerge without the aid of even a foot of rope—such a person would answer you regarding the meaning of his coming from the West.
The monk said, “Recently, Master Chang of Hunan has appeared in the world; he also speaks to people with words here and there.”
The Master called to the śrāmaṇera and said, "Drag this corpse out! (The śrāmaṇera was Yangshan. Later, Yangshan asked Danyuan, "How can one get the person out of the well?

Danyuan said, "Tsk! You fool! Who is in the well? Yangshan then asked Guishan. Guishan called out, "Huiji! Yangshan responded. Guishan said, "He is out. After Yangshan became the abbot, he frequently cited these previous words, saying to the assembly:
"I gained my name from Danyuan; I gained my ground from Guishan.")
Chan Master Shenzan of Guling in Fuzhou was originally ordained at Dazhong Temple in his native prefecture. Later, while traveling on pilgrimage, he attained enlightenment under Baizhang.
Upon returning to his home temple, he asked his original teacher, "While you were away from me, what accomplishments have you gained?"
[The Master] said, "I have no business at all," and consequently sent him to perform manual labor. One day, while bathing his body, he ordered the Master to remove the dirt from his back.
The Master then patted his back and said, "A fine Buddha hall, yet the Buddha is not holy. The Master turned his head and looked;
the Master continued, "Though the Buddha is not holy, he is at least able to emit light. On another day, while the Master was reading a sutra by the window, a bee flew in.
The master looked at him and said, "The world is this vast and wide, yet you are unwilling to leave it; you merely bore into old paper—when will you ever get out? He then spoke a verse:
"The Gate of Emptiness you refuse to leave, Yet you throw yourself through a window—how very foolish! For a hundred years you have bored into old paper;
On what day will you finally emerge? His original teacher then set down his scriptures and asked, "Whom did you encounter while traveling on foot?"
"I have seen you before and after, and your speech has always been extraordinary. The Master said, "I, this humble one, was shown a place of rest by Venerable Baizhang;
I now wish to repay his compassionate virtue. Thereupon, the Abbot informed the assembly and prepared a vegetarian feast, requesting the Master to preach the Dharma.
The Master then ascended the seat and proclaimed the tradition of Baizhang, saying: "The spiritual light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.

Its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters. The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally perfected from the beginning. Simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
Upon hearing these words, the Founder attained awakening, exclaiming: "Who would have thought that in my old age I would hear such ultimate matters?"
Later, the Master resided at Guling. After gathering disciples for several years, as he was about to pass away, he bathed and shaved his head.
Ringing the bell, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you all recognize the samādhi of no-sound? The assembly replied, "We do not recognize it. The Master said, "Listen quietly."
"Do not think of anything else. The entire assembly listened intently. The Master remained solemn and passed into stillness (*parinirvāṇa*). His stupa remains at his original mountain.
Chan Master Tong of He'an Temple in Guangzhou was ordained at Shuanglin Temple in Wuzhou. From childhood, he spoke little; people of the time called him "The Silent Tong.
Once, while he was prostrating before a Buddha, a Chan practitioner asked him, "What is it that you, the Dharma Master, are prostrating to?"
[The Master] said, "It is a Buddha. The Chan practitioner then pointed to the image and asked, "What is this? The Master had no reply.
That night, he prepared his formal robes and paid his respects, asking, "Regarding what I asked today, I do not yet know its meaning.

The Chan practitioner asked, "How many years of summer retreats (*kṣānti*) have you completed as a lecturer? The Master replied, "Ten years. The Chan practitioner asked, "Have you ever left the household life [to become a monk]? The Master—
He was utterly bewildered. The meditator said, "If you do not understand, what have you been doing for a hundred summers? He then ordered his fellow practitioner Mazu to go with him.
When they arrived at Jiangxi, Mazu had already passed away, so he went to see Baizhang, where his doubts were suddenly dispelled.
Someone asked, "Are you a Chan master? The Master replied, "I, a poor monk, have never studied Chan. After a long silence, the Master called out to the man; the man—
He assented. The Master pointed to a coconut tree and the man had no reply. One day the Master summoned Yangshan and said, "Bring me the small bed.
When Yangshan had brought it there, the Master said, "Return it to its original place. Yangshan did so. The Master then called Huiji (Yangshan’s name), and he responded.
The Master asked, "What is that object over there by the bed? Yangshan replied, "A pillow. The Master said, "The pillow..."
"What is this over there? Dashi said, "Nothing. The Master called out, "Huiji! Dashan responded, "Yes.
The Master asked, "What is this? Dashan had no reply. The Master said, "Go."
A monk asked Chan Master Longyun Tai of Jiangzhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Last night, the ox was lost in the pen."
Chan Master Dao of the Weiguo Monastery in Jingzhao arrived for an audience. The Master asked, "From where have you come? The monk replied, "I have come from Henan.

The Master said, "Has the Yellow River cleared yet? The monk had no reply. (Miaoyan of Mount Wei spoke on his behalf: "A small fox cub wishes to cross; let it cross—why harbor doubt? The Master was unwell and did not receive visitors.
When someone came to pay their respects, he said, "I have long heard of the Venerable’s virtue and character; I am honored now to receive your Dharma..."
His physical condition was unwell, so he briefly requested to see the Master. The Master took his bowl and its stand, had an attendant carry them out and present them, at which the man had no reply.
A monk asked Master Wansui of Zhenzhou: "The great assembly has gathered; what should we discuss? The Master said: "Chapter One:
The Prologue" (Ruizong Rong’s variant says: "After prostrating, depart").

A single statement regarding Nanquan’s passing may be said to outshine the past and surpass the future; it is rarely heard in all time. The Master remained silent.
A monk asked, "What is Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles. The monk asked, "What is Avalokiteśvara?
The Master said, "Sounds and speech. The monk asked, "What is Samantabhadra? The Master said, "The minds of sentient beings."

[The student] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "It is the physical body (*rūpakāya*) of sentient beings. [The student] asked, "Since the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical, why are there various names for them?
The Master said, "Returning to the source through the faculty of sight is called Mañjuśrī; returning to the source through the faculty of hearing is called Avalokiteśvara;
returning to the source through the mind is called Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Avalokiteśvara... [text fragment ends]
Sound is the Buddha’s unconditional great compassion; Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous, unconditioned practice;

these three sages are the Buddha’s sublime function, and the Buddha is the true essence of these three sages. In terms of function, there are as many provisional names as there are sands in the Ganges;
in terms of essence, they are collectively named as one Bhagavān. Question: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. How is this principle to be understood? The Master said: "Listen."

The Old Monk’s Verse: "Where there is obstruction, it is not a wall; where there is passage, it is not empty space. If one understands in this way, mind and form are fundamentally the same. He further said:
"The Buddha-nature manifests with majestic dignity, yet sentient beings who dwell within its nature find it difficult to see.
If you awaken to the selflessness of sentient beings, how does my face differ from the Buddha's face? Having thus concluded the inquiry into the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
In the end, there is no substance. How, then, can one speak of transforming the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom?
The Master showed them a verse: "The seven arise depending on the one; the one ceases while sustaining the seven. When the one ceases, they all cease;
the six and the seventh never migrate. Question: "When an earthworm is cut into two segments, both ends move. We do not know which end possesses the Buddha-nature. The Master said:

[The student] asked, "How can one deal with deluded thoughts? The Master said, "How can you deal with movement? [The student] said, "I do not know how fire and wind have not yet dispersed. The Master said, "Do you not know that fire and wind have not yet dispersed?
[The student] asked, "How can one turn back mountains, rivers, and the lands to return to oneself? The Master said, "How can one turn back oneself?"
[The monk] said, "I have gone to form mountains, rivers, and lands. The Master said, "I do not understand. The monk replied, "Under the city walls of Hunan, it is good for raising the people;
rice is cheap and firewood is plentiful, sufficient for all four neighbors. The monk was speechless. The Master presented a verse, saying: "Who asks about the turning of mountains and rivers?
Mountains and rivers turn toward whom? Perfect penetration has no two sides; The Dharma-nature fundamentally has no place of return. The Huayan Seat-Master asked, "Is space..."
[The student asked: "Is this definitely existent? Or is it definitely non-existent? The Master said: "To say it is existent is acceptable; to say it is non-existent is also acceptable.
When space is said to exist, it is merely a provisional existence; when space is said to be non-existent, it is merely a provisional non-existence.

[The student] asked: "Regarding what the Master has said, what scriptural authority is there for it? The Master said: "Virtuous One, have you not heard? The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* says: 'The space of the ten directions arises from your [mind]...'"
Within the mind, it is like a single fleck of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky—is this not the time when space arises?

It is merely the arising of a provisional name. Again, it is said: "If even one person among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty spaces of the ten directions will all vanish away"—is this not the time when space ceases?
It is merely the cessation of a provisional name. This is why I, the old monk, say: existence is provisional existence; non-existence...
"This is provisionally non-existent. He asked again, "The sutra says: 'As if within pure lapis lazuli, the image of true gold appears within. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Take pure lapis lazuli as the essence of the Dharma-realm; take the image of true gold as the essence of untainted wisdom."
It can give rise to wisdom; wisdom can penetrate the essence. Therefore it is said: "As within pure lapis lazuli, the image of true gold appears within.
Question: What is the sphere of activity for those of the highest rank? The Master said: "Like the eyes of a dead man. Question: When those of the highest rank meet one another, what is it like?
The Master said: "Like the hands of a dead man. Question: Why did Sudhana travel through the universes for immeasurable kalpas?
[The student] said, "The world is not pervasive within the body of Samantabhadra. The Master said, "From immeasurable kalpas past until now, have you ever traveled throughout it all?
[The student] asked, "What is the body of Samantabhadra? The Master said, "Seeking Chang'an inside the Han-yuan Palace. [The student] asked, "What is the mind of a student?
The Master said, "The entire world of the ten directions is your mind. [The student] said, "If that is so, then for this student..."
"Is this where you attach your body? The Master said. The monk asked, "What is the place where one attaches the body?
The Master said, "The great ocean is deep, yet deeper still. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Fish and dragons come and go; they rise and sink as they please.
A monk asked, "When someone asks the Master, you answer according to the circumstances. But when no one asks the Master, what then?"
The Master said, "When weary, one sleeps; when vigorous, one rises. A monk asked, "How should a student understand this?
The Master said, "In summer, one is bare-boned; in winter’s cold, one must have a robe. A monk asked, "Where has the deceased monk gone after his passing? The Master showed him a verse, saying:
"Unaware of the diamond body, Yet calling it 'conditioned arising. The ten directions are truly quiescent; Who is there, and who remains?"
"Who is traveling? The Master praised Nanquan Zhen, saying: "Majestic is Nanquan, the source of the three periods. The Vajra-body abides eternally; throughout the ten directions it is boundless.
Birth and Buddhahood are inexhaustible; having manifested, they return once more. Having long relied upon Nanquan, there is a verse on hitting the mark that says:
'Today I return home and enter the great gate; Nanquan’s direct path pervades the universe. Every dharma is distinct and clear.'"
The Patriarch turned his head and said with shame, "What fine descendants! Nanquan replied, "Today’s opportune matter need not be discussed.
Nanquan does not say it pervades the entire universe; returning home is entirely the business of descendants, for the patriarch has never gone out the door."
The Verse on Encouraging Study says: "Even atop a ten-thousand-fathom pole, one must not rest; Majestic is the path, yet few travel it.

The Master (Xuedou) therefore composed a verse: "The myriad dharmas are of one suchness—there is no need for selection. In this one suchness, who is there?"
Whether one discriminates or does not discriminate, this very life-and-death is fundamentally bodhi; the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time share the same eye.
A verse admonishing the felling of pines and bamboos says: "A thousand-year bamboo and a ten-thousand-year pine—branch by branch and leaf by leaf, they are all the same.
I inform you, seekers of the profound from the four quarters: whenever you raise your hand, you are none other than touching the Patriarch."

He left home to become a monk at a temple and received full ordination according to his seniority. Later, he entered the quarters of Nanquan and eventually traveled to Matishan in Quzhou, where he settled in a thatched hut for his daily life.
In the second year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, a local resident named Weng Qiangui offered the Zihu (Son Lake) area below the mountain and established a monastery there.
The Master hung a wooden plaque at the entrance that read: "At Zihu there is a dog; it takes people's heads."
In the middle he seizes the person’s heart; at the bottom he seizes the person’s feet. To hesitate for a moment is to lose one’s body and life.

Under Linji’s assembly, two monks were traveling to visit other teachers when they lifted the curtain. The Master shouted, “Look out for the dog! The monks looked back, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.

While tilling the garden with Master Shengguang, the Master suddenly struck the hoe down and, looking back at Guang, said: “The matter is not non-existent, but as soon as you conceive a thought, it is already gone.”
"Go away. Guang then asked, "What is the matter? The Master stepped forward, tripped him by treading on his chest, and knocked him down.
From this, he attained realization. When the nun arrived for an audience, the Master said, "Are you not Liu Tiemo? She replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "Turn left! Turn right!
She said, "Master, do not act so perversely. The Master then struck her. One night, the Master shouted in front of the Sangha hall, "Thieves! The assembly—
Everyone was startled. A monk came out from inside the hall, and the Master seized him, saying, "The *vinaya-dhara* has caught you!
He has caught you! The monk said, "It is not I. The Master said, "It is indeed I; it is simply that you are unwilling to take responsibility.
He then presented a verse to the assembly, saying: "For thirty years I have dwelt at Zihu; For two meals a day, my strength has been coarse on rice gruel. There is nothing to do."
He went up the mountain once; when asked if people of the time understood him, [he replied that they did not]. During the Guangming era, he passed away peacefully without illness.
His stupa was erected at his home mountain.
Chan Master Tanzhao of Baima in Jingnan often said, "How happy! How happy! Yet, when the time of his death arrived, he cried out in agony.
"Alas! Furthermore, King Yama has come to take me. The head of the monastery asked, "When you were thrown into the water by the Military Commissioner at that time, your countenance remained unmoved.
How can you now be like this? The Master raised his pillow and said, "Tell me, was it so then, or is it so now?
The head of the monastery had no reply. (Fayan spoke on his behalf: "At such a moment, simply cover your ears and leave.")

Chan Master Yiduan of Xiangyan in Dengzhou ascended the hall and said: "Brothers, since we have not yet resolved our mutual doubts, what matters are there for us to discuss together?
In three or five days, I shall depart. Those who study now must reach a final resolution."
Set aside the present moment. Do not merely crave the "nothingness" of those superior men.
Brothers, even if you should learn all manner of diverse paths of meaning, you will never be able to substitute them for your own realization; you must ultimately exert effort to achieve it.
Merely memorizing others' clever phrases will only lead to increasing confusion. If you wish to attain accord with the truth, simply be reverent and diligent in every way.
"Do not linger for even a hair’s breadth; only when you are like empty space will there be a small measure of it.
For empty space has no locks or gates, no walls or enclosures, no shape or segments, and no eyes or mind. At that time, a monk asked, "How was it when the ancients met?
The Master said, "I have never met the ancients. The monk asked, "In these times, where the life-lineage remains unbroken, how can one resemble them?"
The Master said, "What is there to admire? [The monk] asked, "I am not asking about trivial matters;
I ask the Master to provide an answer. The Master said, "What more do you seek from me? [The monk] said, "It is not for the sake of trivial matters. The Master said, "Then you are making me speak.
He then said, "Brothers, the Buddha is dust; the Dharma is dust. You spend your whole days racing and seeking—what rest can there be? Simply..."
In the midst [of practice], do not allow sentiment to hang upon you; let sentiment not hang upon things. There is no good to be grasped, and no evil to be discarded.
Do not let yourself be caged or obscured by them—this is the true place of training. A student asked, "I once took my leave from an elder master.

He said, 'When you go, stay close to virtuous associates and attach yourself to good friends. Now I take my leave of the Master; I wonder what instruction you have for me? The Master said, "Pay your respects."
[The Master] bowed. The monk prostrated. The Master said, "As for bowing, you may bow as you please; do not mistake a servant for a lord. He ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "What is the direct source? The Master then cast down his staff and immediately returned to his quarters.
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Beyond speech and silence, there is a path. This old monk’s mouth is too narrow;
I cannot explain it to you. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, a monk asked: "For what reason is the true cause (zheng yin) without affairs?

The Master replied: "I have never paused. He then continued: "Even if one were to strip away everything layer by layer until nothing remains and there is no lingering trace, [it is merely] provisional..."
The "provisioning" at that time is also a skillful means for guiding people. If it were a matter of the other shore [of ultimate reality], such a thing would be impossible.
Chan Master Xian of Lingjiu in Chi Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "This is the fundamental task for each of you.
If I were to tell you, this old monk, how to do it, it would be like drawing legs on a snake. At that time, a monk asked: "I do not ask about drawing legs on a snake; how about this?"
"This is the fundamental matter," the Master said. "Venerable, try to speak on it. When the monk was about to ask again, the Master said, "Why do you paint your feet?
Master Mingshui asked, "What is the sudden attainment of the Dharmakāya? The Master replied, "Once you have passed through the Dragon Gate, look toward the clouds beyond;
do not be like a fish that strikes its forehead against the Yellow River. Yangshan asked, "When all is silent and speechless, how does one see and hear?"
The Master said, "Before the seamless stupa, there is much rainwater. A monk asked, "What is it like when both of them are silent? The Master said, "It is the constant.
The monk asked, "Is there anything that transcends the constant? The Master said, "There is. The monk said, "Please, Master, sing it forth.
The Master said, "The mysterious pearl shines of itself; why need one seek light from beyond the wall? [The monk] asked, "Today we make offerings to Great Master Wuran of West River."
"Is it not yet certain whether he will return? The Master said, "Originally there was nowhere to go; how could he now turn with the wind?
[The monk] asked, "If that is so, what is the use of making offerings? The Master said, "The power of conditioned effort does not interfere with the nature of ultimate meaning."
A monk asked the Venerable Master of Mount Song at Luojing, "What is it like when the ancient road is level? The Master said, "It does not go forward.
The monk asked, "Why does it not go forward? The Master said, "Because there is no obstruction. The monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Song? The Master said:
"The sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west. The student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "I do not understand 'east' or 'west' either.
The student asked, "What is it like when the six consciousnesses arise together? The Master said, "They are different. The student asked, "Why is it so? The Master said, "They are the same."
When Master Rizi was visited by Yaxi for an audience, the Master made a gesture of rising. Yaxi said, "This old mountain ghost still sees me here.
The Master said, "My fault, my fault; just now I failed to respond. As Yaxi was about to offer further words, the Master gave a shout.
Yaxi said, "Standing before a great battle array, it is indeed difficult to resist. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. Yaxi said, "It is not so."
"Not so" (Zhaozhou said: "Pity these two fellows; they do not know the phrase for turning around").
A monk asked West Chan Monastery Master of Suzhou: "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings.
What is the very intent of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master raised his whisk and showed it to him. The monk did not prostrate himself, but departed immediately.
Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Zhejiang. Xuefeng said, "Where were you this summer? The monk said, "At Xichan. Xuefeng asked, "Is the Master well?
The monk replied, "When I arrived, he was in full health. Xuefeng said, "Why did you not stay there at ease?
The monk said, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. Xuefeng asked, "What is the matter? The monk recounted the previous conversation. Xuefeng said, "You..."
"How is it that you do not accept him? he asked. [The monk] replied, "He is an object. Feng said, "Do you see the men and women in the houses within the city of Suzhou?
He replied, "I see them. Feng said, "Do you see the trees, groves, ponds, and marshes along the road? He replied, "I see them.
Feng said, "In all cases, when one beholds the men and women in houses, the great earth, the forests, and the ponds—all are objects. Do you accept this? He replied, "I accept it. Feng said:
"As for the mere act of raising the whisk, why do you refuse to accept it? The monk then prostrated and said, "I, your disciple, have spoken thoughtlessly;
I beg the Master’s compassion. Feng said, "The entire universe is this single eye.
Where will you sit and crouch? The monk was speechless.

The Grand Master Lu Xing, the Prefectural Governor of Xuanchuan, asked Nanquan: "An ancient once raised a gander in a bottle. As the gander grew larger, it could no longer get out of the bottle. Now, one must not break the bottle, nor may one harm the gander. How, O Monk, does it get out? Nanquan called out, "Grand Master! Lu responded, "Yes. Nanquan said, "It has come out. From this, Lu attained awakening. Thus it is said: The gander grows within the bottle; The bottle grows with the gander. If you wish to see the gander emerge, Do not destroy the bottle, do not harm the gander. Nanquan calls out, "Grand Master! Lu responds, "Yes. Nanquan says, "It has come out. At these words, the Grand Master was liberated. Thus it is said: "The gander grows within the bottle; The bottle grows with the gander. He paid his respects with a formal expression of gratitude. When Nanquan passed away, the Abbot of the monastery asked, "Why did you, Great Officer, not weep for the late Master?
Lu said, "If the Abbot could speak [the truth], then I would weep. The Abbot was speechless. (Changqing spoke on his behalf: "Whether it is appropriate to weep or not.")
One day, the lay practitioner Gan-zhi of Chizhou entered Nanquan’s hall to provide a vegetarian feast. Huangbo was serving as the head seat. The practitioner requested that alms be distributed.

The head seat said, "The two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are equal and without distinction. Gan-zhi said, "How can such words justify my offering of a *dakṣiṇā* (alms-offering)? He then took [the offering] and went out.
A short while later, he re-entered and said, "Please grant me the gift of material wealth. The head seat replied, "Material wealth and the Dharma..."

The two patrons were equal and made no distinction between them; Gan then proceeded to distribute the alms. On another day, he entered the monastery to provide gruel and invited Nanquan to perform the recitation.
Nanquan struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the wildcat and the white ox.
Gan shook out his sleeves and departed. After the meal, Nanquan asked the steward, "Where is the practitioner?"
Zuo said, "He would have left right then. Quan immediately smashed the cooking pot. Gan Chang received guests and visitors;
once, a monk asked him, "It is no easy matter for a lay practitioner to receive guests. Gan replied, "It is like feeding a donkey or feeding a horse," whereupon the monk withdrew.
There was a monk living in a hermitage who was soliciting donations for household goods. Gan said, "I have a question; if you can answer it, I shall give you something.

He then wrote the character for "mind" (心) and asked, "What character is this? The monk replied, "The character for 'mind'. Gan then asked, "What character is this for [your] wife? The monk replied, "The character for 'mind'."
Gan said, "My wife should also live in this hermitage. The monk remained silent, and Gan likewise gave him nothing.
He then asked another monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Mount Gui. Gan said, "Once a monk asked Mount Gui, 'What is the meaning of the coming from the West?
Mount Gui raised his whisk. How do you understand Mount Gui's meaning? The monk said:

"Using phenomena to clarify the mind; attaching to objects to manifest the principle. Gan said, "It would be better to return to Mount Mui. (Upon hearing this, Baofu raised his hands and then turned them palm-down.)

National Teacher Anguo of Yanguan was a successor of Chan Master Chang of Guannan in Xiangzhou. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the West? The Master raised his staff and said, "Do you understand?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master then struck him. Whenever he saw a monk coming to pay his respects, he would most often [use] his staff.
"Chasing after. Some say, "A moment too late," while others say, "Beating the drum of Guannan. Yet among his contemporaries, few could sing in response.
When Chan Master Xuanzhen of Shuangling in Hongzhou first asked Wudeng, "Why is it that the Bodhisattva Without Supernatural Powers..."
"His traces are difficult to find," I said. "Only those on the same path will know. The Master asked, "Does the Abbot know them?
I replied, "I do not know. The Master asked, "Why do you not know? I replied, "Because you have departed, you do not recognize my words.
Later, the Master attained realization of the essential meaning under Yanguan.
Chan Master Jiǎnzōng of Jìngshān in Hángzhōu was the son of the Qián clan of Húzōu. He left the household life under the Venerable Gāoxián of Kāiyuán Monastery in his native prefecture;
he mastered the *Sīyì jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) and was well-versed in the Pure Land teachings. Later, he went to Yànhuán to resolve his lingering doubts and obscurities.

In the third year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, while residing at Mount Jing, the Master had a junior disciple named Hongxin (Hongxin was the Great Master Fajie), who prided himself on his skill in lecturing and debate.

The Master said to him, "The True Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is direct and beyond verbal expression. Your calculation of grains of sand in the ocean—what benefit does this have for the ultimate principle?
You need only refrain from maintaining cognitive views, extinguish all external conditions, and detach from every state of mind; this is your true nature. Hongxin...

He was utterly bewildered and, having paid his respects and taken leave, traveled to various regions. Upon reaching Mount Gui, he finally realized the profound essence of the teachings and subsequently became a successor to Mount Gui.
The Master passed away in the seventh year of the Xiantong era; he was posthumously honored with the title Great Master Wushang (Supreme).
Chan Master Lingxun of Mount Furong in Fuzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Guizong Chang. When he first visited Guizong, he asked, "What is the Buddha? Guizong replied:
"I have told you this; will you believe it? The Master said, "If it is the Honored One’s sincere word, how would I dare not believe it?
Zhaozhou said, "It is precisely you yourself. The Master asked, "How does one maintain this? Zhaozhou said, "A single speck of film in the eye, and empty flowers fall in confusion.

(Fayan said: "If there were no subsequent words, how could there be a 'returning to the source'? The Master took his leave. Zhaozhou asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going back to the mountain ranges."
Zhong said, "You have been here for many years; now that you have finished your preparations, come and let me speak some Dharma for you.
The Master packed his belongings and went up. Zhong said, "Come closer. The Master drew near. Zhong said, "The weather is cold on the road; take good care of yourself.
Upon hearing these words, the Master’s previous understanding was suddenly forgotten, and he passed away in tranquility. He was posthumously titled Great Master Hongzhao.
A monk came from Jia Shan to pay his respects to Master Gaoting of Hantan. As soon as he prostrated, the Master struck him.
The monk said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects; why do you strike me? The monk prostrated again, and the Master struck him once more and drove him away.

When the monk returned and reported this to Jia Shan, Jia Shan asked, "Did you understand? The monk replied, "I did not understand. Jia Shan said, "It is fortunate that you did not understand. Had you understood, then..."
At the mouth of the Jia Pass, the Mute One.
Master Daemao of Silla ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to recognize the Teacher of all Buddhas, recognize him within the mind of ignorance.
If you wish to recognize the eternally abiding, unfading nature, recognize it amidst the constant transformation of the myriad things. A monk asked: "What is..."
At Dayumao (Daomaofeng). The Master said, "The blade is not revealed. [A monk] asked, "Why is the blade not revealed? The Master said, "Because there is no one who can meet it.

Zen Master Zhitong of Mount Wutai (who called himself the "Great Zen Buddha") was initially residing under the assembly at Guizong. One night, he suddenly cried out repeatedly, saying, "I have attained great enlightenment!
The assembly was startled by this. The next day, when the assembly had gathered for the hall discourse, Guizong said, "Last night..."
The Master came forward and said, "I, [Name]. Yunmen asked, "What principle have you realized that you speak of 'Great Enlightenment'?
Try to explain it. The Master replied, "A nun was originally made by a woman. Yunmen marveled at this. The Master then took his leave.
As Yunmen saw him off at the gate, he offered him his straw rain-hat. The Master took the hat, placed it on his head, and walked away immediately, without a word.
Looking back, he later resided at Fahua Temple on Mount Tai. At the time of his death, he spoke a verse: Raising my hand, I grasp the Southern Dipper;
Turning my body, I lean against the Northern Pole Star. I emerge my head to gaze beyond the heavens: Who else is there like me?
A monk asked National Teacher Kazhi of Silla, a successor of Chan Master Dame Chang: "What is the meaning of [the Patriarch’s] coming from the West?
The Master said, "I will tell you when you come from within. The monk asked, "What is the essential purport of Dame? The Master said, "Curdled milk is originally all at once."
"Thrust!
Thus spoke Master Tiantong of Hangzhou while ascending the hall for the assembly: "Do not wait for this old monk; when it is time to come, simply come;
when it is time to go, simply go. Each of you possesses the ocean of the nature of the Flower Treasury (Huazang), complete with merit and unimpeded radiance. Each and every one...
Take this up. Be careful. A monk asked, "How does one go forth beyond the three realms? The Master said, "Where are you right now?
[He was] the Dharma successor of Chan Master Foguangman.
Bai Juyi, styled Ledu, was the Prefect of Hangzhou. He had long attended upon Foguang, through whom he attained the Dharma of the Mind and simultaneously received the Mahāyāna Vajra Jewel Precepts.
During the Yuanhe era, he visited the Dharma Hall of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao and posed four questions (the words of which appear in the "Yushan Chapter").
In the fifteenth year [of the Yuanhe era], while serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, he visited Master Niaoke; their dialogue and exchanges are recorded (as seen in the "Niaoke Chapter").

I once sent a letter to Dharma Master Ji, arguing that since the Buddha possesses unsurpassed great wisdom and has expounded the principles of the teachings, how could there be a situation where he accommodates the varying capacities of beings and responds to their diverse ailments in ways that contradict the doctrine of the single flavor of equality?
I cited six scriptures, including the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Vajrasamādhi*, to refute his two-fold interpretation. Furthermore, regarding the five aggregates and the twelve...

Regarding the explanation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the preceding and succeeding sections differ in character. Establishing principles to investigate them, [the author] probes the profound and seeks out the hidden, penetrating the obscure and illuminating the subtle.
Yet, I have not seen the Dharma Master’s response, nor have there been many who have come forward to provide an answer on his behalf.

Furthermore, having received the eight stages of gradual cultivation (*aṣṭau krama-śikṣā*) from Master Ning of the Eastern Capital, I shall expand upon each single word into a verse to explain its essential meaning.

From the shallow to the profound, his works are like pearls strung together. Wherever he served in official posts, he frequently sought out the ancestral Way. He held that there should be no fixed teacher for learning.
Later, serving as a Palace Attendant (*Binkè*) stationed in the Eastern Capital (*Dōngdū*), he exhausted his own stipend to restore Longmen Xiangshan Temple.

Upon its completion, he composed the inscription himself. In all his writings, he invariably addressed matters of edification; there was nothing that did not praise the Buddha Vehicle (*Fóchéng*). This is evident in his collected works. His...
The sequence of his official appointments and his final return to complete the ancestral sacrifices are recorded in the historical records.
Chan Master Mo of Wuxi was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Zhengyuan of Guishan in Fuzhou;
he was the son of the Cai family of Xuancheng. He once composed a verse to instruct his disciples, the first of which says:
How many times has the vast ocean turned into mulberry fields? Only empty space remains uniquely serene. Those who have already reached the shore need no longer cling to the raft;
those who have not yet crossed must surely rely on the boat. Second: Having sought the teacher and recognized the source of one’s own mind, both banks are profound while the center is not.
If you are already a Buddha, there is no need to seek another Buddha; it is simply because of this that you forget all conditions. Xiantong.
[He lived for] ten years and passed away at his native mountain. He was posthumously titled Master Xingkong (Nature-Emptiness).
A monk asked Su Xi Worthy One, "What is the Buddha Dingguang? The Master said, "A duck swallows a snail.
The monk asked, "Does this allow a student to turn back? The Master said, "The eyes protrude outward."
The Master Puhua of Zhenzhou, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Panshan, was a man of unknown origins. He served Panshan as his teacher and secretly received the true instructions;
however, he feigned madness and spoke without restraint. Following the passing of Panshan, he went to the northern regions to practice his teachings, or—
In a city or among the graves, he shook a single bell and said: "If it comes from the bright side, strike it on the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, strike it on the dark side;
if it comes from the four quarters and eight directions, strike it with a whirlwind; if it comes from empty space, strike it with a continuous barrage.
One day, Linji had a monk seize him and asked, "What if it does not come in any of these ways? The Master pushed him away and said, "Come tomorrow, Great Compassionate One."
There was a vegetarian feast in the monastery. When the monk returned, he recounted this to Jie. Jie said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Whenever he saw anyone, regardless of their status, he would ring his bell once; he was thus known at the time as Master Puhua.
Sometimes he would ring the bell right by a person's ear or against their back. If someone turned around, he would immediately open his hands and say, "Give me a coin."
He would also eat food at improper times. Once, as evening fell, he entered Linji’s monastery and ate raw vegetables.
Linji said, “This fellow looks exactly like a donkey. The Master then brayed like a donkey. Linji said to the steward, “Give him plenty of fodder.
The Master said, “The people of Shaoshi did not recognize me; now I have come again to Jinling. Linji’s single eye sees through everyone everywhere.”
He opened [the gate]. Seeing the cavalry officer, the Master stepped forward and shouted, "Watch out! The officer also shouted, "Watch out! and assumed a wrestling stance.
The officer ordered his men to strike the Master with five blows of the staff. The Master said, "It resembles it, but it is not it. Once, while the Master was in the midst of the marketplace...
Shaking a bell, he sang out: "I cannot find a place to go. At that time, Daowu encountered him, seized him, and asked:
"Where do you intend to go? The Master replied: "Where have you come from? Daowu was speechless. The Master jerked his hand away and departed.
One day, Linji and the Elder of Hetang Muta were sitting together in the Sangha Hall. Just then—
It was said that the Master was daily in the marketplace, acting like one who had lost his wits; no one knew whether he was an ordinary man or a sage.
Suddenly, the Master entered, and Linji asked him, "Are you an ordinary man or a sage? The Master replied, "Now tell me, are you an ordinary man or a sage?
Linji then gave a shout. The Master pointed his finger and said, "The bride of He-yang; the old woman’s Zen of the wooden pagoda; Linji’s little..."
"That fellow has, however, one eye open. Ji said, "This thief! The Master said, "Thief! Thief! and then went out.
At the beginning of the Tang Xiantong era, as he was about to pass into extinction, he entered the marketplace and said to the people, "I beg for a *zhidu* (monastic robe).
Some people gave him a padded jacket, others gave him a cloth cloak, but he accepted neither; shaking his staff, he departed. Linji had someone deliver [a robe] to him.
The coffin was brought. The Master laughed and said, "Linji’s brat is so talkative," and then accepted it. He then took leave of the assembly, saying, "Puhua will die at the East Gate tomorrow.

The people of the district followed one another to escort him out of the city. The Master spoke in a stern voice, "A burial today would not accord with the principles of the *qingwu* (the art of geomancy).
He then said, "Tomorrow he will pass away at the South Gate. The people followed him there as well. Again he said, "Tomorrow..."
It was auspicious for him to depart through the western gate. As people gradually became scarce, he emerged and then returned. The people’s resolve grew somewhat slack.

On the fourth day, he personally carried his coffin out through the northern gate; shaking a bell, he entered the coffin and passed away. The people of the commandery rushed out of the city, lifted the coffin to look within, but he was no longer there.
Only the sound of the bell was heard in the air, fading into the distance, its cause unfathomable.
Chan Master Liaosu of Shouzhou, a successor of Chan Master Magu Cheshan, went to visit Magu. When Magu saw him approaching, he took up a hoe and went out to weed.
Upon reaching the spot where Magu was weeding, Liaosu found that Magu paid him no attention at all; instead, he returned to his quarters and shut the door. The following day, Liaosu went there again.
Dagu again closed his door. The Master knocked on the door. Dagu asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "Liangsui. As soon as he uttered his name, he suddenly attained realization.
He said, "Preceptor, do not deceive Liangsui! Had I not come to pay my respects to you, Preceptor, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for the rest of my life.
Dagu then opened the door and they met. Upon returning to his lecture hall, he said to the assembly:
What all people know, Liang-sui knows entirely; what Liang-sui knows, all people do not know.
When Chan Master Huichao of Shushan in Jizhou—a successor of Chan Master Huihui of Dongsi—came to pay his respects, the Master said, "You have already occupied one [position]."
“Just now you were at Fang; why have you come here? He replied, “Liang-jia can do nothing with my doubts, so I have come specifically to see the Master.
The Master called out, “Liang-jia! He responded, “Yes? The Master said, “What is it? Liang-jia was speechless. The Master said, “A fine Buddha indeed, but he simply lacks radiance.”
A monk asked Chan Master Chuwai of Qianzhou, successor to Chan Master Xitang Zang:

"Regarding the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, when one realizes their principle and attains the subtle, are the intent of the Patriarchs the same as these, or are they different?
The Master said: "One must discern beyond the six propositions; one must not be turned by sounds and forms. The monk asked: [The Master continued: "..."
"What are the six phrases? The Master said, "Speaking, silence, neither speaking nor silent, both together, neither together, and how would you do it?
The monk had no reply. He asked Yangshan, "What is your name? Yangshan said, "Huiji. The Master said, "Which one is wisdom (hui)?
Which one is stillness (ji)? Yangshan said, "It is right before my eyes. The Master said, "There is still something before [you]."
Later, while at Mount [Name Omitted], he said, "Setting aside for a moment the 'before' and 'after,' what have you seen, Master? The Master replied, "Go drink tea.
Chan Master Huaiyun of Zhangjing was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Hongbian of Da Jianfu Monastery in Jingzhao.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang Dynasty, the Emperor asked, "Why is there a Northern and Southern school in the Chan tradition?"
He asked for his name. [The Master] replied, "In the Zen school, there is fundamentally no distinction between North and South.

In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, and it was transmitted from one to another until it reached the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma. He came to this land and became the First Patriarch.
Subsequently, when the Fifth Patriarch, the Great Master Hongren, was expounding the Dharma at Mount Dongshan in Qizhou, there were two younger brothers [who studied under him]."
One was named Huineng; he received the robe and the Dharma and resided in the region south of the Ling Mountains, becoming the Sixth Patriarch.
The other was named Shenxiu; he propagated the teachings in the north. Later, Shenxiu’s disciple Pujì established Xiù as the Sixth Patriarch and claimed himself to be the Seventh Patriarch.
Although the Dharma they attained was one and the same, there was a difference between them in their methods of guidance and awakening—namely, the sudden and the gradual. Thus it is said:
The Southern Sudden and Northern Gradual [teachings]—these were not originally titles of "North" and "South" belonging to the Chan school.
The Emperor asked, "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? He replied, "To prevent wrongdoing and cease evil is called precept. The Emperor asked, "What is 'concentration' (samādhi)?

He replied, "When the six sense organs encounter objects, the mind does not follow after conditions; this is called concentration. The Emperor asked, "What is 'wisdom' (prajñā)? He replied, "When both mind and objects are empty, [the mind] illuminates..."

To survey all things without delusion is called wisdom (*prajñā*). The Emperor asked, "What constitutes skillful means (*upāya*)? He replied, "Skillful means is the gateway of provisional expediency that conceals the reality and covers the true marks.
To provide guidance for those of middling and inferior capacities by employing indirect methods of instruction is what is termed skillful means.
Even to speak of abandoning skillful means and teaching only the Unsurpassed Way for those of superior faculties is itself a discourse of skillful means. This continued until the Patriarch...

The Master spoke of the profound mystery: "One forgets all achievement and severs all designations; there is likewise no trace of expedient means. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes the Buddha-mind?

He replied, "Buddha is a term from the Western Heaven; in the language of Tang, it means 'Awakening. It refers to the wisdom and illuminating awareness possessed by a person, which constitutes the Buddha-mind.
'Mind' is an alternative name for the Buddha, possessing hundreds of thousands of different appellations, yet its essence is but one. It has no form or shape, and is not—"

The characteristics of blue, yellow, red, and white, male and female, and so forth—whether appearing as devas or non-devas, humans or non-humans, manifesting as gods or men, and capable of being male or female—are neither beginning nor end, and are without birth or extinction; therefore, they are called the nature of numinous awakening.
Just as Your Majesty responds to ten thousand affairs daily, this is precisely Your Majesty’s Buddha-mind. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to transmit it together, it would not...
[The Master] thought that there must be something else to be attained. The Emperor said, "Suppose there were someone today who practices the mindfulness of the Buddha; how would it be?

He replied, "When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he acted as the Teacher of Gods and Humans and as a Good Spiritual Friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). He taught the Dharma according to their respective capacities (*indriya*).

For those of superior faculties, he opened the path of the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*) so they might suddenly awaken to the ultimate principle. Those of middling or inferior faculties could not yet understand it all at once; therefore, for the sake of Vaidehī..."
It is hoped that you will temporarily open the gate of the sixteen contemplations to lead those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. Outside of the mind there is no Buddha; outside of the Buddha there is no mind. The Emperor asked:

"If there are people who uphold this sūtra, practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and recite mantras seeking the Buddha, what do you think? He replied: "The Tathāgata’s various expositions and praises are all for the sake of the Supreme Vehicle."
"Vehicle. Just as the myriad streams and currents of the hundred rivers all flow toward the sea, so too do these various differentiated numbers all return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
The Emperor asked, "Since the Patriarch has already attained the seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*), how is it that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of 'dharmas that can be attained'?
He replied, "In the Buddha’s entire dispensation, there is truly not a single dharma given to anyone; he merely shows all people their own [nature]."
Each possesses the same single Dharma-treasury by nature. At that time, when the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara merely certified Śākyamuni’s original dharma, there was nothing to be attained;
only then did he accord with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent. Thus the Sūtra says: "There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
This dharma is equal. Cultivate all wholesome dharmas, yet do not dwell in signs. The Emperor said: "Since the Chan Master has already..."

[The Emperor] asked, "Do you understand the intent of the Patriarchs? Do you still prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sutras? He replied, "The śramaṇa sons of Śākyamuni prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sutras;
this is the constant law for those who maintain the office. There are four kinds of retribution.

Nevertheless, they cultivate their persons according to the Buddha’s precepts, seek out wise teachers, gradually practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and tread upon the tracks left by the Tathāgata. The Emperor said, "What is sudden realization? What is gradual cultivation?"

Xiu replied, "I have suddenly realized my own nature and am the equal of the Buddhas. However, because of the defiled habits accumulated since beginningless time, I must rely on gradual cultivation and remedial practices to allow the functions of this nature to arise in accordance with it.
It is like a person eating rice: one cannot be full after a single mouthful. On that day, Xiu responded to questions for seven *ke* (approximately forty-two minutes).

The Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes and a square-cut cassock, conferred upon him the title Chan Master Yuanzhi, and further issued an imperial decree to repair all ancestral pagodas throughout the empire.
Each was ordered to guard [the teaching].
Chan Master Zhiju of Guishan in Fuzhou was the son of the Liu family of Yangzhou. Initially, he went to visit Zhangjing.
Zhangjing asked, "From where have you come? The Master replied, "I have come to nowhere; I have come from nowhere. Although Zhangjing remained silent, the Master likewise [proceeded on his way].

Wu awakened. After his formal installation, he ascended the hall and said: "A movement of the countenance or a blink of the eye—nothing emerges outside the single thought-moment of one's own pure mind, which is fundamentally Buddha.
He then spoke this verse: "The mind is fundamentally free from dust; what need is there to wash it? The body is without illness; why seek out a physician?

If you wish to know the place where the Buddha is not the body, Look at the bright mirror when it has not yet reflected anything. Later, during the reign of Emperor Wuzong, [the monastic community] underwent the purge. There was...
He addressed the assembly in verse: An imperial decree falls like thunder from the emerald peaks; Before the wind, he sheds tears and casts off his dhyāna robe.

Amidst the clouds lies a temple where he cannot remain; In the dust there is no home—where shall he return? The bright moon divides its form, ever new in every place; How could a layman fall away from one who has realized emptiness?
Who says that being in the secular world hinders the cultivation of the Way? Kanakamuni once took the body of a lay devotee.
