When the sage Rishyaśṛṅga sat in meditation beneath the forest trees, he was once maimed by the King of Singers; how much less could such a thing occur in our sagely dynasty?
To merely command him to cease his practice of the Way—what cause for sorrow is there? Upon the restoration of the reign by Emperor Xuanzong, he no longer donned the black robes.
In the sixth year of the Xuántóng era, he passed away at his native mountain, posthumously titled Chan Master Guījì.
Chan Master Cao of Jinzhou invited Master Mi for a meal. He did not arrange any seating positions. When Master Mi arrived, he spread his sitting cloth and prostrated;
Master Cao descended from his meditation seat. Master Mi then took the master’s seat, while Master Cao sat on the floor instead.
When the meal was finished, Master Mi departed. An attendant said, "The Master is revered by all people, yet today your seat has been usurped by another."
The Master said, "If he comes after three days, I shall accept him as saved. After three days, the man indeed arrived and said, "The other day I encountered bandits.

[A monk asked Jingqing, "What was the meaning of the ancient saying, 'The other day I encountered bandits'? Jingqing replied, 'I see only the sharpness of the awl's tip; I do not see the squareness of the chisel's head.']
Whenever Master Gudī of Langzhou saw a monk approach, he would simply say, "Go away; you have no Buddha-nature. The monks were unable to respond.
Even those who did respond failed to grasp his intent. When Yangshan arrived for an audience, the Master said, "Go away; you have no Buddha-nature."
Dongshan joined his palms, stepped forward three paces, and responded with an assent. The Master smiled and said, "From where did you obtain this samādhi?
Dongshan replied, "I received my name from Danyuan; I obtained my ground at Guishan. The Master asked, "Are you not then Guishan’s son?
Dongshan said, "In terms of worldly convention, it is not that I am not; however, regarding the Buddha-dharma, I do not dare. Dongshan then asked, "Master..."
"From where did you obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Zhangjing.
Baoshan sighed, saying, "It is inconceivable; it is difficult for those who come here to find a place to settle."
A monk asked Master Gongji of Hezhong Prefecture, “What is the Way? What is Chan? The Master showed him by means of a verse, saying:
“That which has a name is not the Great Way; right and wrong are both not Chan. If you wish to know the meaning within this, it is like using yellow leaves as money to stop a child’s crying.”
When Chan Master Jieling of Shanglin in Hunan first visited Chan Master Yongtai Tuan, the latter asked him, "Virtuous One, what have you come for?"
The Master said, "Your armor and helmet are fully equipped. Yangshan said, "Strip them all off before you may meet with the Virtuous One. The Master said, "I have stripped them off.
Yangshan scolded him, saying, "The thief has not yet been beaten; why are you stripping yourself? The Master had no reply. Yangshan spoke on his behalf, saying:
"Please, Preceptor, clear those around you. Guishan made a gesture with his hand and said, "Yes, yes. Later, when the Master visited Yongtai, Yongtai finally explained the meaning of this to him.
The Master of Bimoyan on Mount Wutai constantly carried a wooden staff; whenever he saw a monk come to prostrate, he would immediately—
Holding his forked staff across his neck, he said: "Which demon-spirit taught you to leave the household life? Which demon-spirit taught you to travel as a wandering monk?
If you can speak, you shall die under this staff; if you cannot speak, you shall die under this staff. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Among the disciples, few were able to respond.

(Fayan spoke on their behalf: "Beg for your life. Fandeng spoke on their behalf: He simply extended his neck to show him. Xuanjue spoke on their behalf: "Old man, you may set down your staff. Huo Shan Tong.
The Master went to visit the Teacher. As soon as he saw him, he did not prostrate, but instead leaped into his arms. The Teacher patted Tong’s back three times.
Tong rose, clapped his hands, and said, "Elder brother, you have deceived me for three thousand li; you have deceived me for three thousand li!
and he immediately turned back.
Every day, Master Zhilin of Hunan would revile Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, calling them both malevolent spirits. Holding a wooden sword in his hand, he claimed to be subduing demons.
As soon as he saw a monk coming to visit him for instruction, he would immediately cry out, "The demon has come! The demon has come! and brandish the sword wildly before returning to his quarters.
He continued this for twelve years. Later, he set aside the sword and remained silent. A monk asked, "Regarding those twelve years ago..."
"Why did he subdue the demons? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor. [The monk] asked, "Why did he not subdue the demons twelve years later?
The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor."
Zen Master Qi’an of Huangzhou, a successor of Zen Master Huayan Zang, ascended the hall and said:
"Words do not fall into fixed phrases; Buddhas and patriarchs can only exert themselves in vain. The profound resonance does not decline."
"Who can know this? A monk asked, "How does one recognize one's own Buddha? The Master said, "When a single leaf is clear, it cannot be exhausted;
when the melody of the pines and wind has ceased, there is no one to lament. The monk asked, "What is one's own Buddha?
The Master said, "The swift horse before the grass is truly difficult to fathom; to reach the ultimate subtlety, one must walk as a beast. Someone asked, "How old are you, Master? The Master—
He said: "Five, six, four, and three cannot be categorized; how could one and two be the same? Truly, they are difficult to fathom. The Master had a verse that says:
"Within the fiercely blazing flames, there is a path for people; atop the swirling wind, one dwells immovably. Constantly and eternally throughout kalpas, who could ever deviate from this?"
The bright sun silently moves its light to illuminate all equally.
Fourth generation descendant of the Nan Yue lineage;
Dharma heir of Chan Master Huangbo Yun.
The Venerable Master of Muzhou was named Daoming. He was a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan. At the time of his birth, a crimson light filled the room and auspicious clouds covered the sky;

these did not disperse for ten days. His eyes possessed the double pupils (*chongtong*), and his face displayed the seven stars. His physical features were extraordinary, setting him apart from the common crowd.
Once, while visiting Kaiyuan Temple to pay homage to the Buddha, he recognized a monk as an old acquaintance. Upon returning home, he informed his father.
The mother wished to seek ordination as a nun; her parents granted permission for her to join the Sangha. Thereafter, she maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and mastered the Tripitaka.

Traveling abroad, she attained realization of the essential meaning under Huangbo. Later, at the request of the fourfold assembly, she resided at Guanyin Yuan, where she was constantly attended by more than a hundred followers.
After several decades had passed, students would come to question and challenge him; he would respond immediately to whatever was asked, using language that was steep and profound.
Since this did not follow conventional paths, those of shallow capacity often mocked him; only those of the Mysterious Learning (*xuanxue*) with keen natures revered and submitted to him.

Consequently, seekers from all quarters flocked to him, and they all addressed him as a "Venerable Elder" (*zunsu*). Later, he returned to Kaiyuan Temple (now renamed Doushuai), where he resided in his quarters weaving *pú* grass sandals.

Because his foster mother was named Chen (蒲), he was known by the sobriquet "Chen the Straw Sandal" (陳蒲鞋). When the Khitan rebels entered the territory, the Master displayed a large straw sandal at the city gate.
The Khitans wished to discard it, but though they exerted all their strength, they could not lift it. They sighed, saying, "There is a great sage in Muzhou," and abandoned the city and departed;
thus, the area was spared from turmoil. One evening, during the late assembly, he said to the multitude, "All of you, have you yet attained this one thing?"
"You have not yet even entered the gate. If you have not yet found a way to enter, you must seek one.
If you do find a way to enter, you must never again let me down. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed, saying, "I shall certainly never let you down, Master.
The Master said, "You have already let me down. He added, "It is clear."
"I have explained it clearly to you, yet you still do not understand; how much less could you grasp it if it were covered over?
He said again, "Since I have been the abbot here, I have never seen a person come who is truly without affairs. Why do you not come forward?
At that time, a monk stepped forward, and the Master said, "The rector is not here; take him away yourself. Outside the Main Gate, give him twenty blows."
[The Master] struck him with his staff and said, "Where does your fault lie? The monk replied, "[I do not know]. The Master said, "To add shackles upon a pillory.

Whenever the Master saw a *chan* monk (*nanseng*) coming, he would immediately close the door. However, if he saw a lecturer-monk (*jiangseng*), he would call out, "Lecturer! When the lecturer responded, the Master would say:
"A man carrying a wooden board. Someone said, "There is a bucket here; give me some water.
One day, while standing on the corridor steps, a monk asked, "Where is the room of the Venerable Master Chen? The Master took off his straw sandals and struck him over the head with them.

The monk then ran away. The Master called out, "Virtuous One! The monk turned his head back, and the Master pointed and said, "Go that way instead. An imperial messenger asked, "The three gates are all..."

The Master opened the door. As the official entered through the gate, the Master called out, "Minister! The official responded with an assent. The Master said, "You have entered through the Gate of Faith.

The official then noticed the murals on the wall and asked, "What were those two venerable ones discussing? The Master struck the pillar and said, "Among the three bodies, which one does not preach the Dharma? A Dharma lecturer came to consult him.
The Master asked, "Are you not a lecturer on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only)? The lecturer replied, "I dare not say so."

The Master said, "Leaving for the Western Heaven in the morning and returning to the land of Tang in the evening—do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Ho! Ho! You do not even observe the five precepts!
The Master asked an elder, "When one has attained realization, a single hair-tip swallows the vast ocean; only then does one know that the great earth is but a single mote of dust.
Elder, what do you say to this? The elder replied, "To whom would you ask? The Master said, "I am asking you, Elder. The elder said, "Why do you not accept [this]?"

The Master said, "You do not understand my words; I do not understand your words. He asked a Dharma Master, "What sutra are you lecturing on? The Master replied, "I am lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Master said, "May I ask about a certain passage of meaning? [The Dharma Master] said, "Yes. The Master kicked at the air with his foot, blew upon it once, and said, "What is the meaning of this?
[The Dharma Master] said, "This meaning is not found in the sutra. The Master said, "You are a fellow who speaks empty falsehoods! (5)
Regarding the meaning of the *Hālāhala* (Baili) lifting the rock, [the monk] instead said, "There is none. When the Master saw a monk, he said, "This is a settled case;
I grant you thirty blows. The monk said, "I am like this. The Master said, "Why does the *Vajrapāṇi* at the triple gate raise his fist?"
[The monk] said, "Even Vajra was like this. The Master then struck him. [The monk] asked, "What is the path that leads upward?
The Master said, "If you want to speak, what difficulty is there? [The monk] said, "Please, Master, speak it. The Master said, "The first and third; the middle nine and the lower seven."
Question: "If one does not remove one layer by means of another layer, that is not what I am asking. How is it when one does not remove one layer by means of another layer?
The Master said: "Yesterday we planted eggplants; today we plant winter melons. Question:
"What is the true meaning of Caoxi? The Master said: "This old monk loves anger and does not love joy. Question: "Why is it so? The Master said: "When meeting someone on the road..."
A swordsman must present his sword; one who is not a poet should not speak of poetry. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "Liu-yang.
The Master said, "When that senior practitioner there was questioned on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, what did he say? He replied, "Throughout the land, there is no path to walk upon.
The Master said, "Did that senior practitioner truly say such a thing? He replied, "He truly did. The Master took up his staff and struck him, saying, "This..."
Mindful of the man from Han, the Master asked an elder, "If a brother were to come, how would you respond?

He replied, "I will wait for him to arrive. The Master said, "Why do you not speak? He replied, "What is it that the Master lacks? The Master said, "Please, do not trouble yourself with such complications.
A monk came to visit. The Master asked, "Are you not a wandering monk? He replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Have you yet paid homage to the Buddha?"
[The monk] asked, "What is the purpose of building mounds of earth? The Master said, "Go away yourself. Another asked, "I am both a lecturer and a traveler;
when I do not understand the meaning of the teachings, what should I do? The Master said, "Truly speaking, you must repent for your words. The monk said, "I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said, "If you had not asked, I would have kept my mouth shut and remained silent. Since you have asked, I shall not [remain silent]."
"You may depart with your mouth shut. The monk said, "I ask the Master to speak directly. The Master said, "The mind bears no grudge against others; the face shows no color of shame.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like when a single phrase exhausts [all expression]? The Master said, "Your meaning has fallen. [The monk] asked, "In what way has my meaning fallen?
The Master said, "Who is there to give thirty blows? [The monk] asked, "Highly bowing to Śākyamuni, one does not prostrate to Maitreya."
"How was it then? The Master said, "Yesterday someone asked this; I chased him out. [The monk] said, "Master, I fear that I am not sincere.
The Master said, "My staff is not here; I will give you thirty blows with the handle of a broom instead. He ascended the hall and said, "I saw Baizhang not knowing good from evil.
As soon as the assembly had gathered, he struck them all down at once with his staff. Then he called out, 'Great..."
[The Master] called to the assembly. The assembly turned their heads. He then said, "What is this? Where is there any common ground for conversation?

Huangbo Zen Master did likewise. Again he called to the assembly. The assembly turned their heads. He then said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind. It is still somewhat inferior [to the truth].
He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "I have been shouted at by you, old monk. The monk—
Again he shouted. The Master said, "After three shouts and four shouts, what then? The monk was speechless. The Master struck him and said, "You are a fellow who only plunders empty space.
A scholar visited the Master and claimed that he understood twenty-four styles of calligraphy.

The Master pointed a single dot in the air with his staff and asked, "Do you understand? The scholar was at a loss. The Master said, "And yet you say you understand twenty-four styles of calligraphy!"
[The Master] did not even recognize the "Eight Strokes of the Character 'Ever'. He ascended the hall and said, "To tear it apart is up to me;
to fold it back together is also up to me. At that time, a monk asked, "What is tearing it apart? The Master said, "Three times nine is twenty-seven.
Bodhi, Nirvana, Suchness, Liberation, 'this very mind is Buddha'—I speak thus for now; what do you say to this? [The monk] said, "I..."
"Not so," he said. The Master replied, "The cup falls to the ground; the saucer shatters into seven pieces. The monk asked, "What is 'gathering together'?
The Master then sat with his hands folded. The monk asked, "Are the meaning of the teachings and the meaning of the Patriarchs the same or different?

The Master replied, "The green mountains are themselves green mountains; the white clouds are themselves white clouds. The monk asked, "What are the green mountains? The Master replied, "Give me back my..."
As a drizzle of rain fell, [the Master] said, "If you cannot speak it, ask the Teacher to speak it. The Teacher said, "The Lotus Sūtra is the vanguard on the battlefield;
the Nirvāṇa Sūtra is the withdrawal after the verse. He asked a monk, "Where have you been this summer? The monk replied, "I will tell you when the Teacher has a place to stay.
The Teacher said, "A fox is not of the lion's kind; a lamp is not as bright as the sun and moon. He asked another monk, "Where have you come from? The monk stared at him with wide eyes.
The Master said, "A Han before the donkey and after the horse. The monk said, "I ask the Master to examine me. The Master said, "A Han before the donkey and after the horse.
Bring me a phrase of the Way. The monk had no reply. While the Master was reading the sutras, Minister Chen Cao asked, "What sutra is the Master reading?
The Master said, "The Diamond Sutra. The Minister said, "Of the translations from the Six Dynasties, which one is this? The Master raised [the book].
The Sūtra says: "All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, bubbles, shadows, and illusions. Following this passage in the sūtra, a monk asked, "Master, what sūtra are you reading?
The Master replied, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The 'Chapter on the Cremation' is at the very end. He then asked the monk, "Where were you this summer? The monk replied, "At Mount Jing.
The Master said, "This fellow who eats his evening meal! The monk asked, "Among the monasteries of venerable elders, why do you say he eats his evening meal?"
The Master chased him out with his staff. Hearing that an elderly master was difficult to approach, he went to visit him in person.
As soon as he entered the abbot’s quarters, the elder gave a shout. The Master slapped his own ear and said, "A double case. The elder asked, "Where does the fault lie?

The Master replied, "This wild fox spirit," and then withdrew. He then asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Jiangxi. The Master said, "Have you worn through your sandals?"
"How many straw sandals? The monk had no reply. While having tea with a lecturer-monk, the Master said, "I cannot save you.
The monk said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master to grant me an instruction. The Master held up an oil cake and asked, "What is this?"
[The Master] said, "It is the dharma of form. The Master said, "This fellow who has entered the boiling cauldron!
When the Venerable Dade in his purple robe arrived and prostrated, the Master took up his hat and its band and asked, "What do you call this? He replied, "A 'Heaven-Pointing Hat' (chao tian mao).

The Master said, "If that is so, then I shall not take it off either. He then asked what field of study he practiced. [Dade] replied, "Yogācāra (Consciousness-Only). The Master asked, "How do you explain it? He replied:
"The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. The Master pointed to the door leaf and asked, "What is this? He replied, "It is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).
The Master said, "When you were granted the purple robe before the imperial curtain and lectured on the sutras before the Emperor, how could you have failed to observe the five precepts?
De was speechless. Another asked, "I have only recently entered the monastic community; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "You do not know how to ask. [The student] said, "Master..."

“Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, “I grant you thirty blows; take them and depart on your own. A monk asked, “I request the Master to provide the essential framework for the meaning of the Teachings.
The Master said, “Just ask what you wish, and I shall tell you. The monk said, “I pray the Master will speak.

The Master said, “Burn incense in the Buddha Hall; join your palms at the Main Gate. The monk asked, “What are the words for unfolding and rolling up [the Dharma]? The Master said, “Measure one’s talent.”
Regarding the appointment to the office: [The Master] asked, "What are words that do not unfold or display? The Master said, "I humbly pray you may enjoy the offering.
While borrowing an axe at Jiaoshan, the Master called to a lad, "Bring the axe here. When the lad brought the axe, he said, "There is no line or rule;
for now, chop roughly. The Master then gave a shout. He further asked the lad, "How is it that you chop your own head? The lad then made a chopping motion.
Shi said, "I cannot chop off your old man's head. The Master asked the scholar, "Which classic do you, sir, specialize in?

The scholar replied, "The *Yi*. The Master said, "The *Yi* says: 'The common people use it daily yet are unaware of it. Now tell me, what is it they are unaware of? The scholar replied, "They are unaware of the Dao.
The Master asked, "What is this Dao? The scholar was speechless. A monk then asked [the Master]: [Note: The text provided ends with "僧問" (A monk asked), indicating the beginning of another dialogue.]
"Can one turn a single breath back and forth to obtain the entirety of the Great Canon? The Master said, "What kind of pastry tongs do you have? Bring them here quickly!
A monk asked, "What is the teaching of this entire lifetime? The Master said, "The 'Shang Daren Qiu Yiji' (The Great Man Shang, the Yi-ji of Qiu).
A monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "A fierce fire frying with oil. A monk came for an audience. The Master said, "Are you a newcomer?"
The monk said, “Yes. The Master said, “Set aside this tangle for a moment; do you understand? The monk said, “I do not understand.

The Master said, “Carrying your shackles and presenting your petition, go out by yourself! The monk then went out. The Master called, “Come here, come here! I am asking you in earnest: where have you come from? The monk said, “Jiangxi.
The Master said, “Do you see that Master Letan is behind you, watching lest you speak nonsense? The monk had no reply.
A monk asked about the *vajra* at the temple gate: "If it is spread out, it is the vastness of heaven and earth; if it is not spread out, not even a hair's breadth is encountered.
What is the case here? The Master said, "Hūṃ! Hūṃ! I have never seen such a thing. The Master then asked, "First you leap three thousand feet forward, then you retreat eight hundred paces backward.
How do you propose to act? The monk said, "Yes. The Master said, "First, I shall issue a written indictment against you," and he struck him.
As the monk was about to leave, the Master said, "Come, let me entangle you in some vines. He spread out his hands and said, "The entire universe and the great earth are here.
Now tell me, how deep is the water in Lake Dongting? The monk replied, "It has never been measured.

The Master asked, "And what of Lake Dongting itself? The monk said, "Precisely because of the present moment. The Master said, "You do not even understand these vines," and he struck him. [Then] he asked: "What about suchness?"
"What is the phrase that is unimpeded wherever one encounters it? The Master said, "I do not speak in such a manner. The monk asked, "How then would you speak?
The Master said, "The arrow has already traveled a hundred thousand li to the Western Heavens; it now waits within the Great Tang Empire.
While reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a monk asked, "What sūtra are you reading? The Master said, "The great cloud of radiance; the azure cloud of radiance."
A purple cloud of light appeared. [The Master] pointed toward the front and said, "What kind of cloud is that over there? [The monk] replied, "It is a black cloud to the south.
The Master said, "There must be rain today. He asked, "The character 'yi' (以) is not formed; the character 'ba' (八) is not correct. What kind of phrase is this?
The Master snapped his fingers once and said, "Do you understand? [The monk] replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The eulogies recited above..."
"Restricting the supreme cause: a frog leaps up into the sky; an earthworm vaults across the Eastern Sea. He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from?
The monk replied, "From north of the River. The Master said, "There is a Venerable Zhaozhou there; have you been to him? The monk replied, "I have just left there.
The Master asked, "What words or phrases did Zhaozhou use to instruct his disciples? The monk recounted the story of the tea. The Master—
He then laughed heartily and said, "How shameful! But tell me, what was Zhaozhou’s meaning?
The monk replied, "It was merely a provisional expedient for the occasion. The Master said, "Alas! Zhaozhou has been splashed with a ladle of dung by you! He then struck him.
The Master then asked the śrāmaṇera, "How do you understand this? The śrāmaṇera immediately prostrated himself, and the Master struck him as well.
A monk who had arrived there went to the śrāmaṇera and asked, "Why did the Master strike you just now? The śrāmaṇera replied, "If it were not for me, the Master would not have struck me.
This newcomer was merely paying his respects. The Master rebuked the newly arrived monk, saying, "Why, Ācārya, did you steal the constant [practice]?"
[The Master] was sitting there eating fruit. [A monk] said, "As soon as this student arrived at the Master's place, why did you say he was stealing fruit?

The Master said, "The stolen goods are right here. He asked another monk, "Where have you recently come from? [The monk] said, "Mount Yang. The Master said, "You do not even observe the five precepts."
[The monk] asked, "Where, so-and-so, is there any falsehood? The Master said, "A śrāmaṇera has no place here.
As the Master was about to pass away, he summoned his disciples and said, "The conditions for this place have ceased; I shall now depart. He then sat in the full lotus posture and entered nirvāṇa.

The people of the district burned his body with fragrant wood, and śarīra relics fell like rain. They then collected his sacred remains and fashioned a statue in the temple. His lifespan was ninety-eight years.
The seventeenth day of the twelfth month, year sixty-six.
Chan Master Chunan of Qianqing Mountain in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Fuzhou.
He first visited Rong, who said to him, "I am not your teacher; your teacher is Huangbo, who is beyond the Yangtze River. The Master took his leave and subsequently went to visit Huangbo.
Huangbo asked, "How is it when you have not yet manifested the images of the triple world? The Master said, "Is there anything at all right now?
Huangbo said, "Setting aside for a moment whether there is or not, how is it right now? The Master said, "Neither present nor past. Huangbo said, "The Dharma-eye of our lineage is already within you.
Later, after he had taken up residence, he ascended the hall and said, "Sons, even if you were to understand the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods..."

Filling a vessel with water and attaining hundreds of thousands of samādhis are not equal to cultivating the path of non-outflow (*anāsrava-mārga*) for a single thought-moment, thereby escaping the fetters of the causes and effects of humans and devas.
At that time, a monk asked, "How does one cultivate the path of non-outflow? The Master said, "Apprehend it at the time when you, O *ācārya*, have not yet come into being.
The monk asked, "If you have not yet come into being, who is taught to apprehend it? The Master said, "The one who apprehends is also non-existent. [The monk] asked again.
"What is easy? The Master said, "To put on clothes and eat food; not needing to read sutras or study the teachings;
not needing to practice the Way, prostrate, burn the body, or scorch the crown of the head—is this not easy? [The student] asked, "What is difficult?

The Master said, "If even a subtle thought arises, one immediately possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The cycle of birth and death within the three realms all proceeds from your single thought. Therefore, the Buddha..."

He instructed the bodhisattvas, saying: "The Buddha protects and keeps me in mind. Although the Master responded to the needs of sentient beings without weariness, he remained constantly in a state of tranquil meditative concentration for periods exceeding a month or ten days.
In the fifth month of the sixth year of the Wende era, he passed away. His stupa was erected in a secluded spot to the west of the monastery.
In the second year of the Dàshùn era, when Sun Rú of Xuānzhōu raided Qiántáng, he opened the stupa and beheld the Master’s entire body, solemn and intact.
With his nails and hair grown long, he bowed in thanks and departed.
Chan Master Lingguan of Mount Wushan in Fuzhou (commonly known as Old Guan) usually kept his door bolted; few people saw him.
Only one lay devotee would arrive at mealtime to deliver offerings, at which point the master would open the door. One day, Xuefeng took the opportunity to knock on the gate. The Master—

He opened the door. Yunfeng suddenly grabbed him by the chest and said, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? The Master spat at him and said, "You wild fox spirit! He then pushed him out and closed the door.
Yunfeng said, "I only wanted to recognize my elder brother. While they were clearing weeds, the Master asked a monk, "Where are you going?
The monk replied, "I am going to West Monastery to pay respects to Master An. At that moment, there was a green snake on a bamboo stalk; the Master pointed at it.
The snake said, "If you wish to recognize the old wild fox spirit of West Monastery, it is simply this.

The Master asked West Monastery, "What kind of thing can be placed upon this plot of ground? The monastery replied, "A Buddha without marks would be well-placed here. The Master said, "A truly fine plot of ground."
"It was defiled by my elder brother's emission. While he was rolling the noodles, a monk came for an audience. The Master rolled some noodles and showed them to him; the monk then departed.
At evening, the Master asked his junior attendant, "Where did that monk go just now? The junior attendant replied, "He left immediately.
The Master said, "It is so, it is so—but he only obtained one peg. (Xuange said: "Where is the one peg missing? He asked: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master extended his tongue and showed it to him. The monk prostrated in thanks. The Master said, "Stop, stop! What did you see that you prostrate?
The monk replied, "I thank the Master for his compassion in showing me the mark of the tongue. The Master said, "These days an ulcer has grown on my tongue."
The monk arrived and knocked on the door. The attendant opened the door and immediately went out. The monk entered and prostrated.
He asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Who was that person who just went out? As the monk prepared to step forward, the Master pushed him out and closed the door.
When Caoshan was traveling as a pilgrim, he asked, "What is the Vairocana Teacher? The Lord of the Dharma-body? The Master—
[Caoshan] said, "If I were to tell you, it would be something else entirely. Caoshan related this to Dongshan, who remarked, "What an excellent point of inquiry!
It only lacks a follow-up question. Why not ask, 'Why do you not say anything? Thereupon, Caoshan came forward and posed that further question.
The Master said, "If you say that I do not speak, then my mouth would be mute; if you say that I do speak, then my tongue would be stammering.
Caoshan returned and reported this to Dongshan, who deeply approved of it.
Chan Master Zongche of Luohan Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Wu family in Huzhou. He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The bone is crushed. (The Master frequently used this phrase in response to questions; at the time, he was called "Master Bone-Crusher.

A monk asked, "What is the Southern School and the Northern School? The Master said, "The mind is the school. The monk asked, "Does one still look to the teachings? The Master said, "The teachings..."

"This mind," he asked, "is often shrouded in the density of the ground of nature (*bhūmi*). How can it be awakened? The Master said, "When the clouds of affliction are swept away by the wind, the great void becomes vast and clear.
[The student] asked, "How does one attain clarity? The Master said, "A single orb, pure and bright, radiates its light across ten thousand miles."
The layman Pei Xiu, styled Gongmei, was a native of Wenxi in Hedong.

While serving as Governor of Xin’an, it happened that Master Yun had recently left the community at Huangbo Mountain in Lingnan and entered the Dà'ān Monastery, where he mingled with the laborers to sweep and clean the halls.
When the Governor entered the temple to burn incense, the administrators received him; upon observing the murals on the walls, he asked about them.
"What kind of image is this? The attendant replied, "It is the true likeness of a high monk. The Duke said, "The true likeness may indeed be viewed;
where is the high monk? The attendant had no reply. The Duke asked, "Is there any Zen practitioner here? He replied, "Recently there was a monk who came to this temple to take up service;
he bears a strong resemblance to a Zen practitioner. The Duke said, "May he be summoned so that we may question him? Thereupon, they hurriedly sought him out.
Huangbo arrived. Upon seeing him, the Duke was delighted and said, "Just now I had a question, but the virtuous ones were reluctant to speak.
I now request the Master to provide a reply in my stead. Huangbo said, "I pray the Duke will pose his question. The Duke repeated the previous story, and Huangbo spoke in a clear voice:
Pei Xiu responded with an assent. Baizhang asked, "Where is it? At that moment, Pei understood the meaning as clearly as if he had recovered a pearl from his topknot.

He said, "My teacher is truly a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Your pointing out of the exact point is so precise; why have I been submerged in this state until now? The assembly of the monastery was stunned.
From then on, he invited the Master into his official residence and performed the rites of a disciple. Although he repeatedly declined, [Baizhang] would not stop. Furthermore—
He earnestly entreated him to reside at Huangbo Mountain to further revitalize the ancestral Way. Whenever he had leisure, he would personally enter the mountain to pay his respects;

if he wished to hear profound discourses, he would invite him into the prefectural seat. Since the Master had thoroughly penetrated the intent of the patriarchs and was also extensively versed in the characteristics of the teachings, the Chan scholars of all quarters remarked that Minister Pei had not come out from the gate of Huangbo in vain. This continued until the Minister’s transfer to the commandery of Xuancheng.
He further contemplated paying homage to him and thus established a monastery, inviting [Guifeng] to reside there.

Although Guifeng was deeply versed in both Chan and doctrinal studies and held in high esteem by Pei, he did not equal those who turned their hearts toward Huangbo with such total devotion and submission.
Furthermore, he composed the epitaph for Guifeng, stating: "I, Xiu, am to the Master a brother in the Dharma, a friend in righteousness, and a son in gratitude."

It is thus evident that spiritual friends serve as both internal and external protectors of the Teaching. Furthermore, [the Master] compiled the *Essential Sayings of Huangbo*, personally inscribing a preface for it to be placed at the beginning of the collection to remain as a guardian of the mountain gate.
He also personally inscribed the titles for five hundred cases of the *Tripitaka*, which have been treasured until the present day.

Moreover, Chan Master Guifeng composed the *Chan-yuan ch'uan* (Exposition on the Source of Chan), the *Yuan-ren lun* (Treatise on the Origin of Humanity), and the *Yuanjue jing* (Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment).

He composed prefaces for the *Sūtra Commentary*, the *Commentary on the Dharma-dhātu Contemplation*, and other works. Devoted to the inner scriptures, he penetrated deeply into the assemblies of the Dharma;
a text of his vow-inscription remains transmitted to the world.
Chan Master Fazu of Daisui in Yizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Changqing An.
A native of the Wang family in Zizhou, he attained awakening at a young age and resolved to seek out teachers.
He left the household life at Huiyi Temple; after receiving full ordination, he traveled south, where he first met Yaoshan, Daowu, and Yunyan.
Dongshan next went to the assembly of Daowei outside the mountain passes. For several years there, his food did not reach satiety and he sought no warmth while lying down;
he refined his practice through austerity, and his conduct was beyond the common. Daowei held him in high esteem.
One day Daowei asked him, "Disciple, while you were with me here, you never once asked a single turning phrase. The Master replied, "Where would you have me apply my mouth?"
Yangshan said, "Why do you not say, 'What is the Buddha? The Master then made a gesture with his hand to cover Yangshan’s mouth.

Yangshan sighed and said, "You have truly attained the marrow. From that time on, his fame spread throughout the four seas. Thereafter, he returned to Shu and stayed at Longhuai Temple in Pengkou Mountain, Tianpeng.
For three years, he brewed tea by the roadside and distributed it universally. Then, while traveling to the mountains behind, he saw one...

There was an ancient monastery called Daisui (Great Following). Towering peaks rose in majestic beauty, and the waters of the mountain stream were clear and cool. Within it stood a tree over forty feet in circumference;
it had a single opening facing south, hollow and unobstructed, naturally forming a hermitage without the need for an axe or hatchet.

At that time, it was known as the Wooden Chan Hermitage. The Master resided there for over ten years, his shadow never leaving the mountains, yet his reputation spread far and wide to all four quarters.

Scholars of the Dark Learning (Xuanxue) flocked from a thousand miles away, drawn by his reputation. The Ruler of Shu held him in high esteem and dispatched envoys to summon him repeatedly, yet the Master declined each time on the grounds of old age and illness.
He was subsequently appointed as the Great Master Shenzhao. Ascending the hall, he said: "This nature is originally pure and possesses all virtues in their entirety.

It is only because of the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise. Thus, the various sages, having awakened to it, employ it exclusively in its pure aspect to achieve the Way of Enlightenment."
Ordinary beings are deluded by this; they exclusively engage in defiled activity and sink into the cycle of saṃsāra. Yet its essence is non-dual; thus the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:
"There is no duality and no division; there is no distinction and no interruption. A monk asked: "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed..."
"I do not yet understand whether this is destroyed or not. The Master said, "It is destroyed. The monk said, "If that is so, then it follows him.
The Master said, "It follows him. The monk did not accept this. Later, he went to Touzi and recounted the previous conversation. Touzi then prepared incense and prostrated from afar, saying:
Xichuan Gufo appeared in the world and said to a monk, "Return quickly and repent. The monk returned to Daisui, but the Master had already passed away.
The monk went again to Touzi, but Touzi had also passed away. [The monk] asked, "What is the mark of a great man?

The Master replied, "There is no notice pasted upon his belly. He asked the monk, "Where are you going? The monk said, "I am going to live in a hermitage on the Western Mountain. The Master said, "I..."

[The Master] called out to him from the top of the eastern hill, "Will you come when called? The monk said, "No. The Master said, "Then you have not yet mastered dwelling in the hermitage. A monk asked, "When birth and death arrive, what then? The Master said, "When you meet tea, drink the tea; when you meet rice, eat the rice. The monk asked, "Who receives the offerings? The Master said, "Close your alms bowl. Beside the hermitage was a tortoise. A monk asked, "All sentient beings... [The Master] said, "The tortoise has eight legs. The monk asked, "What about the Buddha-nature? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Buddha-nature. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one attain liberation? The Master said, "The tortoise has no liberation. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one enter the Way? The Master said, "The tortoise has no way to enter. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one realize the fruit? The Master said, "The tortoise has no fruit to realize. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one become a Buddha? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Buddha to become. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one transcend the world? The Master said, "The tortoise has no world to transcend. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one escape suffering? The Master said, "The tortoise has no suffering to escape. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one attain Nirvana? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Nirvana to attain. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one achieve Buddhahood? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Buddhahood to achieve. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one reach the ultimate? The Master said, "The tortoise has no ultimate to reach. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one see the nature? The Master said, "The tortoise has no nature to see. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one realize the truth? The Master said, "The tortoise has no truth to realize. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one attain enlightenment? The Master said, "The tortoise has no enlightenment to attain. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one manifest the Way? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Way to manifest. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one turn the wheel of Dharma? The Master said, "The tortoise has no wheel to turn. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one preach the Dharma? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Dharma to preach. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one save sentient beings? The Master said, "The tortoise has no sentient beings to save. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one uphold the precepts? The Master said, "The tortoise has no precepts to uphold. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one practice meditation? The Master said, "The tortoise has no meditation to practice. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one cultivate wisdom? The Master said, "The tortoise has no wisdom to cultivate. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one enter the realm of reality? The Master said, "The tortoise has no realm of reality to enter. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one dwell in the state of non-action? The Master said, "The tortoise has no state of non-action to dwell in. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one realize the unborn? The Master said, "The tortoise has no unborn to realize. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one attain the unconditioned? The Master said, "The tortoise has no unconditioned to attain. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one manifest the great function? The Master said, "The tortoise has no great function to manifest. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one turn the great wheel? The Master said, "The tortoise has no great wheel to turn. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one ascend the high seat? The Master said, "The tortoise has no high seat to ascend. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one receive the transmission? The Master said, "The tortoise has no transmission to receive. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one become a patriarch? The Master said, "The tortoise has no patriarchate to become. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a teacher of men? The Master said, "The tortoise has no men to teach. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a guide for the world? The Master said, "The tortoise has no world to guide. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a vessel of the Dharma? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Dharma to hold as a vessel. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a field of merit? The Master said, "The tortoise has no merit-field to be. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a refuge for all? The Master said, "The tortoise has no refuge to provide. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a protector of the teachings? The Master said, "The tortoise has no teachings to protect. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a support for the Sangha? The Master said, "The tortoise has no Sangha to support. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a lamp in the darkness? The Master said, "The tortoise has no darkness to illuminate. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a bridge across the stream? The Master said, "The tortoise has no stream to cross. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a boat on the ocean? The Master said, "The tortoise has no ocean to sail. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs. The monk asked, "How can one be a medicine for the sick? The Master said, "The tortoise has no sickness to cure. The monk asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Because it has eight legs."
"Skin inside the bone. Why is it that this sentient being has skin inside the bone? The Master picked up his straw sandals and placed them over the back of a turtle;
the monk was speechless. The monk asked, "What is the essential dharma of all Buddhas? The Master raised his whisk and said, "Do you understand?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A fly-whisk. The monk asked, "What is the student’s own self? The Master said, "It is I."
[The monk] asked, "Why is it, then, that it is the Master himself? The Master said, "It is your own self. He asked, "What is the singular matter of Dàsui?
The Master said, "East, west, south, north. He asked, "Since the Buddha-dharma pervades all places, where should a student station their feet?
The Master said, "The great ocean allows the fish to leap; the vast sky permits the birds to fly."
A bird flies away. [A monk] asked: "When father and son, who are most intimately related, must part ways at a fork in the road, what then?
The Master said: "Because there are father and son. [Another] asked: "What is the seamless stupa? The Master said: "Five feet high. [The monk] said: "I do not understand.

The Master said: "A solid brick. [Another] asked: "After the Master passes away, to whom will the Dharma be entrusted? The Master said: "The pillar and the brazier. [The monk] asked: "Is it so? The Master said: "Yes."
"Reception is also non-existent. The Master said, "The brazier and the pillar. The practitioner led the assembly to visit him.
The Master asked, "When one who has attained realization calls out 'East,' what does he mean? He replied, "One cannot call it 'East. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You stinking donkey!
If you do not call it 'East,' what do you call it? The practitioner was speechless. [Another] asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Red earth."

[The Master] drew a winnowing basket and said, "I do not yet understand this principle; how is it? The Master said, "A winnowing basket has lips; rice cannot leap out. He asked a monk, "What teaching do you lecture on?
The monk replied, "The *Śata-dharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas). The Master picked up his staff and said, "From what does it arise? The monk replied, "It arises from conditions.
The Master said, "Alas! Alas! He asked another monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "To Mount Emei to pay homage to Puxian [Samantabhadra]."
The worthy one departed. The Master raised his whisk and said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here. The monk drew a circle, threw it behind him, and then prostrated.
The Master called to his attendant, "Give this monk a cup of tea. After the assembly had finished their formal inquiry, the Master spoke again.
The Master made a gesture with his mouth as if suffering from a wind ailment and said, "Is there anyone who can cure my mouth?
The monks vied with one another to send him medicine, and when the laypeople heard of it, they also sent much medicine. The Master accepted none of it.
After seven days, the Master pinched his own mouth to straighten it and said, "For all this time, I have been beating these two pieces of skin; even until now, no one has cured me."
He attained [enlightenment] and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Rumen of Lingshu in Shaoyang was a native of Min. The Liu clan, who ruled Guangzhou, held him in high esteem for generations and appointed him as the Great Master Zhisheng.
A monk asked, "What is the ultimate principle of the Buddha-dharma? The Master simply extended his hand. [The monk] asked again, "How about this?"

"This is the family style of our Preceptor," [the monk] said. The Master replied, "A field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners. [The monk] asked, "What is meant by 'a field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners'?
The Master said, "The dilapidated house has no one to repair it. [Another monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the West's coming?
The Master said, "Child, do not act like a common laborer. [The monk] said, "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "You have come from Qianzhou. [The monk] asked, "Is this..."
"What makes it so difficult to understand? The Master said, "A windmill atop the head of the Fire God. A nun presented a ceramic bowl to the Master;
the Master lifted it up and asked, "From what did this emerge? She replied, "It emerged from Dingzhou. (Fadeng offered an alternative reading: "Do not hastily [judge] this place.
The Master then smashed it to pieces, and the nun was left speechless. (Baofu spoke on her behalf: "He who seeks to deceive the enemy perishes. He asked, "How old are you, Preceptor?"
The Master said, "Today I am born; tomorrow I shall die. He was asked again, "Where, O Monk, is your place of birth? The Master replied, "The sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west.
For over forty years, the Master transformed those in the region south of the Ling Mountains, leaving behind many extraordinary traces.

When the Lord of Guangzhou was about to mobilize his army, he personally visited the monastery to request the Master’s judgment on whether the enterprise would be auspicious or not. The Master had already known this beforehand; he sat peacefully and passed away. The Lord [was deeply moved].
The angry administrator asked, "When did the Master fall ill? He replied, "I have never been ill. Just now, I sealed a letter and instructed that it be presented to the Great King.
When the administrator opened the letter, he found a note that read: "The Eye of the Human and Heavenly Beings, the Senior Seat in the Hall; the Master has realized the Teacher's intent.
Thereupon, [the King] called off the military campaign and summoned the First Seat to open the hall and preach the Dharma (this was Yunmen). [His] reliquary stupa.
The ritual for interring him in a stupa was extensively prepared by the ruler. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Lingshu, and a true-body stupa was erected for him.
Chan Master Lingyun Zhiqin of Fuzhou was a native of Changxi in that same prefecture. Initially at Mount Gui (Weishan), he attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms.
He composed a verse which said: "For thirty years I have sought the swordsman; how many times have the leaves fallen and sprouted again?"

Zhizhi said: "Ever since I first beheld the peach blossoms, until this very day I have had no further doubts. When Guishan examined the verse and interrogated him regarding his realization, he found it to be in perfect accord with the Dharma.
Guishan said, "Your awakening through these conditions shall never again be lost; guard and maintain it well."

Only the root that carries consciousness remains constant. Those of superior faculties encounter virtuous friends who clarify the truth for them; they attain liberation on the spot, which is itself the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*).
Those of middling or inferior faculties are deluded and ignorant; unable to awaken through insight, they remain submerged in the triple world, wandering through birth and death. Thus it is explained.
