The Dharma Heirs of National Teacher Mazu Daoyi. 1. Chan Master [Mazu]. His Dharma Successors.
Chan Master Daowu of Jingzhou was a native of Zhugong. His secular surname was Cui; he was a descendant of Ziyu.
At the age of fifteen, he followed Vinaya Master Tanchu at Changsha Temple to enter the monastic life. At twenty-three, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.
At thirty, he visited Shitou, where he repeatedly received instructions, yet for some time he failed to grasp the essential point. Subsequently, he called upon National Teacher Huizhong. Three...
14. Together with Guoshi Shizhe Yingzhen, he returned south to pay his respects to Mazu. Mazu said: "Recognize your own mind; it is originally the Buddha.
It does not belong to gradual stages, nor does it depend on cultivation. Its essence is naturally suchness (tathatā), and its myriad virtues are perfectly complete."
The Master attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. The Patriarch instructed him, saying, "If you take up residence as an abbot, do not leave your former location.

Having received this guidance, the Master returned to Jingmen. Not far from the city walls, he constructed a thatched hut. Later, when the Regional Inspector (Jieshi) inquired about him, his attendants provided the details.
The Regional Inspector personally came to visit him for instruction; seeing that the path was so narrow it was difficult for carriages and horses to pass, he was struck with wonder.
Seeing that the overgrown thickets had never been cleared or trimmed, he was provoked to anger and ordered his men to seize the Master and cast him into the water.
Just as his banners and pennants were returning, they saw fire break out throughout the entire yamen; flames blazed both inside and out, making it impossible to approach.

Only the voice from the air could be heard, saying, "I am the deity of the Heavenly King! I am the deity of the Heavenly King! Upon hearing this, the regional inspector turned his heart back toward faith and prostrated himself; the smoke—

The flames were completely extinguished, and he appeared exactly as he had been before. He then proceeded to the riverbank, where he saw the Master standing in the water without his robes being wet at all.

The regional inspector (Jieshi) again offered a profound confession and invited him to the government office to receive offerings. To the west of the prefecture, he built a temple, naming it Tianwang (Heavenly King).
The monk Longtan asked, "How is the matter that has been transmitted from the ancestors? The Master said, "It is not that you cannot see where you have come from.
Longtan said, "How many people possess such an eye? The Master said, "In shallow grass, it is easy for tall reeds to grow.
The Master often said, "Happy! Happy! Yet when he was approaching his end, he cried out, "Suffering! Suffering! and further remarked, "King Yama!"
"Come and take me! The head of the monastery asked, "When the Master was cast into the water by the Regional Inspector, your countenance remained unmoved.
How can you now act like this? The Master held up his pillow and said, "Tell me, which was it: that time, or now?
The head of the monastery had no reply and then entered nirvana. This occurred in the tenth month of the third year of the Yuanhe era, the Wuzi year.
On the thirteenth day, at the age of eighty-two and having completed sixty-three summer retreats, he passed away.

He had one successor in the Dharma, named Chongxin, who was Longtan. (Song Dachuan states: "By collating the two steles by Qiu Xuansu and Fu Zai, it should be established that Tianwang Daowu succeeded Mazu, and Longtan Chongxin succeeded him;

only then will the lineage be free from error. According to the *Zhuyuelu*, Tianwang Daowu succeeded Mazu, and Longtan Chongxin succeeded him. This was composed by Qiu Xuansu. There is also the *Nanyue Stele* by Gui Deng, a renowned man of the Tang, and Guifeng’s reply to Pei Guo[wei].)

In the *Zongqu zhuang* (Account of the Essential Tenets) and Quan De’yu’s *Mazu Taming*, both treat Tianwang as the successor of Mazu. However, Fokuo Bai, Da Guanying, Lü Xiaqing, and Zhang Wujin all composed refutations to prove that the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) contains an error.

According to the *Zhengming lu* (Record of Correct Names), among the various pieces of evidence provided by these scholars based on historical records, the words of Zhang Wujin are the most profound and incisive. Wujin stated: "Shitou received [the Dharma] from Yaoshan; Yaoshan received it from Caoxi and Dongshan. Their teachings, principles, practices, and fruits were expressed through subtle and winding discourse.

Under Huangbo and Daowu, Zhou Jingang appeared, whose fierce rebukes and scoldings were such that even Buddhas and Patriarchs dared not meet his edge. He further noted that he feared the character "Huang" (皇) was a scribal error for "Qiu" (丘). Later, he found corroboration in the writings of Qiu Xuansu and Fu Cai.

There are two steles. He showed them everywhere to all quarters, saying: "I have long suspected that although Deshan and Dongshan both emerged from under Shitou, why was it that where they extended their hands, their approaches to life and death were not the same? Now, by means of these two steles of Qiu and Fu, the matter is clearly and brightly revealed."

Only now do I realize that my selection of the Dharma and my examination of men were not in error. This has been established directly from the point of provisional designation; a single word settles doubts spanning a thousand ages. It is like a person in the world whose lineage is disputed:

while one may clarify the matter by examining the family genealogy, a single drop of blood will immediately distinguish the true from the false. These inexhaustible words may be called "obtaining the truth through a drop of blood. According to what is recorded in the *Sankē* (Three Volumes), the evidence is precise and the discussion is thorough;
a case of doubt that has persisted for a thousand years is resolved in an instant.
The Third Generation under Mount Nanyue:
Chan Master Longtan Chongxin of Lizhou was a native of Zhugong. His family sold cakes. The Master was brilliant from his youth.
This was unusual. Initially, when Master Wu of Shangwu received the patriarch’s prediction of his future enlightenment, he later resided at Tianwang Temple.
No one could fathom him. A man from the temple lane would daily bring ten cakes to offer him.

When the Master of Tianwang accepted them, after each meal he would invariably set aside one cake, saying, "I give this to you so that it may provide shade for your descendants. One day, the man thought to himself: "The cakes were brought away by me."
"Why have you returned these to me? Is there some other underlying meaning? He then went to see the king and asked about it.

The king said, "These were brought by you; what fault do I have in returning them to you? Upon hearing this, the master somewhat understood the profound principle (*xuanzhi*) and consequently renounced his home life.
The king said, "In the past you honored merit and goodness; now you have faith in my words. You may be named Chongxin (Venerable Faith). Thereupon, he served diligently at the king's side. One day...
The Master asked, "Since I arrived, I have not received instruction on the essential point of the mind.

The King said, "From the moment you arrived, there has never been a time when I have not pointed out the essential point of your mind. The Master asked, "Where did you point it out? The King said, "When you brought me tea, I accepted it for you;
when you brought me food, I received it for you; when you bowed in greeting, I lowered my head. Where [else] was it not pointed out?"
[The Master] did not point out the essential heart-instruction. The Master lowered his head for a long time. The King said, "If you see, see directly;
if you deliberate, you are already mistaken. At that moment, the Master attained realization. He asked again, "How does one maintain this? The King said, "Wander freely according to your nature;
roam at ease following conditions. Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no separate 'sage's understanding'. Later, the Master went to Longtan in Liyang to reside there.
A monk asked, "Who can obtain the pearl within the topknot? The Master said, "One who does not prize or play with it obtains it.
The monk asked, "Where is it placed? The Master said, "If there is a place, then tell me where it is. A nun asked, "How can one become a monk?
The Master said, "It has been quite some time since you came here as a nun. She asked, "Is there ever a time when one is a monk? The Master said, "What are you right now?"
Mo said, "I am currently in the body of a nun; how could you not recognize me? The Master said, "Who recognizes you?
Governor Li Ao asked, "What is true suchness and prajñā? The Master said, "I have no true suchness or prajñā. Li said, "It is fortunate to have met the Master.
The Master said, "These are still words that go beyond the mark."
Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Dingzhou, a successor in the fourth generation under the lineage of Chan Master Longtan Xin of Nanyue,
was the son of the Zhou family in Jianzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of seven and received full ordination according to his years.
He was fully equipped with mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka and had thoroughly penetrated the essential meanings of the various sūtras on the nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of phenomena.

He frequently lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and his contemporaries called him "Zhou the Vajra. Once, he said to his fellow students: "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no loss;
a tiny speck is cast upon a sharp blade, yet the blade remains unmoved. Whether one is still learning or has completed learning—only I know this. Later, he heard of the Chan [teachings] in the South.

The assembly was quite grand. The Master felt indignant and said, "A renunciant may study the Buddha’s majestic deportment for a thousand kalpas and the Buddha’s subtle practices for ten thousand kalpas, yet still fail to attain Buddhahood.
Yet this 'demon-child' from the South dares to speak of 'directly pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
I shall tear open his den and exterminate his kind, thereby repaying the Buddha's grace. Thereupon, he took up the Blue Dragon.
As the Master was traveling from Shu with his commentaries and sub-commentaries (*shūshō*), he reached the road through Liyang and saw an old woman selling cakes.

Stopping to rest his shoulder, he bought some cakes for refreshment. The woman pointed to his pack and asked, "What kind of text is this? The Master replied, "The *Qinglong Shūshō* (Commentaries and Sub-commentaries of Qinglong).
The woman asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? He replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman said, "I have a question; if you can answer it, I shall give you [these cakes]."
He offered him some refreshments. When [Xuefeng] replied that he could not, the other said, "Then go elsewhere for a while. [Xuefeng] thought, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
'The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. I wonder which of these minds the Venerable One is pointing to?
The Master remained silent. He then went to Longtan. Upon reaching the Dharma Hall, he said, "I have long heard of Longtan; now that I have arrived..."
The pond was no longer visible, nor did the dragon appear. The Pond Master extended his body and said, "You have personally arrived at the Dragon Pond.

The Master was speechless and subsequently took up residence there. One evening, while standing in attendance, the Pond Master said, "It is deep in the night; why do you not go out? The Master said, "I shall take my leave," and then departed.
Upon returning, he said, "It is dark outside. The Pond Master lit a paper candle and passed it to him. As the Master reached out to receive it, the Pond Master [snuffed it out].
[The candle] was blown out. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Longtan asked, "What have you seen?
The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.

On the following day, Longtan ascended the seat and said to the assembly, "Among you there is a fellow whose teeth are like a forest of swords and whose mouth is like a blood-basin; he would strike with a single blow—"
Without looking back, he said, "In time, I shall stand upon the summit of a solitary peak and establish my Way.
The Master then piled his commentaries and sub-commentaries before the Dharma Hall, raised a torch, and said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void;

to exhaust all worldly pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. He then burned them. Thereupon, [the Master] paid his respects and took his leave, proceeding directly to Mount Mí.
Carrying a double-layered mat, he ascended the Dharma Hall, walking from west to east and from east to west. Looking toward the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), he asked, “Is there anyone here?
Is there anyone here? As the Master sat there, he did not look up at all. The Master said, “No one, no one,” and then went out.
Reaching the entrance, he said, “Even though it is so, one must not be careless. He then prepared his formal demeanor and re-entered to have an audience. Just as he stepped across—
Dongshan picked up his sitting mat and said, "Preceptor. As Shangu was about to take the whisk, the Master gave a shout and, shaking out his sleeves, departed.
That evening, Shangu asked the Head Seat, "Is the newcomer still here today?

The Head Seat replied, "At that moment, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went out wearing his straw sandals. Shangu said, "In the future, this man will settle upon the summit of a solitary peak."
"A thatched hut—there he goes, reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs. The Master resided at Liyang for thirty years;

during the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang dynasty, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he took refuge in a stone grotto on Mount Dufu. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Xue Tingwang, the Governor of Wuling, [invited him].

He restored Chongde Mountain Hermitage and renamed it Gudeng Chan Monastery. Intending to seek out a wise master to serve as its abbot, he heard of the Master’s spiritual conduct and repeatedly invited him to descend from the mountain.
However, Wang Tingwang devised a deceptive scheme and dispatched an official to falsely accuse him of a shortage of tea and salt.

Regarding the violation of prohibitive laws: he took his master to the prefecture, where he paid his respects, made earnest entreaties for him to reside there, and extensively propagated the style of his school.
He ascended the hall and said: "If you have no affairs within yourself, do not seek falsely; even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would not be true attainment.

You need only be without affairs in the mind and without mind regarding affairs; then you will be spiritual within emptiness and wondrous within voidness. Even a hair-tip's worth—" [He ceased speaking.]

To investigate the fundamental origins and final ends of these things is entirely to deceive oneself. Why? Because a single thought tied to even a hair’s breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms;

a fleeting emotion gives rise to shackles that bind one for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds; extraordinary features and inferior forms are all but illusory colors.
If you seek them, will you not bring about entanglements? When you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction. In the end—
"It is of no benefit. He gave a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*) to the assembly, saying: "Tonight I will not answer questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff.
At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated. The Master struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question; for what reason does the Master strike me?
The Master asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "From Silla (Korea). The Master said, "Before you have even stepped onto the boat—"

"Railing! Well-deserved thirty blows! (Fayan said, "The Great and Small Deshan have split their talk into two pieces. Xuangjue said, "In the monastic community, this is called 'separating the words. Let us set that aside for a moment;
as for Deshan’s statement, 'Thirty blows for one who asks a question,' what was his intention? A monk came to visit. The Master asked the rector, "How many new arrivals are there today?
He replied, "Eight people. The Master said, "Call them here and press them down all at once. Longya asked, "I, a student, rely upon the sword of Mohe. I intend—
When Ya was about to take the Master’s head, the Master extended his neck forward and said, "Fa" (Dafayan alternatively said: "Where do you intend to strike?").
Ya said, "The head has fallen. The Master laughed loudly. Later, Ya went to Dongshan and recounted the previous conversation.
Dongshan asked, "What did Deshan say? Ya replied, "Deshan was speechless. Dongshan said, "Do not say he was speechless; let us consider Deshan for a moment."
He threw it down at his feet and presented it to the old monk to look at. Only then did Ya realize his mistake; he immediately apologized and repented.
A monk reported this to the Master (Zhaozhou), who said, "The old man Dongshan does not know good from bad. This fellow has been dead for so long—what use is there in saving him?
A monk asked, "What is Bodhi? The Master struck him and said, "Get out! Do not defecate here."

A question was asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The Buddha is an old bhikṣu from Western Heaven. Xuefeng asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the school, does a student still have a share in it?
The Master struck him with a staff and said, "Say something! Xuefeng said, "I do not understand. On the following day, he requested further instruction.
The Master said, "In my school there are no words or phrases; truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Because of this, Xuefeng attained realization.
There was a realization. When Yantou heard of this, he said, "The old man Deshan has a backbone as hard as iron; it cannot be bent.

Nevertheless, even so, within the gate of proclaiming the Teaching, he still falls short by a small measure. (Baofu asked Zhaoqing, "As for Yantou’s appearance in the world, what teachings did he have that surpassed Deshan, such that you speak in this way?

Qing replied, "Have you not seen how Yantou said, 'It is like a person learning archery; only after a long time will they hit the mark'? Baofu asked, "After hitting the mark, what then? Qing replied, "Unfurl it, Layman; there is nothing that is not.")

Shi Tongyang said, "Master, today you have not merely raised a story. Qing said, "What kind of mental activity does this Reverend Zhangli possess? Mingzhao said, "Even the great Zhaoqing has misapplied terminology. He then addressed the assembly, saying:
"Whether you can answer it or not, you shall receive thirty blows. When Linji heard of this, he said to Luopo, "Go and ask him:
'Why do you give thirty blows even to one who can answer? Wait until he strikes you; catch his staff and give it a shove. See what he does then.
Luopo followed these instructions and asked the question. The Master struck him immediately. Luopo caught the staff.
As he was seeing him off, the Master returned to his quarters. When Pufu returned, he related this to Linji. Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Even so, do you recognize Deshan? As Pufu hesitated, Linji struck him. (Yantou said, "The old man Deshan usually relied solely on a single white staff;

he would strike even a Buddha who came, and he would strike even a Patriarch who came. Yet, alas, there was still something lacking. Dongchan Qi said, "As for Linji saying, 'I have always suspected this fellow'—")

"This is speech that is acceptable; this is speech that is unacceptable. There must surely be another principle at work here—try to judge it for me. He ascended the hall. [A monk] asked a question, yet there was a fault in doing so;
not asking was likewise contrary to the Way. A monk came forward and bowed. The Master struck him immediately.

The monk said, "I have only just bowed; why did you strike me? The Master said, "If I wait for you to open your mouth, what would be worth doing? The Master ordered his attendant to summon Yicun (who was Xuefeng). Yicun came forward.
[Someone] approached. The Master said, "I am calling for Yicun myself; why have you come here again? Yunmen had no reply. He ascended the hall and said:
"The realization of my ancestors was not like this. Here there is neither patriarch nor Buddha. Bodhidharma is an old hirsute barbarian; Śākyamuni is a dried-up dung-club;
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are dung-carriers; Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment are..."
To break the attachments of ordinary people: Bodhi and Nirvana are tethering stakes for donkeys; the twelve divisions of the teachings are registers of ghosts and spirits;
the four fruits of sainthood are mere paper for wiping sores. The noble ones of the first thought-moment and the ten stages are ghosts guarding ancient tombs, unable even to save themselves.
When a monk came to visit him, he stepped forward and assumed the stance of a wrestler. The Master said, "Such rudeness deserves a beating."
The mountain monk held up his staff. The monk brushed aside his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "Even if you were as capable as this, you would still only have attained half.
The monk turned around and gave a shout. The Master struck him, saying, "It must be I who strike you before it is right.

The monk said, "There are those with clear eyes in all quarters. The Master said, "Naturally, there are those with eyes. The monk opened his eyes wide and said, "Cat! Then he went out. The Master said:
"The Yellow River clears once every three thousand years. When a monk approached, the Master closed the door. The monk knocked on the door, and the Master asked, "Who is it?
The monk replied, "A lion cub. The Master then opened the door; the monk prostrated, and the Master mounted the monk's shoulders, saying, "Where have you come from, you beast?
Xuefeng asked, "Regarding Nanquan’s beheading of the cat—what was his intent? The Master then...
He struck him and pursued him, then called out, "Do you understand? Feng said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Even my 'old woman's heart' does not understand.
A monk asked, "How far apart are the ordinary person and the sage? The Master then shouted. Once, while the Master was ill, a monk asked, "Is there anyone who is not ill?
The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "Who is this one who is not ill? The Master said, "A-ya, A-ya."
[The Master] said: "To grasp at empty space and pursue echoes is but to weary your mind and spirit. When one awakens from a dream, one realizes it was not real;

in the end, what event has actually occurred? Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. This was the third day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty.
The posthumous title of Zen Master Jianxing was conferred.
A monk from Le Tan Bao Feng in Hongzhou came for an audience. The Master asked, "The matter within [the realm] is easy to speak of;
the matter that does not fall within it is difficult to speak of from beginning to end. The monk replied, "When I was on the road, I already knew this one thing."

The questioner asked, "Master, even if you were to travel for another twenty years, it would not be too much. The Master said, "Does this not accord with your own understanding? The questioner replied, "Is it that it does not accord with your meaning, Master?
The Master said, "A bitter gourd is no fit thing to entertain guests. He then asked a monk, "The ancients had a single path to receive those who are beginners and those of later generations;
do you know it? The monk replied, "I ask the Master to point out that single path of the ancients. The Master said, "If that were so—"
The *ācārya* understood and said, "To place a head upon a head. The Master said, "It was not fitting for Baofeng to ask you, sir.
The *ācārya* said, "What harm is there in asking? The Master said, "No one here has ever been allowed to prattle on about principles.
Begone! A monk from Yantou came to visit. The Master held up his whisk and said, "Those who fall into this trap have not yet developed the eye."
The monk intended to step forward. The Master said, "Just then, you fell into this trap. The monk returned and related this to Yantou.
Yantou said, "If I had seen him at that moment, I would have snatched away his whisk; let us see what he would have done then.
Upon hearing this, the Master said, "I would have held up my whisk for him to snatch. But when no object is presented at all, what then? When Yantou heard this, he said again:
Without the scales of the stars, how could there be any means of discernment?
This is the lineage of Chan Master Deshan Jian, the fifth generation descendant of Nanyue.
Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo of Ezhou was a native of the Ke clan in Quanzhou. In his youth, he paid respects to Master Yi of Qingyuan to receive the tonsure.
He subsequently traveled to Baoshou Temple in Chang’an to receive full ordination and studied various sections of the Sūtras and Vinaya.

He moved freely within the garden of Chan, befriending Xuefeng and Qinshan. From Daci Mountain in Hangzhou, he proceeded by stages to visit Linji, arriving just as Linji was returning from his travels.
Ji went to visit Yangshan. As soon as he entered the gate, he held up his sitting cloth and said, "Venerable Master!
Yangshan took up his whisk, intending to raise it, whereupon the Master said, "A truly skilled hand. Later, he visited Deshan; holding his sitting cloth, he ascended the Dharma hall and gazed about.
Mount [Shishuang] asked, "How so? The Master gave a shout. The Mountain asked, "Where does the old monk’s fault lie?
The Master said, "A double case," and then went down to attend the hall. The Mountain remarked, "This master is somewhat like a true traveler.
On the following day, when the Master came to pay his respects, the Mountain asked, "Is the *dārala* (junior brother) the one who arrived yesterday? He replied, "I am. The Mountain asked, "What..."
He had acquired this superficiality during his studies. The Master said, "Quanhuo never deceives himself.
Shanshan said, "In the future, you must not let the old monk down. One day, he went to visit Deshan; as soon as he stepped across the threshold, he asked, "Is this ordinary or is it holy?
Deshan shouted. The Master bowed. Someone reported this to Dongshan, who said, "If it had not been Master Huo, it would have been very difficult."
[The monk] accepted [the challenge]. The Master said, "The old man Dongshan did not recognize good from bad; he wrongly applied these words and phrases.
At that time, I would have used one hand to lift up and one hand to press down. Xuefeng was serving as the head cook at Deshan’s monastery.

One day, when the meal was late, Deshan held out his bowl and went down from the Dharma Hall. Seeing this, Xuefeng, who was drying his hand-towel, said, "The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded."
"Where are you going on your alms-round? De Shan then returned to his quarters. Feng reported this to the Master [Linji], who said, "Great as De Shan may be, he has not yet realized the final word.
Upon hearing this, De Shan ordered his attendant to summon the Master, asking, "Do you refuse to acknowledge me, old monk?

may I ask how you, the Master, handle this? The Master held up the whisk. The monk then bowed his head.
[The monk] went out. The Master did not look back. (Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "The assembly, look at this one warrior! Question:

"Are the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings expounded for the sake of ordinary beings, or are they not expounded for the sake of ordinary beings? The Master said: "A single song of the willow branch is not enough. The Master said to Jingqing:
"In the past, there was an elder who led an official on a tour of the hall and said: 'This entire assembly consists entirely of students...'"
"Buddha, Dharma, Sangha. The official said, "Though gold dust is precious, what then? The old master had no reply.

Qing Dai remarked, "Recently, he has been throwing bricks to draw out jade" (Fayan offered a different reading: "How can you, sir, value the ears and despise the eyes?"). Ascending the hall, the Master held up his whisk and said, "This one is for those of middle and lower capacity.
A monk asked, "What about when a person of the highest capacity arrives? The Master held up the whisk. The monk said, "This..."
[The Master] said, "This one is of middle-lower capacity," and he struck him. He was asked, "What was the meaning of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant?

The Master then rose and entered the abbot’s quarters. He asked a monk, "Where have you been this summer? The monk replied, "At Yongquan. The Master said, "Is it a long-term surge? Or a temporary surge?
The monk said, "The Master has not grasped the point. The Master said, "I am the one who has not grasped the point. The monk said, "That is so. The Master then struck him.
During a communal work session (*fusshō*), the Master encountered a macaque on the road. The Master said, "Every person possesses a mirror of antiquity;
this macaque also possesses a mirror of antiquity. Sansheng said, "It has been nameless throughout kalpas of time; how can it be manifested as a 'mirror of antiquity'?"
The Master said, "A flaw has arisen. Shengsheng said, "What kind of desperate urgency has this old fellow fallen into?
He does not even recognize the pivot of the teaching. The Master said, "This old monk’s duties as abbot are many. A military commander from Min offered silver and a folding chair.
A monk asked, "The Master receives such offerings from the Great King; with what will you repay him? The Master struck the ground with his hand and said, "Strike me lightly! Strike me lightly!"

"I. (A monk asked Shushan, "Xuefeng said, 'Lightly strike me. What was his meaning? Shushan said, "A melon-pickle stuck in his hair; the tail hangs down level with his heels. Question: "What is it like when one has swallowed all of Vairocana?
The Master said: "Have you returned safely from Fudang? Are you doing well? Ascending the hall, he said:
"If I speak of east and west, you will seek out the words and chase after the phrases. If I am like a wild goat hanging by its horns, where will you search for me?"

A monk asked Baofu, "As for Xuefeng, what kind of teaching did he have that was like a wild goat hanging from a tree branch? Baofu replied, "I cannot fail to be a disciple of Xuefeng. The master’s Dharma seat was never less than fifteen hundred followers.
In the third month of the Wuchen year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, he manifested illness. The military governor of Min ordered a physician to attend him.

The Master said, "I am not ill. He ultimately refused to take medicine. He left behind a verse to entrust the Dharma. On the second day of the fifth month, he went out to Lan-tian in the morning and returned in the evening;
after bathing his body, he entered nirvana at midnight.
When Master Ziguang of Gantan in Hongzhou was asked by Baizhao, who had come to offer condolences because a family member’s funeral was taking place at home, the Master said, "How painful!
Alas for Heaven! Baizhao replied, "Father is dead; mother is dead. The Master struck him and drove him out. In all his encounters with students, the Master acted in this manner.
Chan Master Huigong of Ruelong on Mount Tiantai was the son of the Luo family of Fuzhou. He visited Deshan, who asked, "Do you understand? Gong replied, "What?
Deshan said, "Please come forward for an audience. Gong asked, "Do you recognize me? Deshan laughed heartily and subsequently permitted him to enter the inner room.
When Deshan passed away, Gong then began to propagate the Dharma.
The Monk Waguan of Quanzhou served as an attendant at Deshan. One day, they entered the mountains together to cut wood.
Deshan gave the Master a bowl of water; the Master took it and drank it immediately. Deshan asked, "Do you understand? The Master replied, "I do not understand."
Sanshan again offered a bowl of water to the Master. The Master accepted it and drank it. Sanshan asked, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not understand.

Sanshan said, "Why do you not strip away that which does not understand? The Master said, "If I do not understand, what more is there to strip away? Sanshan said, "You are very much like an iron stake.
Later, after [the Master] had established his own residence, Xuefeng visited him. While they were conversing over tea, Xuefeng asked:
"How was it when you were cutting wood at Deshan at that time? The Master said, "At that time, my former teacher approved of me.
Feng said, "The Master left your teacher too early. At that moment, there happened to be a bowl of water before him.
Feng said, "Bring me some water. The Master then passed it to him; Feng took it and immediately poured it out. (Yunmen said: "Do not degrade the noble by treating them as base.")
Chan Master Jianting of Xiaozhou went to visit Deshan. As soon as he saw him from across the river, he called out, "I hope you are well.
Deshan then waved his fan to beckon him over. At that moment, the Master suddenly attained awakening; he then strode straight across and departed without looking back once more.
Chan Master Shiyuan of Ruiyan in Taizhou,
a descendant of the sixth generation under Nanyue and a successor of Chan Master Yantou Huo,
was born into the Xu family of Min. Having donned the monastic robes from childhood, he maintained the precepts without fail.
[Fragmentary. When he first paid his respects to Yantou, he asked, "What is this fundamental, eternal principle? Yantou said, "Movement. He asked, "What is it like when there is movement?

Yantou said, "It is not the fundamental, eternal principle. After the Master had remained silent for a long while, Yantou said, "If you consent [to this], you have not yet shed the sense-bases and their objects."

Unwilling to remain forever submerged in birth and death, the Master finally attained realization and prostrated himself. Whenever the Head spoke with him, their exchange was never at fault. Later, he visited Jia Shan.
Jia Shan asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Wo Long. Jia Shan said, "When you arrived, had the dragon yet risen? The Master then looked back at it.
Jia Shan said, "To apply more moxa burns upon a scar from a previous one. The Master said, "So be it."
The Master said, "What is the point of the Abbot suffering so much like this? Shishuang ceased his activity. The Master then asked Shishuang, "In this way it is easy;
in another way it is difficult. In this way and this way one is alert; in that way and that way one dwells in the realm of emptiness.
'In this way' and 'not in this way'—I ask the Master to speak quickly. Shishuang replied, "I am deceiving you, my friend."
The Master shouted, saying, "This old monk! What kind of time is this now? and he immediately went out. (Later, a monk reported this to Yantou. Yantou said, "Alas!
This branch of our Buddha-dharma is being carried away in such a manner. The Master subsequently resided at Ruiyan in Danqiu. He sat upon a flat rock all day long as if he were a fool.
Every now and then, he would call out to himself, "Master! and then respond, "Yes. He would then say, "Stay alert! In the future, do not let others deceive you."

[This is] deceptive. (Later, a monk visited Xuansha. Xuansha asked, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Ruigyan. Xuansha asked, "What words or phrases did he show to his disciples? The monk recounted the previous story.

Xuansha said, "In one sense, it is all a matter of playing with the spirit; yet, how extraordinary! Why did you not simply stay there? The monk replied, "He has already passed away. Xuansha asked, "Can you still call out for him now and get a response? The monk was speechless. The Master led the assembly with strict discipline, earning praise throughout the Jiangbiao region.
A monk asked, "When the jeweled canopy appears above the head and clouds arise beneath the feet, what then? The Master said, "Wearing a cangue."
Dai Suohan asked, "When there is no jeweled canopy above one's head and no clouds arising beneath one's feet, what is it like at such a time?
The Master said, "You are still not out of the cangue. He asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "I am weary after the midday meal. Jingqing asked, "The heavens cannot cover it."
"The earth cannot support it; is this not so? The Master said, "If it were so, it would be covered and supported. Qing said, "If it were not so, I would have nearly met my end at Ruiyan.
The Master called himself by the name Shiyuan. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A stone ox.

[The monk] asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "A little stone ox. [The monk] said, "In that case, they are not the same. The Master said: [Note: The final response from the Master is omitted in the source text.]
[The monk] said, "They cannot be joined. [The Master] asked, "Why can they not be joined? The Master said, "There is no sameness with which to be in sameness; what would you join?
[The monk] asked, "How should one deliberate so as not to fall into stages? The Master said, "They cannot be arranged. [The monk] asked, "Why can they not be arranged?
The Master said, "From the beginning, they have had no stages. [The monk] asked, "In what position do they reside? The Master said: *This is the end of the excerpt.*
He did not sit in the Hall of Universal Radiance. Someone asked, "Is there no longer any returning to transform through principle? The Master said, "His fame is so great throughout the three realms;
where would he not return to court? One day, a village woman came to pay her respects. The Master said, "Return quickly and save several thousand lives.
When the woman returned to her house, she saw her daughter-in-law gathering field snails. She immediately released them by the water's edge. This was the Master’s marvel.

His traces [of activity] were numerous; they are not recorded here in detail. After his passing, he was enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain and posthumously titled Chan Master Kongzhao (Empty Illumination).
Chan Master Yan of Xuanshui in Huai Prefecture was asked by a monk, "What is one who is on the Way? The Master said, "The sun sets and one seeks lodging in a solitary inn.
He was further asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The three sons of the Zhang family. When the monk said, "I do not understand," the Master... [replied].
[The student] said, "Not [the first, second, or third month]. He asked, "What is the one phrase prior to sound? The Master said, "HŪṂ.
He asked, "How is it after turning back? The Master said, "What is it?"
Chan Master Daoxian of Luoshan in Fuzhou was a native of the Chen family of Changxi. He left home to become a monk at Guishan; upon reaching the required age, he received full ordination.
He traveled extensively throughout various regions and once visited Shishuang to ask: "What is it like when one cannot find peace whether staying or departing? Shishuang replied:

"You must simply exhaust [all attachments]. The Master did not find this to his satisfaction, so he went to study under Yantou. He asked the same question as before, and Yantou said, "He goes and stays according to his own will;
what is the use of managing him? Thereupon, the Master took these words to heart. The Military Governor of Min, having tasted the flavor of his Dharma, invited him to reside at Luoshan.
He was titled Chan Master Fabao. Upon ascending the seat to open the hall, as he was just adjusting his robes, he said, "Take care.
The assembly did not disperse. After a long silence, the Master spoke again: "Those who have not yet recognized it, come forward! A monk stepped forth and bowed.
The Master raised his voice and said, "How truly bitter! As the monk prepared to ask a question, the Master shouted him out. He then asked, "What is the extraordinary phrase? The Master—

[The Master] said, "What do you say? A monk asked, "How does one discern and clarify matters that confront one directly? The Master raised his fly-whisk. The monk said, "I beg the Master to show us compassion.
The Master said, "It is far too late. A monk asked, "In this urgent pursuit, I request the Master to grant me an encounter.

The Master said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The arrow has already passed. A monk asked, "When the nine women did not carry [the child], who was it that held him up? The Master—
The Master said, "Ask with a loud voice. As the monk prepared to ask again, the Master said, "Where have you gone? Another monk came to attend upon him. The Master asked, "What is your name?
He replied, "Mingjiao (Teaching of Clarity). The Master said, "Do you understand the Teaching yet? He replied, "As best as I can.
The Master raised his fist and said, "At the assembly on Vulture Peak, what did they call this? He replied, "The Fist-Teaching. The Master laughed and said, "If it is so..."
[The Master] called it the "Fist Teaching. Then, extending his two feet, he said, "What teaching is this? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Do not call it the 'Feet Teaching'?
While the Master was at Heyoshan, as he was seeing off the elder Gu who was traveling with him, he took up his staff and thrust it toward the front of Gu.
Gu had no reply. The Master said, "A stone ox blocks the ancient road; a single horse gives birth."

"A pair of colts. (Later, a monk cited this to Shushan. Shushan said: "A stone ox blocks the ancient road; one horse gives birth to three tigers. A monk took his leave of Baofu. Baofu asked, "Where are you going?"
Baofu said, "Bow to Mount Luo. Baofu said, "Tell Mount Luo that I, Baofu, will go to the capital this autumn to have an audience with the Great King.
I shall prepare forty questions to ask the Master; if even a single phrase does not accord with the truth, do not say I did not warn you.
A monk reported this to the Master (Xuedou). The Master laughed heartily and said, "Since Old Teacher Chen entered Fujian, he has been saying..."
"Hongtang. I have never seen a single watchtower beneath this bridge. A 'hair-tip star' has appeared. You and I shall ask Congzhan:
Master Chen has no such questions; he possesses only a single sword. Beneath that one stroke, there must be the intention of manifesting a division of self, as well as a path for the self to emerge.
If one does not understand this, one will surely be reduced to dust. The monk returned and related this.

Fufu appeared to be acting as if he were being pious. Fufu said, "At that time, I was merely joking with him. When autumn arrived and it was time for the formal audience, the Master specially prepared a tea ceremony and invited Fufu.
Fufu did not go, but instead said to a monk, "I had made some joking remarks in the interim; I fear the Master might ask about them.
The monk returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "Tell him: 'A fierce tiger will never eat meat that has already been submitted.'"

The monk departed and Fú arrived. The Elder Wúzhèn asked, "Regarding Yàntóu’s statement, 'Dòngshān’s Buddha is simply without light,' I wonder what deficiency Dòngshān had that he was told to be 'without light'? The Master called out, "Zhèn!
Zhèn responded. The Master said, "Truly, it is a fine Buddha, but he is simply without light. Zhèn asked, "Why did the Great Master dismiss him [by saying this]?"
Wu-zhen spoke. The Master said, "Where did Old Teacher Chen shift your words? Speak quickly, speak quickly! Zhen was speechless.
The Master struck him with thirty blows and drove him out. Zhen reported this to Zhaoqing, who spent the entire summer reviling him.

At the end of summer, he came in person to inquire. The Master then explained the matter clearly to him. Xingqing immediately prostrated himself and repented, saying, "I have indeed wronged the Great Master.
A monk then cited a poem by Hanshan and asked, "When the white crane holds the bitter peach, what then? The Master said:
The Chaste Woman Sings in Her Chamber: "Taking a thousand li as a single breath—what is it like? The Master said: "Seeing off guests outside the post station.
"Setting out for Mount Penglai—what is it like? The Master said: "Leaning on a pillow, watching a macaque. "Using this as provisions for the journey—what is it like?
The Master said: "An ancient sword before a skull. [He] asked: "What is the tip of the hundred grasses? The Master said: "A staff leaning against a wall."
"Everything above is the meaning of the Patriarchs. The Master said, "I have pierced your eyes through. A monk asked, "What is the Way?
The Master said, "It is currently stuck on the wall. A monk asked, "In front is a ten-thousand-fathom deep ravine; behind are tigers, wolves, and lions.
At such a time as this, what then? The Master said, "Free and at ease. A monk asked, "Who is the master of the three realms? The Master said, "Do you even know how to eat your rice? Linji.
Upon ascending the hall for his final teaching before passing away, he gathered the assembly. After a long silence, he extended his left hand;
the administrators did not know what this meant, so he ordered the monks on the eastern side to step back. He then extended his right hand and ordered the monks on the western side to step back.
He then said, "To repay the Buddha's kindness, nothing surpasses the propagation of the Great Teaching. Go back! Go back! Take care! Having finished speaking, he smiled gently and passed away.
Ji. Chan Master Congfan of Xiangxi in Fuzhou arrived for an audience. The Master said, "Are you not a monk from Gushan?
The monk replied, "I am. The Master said, "Why does the jewel upon your brow not appear? The monk was speechless. When the monk took his leave, the Master saw him off at the gate.
He summoned the Elder again. The monk turned his head. The Master said, "Your belly is full of Chan. The monk asked, "What kind of mind is the Master's? The Master simply laughed heartily.
As the Master put on his patched robe (*kāṣāya*), he spoke this verse: "The upper robe of Kāśyapa, When donned, requires swift wit.
As soon as the arrow of the call is distinguished, The hidden tortoise is revealed without concealment."
While Chan Master Yan of Shengshou Monastery in Fuzhou was mending his robes, a monk approached him for instruction. The Master held up the robe to show him, saying:
"This mountain monk has a single robe; I spread it out for all to see. The two strips of cloud-patterned cloth are divided—do not let the needles and thread be exposed.
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The monk had no reply. The Master said, "For so long a time, what have you been doing?"
Chan Master Huizong of Lingyan in Jizhou was a native of the Chen family of Fuzhou. He received his monastic training at Guishan. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Lingyan?
The Master said, "Pine and cypress trees stand in dense, thick rows. The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm?
The Master said, "Every night there is the cry of a monkey. [The monk] asked, "What is the student’s own fundamental matter?"
The Master said, "Why do you cast away pure gold to pick up shards and rubble?
Chan Master Xuan Sha Shibei Zongyi of Fuzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Xuefeng Cun. He was the son of the Xie family of Min. From his youth, he delighted in fishing. Once, while drifting...

On a small boat upon the Nantai River, he associated with the fishermen. At the beginning of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, when he was only thirty years old, he suddenly felt a longing to transcend the mundane world.
He then abandoned his boat to seek ordination under Chan Master Xun of Furong, shaving his head. He went to Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang to receive full precepts.

Wearing a coarse cotton robe and straw sandals, he took only enough food to sustain his breath; he often sat in meditation throughout the entire day, which caused everyone to marvel at him. Together with Xue...
Feng was originally a fellow practitioner of the Dharma-gate, yet they related as teacher and disciple. Because of his ascetic practices, Feng called him "Dhūta.
One day, Feng asked, "Which one is Dhūta Bei? The Master replied, "I would never dare to deceive anyone."
On another day, Feng summoned him, saying, "Dhūta Bei, why do you not travel extensively to seek instruction? The Master replied, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land;

the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Feng approved of this. When they ascended Mount Xianggu, he and the Master labored together to build the monastery. Disciples from afar flocked there.
The Master entered the inner quarters to consult and resolve his doubts, never flagging whether morning or evening. Furthermore, he studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and attained realization.

He clarified the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*). Consequently, his responses were swift and nimble, in perfect resonance with the *Sūtras*. Whenever scholars from various regions encountered points they could not resolve, they would invariably seek instruction from him.
Even when engaging in rigorous inquiry with Xuefeng, he did not shrink from the responsibility of benevolence.
Xuefeng remarked, "Bei Touduo is a man who has returned for a second birth. When Xuefeng ascended the hall, he said: "If you wish to understand this matter, it is like an ancient mirror."

[The Master] was presiding at the high seat. "When a Hu comes, he appears as a Hu; when a Han comes, he appears as a Han. A monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "What if a bright mirror were to suddenly arrive?
Feng said, "Both Hu and Han would be hidden. The monk said, "Old Monk, your heels have not yet touched the ground."

After residing [there], he ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha-way is vast and open; it has no fixed path. It is the gate of liberation that has no gate, the intention of the Way-man that has no intention.

It does not abide within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be subject to rising or sinking. To establish it is to deviate from the truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned creation.
Movement gives rise to the root of birth and death; stillness leads to intoxication in the land of dullness. When both movement and stillness are simultaneously extinguished—"
Falling into emptiness and oblivion—this is where movement and stillness are both grasped. To realize the Buddha-nature in its full, unadorned vastness, one must face the dust and encounter objects;
like withered wood or cold ashes, when applied according to the occasion, one does not fail in what is appropriate.

Like a mirror reflecting all forms without its radiance being disturbed, or a bird flying through space without being mixed with the color of the void, for this reason, throughout the ten directions there are no images, and within the three realms there is no trace of movement. Thus, one does not fall [into error].
The mechanism of coming and going does not abide in the intermediate state of mind. Within the bell there is no sound of the drum; within the drum there is no sound of the bell.
Bell and drum do not intersect; in every phrase there is no before or after. It is like a strong man extending his arm—relying on no external force.
A lion roaming—how could it seek a companion? The nine heavens are free from obscuration; where is there any need for piercing through? This single segment of luminosity has never been darkened.

Obscure! If one reaches this state, the essence is tranquil and still, eternally lucid, blazing with the brilliance of the sun, beyond all boundaries. Within the empty space of perfect enlightenment, it does not waver;
it devours and illuminates heaven and earth, shining forth in total isolation. Now, as for the Buddha appearing in the world, there is fundamentally no coming or going.
Therefore it is said that there is no substance. The Way is fundamentally suchness; phenomena are naturally and truly as they are. It does not consist of cultivation or realization;

it simply requires being empty and at ease, yet not obscuring one's functioning, so that one’s activity does not involve the mire of the mundane. Within this, even a hair’s breadth left unspoken constitutes belonging to the retinue of Māra.
The preceding and following phrases are the difficult points for students. Thus, when one phrase accords with the Way, the eighty thousand gates are forever closed.

To sever birth and death: even if you attain a state like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—unimpaired by being struck and undispersed by touching the waves—it is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. Where a man of the Way acts, it is like fire melting ice;
the ice never reforms. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return. Therefore, it cannot be caged.

Willingly abiding, they do not turn their heads when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements; to this day, there is no fixed location. If you reach this point, you ascend the profound at every step;

it belongs neither to the heterodox nor the orthodox. Consciousness cannot perceive it; wisdom cannot know it. To move is to lose the source; to awaken is to become deluded regarding the ultimate meaning.
The followers of the Two Vehicles tremble with fear, and those of the Ten Stages are struck with terror. The path of speech is cut off; the sphere of mental activity—
Extinction. Directly, Śākyamuni closed his room in Magadha; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī; Subhūti proclaimed "no teaching" to manifest the Way;
and Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening as flowers rained down. If you see it before you in this manner, what else could you doubt?
There is no place to settle; one is detached from past, present, and future; it cannot be delimited or constrained; the paths of mind and thought are cut off; it does not depend on...
Adorned from the beginning, it is truly pure; in every movement of speech and smile, it is clearly manifest everywhere, lacking nothing at all.

People of the present age do not awaken to this underlying principle; they recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust, becoming stained and attached at every turn and bound by every circumstance.

Even if they were to awaken, the realms of sensory objects remain chaotic and their names and forms unreal; they then attempt to settle the mind and withdraw their thoughts, seeking to withdraw from all phenomena.

To return to emptiness, closing the eyes and hiding the pupils, yet ultimately having thoughts arise—though one may gradually break them down, as soon as subtle conceptions are born, one must immediately suppress them.
A view such as this is precisely that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism, a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Obscure and vast, without sensation or cognition; one who plugs their ears to steal a bell merely deceives themselves.

To make such distinctions here is not the case. It is not a matter of hiding behind doors or leaning against walls; every phrase is manifest before us. It cannot be deliberated upon and does not involve literary ink.
Fundamentally severed from the realm of dust, it fundamentally has no rank or position. Provisionally named a "renunciant," it ultimately leaves no trace.

The traces—whether True Suchness, ordinary beings, sages, those in hell, or humans and devas—are merely expedient methods for healing the madness of a son. Since even empty space undergoes no change, how could the Great Way have any rising or sinking?
To awaken is to move freely in all directions without departing from the fundamental limit. If you reach this point, [you will realize this].
Ordinary people and sages alike have no place to stand. If you direct your attention toward the words, you will be drowned and destroyed.
If you run outward in pursuit, you fall into the realm of demons. As for the state of suchness, there is nothing to be contrived; it is just like a blazing furnace that harbors not even a mosquito.
This principle is fundamentally level—what need is there to clear it away? Whether moving or still, whether raising an eyebrow or not, this is true liberation.

The Way does not consist in forcefully applying one's own intentions or calculations; to establish such views is to deviate from the truth. If you arrive here, do not admit even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization.
To point toward it with the intellect is already an error; even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not place a single word upon it.
Long stay; take care. [Ascending the hall: I now ask you all: what matter can you actually take responsibility for? In what world do you abide? Where do you rest?
To establish one’s life upon the body—can you still discern this? If you cannot discern it, it is just like seeing flowers in the air when pressing on the eyes;

as soon as you perceive things thus, you err. Do you understand? What you now see before you—the mountains, rivers, and great earth, form and emptiness, light and darkness, and all such various things—are all but the phantom flowers of a weary delusion;
they are called inverted views and perceptions. As for those who have left the household life, they must recognize the mind and attain realization.

This is the fundamental source; therefore, one is called a śramaṇa. Since you have now shaven your hair and donned the robes, assuming the appearance of a śramaṇa, you possess the capacity to benefit both yourself and others.
Yet, as I look at you now, you are entirely black and murky, like ink.
If you cannot even save yourself, how can you claim to have attained the Way? O benevolent ones, the matters of the Buddha-dharma involve profound causes and conditions;
do not treat them with indifference or superficiality. Do not gather together to engage in idle chatter and confused talk, wasting time in empty praise. Time is difficult to obtain—how regrettable!
You who are great men, why do you not examine yourselves and look into what this matter truly is? As for the ancestral school from of old...
This is the lineage of the crowns of all Buddhas. Since you are unable to uphold it, I have therefore expediently exhorted you to simply follow the gate of Kāśyapa, attaining immediate transcendence.
This single gate transcends the cause and effect of ordinary beings and sages; it transcends the wondrously adorned world-ocean of Vairocana;
it transcends the other expedient gates of Śākyamuni; and from this very point downward through eternal kalpas, it does not allow for [gradual] instruction.
There is one thing that I shall show you with my own eyes. Why do you not investigate it with urgency yourself?
It is not necessarily the case that one must wait for three or two lifetimes to accumulate pure karma over a long period. O worthy one, what is the matter of the *zongcheng* (the core teaching)?

Chan Master Hui-ling of Changqing in Fuzhou was a native of Yanguan in Hangzhou. His surname was Sun. By nature, he was pure and serene.

On the day of opening the hall, the official approached the corner of the dais wearing court robes and said, "I request the Master to preach the Dharma. The Master asked, "Do you hear me?
The official prostrated himself. The Master said, "Even so, I fear there may be those who do not agree. A monk asked, "What is the True Dharma Eye?"

The Master said, "If there is a vow, one does not scatter sand. One day, Imperial Preceptor Wang entered the monastery and, seeing that the gate of the abbot’s quarters was closed, asked Attendant Yan, "Is there anyone who would dare say the Grand Master is here?

"What is this matter that is not separated by even a hair’s breadth? The Master said, "Whether it is right or not.

The monk asked again. The Master sat with his shoulder bared. The monk prostrated. The Master said, "How do you understand this? The monk replied, "Today the wind has risen.
The Master said, "To speak in such a way is merely the view of one who is not yet settled. Among the ancients and the present, what essential point do you have that can equal Changqing?
If you can bring it forth, I will allow you to be the host of this discourse. The monk simply remained standing.
The Master then asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "A man from the north. The Master said, "Having traveled three thousand li from north to south, why do you practice such falsehood?

The monk was speechless. Later, while presiding over the assembly, the Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Do not say that tonight’s [teaching] is but a trifle," and he descended from his seat.
A monk asked, "When many hands sift gold together, who is the one who obtains it? The Master replied, "It is the one who possesses skillful means."
[The monk] said, "I have attained it. The Master asked, "Does a student still attain anything? The Master said, "It is very far away. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"If you encounter a fellow traveler on the Way and pass each other with shoulders touching, the lifelong task of study is finished. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:

"When everything has been swept clean and put in order, someone steps forward and asks me for the self. I strike them a blow across the spine. If that blow reaches you, you must feel shame and remorse; if it does not..."
“One blow reaches you. Where else would you turn to understand it? [The monk] asked, “What is it like when the antelope hangs its horns in the trees?

The Master said, “A fellow among the grass. [The monk] asked, “What is it like after the horns have hung there? The Master said, “He is crying out in confusion. [The monk] asked, “Ultimately, what is it?”
The Master said, "The business of the donkey has not yet gone, and the business of the horse has already arrived. He asked, "How does this accord with the words of the Sage?
The Master said, "Great and small Changqing would have their mouths like flat carrying-poles at your single question. He asked, "Why is it so? The Master said, "What was it you asked just now?
He ascended the hall and said, "If I were to purely uphold and proclaim the Dharma-vehicle (zongcheng), I would have to close the doors of the Dharma Hall."
"By means of the Way, the Dharma is exhausted and there are no people. A monk asked, "I am not afraid of having no people; I ask the Master to exhaust the Dharma.
The Master said, "Do you understand where it falls? A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the West? The Master said, "Xiangyan has already spoken it; [you] are all sitting there at once."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said, "If everyone were like today, Old Hu would have cause for hope. Baofu said, "If everyone were like today, Old Hu would be utterly hopeless.
(Xuánjué remarked: "To speak thus—is this a word of meeting, or is it not a word of meeting? When National Teacher Ān-guó received his monastic title, the Master went to offer his congratulations.
As Ān-guó came out to receive him, the Master asked, "Has your title arrived? He replied, "It has arrived. The Master asked, "What is the title? He replied:
Mingzhen. The Master then extended his hands. Guo asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I almost failed to ask about your transgression.
He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? [The monk] said, "From Gushan. The Master said, "Gushan has a phrase that does not cross the stone gate.
If someone were to inquire about it, what would you say? [The monk] said, "Last night I stayed at Baoci. The Master said, "A back-breaking blow for you!"
Again, [the monk] asked, "How so? The Master said, "If the Abbot were to apply this staff, he would not have received the offerings of devas and humans in vain.
The Master continued, "How could you have let him off with such ease? A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'When meeting, do not bring it forth;

when a thought arises, one knows it immediately. What about such a time? The Master said, "Do you even know it yet? [The monk] again asked Baofu. Baofu said, "Whose words are these? [The monk] replied, "Danxia's words. Baofu said, "Go away! Do not disturb me while I am sleeping."
The Master entered the Sangha hall, held up the head of the memorial document, and said, "To see it is not to see it. "Do you see it? The assembly had no reply.

where the Monk cannot reach with an answer, the student will simply not ask. The Master then grabbed him and said, "Is this my principle? Is it your principle? [The monk] said, "If the Monk strikes the student, the student shall also strike the Monk. The Master said: **Answer:** The Master said, "Jingqing has suffered a loss today. [The monk] asked, "Regarding a place where the student cannot reach with a question, I request that the Master not answer;

regarding a place where the Monk cannot reach with an answer, the student will simply not ask. The Master then grabbed him and said, "Is this my principle? Is it your principle? [The monk] said, "If the Monk strikes the student, the student shall also strike the Monk. The Master said:
"You may plow against the grain. He asked, "I have heard it said that in all quarters, those who are not 'running people' are 'caging people' or 'netting people.
I wonder, Master, what do you say to this? The Master replied, "Because you have posed this question, I am left with nothing but my teeth falling out right before the gate.
One day, when the assembly had gathered, the Master threw down his staff and said, "The whole assembly has moved! (2)
"Ten blows! Twenty blows for not being moved! At that time, a monk came forward, took up the staff, placed it on his head, and walked out.

The Master said, "Jingqing has lost today. He asked another monk, "What is that sound outside the gate? The monk replied, "The sound of raindrops falling. The Master said, "Sentient beings are inverted;
deluded about themselves, they pursue external objects. The monk asked, "How about you, Master? The Master said, "I have never been deluded."

[The monk] said, “I have reached the point where I am no longer deluded about myself; what is the meaning of this? The Master said, “To leave one’s body may still be easy, but to cast off one’s entire being to realize the Way is difficult.
[The monk] asked, “What is the same aspect (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)? The Master took a fire-tongs and thrust it into the brazier.

[The monk] asked, “What is the distinct aspect (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)? The Master again took the fire-tongs and thrust them to one side. (Fayan commented: “The question was not in accord with the principle. There was a monk who brought along a young boy.
The Master’s son arrived and said, "This youth constantly loves to question others about the Buddha-dharma; I request that the Master examine him.
The Master then ordered tea to be prepared. When the youth brought the tea, the Master drank it and passed the cup and saucer to the youth. The youth stepped forward to receive them.
The Master withdrew his hand and said, "Can you say anything about this? The monk replied, "Please ask me. (Fayan offered a different version, saying: "Venerable Sir, would you like more tea?
The monk asked, "What is the level of understanding of this boy? The Master said, "He is merely a monk who has maintained the precepts for one or two lifetimes.
He passed away at the beginning of the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty and was interred in a stupa on Longce Mountain.
Chan Master Huaiyue of Ba’en Monastery in Zhangzhou was a native of Quanzhou. A monk asked, “How should one conduct oneself throughout the twelve periods of the day?
The Master said, “Movement is death. The monk asked, “What about when there is no movement? The Master said, “You are still a ghost guarding an ancient tomb.
The monk asked, “What is the place where a student emerges? The Master said, “What fetters are binding you? The monk said—
"But what can be done? One simply cannot emerge from it. The Master said, "In whom does the fault lie? Question: "What is the one spiritual entity that repays kindness?
The Master said, "Why are you eating all this wine dregs? Question: "Does it still manifest its hands and feet? The Master said, "What kind of place is this? Question:
"How was it before Oxhead saw the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said: [He was like]... (text fragmentary)

"Ten thousand *li* of sky, a single sheet of cloud. [The student] asked, "After seeing this, what then? The Master said, "A vast, open ground. [The student] asked, "When black clouds suddenly darken the sky, who is it that brings the rain?
The Master said, "It pours first where the terrain is steepest. [The student] asked, "Since the Dharma-gate (*zongcheng*) cannot be rejected, how should one proclaim it?
The Master said, "The mountain does not call itself; the water flows without interruption. [The student] asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? The Master said, "You..."
"How can one know? He asked, "What is it like when one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha? The Master said, "In what year did you come to see him?
He asked, "What is it like when the lion is in its den? The Master said, "What kind of equipment does a lion possess?
He asked, "What is it like when the lion emerges from its den? The Master said, "Where is the lion? He asked, "What is the Buddha of the present moment? The Master said, [silence].
The Master said, "Quickly prostrate yourselves. On the occasion of his imminent passing, he ascended the hall and said, "For twelve years, I have expounded the teachings and the tradition.
In what way have you all found me strange? If you wish to hear the Three Sutras and Five Treatises, the Kaiyuan Temple is but a few paces from here.
Having finished speaking, he entered nirvana.
Chan Master Hongming Zhen of Anguo Monastery in Fuzhou was the son of the Chen family of Quanzhou.
He visited Xuefeng, who asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangxi. Xuefeng said, "Where did you see Bodhidharma?
He replied, "I told the Master clearly. Xuefeng asked, "What did you say? He replied, "Where have you been coming and going? One day, Xuefeng saw him...
The Master suddenly grabbed him and said, "The entire universe is this gate of liberation. I am holding his hand and pulling him, yet he refuses to enter.
Feng replied, "Master, you cannot blame Hongren for this. Feng pushed him away and said, "Even so, what can be done about all these monks behind him?
The Master then cited the inscription on the National Teacher’s stele, saying: "To attain it in the mind—then the orchid becomes the banner."
The *tán* tree has lost its essence; nectar has become a garden of thorns. He asked a monk, "A single phrase must encompass both the meanings of gain and loss.
How would you say it? The monk raised his fist and said, "One cannot call this a 'fist. The Master did not approve.
He also raised his fist and said differently, "It is precisely because one calls this thing a 'fist' [that it is so]. He then left the world. (Quotation from *Chushi*)
Later, the Military Governor of Min ordered him to reside at Anguo Monastery, where he greatly propagated the profound teachings of the Dharma.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "It is indeed so; do not misunderstand. The monk asked, "What is the First Phrase? The Master said, "Question! Question!

The monk asked, "As a student who has come here, I have not yet exhausted your skillful means; I pray that the Master will exhaust his skillful means for me. The Master remained silent for a long while. The monk bowed. The Master said:
Suddenly arriving at another place, someone asked him, "How would you present [the teaching]? He replied, "I would never dare to present it incorrectly.

The Master said, "Before you even stepped out the door, you were already seen with a smile on your face. He asked, "What is the mind transmitted by Bodhidharma? The Master said, "It has never been a track for later followers.

He asked, "Regarding the pivot that does not fall into existence or non-existence, I ask the Master to speak it in its entirety. The Master said, "Try to judge it for me. He asked, "As for... [The text ends here.]

"What is this matter of a single hair-tip? The Master picked up his *kāṣāya*. The monk said, "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "One who embraces the raw jade need not shed tears repeatedly;
tomorrow morning, present it again to the King of Chu. A monk asked, "What is it like when all is silent and wordless? The Master said, "Take another step forward.

A monk asked, "Generally, whenever there are words or phrases, they all fall within the realm of causes, conditions, and skillful means (*upāya*). What about that which does not fall [into these]? The Master said, "Even so, you have already fallen."

"How are the matters of causes, conditions, and skillful means? The Master said, "Those who use the well-sweep (gēgāo) are frequently encountered; those who carry water in jars (bàosòng) are rarely met.
The questioner asked, "It is said that the path above [the ordinary] has not been transmitted by the thousand sages.

I do not know how you, Reverend, transmit it. The Master said, "For now, keep your mouth free to eat your rice. The questioner asked, "What is a person of noble character? The Master said, "By the riverbank, there is no washing of ears."

"Excellent. One asks: Does a person who constantly dwells in the position of correctness still deserve the offerings of devas and humans?

The Master said, "One who puts on clothes and eats food deserves them. The Master then cited when Master Ling was residing at Zhaoqing. At that time, in...
Standing at the eastern corner of the Dharma Hall, he said to a monk, "A good question can be posed here.
